en: Preface:
In the world, there are things that can be transmitted through words; there are things that cannot be transmitted through words;

and there are things that can be transmitted through words yet ultimately cannot be transmitted through words. Those that can be transmitted through words are the manifest aspects of principle (*li*).
That which people can perceive and point to is that which is subtle in principle and which no one can perceive or point to.
That which can be transmitted through words yet ultimately cannot be transmitted through words—its principle is both most manifest and most subtle;
it is as if near yet distant, as if shallow yet deep. One might point to it and claim it exists.

I do not know where one might see something and take it to be existent, or point to something and take it to be non-existent; nor do I know where one might see something and take it to be non-existent.

Alas! It is difficult to speak of this. In my youth, I perused the classics and histories, and I privately lamented that the words of the sages and worthies were so vast and flowing, so brilliant and magnificent, like the sun and moon adorning the heavens or the rivers and streams coursing along.
As for the stages (*bhūmi*), who is there that cannot see them? And who is there that cannot point them out?
Yet when it comes to their subtle words and wondrous meanings, if one understands them with the heart and realizes them through the spirit, they mostly lie beyond language and writing.
Alas! How, then, could these be pointed out? As for the words of the Śākya clan, I have certainly never crossed their shores; how, then, could I know anything of them?
Even these solitary words and fragmentary phrases are sufficient to illuminate both the present and the past.

If one were to abandon the refined and substantial principles of our own Confucian tradition and instead immerse oneself in that school of emptiness and extinction, it would be like leaving the broad highway to gallop one’s feet along a narrow, winding path of nine bends—is this not excessively eccentric? Niezi Le of Wumen, a diligent reader, investigated...
Having thoroughly mastered the Classics and Histories, he further immersed himself in the teachings of the Chan school.
Following Master Juefan Huihong’s *Yuezilu* (Record of Pointing at the Moon), he compiled the subtle words of the Chan vehicle for over five hundred years from the Southern Song dynasty onwards.

He traced the sources and lineages, meticulously verifying the genealogical branches, and synthesized them into a single work titled *Xuzhuyue* (Continuation of Pointing at the Moon). Alas! The resolve of Master Nie may truly be called diligent.
Seven or eight years ago, Nie Ziyou presented this compilation to me, saying: "The life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is as fragile as a single thread.
The Dharma wheel is entrusted to the two branches and five schools; I pray that you, my son, will fulfill this great vow for me.
At first, I had no leisure to reflect upon it, yet I secretly laughed at the eccentricity of his preferences and the intensity of his resolve. Last spring, I came to Hunkoung. [At] Wuyuan...
Next, Master Jie came to see me and said, "I have received a dream-omen; this book must await you to be completed.
Could this not be due to a karmic affinity from former lives? I started in surprise and said, "Is that so? Your devotion is indeed singular. How could I dare decline?
Furthermore, there were Master Liu Ju-an of Zhongshan and Master Sun Xiaoze of Qinyou who participated.
They collated and verified one another’s work. Thereupon, they widely solicited donations and assembled craftsmen to prepare the printing blocks, publishing it with great haste.

However, I have heard that in the learning of the Śākya clan, being "unclad by even a single thread" is considered the supreme vehicle (*agrayāna*), and the "emptiness of all mental concerns" is regarded as the ultimate virtue.

They do not establish written texts nor provide sub-commentaries; it is like pointing toward the moon—afterward, those who speak of the moon or listen for the moon all take the finger itself to be the moon.
An Allegory. Alas! Can it be transmitted through words? Or can it not be transmitted through words?
Or can it be transmitted through words yet ultimately cannot be transmitted through words? I am unable to point to any of these with certainty.
Should those who read this hereafter take the very reason I laughed at Master Nie and instead laugh at me, what more could be said?
Colophon.
On the first day of the Lantern Festival in the first month of the nineteenth year of the Kangxi era, his younger brother Jiangxiang of Guśi respectfully inscribed this at Wensuanlou in Guangling.
Continuing with the Preface to the *Zhuyuelu*:
The Marquis of Wei, Wu Ji, forged and stole the military tally, struck down Jin Pi, and seized his troops to save Zhao.
When Li Guangbi was serving as Grand General, the Censor Cui Zhong violated military law; he marshaled his troops, intending to execute him, just as the Vice Minister of the Household—
When the execution order arrived, Li Guangbi said, "If I am an Inspector, I shall execute the Inspector; if I am a Minister of the Interior, I shall execute the Minister.

He subsequently executed him and only then reported the matter to the throne. Only with such courage and resolve can one discern whether the fundamental principles of governance are severed or continued.
When Han Xin was serving as the Commandant of Grain under the Han dynasty, he deserted on the way. Xiao He pursued him and presented him to the King of Han.
He was appointed as Grand General, and the entire army was struck with awe. When Han Qi was stationed at Yan'an, an assassin entered his tent to carry out a murder.

As Qi rose from his seat, he asked: "Who sent you to come here? Take my head and go! Only one with such discernment and resolve is fit to establish the rank and position of the fundamental principles of governance.
Fu Jian led a million troops to the banks of the Huai and Fei rivers; then Xie Xuan entered...
When Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei requested an audience, Xie An displayed an expression of total fearlessness and said, "I have already received another imperial decree.

When Xuancheng defeated Shi Le, Xie An likewise showed no sign of joy and said, "The young brats have finally defeated the rebels. During the campaign at Shanyuan, Kou Qianzhi urged Emperor Zhenzong to cross the river.
The True Sect (Shinshū) sent a spy to observe his conduct; only then did he close the gates and allow his servants to indulge in drinking, gambling, singing, and shouting.
It was only when the Khitans were struck with fear and requested an alliance that he spoke such words as "dividing the principles and lineages. Alas!

Is this not truly lamentable? In recent times, demonic and heterodox teachings have flourished while the true lineage has declined. People wield blind staffs and shout blindly, claiming to be sages and boasting of their own prowess.

Yet, upon examining their learning, those at the lowest level cannot even recognize a single character, and those at the highest level possess nothing more than a single volume of the *Record of Pointing at the Moon*.
To deceive others with such things is in fact to deceive themselves; to hoodwink others with such things is in fact to hoodwink themselves.
Deceit and fraud cannot be the way of a human being; how then can one practice the Way?
If one cannot practice the Way, how can they occupy the seat of the Dharma King, wield the Vajra sword, claim to be the legitimate heir of the West, and raise the True Seal of the Tathāgata?
Therefore, I have often said that those who study Confucianism must read the books of the Four Treasuries and Seven Supplements.

Without having beheld the complete corpus of the classics and histories, they consider themselves erudite merely on the basis of the *Tongjian jiyao*, *Shidu*, and *Shicao*, and thus style themselves "Universal Scholars" (*tongru*).
This is like a practitioner of Chan meditation who does not read the entirety of the Great Canon of Sutras.

Failing to behold the complete collection of the sutras, śāstras, and commentaries, they rely solely on the *Yizhuyulu* (Record of Pointing at the Moon) as their conversational tool, and thus presume for themselves the title of "Good Knowledgeable One" (*kalyāṇamitra*).

These are all those who deceive and delude themselves. Therefore, it is truly the merit of Master Gu (Hanshan Deqing) that the fundamental principles of the successive patriarchs have become so far-reaching and enduring—like water returning to its valley—that even those who wield the blind staff and shout blindly have come to possess some understanding.
To partially understand this as being like someone who steals fire from a firefly is also the fault of Master Gao (Mencius). Someone might say:
"In that case, was Master Nie’s continuation of this record a merit or a fault? I replied to him: "As for Master Nie, he possessed merit and was without fault.
Why do I say this? The previous record ended with the Longxing era of the Southern Song. Longxing..."
Regarding the lineages of the thirty-eight generations that followed, and the lamp of wisdom spanning five hundred years from top to bottom, they were utterly ignorant.

Had there not been a *Xu lu* (Continued Records) to sustain the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom, it would have been impossible to distinguish between what was severed and what remained continuous, nor could the levels of attainment have been determined.

The words and phrases are not distinguished. A person who practices meditation is like one who is blind and without sight; how could they possibly be like the wolf of the Yue-guo, sniffing for gold in the darkness?
Therefore it is said that Master Nie had merit but no fault. Furthermore, Master Nie exhausted thirty years of his blood and labor, with calloused hands and cracked feet, to compose this book.
Like those who cleared the forests with basket-hoes and coarse garments, he forged the metal [of his resolve].
He cast cauldrons to ward off *chimei* demons; he was like a king of geese selecting milk from water without leaving anything behind, and like a Persian identifying jewels without any error.
He took what was hidden and made it manifest, achieving double the merit with half the effort. Therefore, I say that Master Nie has merit and no fault.
Others have further said: "Master Nie is a Confucian scholar, yet he forcibly engages in the affairs of the Buddhist school."
"How can he be considered free from fault? I replied to him: "This, indeed, was the fault of Master Nie. For Master Nie was truly a Confucian;
yet he did not shrink from rebukes nor disregard insults, provoking the wrath of the multitude and braving great peril.
He worked until his hands were calloused and his feet were cracked to compose this book. He was like Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu in establishing the orphaned prince, or like Nan Jiyun..."

Lei Wanchun’s defense against the rebels was merely intended to ensure that the lineage of thirty-eight generations since the Longxing era and the lamp of wisdom spanning five hundred years would remain clear and bright.
Even if he were to encounter the rebukes of those with discerning eyes or the harsh censures of various quarters, he would accept them with composure.
Furthermore, Master Qu also considers this to be like the tempering of the sword by Zichan.
The clogs of Yao Ji waddle and caper amidst the bellows, the fire, the wax, and the crucibles; yet he ridicules his own eccentricity. Niezi is just like this.

If this record were to be widely disseminated throughout the monastic groves and circulated through the entire Dharma realm, would it not be like what Panshan spoke of—that "the moon of mind hangs solitary, its light swallowing the ten thousand phenomena"? People of all times and eras are the same.
It is impossible to know how they differ. Alas! How difficult this is! Written by the layman Guangxia, Yu Huai of Putian, at the Yanshan Cottage in Wumen.
Preface to the Continued Record of Pointing at the Moon, Compiled by Subscription:
The Elder of Songyang, a sage of Eastern Wu, has produced this record with his fine brush, cataloging the genealogy of the Chan school. The single flower and five petals are clearly distinct;
like the moon, one follows the finger to see the moon. Recently, there has appeared another "Three-Eared One" (San-er-sheng), who composes poems and inscribes objects in great abundance.
The Sound of Ability. Continuing this record during times of hardship and peril: Neither the monkey’s cage nor the chicken’s coop startles me. I am ignorant of both branches of the Chan school;
Yet upon reading this book, I have always understood it clearly. The hundred rivers all come from the Min River; Mount Tai and Mount Hua still borrow the surrounding embrace of their descendants.
I have heard by hearsay that Cao and Ji split into two schools; East and West gather for debate and yet attack one another. Who would have known?
Now, whether people encounter the sudden or the gradual [teachings], all is contained within the plucking of the flower and the single smile.

Thus, I present this compilation to my fellow practitioners. The Great Dharma has flowed through thirty-eight generations; though the honey is divided among many mouths, its sweetness does not differ. The ears of grain form upon a thousand fields, and the benefit is equal for all.
I pray that you will together give rise to a heart of joy, so that the carving upon jade and stone may deepen our mutual benefit. Otherwise, please follow the path of darkness.
Looking at it from within, light emanates from every stroke of the calligraphy, all of which is pure gold.
Thus, the layman Wu Qiyuan Ci bows and writes:
"The unsurpassed Dharma of the world takes the Buddha as its dhāraṇī. Throughout the forty-nine years [of his teaching], he established sites of practice wherever he went."
The secret truth was bestowed and spread; it did not manifest solely through written characters. Reaching the patriarchs of the Eastern Land, a single reed crossed the sea.
The lamp-flower shone brilliantly upon five petals, illuminating all directions. Mind-to-mind, the wondrous seal of realization has remained without omission throughout kalpas.
The eighteen hundred koans—by a snap of the fingers, their true meaning is fully revealed. For those who have not yet seen the moon, Mount Yu has unveiled its essential principle.
The successor to the seat was Zhengbianzhi, whose influence spread throughout the four worlds. To this day, thirty-seven generations have passed; who shall compile these into a final collection?
The lay practitioner Nie of Wumen personally inherited the great Dharma-treasure. Relying on his own innate wisdom-faculty, he manifested as a treasury of radiance.

He sought certification from venerable elders and traveled extensively to consult those with the true eye. He investigated matters without weariness for detail and refined his work without weariness for craftsmanship.

How could such meritorious efficacy be easily accumulated? It extends widely to the virtues of the masses of faithful believers. How excellent is the Wheel-Turning King! This is no ordinary person’s task.
Through the accomplishment of the six perfections, he brings benefit; he truly relies upon great donors. Gold is spread everywhere like the earth; flowers rain down as tokens of his wondrous marks.
I have indeed heard these words. The devas and nāgas responded with assent. May all the virtuous ones universally aspire to give rise to a heart of joy.
Written by the Lingyan student Fan Guolü, respectfully composed.

Regarding the origins of this work: an ancient author composed a book that touches upon matters of a thousand ages. Although he passed through hardships and perils, his vow remained steadfast and sincere.
Thus, it became imperishable, and his composition has been transmitted for a millennium. If people of today can emulate the ancients, they may truly be said to be without shame.
The sources of Chan are set forth as five schools, their continuity spanning many years. School after school, the transmission is inexhaustible; they are numerous, each raising its own banner.

It is like the descendants of the third and fourth generations, vying with one another to claim that their ancestors are the same. Who can trace back to the source and the stream, so that they shall not contend or incite strife?
In my hometown, Master Qiu has pointed out the sequence of generations in the *Zhizhuyue* (Pointing at the Moon). With the mind of that layman, he regards all with equanimity;
his biographical records are as clear as a row of eyebrows. Through the lineage of robes and fly-whisks, the lamp of the ancestral temple from the West shall, it is hoped, not fall to the ground.
From the Song and Yuan dynasties onward, the Chan lineage lacked successors; it was suspended and painfully severed. Nie Zifa heaved a long sigh and, filled with lamentation, continued this record.
Through diligent and exhaustive searching, he recounted and elucidated the subtle words, proclaiming and upholding the grand tenets.
On the first day of the new year in the Year of Ding-si, I began this compilation. As my brush moved, dragon-elephants appeared; as my pen stirred, lions and maned beasts gathered.
From summer through autumn, I edited and refined it without regard for exhaustion. Looking back to the patriarchs from the time of Chan Master Liang Gao, the lineage reaches thirty-eight generations.

I have traced the currents to their end and sought the source from its beginning; through consultation and collation, nothing has been omitted. In the past, Master Lingyan spoke of this book’s *nidāna* (origination).

In the preceding volume, there are two "Eye-Born" ones (referring to Qu Huankui); in the subsequent volume, there are three "Ear-Sons" (referring to Nie Ledu). Through these ears and eyes, the source of Chan is elucidated, bringing joy to both humans and devas.
Who would have expected that before the book was finished, a fierce wind arose, causing me trembling fear? Master Nie said it was no cause for concern, as [this work] was his long-cherished...

Calamities and snares have converged; yet, by the power of wisdom, I have maintained patience and remained diligent and cautious. In haste and with failing strength, I have written this, urgently seeking to fulfill my original vow.

Biting through the snow and breathing upon the ice, I have compiled and examined these texts, forgetting both sleep and food. Within the circular prison, light was emitted, and a profusion of flower-rain fell.
Once the matter was resolved, I returned to Guangling, where I observed the surging waves at will. That this teaching may circulate depends upon you, Illustrious Lord; may it be widely disseminated.

The golden [scripture] reveals its secret meaning. It is like transmitting fire by means of wood, or like transmitting a spark by means of a lamp. When the fire is exhausted, the wood is not; the lamp transmits, and the spark transmits.
It is like using a finger to point out the moon: one sees the moon and does not see the finger. Yet, through the finger one can obtain the moon; seeing the moon, one then sees the finger.
I am originally but a man bound by the dust of the world; I gaze toward the Way but have not yet reached it. How great is the book of Master Nie! To investigate—
Refining his efforts and applying profound reflection, a definitive assessment has been reached after a thousand years.
This is now inscribed so that there may be no further confusion. Written with reverence by the student Shanhaiyin, Chen Jianlong.
Mr. Sun Xiaozhe’s letter:
Yesterday at the Western Gate, I waited expectantly for your immortal vessel, but in the end it could not be found. I remained despondent for a long time.

Just as I was planning to set sail from Guangling tomorrow morning to pay my respects and meet you and your attendants at Jingzhong Temple, I received your gracious letter; I am delighted that you have indeed not forgotten me.

This is far from the mark. You have already instructed your attendants to invite me to receive the Great Teaching; yet you further claim that I am like a wild duck drifting elsewhere, unable to meet with you, and thus feel compelled to decline reading the texts you have shown me.
To know that the venerable elder considers himself a custodian of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' life-force, not sparing even his own eyebrows—this is truly worthy of praise.
I venture to offer my humble views to assist your lofty wisdom. Lately, among the circle of monastics...
There are many narrow-minded views; moreover, their teeth are sharp and jagged. We must certainly cause them to bow their heads in submission before we can hope for peace throughout the world.

For instance, the recent descendants of Dongshan overturn the established lineages, and while their arguments are never lacking in firmness, those of the Jishi school each harbor a sense of grievance, many of whom clamor at me, my younger brother, with only the intent to [preserve] the blue...
Tian Cangtian replied in a single word: "I have observed that your extensive compilation is detailed regarding genealogy; it could indeed serve as a successor to the *Chuan deng lu*.
However, the title of your work is 'Pointing at the Moon. Considering the meaning of the name, 'pointing at the moon' emphasizes the essential Dharma rather than the lineage."
If one takes genealogical lineage as the primary concern, then one must decisively refute it to effectively silence such views;
otherwise, it merely serves as a topic for idle discourse, leading others to claim that our school has become muddled and superficial regarding the two characters "Pointing at the Moon.

However, if we rely on the essential Dharma, then despite differences in detail or brevity, and variations in beginning or end, we need only deliberate upon the further advancement of the staff (the Zen path). Now, while these woodblocks are first being carved...
"Try it. Would it be acceptable to continue using the name 'Chuan-deng' (Transmission of the Lamp)? Only you, O Illustrious One, can correct me.

Although I, your younger brother, have been traveling about among the various quarters in a haphazard manner, I have never had any real insight. If you say my feet follow others, I have long since ceased to have such a mind.
As for adorning my writings with ink, I dare not let them fall into anyone's category. Master Jiang Hu-lao does not know that among the various quarters..."
I wonder if you have been well. I have had the opportunity to converse with my younger brother morning and evening, and have gained a rough outline of the situation.

You may write to me at your convenience so that I may separately request your further instruction. A fine meeting at Wensuanlou is not far off. I cannot express all that I wish to say. Your brother, Zongyi, bows his head in respect.

(Recently I have examined various editions from the Zhejiang region; they overturn the chronological order of the lineage, with each text differing from the others. Those who understand this grieve over it. Master Xiaozhe is a venerable elder of the Dharma gate in our own time.

Your letter earnestly emphasizes the importance of the transmission lamp’s genealogy, which perfectly accords with my own diligent efforts in compiling and recording these works for the sake of joyful study. May the Zen of Words be forever protected by the Dharma. It is certain that the Buddhas, Patriarchs, Dragon Kings, and Heavenly Beings will join their voices in praise and support. Recorded by Jiangxiang of Jiyang.)

Coming home, the child is spoiled by wealth; he heads toward the riverbank to dangle his painted oar. He entices his father until the old man cannot hold back, and so comes aboard the boat to join in the singing.
Ascending the hall, Yongjia said: "The single moon universally appears in all waters."
"All waters and moons are encompassed within a single moon. Raising his whisk, he said: "Look! Look! A thousand rivers compete to pour forth; ten thousand streams vie to flow.
If you are already skilled at rowing a boat, you will understand the currents of the water; you can then wander leisurely through the ocean of nature and laugh at ease amidst the misty waves.
If this is not yet so, return for now to sit beneath the forest trees and wait for the time when the moon is bright. (Tàipíng Qín, successor).
Master Baozang Ben of Taizhou ascended the hall and said: "More than ten days have passed since Qingming;
the rain of flowers has thinned, yet the depths of one's heart remain profound. Spring colors vex the person, making sleep impossible; a yellow oriole flies past the green willow shade.
He then laughed loudly and descended from the seat. (Tàipíng Qín was his successor.)
When Chan Master Qinghai of Dazhong Xiangfu in Jizhou first met Fojian, Fojian asked:
"If the Buddhas of the three periods of time have been swallowed whole by a single mouth, where else could there be sentient beings to be taught and transformed? What is the principle of this?

As the Master was about to offer a reply, Fojian shouted at him. Suddenly, the Master realized the meaning and composed a verse, saying: "The reality-limit has never been subject to dust; within it..."
"There is neither old nor new; the green mountains, moreover, are the property of my own house. There is no need to seek the house or ask for another ford.
Yuanjian said, "Put it down. The Master bowed and departed (Tàipíngqín was his successor).
Chan Master Jingzhong Fuzhen Liaocan of Zhangzhou, a native of the Luo family from Quannan, ascended the hall and said:
"The Double Ninth, the ninth day of the month—the chrysanthemums are fresh. A single phrase, luminously clear, spans from antiquity to the present. Yang Guang’s camel is nowhere to be found;
last night its tracks were left beneath the pines. (Tàipíngqín was his successor.)
Chan Master Longxing Gu Shan ascends the hall: "One mention is not repeated; it has already fallen into two or three.
Meeting face-to-face without raising an eyebrow results in artificial fabrication. To speak is to move the strings and change the melody; to announce the past is to know the future.

Seeing the shadow of the whip, one should immediately set out; seeing the flagpole, one should turn back. At his very heels, he deserves thirty blows of the staff—how much more so for those who further pursue this..."
Gathering the sparks from rubbing stones and catching flashes of lightning—this labor is but a trivial matter; it makes the blue-eyed barbarian from the West laugh to his heart’s content.
(Zhuo the staff, he descends from the seat. (Taiping Qin succeeded [the previous masters]; the above totals seven persons).
Chan Master Fayun of Baiyang in Fuzhou was the son of the Wen family of Mianzhou. He relied upon Fuyan for training and heard his general discourses (*pushe*).
Fuyan cited the *Heart-King Inscription* by the Great Being Fu Dashi, saying: "The flavor of salt in water; the glue and blue pigment within color. It is certainly there."

He did not see the Master’s physical form. Upon these words, the student attained realization. Later, while watching the revolving scripture repository (lunzang) turn rapidly, he suddenly clarified the Great Dharma.
He hurried to the Master’s chamber to pay his respects and presented this verse: "A peak atop my head, clouds drift lazily; The source has no separate branches, the water flows coolly.
If one wanders the mountains without reaching their very end, In the end, the green mountains will obstruct the eyes. The Master smiled at him.
After he had taken up residence, he ascended the hall and said: "Good matters come piling up one after another; there is no need for fabrication or arrangement.

Yellow leaves falling in the forest are swept away by the water; white clouds drifting across the valley are rolled back by the wind. With a single cry from a cold wild goose, all worldly thoughts and attachments are severed."
"As soon as the frost-bell strikes, my mountain crumbles. Yet the white poplar has something even more extraordinary: all night long, it stirs the dead ashes in a cold hearth.
Suddenly, a monk comes forward and says, "Old man, you are showing off too much! Why do you act so wretched and beggarly?"
The mountain monk simply said this to him, yet you have caught me in it. [Circle] Ascending the hall, he said: "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand?
The Southern Star and the Northern Dipper in the heavens. How is my foot like a donkey’s foot? All past matters are forgotten.
Every person has their own karmic affinity; each one has square feet and a round head. Standing at the banks of Dayu Rapids, the solitary moon’s reflection shines forth."
Deep bay; it cannot be reached. To see it and return is difficult. A single melody of a fisherman’s song passes over the distant shoals. Addressing the Assembly:

The conditions for defilement are easily met, but the work of the Way is difficult to accomplish. Failing to understand the myriad distinctions of present conditions, one sees only the vast, surging winds of external objects.

The forest of meritorious virtues is ravaged; the fire of the mind blazes fiercely, consuming the tree of Bodhi. If one’s aspiration for the Way were identical to one’s affection for kin, Buddhahood would be attained long ago.

If one acts for the sake of the multitude as if for oneself, both self and others will achieve their goals. Seeing neither the faults of others nor one's own righteousness, one will naturally show reverence to superiors and humility to inferiors.
Thus, the Buddha-dharma will manifest at every moment, and one will be liberated from afflictions in every particle of dust.
○ A Teaching to the Assembly on Account of Illness I have been ill for a long time, yet I have never moved my wooden pillow.
When people come, they mostly ask, "How is it? I, this mountain monk, answer according to the circumstances as they arise. Outside the window, the yellow oriole’s voice is even more abundant.

As for this seven-foot frame—where does the illness reside? Those among you with the eye of discernment, please point out the source of the illness for me. The assembly offered various responses, but none were accepted.
[The monk] did not respond. The Master himself clapped his hands once and made a sound like vomiting. He said again, "What a fine wooden pillow! The Master disciplined himself with austere purity;
when traveling, he went alone with only his staff and hat. Later, when he passed away, his body was cremated.

His relics—including his eyeballs, teeth, tongue, and prayer beads—were collected and enshrined together with his sacred bones in a stupa to the west of the temple (Longmen was his distant successor).
Chan Master Ni Huiwen of Jingju in Wenzhou ascended the hall and said: "The Master Fayan once addressed the assembly, saying:
'When the three rolls of the drum have ceased and everyone has crowded up, the affairs of both the Buddha-dharma and human relations are all settled at once. The Master [Huiwen] said:

'As for this mountain monk, when the three rolls of the drum have ceased and everyone has crowded up, the staff is not here; with a mere broom handle, I shall give you thirty blows. (This was recorded by Longmen Yuan, the second successor).
Chan Master Yue’an Shanguo of Daming in Tanzhou, a native of the Yu family of Xingzhou, ascended the hall and said: "When the mind arises, phenomena also arise;
when the mind ceases, phenomena also cease. When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, one calls a tortoise a turtle. O virtuous practitioners of Chan!
"Have you spoken yet? If you have spoken, Daolin will give you my staff. If not, return to the hall and drink tea.
A monk asked, "What was it like when Bodhidharma sat facing the wall for nine years? The Master said, "When the fish swims, the water becomes turbid.
The monk asked, "When the Second Patriarch prostrated himself three times, why did he receive the marrow? The Master said, "The earth is rich; the eggplants grow large."
"Dà said, 'It is simply like a flower opening into five petals; the fruiting occurs naturally of itself. [Dà] asked, 'What matter does this clarify?
The Master said, 'A thief uses his loot as proof. [Dà] said, 'Sometimes riding upon a fine moon, one does not realize one has passed the Cangzhou.
The Master said, 'The Acharya has no share [in this] (Kāifú Níng was his successor).'"
Chan Master Yuchou Jujing of Husheng in Tongchuan was the son of the Yang family of Chengdu. At the age of fourteen, he left home to become a monk and visited Nantang.

When Nantang raised the koan of Xiangyan regarding the dragon crying within a withered tree, the Master engaged in a series of exchanges and inquiries until he attained great enlightenment beneath those words.
One day, Nantang asked him: "Do not guard the green grasses on the cold cliff; sit amidst the white clouds and realize the essence."
"Not good. What will you do? The Master said, "You must brandish the sword. If you do not brandish the sword, the fisherman will nest in his hut.
Huangbo was startled and said, "This little fellow! The Master said, "Take care," and departed. While residing at Dongyan, he ascended the hall and said: "The moon gives birth to one.
Having newly settled at Dongyan, my sorrow and stillness increase. The dusty paths of the world have many twists; the storehouses of rice and flour..."
No grains of dust; the cliffs form the boundary, the springs are its companions. A brisk, clear wind comes and enters the chamber; the local deities of the Mountain King are busy in the dark.
The cloud-slabs, bells, and fish-shaped chimes secretly shed teardrops. Let not the people of the world say he merely guards an empty crag;
there is also one who strikes the eastern fence against the western wall (Da-sui Jing-si).
Chan Master Sheng of Nan’an in Jianzhou ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "To protect life, one must kill; only when all are killed does one dwell in peace.
If you understand the meaning within this, you are clearly still halfway there. Now tell me, what about the single phrase for reaching home?

Śākyamuni and Maitreya have vast capacities, yet it appears they are still merely his servants. A monk asked: [The Master replied: "Śākyamuni and Maitreya have vast capacities, yet it appears they are still merely his servants."
"I do not ask about the five ranks of letting go; what is the matter of holding fast to the three barriers? The Master said, "Holding the Mohe sword crosswise, I issue the full command.
[The student] asked, "I have received your instruction on holding fast to the three barriers; how is the matter of letting go of the five ranks? The Master said:
"In the Great Peace of the Universe, the foolish and obstinate are severed. [The student] said, "If that is so, then under the gate of Nan-yen, the land is vast and people are few.
The Master said, "A sharp and clever monk requires only a single spark. [The student] asked, "From antiquity to the present, when it comes to being born together and dying together, what then?
The Master said, "A house-thief is difficult to guard against. [The student] said, "Today this student has gone out small and encountered something great. The Master then—
He struck [him] and said, "I must strike you, old monk, before it will do" (Da-sui Jing-si).
Zen Master Mo-tang Shao-wu of Neng-ren in Jia-zhou ascended the hall and, citing the case of Zhaozhou visiting the two hermitage masters, offered this verse:
"One mountain ends, then another mountain begins; Severing the solitary peak, look closely. The mist rolls back and the clouds..."
The mountain peaks withdraw into stillness; the Chu sky is vast and open, a single cold wheel [of the moon] (Dasuí Jìngsì).

Zhìtuózi, the Hermit of Tǔxī in Pēngzhōu, was a native of Miānzhōu. When he first arrived at Dàsuí, upon hearing the verse that Shítóu Huángshān recited to the assembly, he suddenly attained realization of the essential meaning.
He returned to live in seclusion at Tǔxī, amidst precipitous cliffs and remote ravines.

There was a rock resembling a crouching exotic beast; the Master carved it into a dwelling. From within, a marvelous spring gushed forth, neither drying up nor overflowing. The fourfold assembly marveled at this.

He resided there for thirty years, and his transformative influence spread widely. On the day the dwelling was completed, he composed a verse: "A single blow completes the stone hermitage; In every direction, spontaneity is attained.
Cool and refreshing, free from the heat of summer; Pure and limpid, with sweet spring water. Vast and expansive, it embraces the sands."
The realm is desolate and severed from all conditions; within it lies boundless meaning. Wind and moon, one sleeps upon a single bed—thus said Dàsuí Jìngsì.
Jiànmén Nán was a man of pure and profound virtue who cultivated the Way. Having attained accord through a single phrase from Dàsuí, he served him with unwearied diligence.
Later, he went to pay his respects to Chónghuà Yūn Chánshī. During their time together, Yūn questioned Nán regarding the Three Seals of the Zen School. Nán—
It is said: "Sealing the sky, sealing the mud, sealing the water. On level ground, cold waves rise in competition.
Even if one manages to go and come with full mastery, it is still like a numinous tortoise dragging its tail. (Da-sui Jing-si and the others above, five persons in total).
Chan Master Gao of Longhua in Qizhou ascended the hall and said: "The elephant king walks; the lion king stays. The barefooted K'un-lun has his eyebrows standing upright.
Hanshan and Shide laugh heartily, pointing at the old pine tree before the gate. But tell me, what is it they are pointing at?
Suddenly, when the wind blows it down, it is a fine pile of firewood. (This was the Five Patriarchs' own succession.)
Chan Master Cháng’ān Zéchóng of Jiànfú Monastery in Ráozhōu was a native of Níngguó. While presiding over the assembly, he gave this discourse. He raised an ancient case:

A monk asked an ancient worthy, “When birth and death arrive, how can one avoid them? The worthy said, “The firewood crackles and the bamboo pops, startling the ears. The monk said, “I do not understand.
The worthy said, “The house dog’s barking is fierce and does not cease at night. The Master said, “Do you all wish to understand? When the firewood crackles and the bamboo...”
A thunderous explosion startles the ears; red dust rises from the bottom of the vast ocean.
The house dog’s snarl does not cease throughout the night; a boat travels thirty thousand *li* across the land. The Earth Goddess Sthāvarā laughs heartily; King Sumeru watches with his eyes and nose.
Grasping hands, he walks east but turns west; the southern mountain responds with its voice within the northern mountain. The Thousand-Handed Avalokiteśvara opens his eyes to behold.
"Whose is this immeasurable compassion? After a long silence, he said, "Long head, short legs; little joy, much anger.
[One day] he ascended the hall and asked his attendant, "Do you still remember the incident from yesterday? The attendant replied, "I do not remember it.
He then looked toward the assembly and asked, "Do you remember? The assembly was silent. He raised his whisk and asked, "Do you remember? After a long silence...
He said, "I have forgotten it. The three horns do not form; even one does not exist. The assembly did not understand.
He then said, "Let us speak of the pillar for a moment; do not open your mouths. He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from the seat. (This was Huanglong Fengsi.)
Hu Wending Gong, the Layman Cao’an, was named An-guo and styled Kang-hou. Having long relied upon Master Xiù of Shàngfēng, he attained the meaning beyond words.
During the Chóngníng era, while passing through Yàoshān, a Zen practitioner raised the story of Nánquán’s “beheading of the cat” and questioned the Gong about it.
The Gong replied with a verse: “The hand digs into heaven and earth; the mechanism of killing and giving life, Arranged at will, lies within [the mind].”
Temporarily: "The jade hall’s hares and horses are not dragons or elephants; the grand function is majestic, yet none know it.
He also sent a verse to Xiu of Shangfeng, saying: "The Peak of Zhurong resembles Du Chengtian; Ten thousand ages of rivers and mountains are before one's eyes.
One must believe that Sīxin has never died; Last night, the autumn moon was once again full together. (Xiu of Shangfeng was his successor.)
Chan Master Fuzhou Puxian Yuansu was a native of Jianning. He ascended the hall and said: "The army follows the seal;
beyond three thousand *li*, all smoke and dust have ceased. The general pursues the talisman; throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, one is pure and naked.

Without the need for iron banners or iron drums, grass bows and wind blow naturally. What necessity is there for the 'seven maneuvers and seven captures' to achieve a state where none submit without thought?"
It is said: "The Great Man wields the sword of wisdom; its prajñā blade is like adamantine flame.
Not only can it shatter the minds of externalists, it has long since struck terror into the hearts of celestial Māras. At such a time, tell me: what kind of person is this commander?
[The Master] lets out a shout. ○ He ascends the hall and says: Nanquan said, "At eighteen, I already understood how to make a living.
My bag had no thread to tie even an ant; my kitchen lacked the crumbs to gather even a fly. Zhaozhou said, "At eighteen, I already understood how to break up the house and scatter the estate.
I bought cheap at the south end and sold dear at the north end. Examining these two statements closely, they deserve thirty blows of the staff each.
Let this one move pass for now. Why? "Once a wanderer, he feels special pity for travelers; naturally, when he craves wine, he spares those who are drunk.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Before a word is spoken, the matter is already entrusted. When you attempt to deliberate, ten thousand mountains stand between you.
Do not say that the Buddha-dharma is nothing more than a trifle; failing to penetrate the Mysterious Barrier is also most difficult. But how, pray tell, does one penetrate the Mysterious Barrier?"
[He] gave a shout and descended from the seat (the seal of succession was bestowed).
Chan Master Sengxun of Shantang at Gushan in Fuzhou, a native of the Ruan clan of that prefecture, ascended the hall and said:
"Huangbo’s sixty blows from his staff—had he not understood the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, he would have been short by a little. [But] under Dayu’s ribs..."
He threw down three fists and said, "Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is nothing more than this. He has truly wearied people to death!
You must know there is one person who, when struck over the head with a great club, does not turn his head; and when struck across the face with an old fist, he likewise pays no heed.
But tell me, who is it? [Ascending the hall: The north wind sweeps the earth, sweeping up the yellow leaves; outside the gate, a thousand peaks show a chilling hue.
At midnight, a tortoise flies with snow; the stone woman frowns her two brows by the stream. [Zhuo] strikes the meditation staff and says, "Everyone is here.
Now tell me, is it the sky that is cold or the people? He lets out a shout and says, "Return to the hall" (this was when Shangfeng first received the Dharma).
Chan Master Biefeng Zuozhen of Gushan in Fuzhou was a native of the Lin clan of Xinghua.

A monk asked, "Zhaozhou circumambulated the meditation seat once and said that he had finished reciting the entire Tripitaka. What is the principle behind this? The Master said, "When painting a dragon, look at its head; when painting a snake, look at its tail.
The monk asked, "The old woman said, 'I have come to request you to recite the complete Tripitaka. Why did you only manage to recite half of it?"
"What do you think about this? The Master said, "If a person lacks far-reaching foresight, they will surely have immediate anxieties.

[The monk] asked, "I do not yet understand where it is that one turns the *Prajñāpāramitā* in eighty thousand lines. The Master said, "If it is not a true connoisseur, it is all in vain to speak of the 'cold of the year.

[Another time,] he ascended the hall for instruction. "Seeking the ox, one must follow its tracks; studying the Way prizes the absence of mind. When the tracks are found, the ox is found; when there is no mind, the Way is realized."
Easy to find. [Fahshi] held up his whisk and said: "This is the track; where is the ox? Even if you can see its horns clearly, its nostrils are still in the hands of Fashí.
[On another occasion, Fahshi] ascended the hall and said: "The path that leads upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages. He struck the ground with his staff and said:
"If you understand it this way, you are still ten thousand eight thousand miles away. After all, what is it? Peach.
The red, white, and purple roses—when questioned about them, the east wind knows nothing at all. Addressing the assembly, he said:

"The Great Way is right before one's eyes, yet for all its presence, it is difficult to behold. If you wish to recognize the true essence of the Great Way, it is not separate from sound, form, voice, and language.
He struck the meditation staff and said: "This is sound. He raised the meditation staff and said: "This is form. "What do you call this? he asked.
"How can this be the true essence of the Great Way? Even if you were to see it here, it would still be like 'a man from Zhengzhou leaving the Cao Gate.
Addressing the assembly: "If we discuss this matter, it is like a person eating rice: when full, one simply stops. If one is not yet full, there will surely be a mind that longs for more food.
Yet if one eats too much, there is the affliction of indigestion. Having reached this point, what is to be done?"
"Go when it is exactly right. After a long silence, he said, "For now, return to the base of the cliff to stay the night; we shall look together upon the bright moon.
(The aforementioned three, including Shangfeng Cai.)
Chan Master Wushi Jiechen of Yuwang Monastery in Qingyuan was a native of the Zhang family of Wenzhou. Upon taking over the duties of the administrative head, he ascended the hall and said:
"A foot has twelve inches; those who can discern this are still rare. A scale has no stars at its tail; do not mistake it for something else.

If you wish to determine the weight of the past and present, or to compare the merits of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, simply ask that you fix a single eye upon this. If you can truly measure one foot..."
Give back those ten inches; eight *liang* are originally half a *jin*. Naturally, there is harmony within and without, and the family and the state will have no affairs.
Today, this mountain monk has already handed it over with both hands. Will you all, sirs, be willing to believe, accept, and practice it?
A ruler and a pair of scissors pervade the world; Master Zhigong was no idle monk. [Ascending the hall, he gave this discourse. Text.
Extraordinary wisdom, the conduct of Samantabhadra, many years and days of practice, Deshan’s staff, Linji’s shout—heroes of a chaotic age!
You people here, as you pass through the Sangha hall and enter the Buddha hall, do you know the peril that exceeds the Iron Ring Mountains?
If you suddenly step upon the crown of Śākyamuni’s head or bump into the forehead of the Holy Monk, you will not escape a calamity. The Master’s nature was stern.
Yi presided over the assembly with ancient methods; at the time, he was known as "Iron-Face Chen" (as recorded by Zhuo Sisi of Tianning).
Chan Master Puming Huelin of Daochang Monastery in Anji, a native of Fuzhou, ascended the hall and said: "The leaky bamboo sieve, the non-leaking wooden ladle;
the white peonies in the courtyard, the red peonies in the railing. Thinking thus of the man who sat facing the wall for nine years—what was his ultimate realization?"
If you do not recognize this one point, tell me: what is this one point? (He strikes the meditation seat with his staff and descends from the seat.
[Ascending the hall: One is many; many is one. Upon the crown of Vairocana, it is as bright as the sun;
yet there is neither one nor many. This is a ready-made case, free of any ambiguity. Picking up the old felt clappers, I manifest the time of clarity.
Singing the Song of Great Peace Together (by Tiantai Zhuo Si).

Chan Master Wuquan Juhui of the Tianning lineage, a native of the Wu clan of this prefecture, presided over the Anji Dharma Assembly where there was no formal succession. He ascended the hall and said:
"In his drunkenness, Zhong Kui sings the Liangzhou; the younger sister at the gate merely nods her head. After the Sea-Roaming Yakṣa has met him, everyone..."
"Clapping hands atop a high tower—if the assembly can understand this, you will lock the tongues of all people in the world.
If you cannot understand it, you will think that this old monk has some other extraordinary secret. [He] ascended the hall and said: "Playing with shadows and games atop a hundred-foot pole."
Not only deceiving you, but deceiving Heaven as well. Laughing at myself for my life spent on the forked path, I have returned in old age with not a single coin.
Ascending the hall, he raised the case: Linji addressed the assembly, saying, "One person is atop a high, towering mountain peak, with no way out.
Another person is at a crossroads, with neither front nor back. Tell me, which one is ahead?"
[The Master] said, "There is one more person who is neither on the high mountain peak nor at the crossroads.
Why does Old Man Linji not know him? He then descended from his seat. (Recorded by Tianning Zhuo Si)
Chan Master Yuanzhi of Songtang at Xianning Temple in Lin’an ascends the hall: The reeds are white; the smartweed is red.
By the stream, the tall bamboos are shrouded in green mist. Vague clouds embrace the secluded rocks; Jade dew drips from the mountain thickets.
Last night the tortoise transformed into a turtle; This morning the water buffalo realizes Perfect Penetration. *Tu!* (Tianning Zhuo’s successor).
Master Wuyuan Liangfan of Anjiu returned to Weian and ascended the hall for discourse: "The events prior to kalpas of dust—the majestic presence has no front or back;
movement and stillness cannot encompass it, and its unfolding and rolling are as swift as lightning. Do not say that ordinary people do not know it; even a Buddha cannot see it.
Where exactly does it reside? Close these two flaps. Whether you realize it or not, I shall further explain it for all of you."
[He drew] a single line. After a long silence, he said: "The world is at great peace; the imperial wind fans forever.
Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "The ultimate Way is not difficult; it simply dislikes discrimination. Is this the nest of people of this age?
Zhaozhou replied, "Someone once asked me this, and for five years I could not provide an explanation. The Master called to the assembly, saying: "Zhaozhou possesses the eye on the crown of his head."
With the eye, distinguish the black from the white within the spark struck from flint; discern the taking and the giving within a flash of lightning.
Why, then, could he not provide an explanation for five years? Do you understand? It is easy to distinguish flour in the snow, but difficult to identify soot in ink. (Tianning Zhuo)
Chan Master Wen Guan Lingguang of Benji, of the Ye clan of Yongjia in the commandery of Wenzhou, ascended the hall and said:

"The Tathāgatas of the past have already perfected this gate—better not to have had such a thing at all. The Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter perfect clarity—better not to have had such a thing at all.
Those who practice and study in the future should abide according to this—better not to have had such a thing at all."
It is better not to have such matters at all. Do you still understand? Aside from Master Chen of Mount Hua, who among people does not walk about carrying both right and wrong with them?
(Tianning Zhu succeeded him; the above totals six persons.)
Chan Master Wuzhenghui Chuchan of Dingshan in Changde was a native of Jingjiang. One day, he ascended the hall and, looking over the assembly, said:
"Do you see? In heaven they form the constellations; on earth they take shape as forms. In the sun and moon they become the waning and the waxing; in the four seasons they become cold and heat.
They are stirred by thunder and lightning, and moistened by wind and rain. But tell me, where do they reside within the realm of the patch-robed monks?"
[The Master] said, "Up! And how about this? With one kick, he overturns the four great oceans; with one punch, he topples Mount Sumeru.
He cannot be contained within the ranks of Buddhas and Patriarchs; yet he blows his fishing pipe at the Bay of Muzhituo. [He] ascended the hall and said:

"On the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, we gather our heads together to raise this [issue]. We blind the Eye of the True Dharma, remove Yunmen’s 'Universal,' and [realize that] Deshan did not understand."
He spoke of Zen, winning the village songs and community dances. "A-he-he! Luo-lo-li! He then performed a dance and descended from his seat.
(Huanglong Zhen succeeded him.)
A monk asked Chan Master Shu of Yanqing on Mount Lu, "Before the Many-Children Stupa, what did they discuss together?
The Master said, "Each time we meet, we grow older; how much longer can we remain brothers? The monk bowed.
The Master said, "Today at Tangxing, I have lost the advantage" (The Abbot Zu was his successor).
Chan Master Puxin of Meng’an at Wanshou on Lian Water ascended the hall and said: "The remaining snow has completely vanished; the spring breeze grows ever more frequent.
If you understand this through the seasons, what then of the Buddha-dharma? Tell me, are the conditions of the seasons and the principles of the Buddha-dharma the same or different?
After a long silence, he said: "A shadowless tree planted where no one sees it; it blooms and bears fruit..."
The fruit naturally emits fragrance (the superior cause silently succeeds).
Chan Master Xingdao Mo’an of Huirì Monastery in Pingjiang ascends the hall: "The gathering clouds are about to snow but have not yet snowed;
the beloved sun seems radiant but does not truly shine. Cold sparrows chirp noisily in the fences; the piercing north wind dances through the curtains. To understand this—"
Shaoyang’s intimate phrase: today, I shall bring it forth face-to-face for you. (He plants his staff upright and descends from the seat. [Recorded by Jing Si of Shengyin].
Chan Master Guo Min of Guangxiao Temple in Guangde, a native of Taoyuan, ascended the hall and cited the story of Nanquan cutting up the cat.
He then said: "Nanquan raised it up and brought down the blade to slaughter; even a six-armed asura could not save him.
Even if both halls had been able to speak it, blood would still have flowed across the streets. (Shengyin, Jing, and Sisi—these three masters above.)
Chan Master Huizhong of Xuefeng Qutang in Fuzhou ascended the hall and said: "All day long one is busy and bustling, yet that matter is not hindered.

Chan Master Yuan of Penglai in Qingyuan lived on the mountain for thirty years without his feet ever crossing the threshold. He was revered by both monastics and laypeople alike.

Chan Master Shouhui of Minyin at Yuantong Temple in Jiangzhou ascended the hall and said: "One merely knows today and then tomorrow;

Master Chan Huanglong Daoguan of Hongzhou ascended the hall and said: "The ancients said: 'Eye and form, ear and sound—the myriad dharmas are thus established.

A monk asked Chan Master Xuanmi Li of Shitai in Yangzhou: "Are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth the same as oneself, or are they different? The Master said:

The Master then pointed to the seat and said, "This platform—if one were to lead a donkey up here, it too would surely defecate upon the ground.

"Thirty [years] with him. Now tell me, where does the fault lie? After a long silence, he said: 'The mechanism was not made by Han Guang;
do not treat your own inner depths as something trivial. (Dahui Zonggao succeeded him.)
Chan Master Dongchan Meng’an Siyue of Fuzhou was a native of Jiangzhou. He ascended the hall and said:
"When Bodhidharma came here, everyone in this land understood the language of India; yet after he departed, everyone in the Western Heaven understood the language of Tang.

If we discuss 'directly pointing at the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha,' it is much like a wild goat hanging from its horns: when the hounds search for its tracks, their single-minded pursuit only leads them further astray."
To say it is useless would mean: "When I came, others laughed at me; I do not know that after I leave, I shall laugh at them.
I have personally transmitted the Chinese and Sanskrit words from of old. When monks eat their vegetarian meals, they fear the night tea.
[The Master] ascends the hall: "I will silence my own mouth, yet you must speak; I will block your ears, yet you must take heed not to miss it. Yesterday someone came from Tiantai, yet he said..."
The Great Sage of Sizhou was sitting in meditation in Hongzhou. What was he selling at the crossroads?
A straw sandal with broken heels and a bamboo hat with a pointed brim (Dahui Zonggao’s lineage).

Chan Master Cigan Shoujing of Xichan Monastery in Fuzhou was a native of this province. He ascended the hall and said: "To discuss the profound and explain the subtle is to scatter excrement and urine;
to wield the staff and shout is to use salt to quench thirst; to establish host and guest is the flowery wall of the ancestral vehicle.
Even if one were to do none of these things, one would still be sitting in a ghost cave. Having reached this point, I, this mountain monk, have already struck you back."
[The Master] struck the drum. He said, "Tell me, when people in their daily lives are filled with indignation in their hearts and constrained in their speech, what should they do?
Do not let your idle academic learning bury the mind of the Patriarchs. [Ascending the hall, he said: "If you clarify only your own self and do not awaken to that which is before your eyes..."
This person has eyes but no feet; if one only awakens to what is before the eyes without clarifying one's own self, this person has feet but no eyes.
Only when the eyes and feet assist one another—like the two wheels of a cart or the two wings of a bird—is it right to pass examination and strike.
[The Master] ascended the hall and said: "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra discuss principle and phenomena; Linji and Deshan employ the staff and the shout. East..."
Meditating alone, one awakens until daybreak. One especially loves the wind blowing from a cool place. *Pah!* Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Close your mouths; speak at all times.
Cut off your tongues; let there be no interruption. No interruption—how most marvelous! How most marvelous! It is but a speck of dust in the eye.
Since it is so marvelous, why does it instead become a speck of dust in the eye? When there is complete understanding, there is nothing to be understood."
"Even the most profound depths of mystery must be criticized" (attributed to Dahui Zonggao).
Chan Master Wanan Daoyan of Donglin in Jiangzhou was a native of Tongchuan. His clan name was Xianyu. Having studied under Yuanwu for a long time, he attained a slight degree of awakening.
When Yuanwu returned to Sichuan, he instructed Daoyan to rely upon Dahui Zonggao and sent a letter to Dahui to this effect.
He said, "The painting of Yanchuan is finished; it only lacks the eyes. Someone else will succeed to this task in the future—the extent of his achievement cannot yet be measured.
Later, when Xuedou Gaofeng resided at Yunmen and Yangyu, the Master was present with him both. Day and night they questioned one another until Gaofeng attained great enlightenment.
[Ascending the hall: "When a single leaf falls, the whole world is autumn. When a single speck of dust rises, the entire earth is gathered up. Niaoke blew on a tuft of cloth-hair."
Thereupon, someone attained enlightenment. Why is it that students of the present day do not recognize their own selves?
After a long silence, he said: "Do not mistakenly blame others. A monk asked, "Regarding the story of Xiangyan climbing the tree—what is its essential meaning?
The Master said, "It cannot be sketched; it cannot be painted. The monk said, "Though Li Ling was a skilled hand, what could he do about being trapped by the barbarians? The Master said, "What?"
Chuchu Lai (Successor of Dahui Zonggao).
Chan Master Fozhao Deguang of Yuyang during the Qingyuan era was the son of the Peng family of Linjiang. At an early age, he entered the hall of Dahui Zonggao. Dahui asked him:
"If you call it a bamboo stick, you commit the fault of 'contact'; if you do not call it a bamboo stick, you commit the fault of 'aversion. You cannot provide an answer."
[The Master] said, "One must not remain silent; speak quickly, speak quickly! The Master [Yunmen] said, "You fabricated old fellow!
You are like hemp and millet. Baogao said, "Which one are you? The Master said, "Today I have caught this old thief.

In the following year, on the anniversary of the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa*, as the Master was prostrating, he thought, "Since the Buddha-body is eternally abiding, how could there be birth and extinction? Before his head had even reached the ground—

Suddenly he attained awakening and immediately informed Daogao. Daogao said, "This time you have reached thorough penetration. When Daogao again took charge of Mount Jing, he invited him to go with him.
Later, he bestowed upon him a verse along with his portrait (dingxiang), saying: "Where there is virtue, there must be radiance; that radiance knows no interruption. Name and reality must correspond;
it is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white... [The text continues: While the Master resided at Lingyin, Emperor Xiaozong...
Zongxuan asked, "When Śākyamuni Buddha entered the mountains to practice the Way for six years, what was it that he accomplished? The Master replied, "I thought Your Majesty had forgotten.
He once stayed overnight within [the palace]. Furthermore, the karmic conditions of his audiences at the Guantang Hall are fully recorded in the original records.
Later, he passed away; his entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Dong'an on Mount Mao (Daoying Huiyuan was a successor of Dahui Zonggao).
Chan Master Zhuduan Zongyan of Huazang in Changzhou was the son of the Zheng family of Fuzhou. Entering the hall, he held up his staff and said:
"If you recognize this, the business of a lifetime of study is finished. "The ancients spoke thus," [Zongyan continued], "but at Huazang, it is not so.
Even if you recognize this, you must still buy straw sandals and travel on foot. Why? To reach the land of Wu by the river."
[The assembly] was exhausted. On the other side of the bank, across the mountains, many [monks] ascended the hall. The Master took the seat and raised the precedent:
Nanquan said, "At eighteen, I already understood how to manage a livelihood. Zhaozhou said, "At eighteen, I already understood how to break up the family and scatter the household.
The Master said, "Nanquan and Zhaozhou were like Xu Liu carrying a single plank; they saw only one side. Huazang has no livelihood to be managed, nor does he have a house to be broken up."
There is no household to be broken; whenever meeting someone, he suddenly throws out an old punch, wishing for them to arrive directly at the point right now.
But tell me, what is it like after arriving? "The thirty-six peaks cannot be viewed enough; yet one comes back to level ground to ride a donkey backward. (Dahui Zonggao was his successor.)
Chan Master Wuyong Jingquan of Tiantong in Qingyuan was the son of the Wu family of Yuezhou.

He ascended the hall and said: "The orthodox lineage of Vulture Peak—those who have attained it still remain deluded. Whether light comes or darkness comes, who can discern the true mark? Whether both are gathered or one is released, who can distinguish the beginning?
Even if a thousand sages were to appear, they would only end up with their tongues tied. Why is this? Because people return to the great kingdom."

Only then is one noble. When the water reaches the Xiao and Xiang rivers, it finally attains clarity. He spoke again: "Just now, Songyuan brought up the story of the bamboo whisk, causing Tiantong to suffer a defeat.
Do you all wish to know? Listen to this verse: 'Grasping the black-lacquered bamboo whisk, A bolt of lightning leaves no time to cover one's ears.
Deshan and Linji are left staring blankly; How can those who are dazed insert their beaks? (Dahui)"

Chan Master Daowen Jian of Kainshan in Jianning was a native of this province. (The details of his enlightenment are recorded in full in the *Jue-an Lu*, in the chapter on Dahui Zonggao. He ascended the hall and said:
"The mind of the Great Sage of the Land of Chu was secretly transmitted from east to west. What is this mind that was secretly transmitted? After a long silence, he said: "Eight."
Moon in Autumn. Where is the heat? [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "Last year there was a June fifteenth;
this year there is also a June fifteenth. Last year’s June fifteenth does not lack this year’s June fifteenth."
On the fifteenth day of the sixth month this year, it is one day more than the fifteenth day of the sixth month last year. Where there is a surplus, there is no need to subtract;
where there is a deficit, there is no need to add. Since there is neither addition nor subtraction, then use what is in surplus abundantly and use what is in deficit sparingly.
Then he gave a shout and said: "Is it much? Is it little? After a long silence, he said: "Within this, can there be any message?"
How many people know (that Dahui Zonggao was succeeded by him)?
Chan Master Nengren Kumu Zuoyuan of Yanshan, Wenzhou, was the son of the Lin family of Min.

He relied upon Dahui at the Yangyu Hermitage, sitting upright throughout the entire day. Miaoxi (Dahui) named him "Zuoyuan Kumu" (Zuoyuan, the Withered Tree). Thereupon, [Dahui] raised the matter of the three generations...
"The Buddhas do not know how to speak. After being questioned and pressed repeatedly, he suddenly attained realization (as recorded in the *Wuyou Zaiqu Lu*).

In the spring of the Yisi year of the Shaoxing era, he went forth to reside at Nengren Temple. Ascending the hall, he said: "Where there is a Buddha, one must not dwell; treading upon a scale-weight, it is as hard as iron.
Where there is no Buddha, pass quickly by; beneath one's feet, the grass is three feet deep. Meeting people three thousand miles away..."
Do not mistake the order of things. The Northern Dipper hangs from Mount Sumeru. If it is so, then one does not go.
With a staff, one picks out the sun and moon. Plucking the willow flowers—plucking the willow flowers! A person with eyes wears embroidered shoes. (He struck his staff and descended from the seat.
He once resided at Fuyan Hermitage in Lianjiang. His dependents were numerous, and daily provisions for food were insufficient. In the hermitage, there was a clay statue of the temple guardian deity.
The assembly was quite large. The Master posted a verse at the shrine, saying: "A small hermitage, meager food, and a small forest— Why should the local deity require eight or nine men?
If you understand how to take turns coming to offer incense, You need not be ground to dust in a single heap.
That evening, the deity appeared in a dream to a lay donor from the mountain front, and everything was exactly as he had warned (Dahui Zonggao succeeded him).
Chan Master Liaoming of Mount Jing in Lin’an stood eight chi tall with a waist ten spans in circumference;

wherever he went, people inevitably gathered to gaze upon him. When Dahui Zonggao was first exiled to Meizhou, the escorting guards were strict and vigilant, and some feared his fate might be unpredictable.
The Master carried his cangue as he traveled, enduring hardships and obstacles without ever showing the slightest slackening. Once he arrived at his place of banishment...
The number of monastics who followed him to seek the Way grew daily. Because alms-food was insufficient and he feared potential calamity, Wuxiaō constantly urged them to leave.
The Master, however, would not consent; he took personal responsibility for the meals and, every day, carried his own begging bowl on his shoulder to wander for alms.
By evening, dozens of people would gather to carry rice, flour, firewood, and vegetables back in a procession. The monastics...

He gathered ten thousand followers, none of whom were not fully endowed [with virtue]. For seventeen years, he remained as if it were but a single day. Most of Gaofeng’s Dharma heirs were guided by him while he was stationed at the military garrison;

all of this was due to the Master’s assistance. When Gaofeng was granted an imperial decree to restore his monastic robes, and subsequently received another decree to reside at Yuwang Monastery, the Master had previously been among his disciples.
Upon Gaofeng’s tenure at Mount Jing, the Master returned to Changlu, and Gaofeng saw him off with [a formal parting].
The verse says: "The world says a filial son emerges from the tip of the staff; I say one who loves their child does not notice their own ugliness.
When the Elder Changlu comes like this, Miaoxi has wasted his mouth for naught. Let the false rumors spread throughout the four seas; A jackal can indeed let out a lion’s roar.
Who says there is nothing to present him as he departs? With a shout, Mount Iron Ring rolls backward! —Postscript.
He received an imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing, where his reputation for the Way grew even more prominent.

Previously, Prince Yang had dreamed of an extraordinary monk who was tall and large-bellied, walking slowly, and saying he wished to purchase a manor in Suzhou. Upon waking, the prince found it strange but did not speak of it.

The following morning, the Master suddenly arrived on foot with staff and sandals; when the gatekeeper shouted to stop him, he would not cease, so the matter was reported to the Prince. The Prince came out to see him.
Gazing from afar at the Master, he found him magnificent and sublime, no different from the one he had seen in his dream. He immediately called his retinue out to behold him.
The entire retinue lit incense and paid their respects. After tea, the Master spoke first, saying, "Your Majesty possesses vast fields and estates;
you might grant one estate in Suzhou as a means to provide offerings for the Buddhas and meals for the monks at Mount Jing. The King did not yet give his consent. Thereupon—
He ordered the preparation of a vegetarian feast. After the master had finished his meal, he departed without further word.

At that time, there was a great commotion both inside and outside [the palace], as word spread that Wang He had offered the estates of Suzhou to the Elder of Mount Jing. This eventually reached the ears of Emperor Xiaozong.
When Wang He entered the court, the Emperor spoke to him, saying: "I have heard that you intend to offer an estate in Suzhou to Mount Jing. I shall grant you an exemption for it."
He was exempted from taxes. Wang and Xie returned home after expressing their gratitude. On the following day, he sent a letter to Jingshan Mountain, requesting that the Master enter the city;
however, two days prior, the Master had already passed away. From then on, whenever Wang and his wife were at rest or awake, [they perceived his presence].

If he grew slightly weary and his eyelids drooped, he would immediately see the Master standing before him, who would say: "Of the six perfections, the perfection of giving is foremost. To begin well and conclude well—this is the ultimate goal.
The King then bestowed a manor and its dependents upon the mountain monastery. This manor yielded one hundred thousand [units of currency] annually;
it was fully equipped with plow-oxen, boats, carts, granaries, and all necessary implements for every task. Furthermore, there was the grace of exemption from taxes. For a long time...
They received his benefits. The Master had a great karmic affinity with both the monastic and lay communities;
throughout Jiang, Zhe, and the two lakes, all hailed him as the rebirth of the Bagua Monk (Da Hui Gao was his successor).
Chan Master Dabao of Daopei in Tanzhou was a native of Fuzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "To call it a 'bamboo stick' is to encounter resistance;
not to call it a 'bamboo stick' is to turn one's back. You must be like a lion that bites; do not act like a hound that chases after clods of earth. A-ha-ha! Do you understand?
Under the feet of the Vajra, an iron Kunlun—catching the doltish Bagua of Mingzhou. [Seal] Above.
The Hall: A thousand words, ten thousand metaphors—intended only to teach you to return home early. Last night a great mass of black clouds arose;
do not let them cause you to lose the path ahead on the mountain. *Tu!* (Dahui Zonggao, successor of Dahui Zonggao).
Chan Master Tanzhi of Yushui in Fuzhou was a native of the Lin family of that same prefecture. Having long relied upon Yuanwu, he considered himself free from doubt.
At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, he went forth to reside at Xiangyun in Xinghua, where his Dharma assembly was quite flourishing.

When Master Dahui Zonggao entered Min, he realized that Tanzhi’s realization was not yet stable; he sent a letter summoning him to come. Tanzhi delayed, so Dahui gave a small lecture (xiaocan), admonishing him with great severity.
He rebuked him and posted a public notice to the fourfold assembly. The Master, having no other choice, broke his summer retreat to visit him. Xiang examined the realization he had attained.

After a while, Xiang said, "With such a view as yours, how dare you claim to be the successor of the Elder Yuanwu? The Master immediately withdrew from the monastery and attended Xiang personally to investigate the mind.
One day, upon entering the inner room for instruction, Xiang asked, "I want someone who does not understand Chan to be National Teacher. The Master replied:

"I have served as National Preceptor and am now departing. Gao gave a shout and drove him out. Not long after, Gao suddenly said to him, "Xiangyan’s place of awakening was not at the point where the bamboo was struck;
Jushi’s attainment was not upon the tip of the finger. At this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.

Later, he resided at Yùquán Temple, where he offered incense for Huìgǎo. He subsequently visited Huìgǎo at Xiǎoxī, where Gǎo ascended the seat and cited an occasion when Yúnmén once held up his staff and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Ordinary people truly take it to be existent; those of the Two Vehicles analyze it and take it to be non-existent."
Pratyekabuddhas call this "illusory existence," whereas Bodhisattvas realize its very substance is emptiness. When a monk sees a staff, he simply calls it a staff;
when walking, he simply walks; when sitting, he simply sits. He must not touch upon it at all.
Gaofeng said, "I am not the old man Yunmen, who digs a hollow in empty space. He then suddenly picked up his staff and said, "Staff! It does not belong to..."
"It exists. It does not belong to non-existence; it does not belong to illusion; it does not belong to emptiness. He struck the ground once and said:
"Ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—all turn toward this very place and, according to their respective capacities, fully obtain its enjoyment.

Yet, within the sphere of the patch-robed monk, it acts as a harm and a grievance. When one wishes to walk, one cannot walk; when one wishes to sit, one cannot sit. To take even one step further, one is obstructed."
The staff-child has lost its way at the head of the path. If you retreat one step, you will have your nostrils pierced by that staff.
Is there anyone here now who is not dissatisfied? Come forth and meet this staff! If there is none, next year there shall be new branches again;
the spring wind’s vexation will never cease. At such a time as this, what should be done? [He] stepped down.
The Master said, "I trouble Yuyuan to bring this forth for the sake of the assembly.

After the Master had ascended the seat and finished his expressions of gratitude, he took up the previous conversation and said, "Just now, when the Abbot made such a critique, it was much like a weary fish resting in a pond or a sick bird perching on a reed."
If it were Yuquan, it would not be so. He took up his staff and said, "This staff can exist and can non-exist; it can manifest illusion and can be empty.
As for ordinary people, those of the two vehicles, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—" he struck the ground once and said, "Here, they are all shattered to pieces."
Only within the realm of the patch-robed monk is it like a dragon finding water or a tiger relying on a mountain;
where one wishes to walk, one walks, and where one wishes to sit, one sits. To take a step forward, heaven and earth tremble; to take a step back, the grass bows and the wind blows.
But tell me, as for this phrase of neither advancing nor retreating—how do you speak of it? After a long silence, he said: "Holding a scroll of scripture, leaning against a pine tree."
"Laughing, he asked the guest from where they had come. (Daoyuan’s *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, Chapter on Dahui Zonggao).
Chan Master Wuben of Jianfu Temple in Raozhou was a native of Jiangzhou. (The details of Wuben’s enlightenment are recorded in full in the *Jueyu Lu*, in the chapter on Dahui Zonggao).
While presiding at Jianfu Temple, he ascended the hall and said: "Śākyamuni shut his room in Magadha; Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth in Vaiśālī; Subhūti proclaimed 'non-arising'..."
As he spoke, manifesting the Way, Śakra and Brahmā ceased their watching and listening and rained down flowers. "O Great Assembly!

This group of incompetent fellows has, for no reason, taken the ancestral fields and gardens and entered into private contracts, each seizing their own four boundaries and divisions according to the dimensions of the plots, dividing them all up at once.
This will cause their descendants in future generations, even after a thousand years, to have nothing above them..."
"A single tile covers the head; below, there is not even enough room to plant a awl.
If Boshan had seen this at that time, he would have dug a bottomless deep pit at the crossroads, called them over, and buried them all at once, sparing us from this mutual dullness and frustration.
Why is this so? Have you not heard it said: "When the family is prosperous, filial sons are born; when the state is hegemonic, there are strategic ministers"? (Dahui Zonggao’s Succession)
Chan Master Danyuan Zunpu, the Great Protector of Beings, was a native of Fuzhou. In his youth, he studied the Way alongside Yuyuan Yi under Yuanwu Keqin at Zhaojue for several years.
Later, he returned to his hometown and assisted Yi at Xiangyun in Pufeng. In the year Jiayin of the Shaoxing era, Dahui Zonggao resided at Yangyu; the Master went there to visit him.
