Better to bury them all at once in a single pit. The Master once offered this verse on the story of the wine dregs: "Within a thicket of brambles he proclaims the wondrous meaning;
In a garden of thistles he radiates beams of light. A thousand words and ten thousand phrases—no one understands them;
Then, following the warbling oriole, they pass over the low wall. (Fóxìng Tàisì)
Chan Master Zhong’an of Lingyan in Lizhou ascended the hall and said: "If one studies Chan without investigating its profound source, every encounter will become an obstruction.
Thus, to cling to stillness and silence to realize a state of quiescent emptiness is to fall into a sea of poison; it is like attempting to overcome the strong with weakness."

Taking oneself as right and others as wrong, one establishes the measure of self and other, resulting in a biased and withered perspective. Consequently, superiority and inferiority cannot be distinguished;
illumination fails to engage with function, and function remains trapped within its nest. This is because the place of study is not profound; it has become entirely mundane.

At this point, one must know that there is penetration and liberation within death, and the concealment of mechanism within life. Even the Buddhas cannot know it, and the Patriarchs cannot fathom it. Therefore:
The ancients said: "Sometimes there is illumination first and then function; let me consult with you on this. Sometimes there is function first and then illumination;
you must be a man of substance before you can grasp this. Sometimes illumination and function are simultaneous—how will you withstand that?
Sometimes illumination and function are not simultaneous—where will you find a place to settle? Do you understand? It pierces through."
Yang Jian’s startling lines were not something acquired on the spot (as recorded by Fóxìng Tái).
Zen Master Zhèngfǎ Hào of Chéngdū ascended the hall and, citing the karmic conditions of Yongjia’s single night at Caoxi, said:
"If you wish to recognize Yongjia, he overturned the seas and mountains in search of a true friend. If you wish to recognize the Patriarch, he..."
Heaven and Earth establish Great Peace; the Two Elders do not know where they have gone. (Holding up his staff) Zuo said:
"The patriarchal wind spreads its glorious fame for a thousand ages. (Fóxìng Tàisī).

Chan Master Bian of Chengdu’s Zhaojue Monastery ascended the hall and said: "A difference of a hair's breadth, and heaven and earth are set apart. A person on the other side of the river sings a *zhègū* lyric;
one mistakenly takes it for the 'Eighteen Taps' of the *hújiā*. Do you wish to understand? If you wish to attain manifestation before you, do not harbor notions of compliance or resistance.
Who contends over the misty waves of the Five Lakes? Since it is so, if one does not return, one will attain it upon returning. (Fóxìng Tài succeeded these four masters.)
Master Juebao Qing of Pingjiang ascended the hall for the formal discourse. He cited a monk’s question to Yunmen: “What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? Yunmen said:
“Water flows uphill on the eastern mountain. The Master said: “The place where all Buddhas emerge is water flowing uphill on the eastern mountain.
A bamboo shoot slants outward, pressed down by a rock; a flower grows upside down, suspended from a precipice. (Daochang Bian was his successor.)
Shouzuo Heshan Ran of Anji was a native of Gusu. He attended Zhengtang Bian for a long time.
On one occasion during his entry into the room, Bian asked, "Why does the cat especially love to catch mice? Ran replied, "When an object meets its master, its eyes stand bolt upright.
Bian was pleased and consequently ordered him to share the seat [at Daofang; Bian was the successor of the aforementioned two].
Chan Master Liaoyun of Chouyan in Yiwu ascended the hall and, citing the story of Zhaozhou’s “The dog has no Buddha-nature,” said:
“Zhaozhou says, ‘The dog has no Buddha-nature. Ten thousand layers of green mountains conceal an ancient mirror;
A barefoot Persian enters the Great Tang, And eight-armed Nalakūvara executes the true command. *Du!* (He was succeeded by Shan Xun of He Mountain.)”
The lay practitioner Pan Lianggui, whose courtesy name was Yirong, was forty years old when he turned his mind toward the ancestral gate.
Wherever he went, he hung up his alms bowl and joined the assembly to seek instruction. While under the guidance of Chan Master Fudeng Xun, he studied for a long time without attaining realization.

Later, while contemplating the story of Nanquan’s killing of the cat, he questioned Xun; upon hearing the words, he attained a profound awakening. His verse says: "My own cat has long since been lost."
A cat belonging to another's house; when asked about it, one laments its loss. Flowers fall and the stream flows; let him act with such impetuosity. (He Shanxun; the two aforementioned individuals).
Chan Master Shouyuan of Suian, known as Wuwai of Hanzhou, was a native of that prefecture. His surname was Shi.

At the age of thirteen, he suffered from blindness in his eyes and went to rely upon Chan Master Huimeng of Qichan. After receiving full ordination, he left the gorges and arrived at Baofeng, where he encountered the Master ascending the hall.
The Master cited Yongjia, who said: "The single moon universally appears in all waters; all water-moons are encompassed by the single moon. The Master...

Upon hearing this, he was relieved and attained realization. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Unify the many into the one. A single moon universally appears in all waters. Return the myriad to the one;
all moons in the water are subsumed within that single moon. When extended, it pervades and encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; when withdrawn, not even a hair’s breadth remains.
Although these processes of extension and withdrawal follow different paths, this matter fundamentally has no distinction. It simply requires that you, at the very root..."
If you can attain even one eye of insight, you will see that all Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations have all manifested from within this.
All of the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the teachings, all the Sūtras, have flowed forth from within this.

Heaven and earth, the sun and moon, and the myriad phenomena of the universe have all arisen and been established from within this. The three realms and nine stages, the seven destinies and four modes of birth—all proceed from here.
All emerge from and submerge within this: hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates, immeasurable subtle meanings, and even all worldly crafts and arts—all these are manifested through its activity.
This is why when the World-Honored One held up the flower, Kāśyapa immediately broke into a smile.
Dharma faced the wall; the Second Patriarch thereby attained peace of mind. When the peach blossoms bloomed profusely, Lingyun’s doubts were completely purified.
Striking bamboo produced a sound, and Xiangyan suddenly forgot all that he had known. This continued until Panshan realized the Way at the head of a meat counter.
Maitreya went into the fish market to meet people. Truly, it must be so even in moments of haste or distress.
Walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—all were within that state.
Since he possessed such wonders and such radiance, since he possessed such vastness and such omnipresence, why is it that you all still have delusion and enlightenment?
Do you understand? Fortunately, there is no place where illumination is partial; yet, there is still a time when it is not clear.
(Lectan Ming-si) Chan Master Wanan Desheng of Yunju in Nankang was the son of He of Hanzhou. At twenty, he received full ordination.

After studying the lectures on the sutras for a long time, he abandoned them to visit Chan Master Wenshu Dao, seeking the essential points of the Buddha-dharma. Wenshu showed him this verse: "Accord with..."
Dan broke into the Persian camp and seized a precious pearl to sell in the village. At the crossroads, a destitute beggar has a bag of elegance hanging from his waist.
As the Master was about to offer a reply, Shu said, "Do not err. The Master withdrew to reflect for three years before finally grasping the essential meaning.
He went to see Foxing, but their spiritual resonance did not meet; he then traveled to Min Province and paid his respects at Gushan, where he immediately asked about the state of the kingdom.
The Master did not step across the stone gate; what was his intention? Zhuan’an responded with a shout: "Idle talk!
The Master immediately attained realization. A monk asked: "I do not ask about Yingzhen’s transcendence beyond the three realms;
what is the 'true person of no station'? The Master said: "Rich and noble when heard, poor and destitute when seen. The monk said: "If you raise your head, you must cover your ears."
He turned his body with the palms of his hands facing outward. The Master said, "Where is the 'Unranked True Person'?
He replied, "Great Master, you do not even recognize the pivot of the teaching. The Master said, "I grant you thirty blows! (Zhuan’an Gui was his successor).
Chan Master Huiwen of Lu’o Monastery on Langshan Mountain in Tongzhou was a native of Fuzhou. His surname was Zheng. He went to Donglin to study under Zhuan’an;

not long after, when Zhuan’an moved to Qianyuan in Min, the Master went there to visit him. Zhuan’an asked, “When emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed; when conceptualization changes, the essence becomes alienated.
Without lingering to harbor further thoughts, bring me a single phrase of the Way. At this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
He spoke in verse: "Having pressed out [the truth], the whole body is mouth; what prevents one from reviling the rain and scolding the wind?
Last night, a fierce tiger in the village ahead bit to death a great beast on the southern mountain. The abbot nodded in approval. Later, after taking up residence, he ascended the hall and said:
"Śākyamuni the Old One spent forty-nine years plotting behind the curtain; Maitreya the Great Being spent ninety-one kalpas dragging through water and mud. These are but ordinary sentiments..."
The measure of the sages cannot eradicate it; though the principle is illuminated through awakening and knowledge, it still remains as a mere proclamation.

To take the Buddha’s intent and the Patriarchs’ intent for what they are, it is like taking fish eyes for bright pearls; to distinguish between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is like mistaking orange peel for a fierce fire.
All you people must open wide the treasure-store within your own chests, bring forth the precious jewels of your own house, and distribute them universally to the poor at the crossroads.
[The assembly] was lacking [in understanding]. Suddenly, a clever fellow emerged from among the crowd and said, "Fine food does not satisfy one who is already full.
The mountain monk simply said to him, "Ouyang Prefecture is still tolerable; what is most distressing is Silla" (Zhuan’an Gui, the successor of Yifeng Hui, and the aforementioned two).
A monk asked Chan Master Ru of Qingyuan in Jizhou, "What was it like before Bodhidharma had not yet arrived? The Master said, "A cast-iron K'un-lun.
The monk asked, "What is it like after he has arrived? The Master said, "A five-colored painted door-god. (Baiyang Shun succeeded him.)
Chan Master Yuanji Yancen of Taiping Yijing was a native of Taicheng. He ascended the hall and, citing Master Zhengtang Bian, raised the question posed in his inner quarters to his students:
"Why does the earthworm transform into a lily? The Master said: "Ten autumns have passed since I stayed at an inn in Bingzhou;
my heart yearns for Xianyang day and night. Without cause, I have crossed the Sanggan River once more, yet I look back..."
Bingzhou is my hometown (Yunju Rushi).
Chan Master Cheng of Ba’en in Ezhou ascended the hall and said: "The autumn rain has grown cold. You people—have you yet completed your Qingzhou cotton shirts?
After a long silence, he shouted: "Today Yunxi puts a fire in a cold place! Then he descended.
The two aforementioned abbots (Yunju Ru and his successor) descended from their seats.
Zen Master Xishi of Xichan Temple in Suining ascended the hall and said: "Autumn has reached its midpoint; the summer heat is gradually fading.
Wild geese cross the void, piercing the azure sky as clear as water. Monkeys cling to the trees, shaking down jade dew like pearls. Even if one were to..."
Regarding this clear opportunity, one cannot help but mistake a tortoise for a turtle. Now tell me: how would you express the phrase "responding to the time and responding to the season"?
"The wild colors merge with the moon over the Three Isles; The stream’s radiance divides the autumn of the Five Lakes. (Xi Chan Lian, successor)
Chan Master Xiu of Tuan’an at Jianfu Monastery in Rǎozhōu ascended the hall and said: "Is it the wind that moves, or the banner? Is it the wind that sounds, or the bell?

It is neither the wind nor the bell that sounds; it is neither the wind nor the banner that moves. This land and the Western Heaven are but a single team of black-lacquered buckets, deceiving and deluding the people of the world.
Look, look! They are about to extinguish the seeds of the Hu [Buddha]. This mountain monk can do nothing about it; I shall chase after them and beat them!"
Hóng. The gourd-curve is winding. A winter melon meets the *lǒngtòng* (Wūjù xíng sì).
Chan Master Huìguān Hui’ān of Guīfēng in Xìnzhōu, a native of Jiānníng, ascended the hall and said:
"For several days the heat has been like burning; a whole body has nowhere to rest. To contemplate it is also a source of affliction for people. This—[the unconditioned]—is yet..."
This is affliction. Furthermore, if there is anything within one's own person that is not yet clear, that too is affliction.

Therefore, when the Great Master Bodhidharma encountered affliction, he wished to swallow it for the sake of all people, but his throat was too small; he then wished to spit it out for the sake of all people.
Furthermore, it was obstructed by his teeth; he could neither grasp it nor let it go. He suffered for nine years.

Had he not obtained [the Dharma] from the Second Patriarch, who did not spare his own life, there would have been no way for him to turn his body [toward enlightenment]. He suffered to the point of wishing for death, as the saying goes: "If the patriarch and father do not resolve [the matter], the son cannot."
The calamity extends to their descendants. Later, when Master Lianhua arrived here, he was vexed and refused to stay;

when Nanyue Huairang went there, he was vexed and refused to descend the mountain. Furthermore, Linji and Deshan exhausted all their own efforts, yet they were vexed that their alms bowls lacked handles.
Today, Guifeng creates afflictions for them over such trivial matters, causing their ignorance to grow.
I shall break it open for you all from the very beginning. [He strikes the meditation staff once and says:
"One person has his cheek exposed behind the head; another has no teeth at the gate of the mouth; and there are several more whose nostrils are missing half.
No need for further investigation. You all should stop standing here dozing off; you simply do not realize that the rice basket and the cooking pot are right in your own home."
At that time, it was completely lost. If you do not believe this, simply return home and examine it for yourself (Wugu Xing succeeded him).
Chan Master Shouren of Qie’an at Changlu in Zhenzhou was a native of Shangyu in Yue. He relied upon Chan Master Wugu Xing and heard him give a general discourse (*pushe*), which said:
"The way our brothers nowadays apply themselves to practice is just like learning archery; first one must steady one's feet."
Later, he practiced that method. Although he subsequently had no conscious intent, because of his long practice, every arrow he released hit the mark.

He let out a shout and said, "The arrow is being released right now! Look, look! The Master involuntarily leaned his body back, making a gesture of dodging the arrow, and suddenly attained great enlightenment.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Among the hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable wondrous gates, today I shall not spare my very life; I shall simply..."
To speak in a single sentence for you all: [he] stood his staff upright and descended from the seat (Wuji Xing was the successor; the three mentioned above).
Chan Master Wuxiang Fadeng of Jingju Nunnery in Wenzhou ascended the hall, held up her staff, struck it, and said:
"Avalokiteśvara goes out; Samantabhadra enters. Mañjuśrī stands wearing boots upon the water. Lifting her head, the hawk flies over Silla. Like a flash of lightning.
A flash of lightning cannot be pursued. (Jingju Wen’s successor).
Chan Master Xiwen Tanben of Wannian Temple in Taizhou was a native of Yongjia. Having recovered from an illness, he ascended the hall to address the assembly.
When Weimo was ill, he spoke of the ultimate principles. When Longxiang was ill, his coughing would not cease; as his coughing would not cease, he spoke of the ultimate principles;
as he spoke of the ultimate principles, his coughing would not cease. You people—do you still recognize the essential meaning within this?
It was originally the wind and cold from the confluence of the Yangtze River that caused the pillar to suffer from a headwind. (Sicheng Ming)

"Not allowing entry from without, not allowing exit from within—strike one decisive blow and all matters are finished. How is this too much?"

If it were Confucius, I would say: 'I have nothing hidden from you. The Master sat in six monastic seats; he never spoke of his own lineage.

It is said: "At the gate is the shop of Sun Bin; in the home dwells the wife of Gan Zhi. Sleeping at night and rising early—who awakens and who remains lost?
There was one who sold rouge and had long practiced the Flower Garland (Avatamsaka) teachings, yet he was quite conceited.

A gentleman presented him with this verse: "Without applying red powder, you are naturally elegant; Yet often Zen practitioners stop short here. Once you have passed through the snares of past and present, [The verse concludes with a seal or mark. "
"Come here and receive this punch! (Tiantong Hua’s successor).
Professor Yan Kangchao was a layman from Changxing in Huzhou. Having met with Ying’an Hua, he attained the essential meaning. His verse says:
"Zhaozhou said, 'The dog has no Buddha-nature. I say, 'The dog has Buddha-nature. Suddenly, upon these words, one knows for oneself where one belongs;
from this point on, one no longer believes the mouth of Zhaozhou. Exert your spirit and shake yourself free. Following behind others, there are no skillful hands.

To ride a cow while searching for the cow is enough to make people laugh to death. Only now do I realize that what I previously held was erroneous. (Tiantong Hua succeeded Yi; the five mentioned above.)
Chan Master Zhong’an Huikong of Fashi Temple in Quanzhou was the son of the Cai family of Ganzhou.
On the day of the Spring Equinox, he ascended the hall, took up his staff, and struck it once, saying: "First, strike the head of the spring ox. He struck it again, saying:
"Afterward, strike the tail of the spring ox. Startling the void, he enters within a strand of lotus fiber; Śākyamuni has no way to hide his tracks, and Maitreya flees in haste.
"A thousand *li*. Manjusri, however, knew where it landed; he clapped his hands and laughed with joy. But tell me, what was he joyful about?

"Last night the spring wind entered the gate; immediately one sees a thousand flowers blooming upon the pestle. Ascending the hall, [he said]: "A thousand houses of pavilions, a moment of autumn wind.
One only knows that a coolness arises in the sleeves, unaware that the leaves have fallen from the groves. At that time—
"Attaining it through recommendation: at every point of contact, the whole is true. If this is not yet so, for now let us meet with mutual greetings of cold and warmth.
[He ascends the hall. He cites the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "The Buddha told Subhūti:

'In all those lands, whatever sentient beings there may be, with their various kinds of minds, the Tathāgata knows them all. Why is this? The Tathāgata says that all these minds are non-minds; this is called...'"
Mind. Do you understand? "The horse's hooves are swift as it enjoys the spring breeze; in a single day, it views all the flowers of Chang'an.
A monk asked, "The former Buddhas established these precedents for the *kaṭhina* ceremony and the summer retreat (*an-gu*). What is their underlying principle?
The Master said, "Mount Sumeru is placed within a lapis lazuli bowl. The monk then gave a shout. The Master then struck him. (Jiaozhong Guangsi)
Chan Master Lin’an Jingci Húnyuán Tánmì was the son of the Lú family of Tiantái. At the age of sixteen, he received full ordination;

having studied the teachings of the Tiantai school, he abandoned them to travel to Mount Jingshan, where he attended upon Dàhuì Zǔgǎo. He subsequently sought further instruction from the Venerable Jiàozhōng Guāng of Quanzhou.
One day, Daokai recounted the karmic occasion of Xiangyan striking the bamboo. Suddenly, he attained realization and composed a verse to present to Daokai.
Daokai then cited the story of Xuansha’s lack of thoroughness to interrogate him; Daokai was unimpeded. Daokai then instructed him, saying: "You may now go see Miaoxi."

The Master accepted his mission and immediately departed for Mei-yang. He served diligently there for four years. Later, while presiding over the assembly at Jingci Monastery, he ascended the hall and said:

"When the Buddhas appear in the world, they commit robbery and murder. When the Patriarchs come from the West, they blow wind and set fires. The good spiritual friends of past and present have mouths like Buddhas but hearts like snakes;
the monks of the world throw themselves into their cages and traps of their own accord. Is there anyone among this assembly who possesses natural magnanimity and exceptional resolve?"

"Venerable sir, are you one who has extended a hand for the sake of our school to uphold the Buddha-dharma? After a long silence, he said, "Even if there were such a person, they would still have to be cut into three pieces.
[One day] he ascended the hall and cited the kōan concerning Yunmen’s question to a monk: "The luminous, tranquil illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges.
The Master said, "Fishing for shrimp on level ground; shooting a soaring falcon across the vast sky. The lame-legged old Yunmen!"
Regarding the "A Thousand Errors and Ten Thousand Errors" (by Jiao Zhongguang):
Chan Master Weiyin Xianan of Qingyuan in Jizhou was the son of the Li family of Changle, Fuzhou.
At the age of eleven, he left Min Province to become a novice under Master Guang of Xunjiang, who was devoted to Chan practice. After five years, he finally received the full monastic precepts.
Fú served for one day as the attendant to Master Gǎng, who was reciting the "Verses on the Fifty-three Spiritual Friends" from the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra* to the lay official Wáng Gōng.
While Fú stood by his side, he heard the lines: "Sometimes one desires to see the Buddhas of the ten directions; when there is nothing to do, observe idly this single mind.

Upon hearing these words, he immediately grasped the essential point. Gǎng marveled at the sharpness of his faculties and sent him back to Fúmīn to pay his respects to Fóxīn Cáiyán. When he arrived...
The elders Dong Chan Guo and Xi Chan Xu were at that time residing at Gui Shan, where Master Hui-ang was staying; the Master went there to seek instruction.
One night at midnight, while searching for his hand towel, he attained a sudden and profound enlightenment. At dawn, he hurried to the abbot’s quarters to communicate what he had realized.
He presented a verse, saying: "Karmic consciousness is vast and boundless; originally it has no basis. Yesterday at the third watch, I turned my head and took a look.
A single segment of numinous light was revealed from the very beginning. The Master did not notice and nodded his head in approval.

Later, he crossed the ridge and met Wanan Yan at Jianfu Temple in Fanyang. During an entry into the inner chamber, his responses were swift and agile. Yan said in a stern voice, "This [is] fortune..."
Zhouzi was corrupted by the teachings of others, and the entire assembly was struck with astonishment. He then went to Mei-yang to see Da-hui Zonggao.
Gao asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master replied, "Meeting face-to-face; there is no other dharma. Gao asked, "How do you maintain this?
The Master replied, "When hungry, I eat; when tired, I sleep. Subsequently, he accompanied Gao back to the north. Gao...
One day he asked, "Of all those who have entered the room, how many have spoken to the point, and how many have not?
The Master said, "Wen, you simply keep watching. Gao suddenly extended his hand and asked, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? The Master said, "The weather is cold;
please, Master, let me fold up your sleeves. Gao struck him with a bamboo staff and said, "Tell me, was that a reward for you or a punishment?"
The Master then expounded upon several dozen kōans of the Buddhas and patriarchs in verse form and presented them to Daokai. The verse on the World-Honored One’s first birth reads:
"To emerge with one's head already out was a mistake from the start; How much more so to open one's mouth and claim supremacy?
Had he known how to keep his tongue deeply hidden at that time, He would have spared his descendants the burden of idle grief. Daokai struck the rhythm of the verse in admiration. (Xiaoxi 3rd year)
In the year Renzi, on the nineteenth day of the fifth month, he manifested illness. He wrote a verse, saying: "The final phrase is handed over face-to-face;

if you deliberate or reflect upon it, it will merely circulate as worldly convention. Thereupon, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. (Jiaozhong Guangsi and the three aforementioned masters.)
Chan Master Zuzhu Dun’an of Gong’an in Jingzhou was a native of Nanping. He ascended the hall and said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
The drool of the wild fox has been drained dry; the lair of the mountain ghost has been kicked over.
Within the level fields and shallow grass, the tawny-tailed tiger reveals itself; amidst the vast and empty void, the magnificent falcon soars through the heavens. A-ha-ha! It is revealed!"
Wind and Bone. Casually brought forth before the assembly—what exactly is it? *Du du!* Ascending the hall, [Donglin Yan Si] said:
"Jade dew hangs from the green grass; The golden wind stirs the white water lilies. A single cry from a cold wild goose Awakens those who have not yet awakened."
Chan Master Fayuan of Ba’en in Tingzhou was a native of Guozhou. One day, ascending the hall, he cited the karmic conditions regarding Juzhi’s raising of a finger.
The Master said: “The beautiful woman rises from sleep, too lazy to comb her hair; She takes up her golden hairpin and inserts it, and that is enough.
For the most part, it is her natural beauty and bone structure that matter; Even without applying rouge and powder, she remains elegant. (The lineage of Yan of Donglin.)
Chan Master Kengtang Yanchong of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an was the son of the Sheng family of Yuqian. He first studied under several elder masters, including Dayuan of Dagu.
Later, he heard Chan Master Ying’an Yan of Donglin say to the assembly: "In this place of mine, there is nothing else mysterious or wondrous;
there is only wood-shavings soup and iron-nail rice for you to chew at will. The Master secretly rejoiced in these words and went to visit him.
He went to report what he had seen. Yan said, "According to your way of seeing, you are sitting right within the mirror-like awareness.
At this, the Master became indignant and cast away everything he had previously attained all at once.

One day, hearing a monk cite Nanquan’s saying, "People of the present day see this single flower as if it were a dream," he silently reached a realization and said, "Beating the grass is only intended to startle the snake."
She-er (Snake-Ear). The next day, he entered the room. Yan asked, "Where was it that Yantou secretly transmitted his meaning?
The Master said, "Today I have caught this old thief in the act. Yan said, "The life of the Great Master Bodhidharma rests in your hands.

As the Master was about to open his mouth, he was suddenly struck a fist across the chest. He attained great enlightenment immediately; sweat poured down his back, and he nodded his head in agreement.
He said to himself, "When Linji said that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma was not much, how could it have been empty words?
He then composed a verse, saying: "To act for others, one must act to the ultimate; To kill someone, one must see the blood. Deshan and Yantou— Ten thousand miles, a single bar of iron.
Yanran entered the hall. "The World-Honored One preached what is not preaching; Kāśyapa heard what is not hearing. He struck the meditation staff.

He said: "The flowing water and yellow leaves—where do they come from? A cow with a cold crow passes through the distant village. Ascending the hall, he raised the example of Xuefeng showing the assembly:
"The entire earth is this gate of liberation; yet, even if one were to grab them by the hand, they would not enter.
The Master said: "How great is Xuefeng! He has split the talk into two pieces. If the entire earth is this gate of liberation, what need is there to drag them?"
Ascending the hall: To go on in this way exclusively—before the Dharma Hall, the grass is ten feet deep.
To come back in this way exclusively—beneath one’s heels, the mud is three feet deep. Tell me, what is it then? Every third year there is an intercalary month;
the rooster cries at the fifth watch. (Yan Sisi of Donglin)
Chan Master Zhizhe Yu’ān Zhēncí of Wǔzhōu was a native of Tóngchuān. His secular surname was Lǐ. He left the household life and received full ordination.

Later, he traveled to lecture halls and listened to discourses on the *Niyuanjue jing* (Complete Enlightenment Sutra). Upon reaching the passage: "The four elements are each separate; where, then, does this deluded body reside?
Ultimately it has no substance and is truly like an illusion," he attained a profound realization. He composed a verse, saying: "A single bright pearl."
While he was among us, whenever he touched or moved anything, light would emanate and the earth would tremble as he presented it to various lecturers, yet none were able to understand it.
Consequently, he traveled south and stayed at the Yuan Tong Monastery on Mount Lu. At that time, Chan Master Wan’an Yan was serving as the West Hall Attendant;
when he entered the room for instruction with the assembly, he raised the following koan: "A monk asked Yunmen, 'When one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha, what then? Yunmen said, 'Buddha.'"
"This too is a dust-mote. The Master, following the sound, immediately shouted and pointed his finger at his chest, saying, "Even the Buddha is a dust-mote.
Having finished the question and the answer, he turned over directly. "I urge you to drink one more cup of wine; once you have passed the Yang Pass to the west, there will be no old friend left.
Yan nodded deeply. A verse on the Samādhi of Dust-Motes: Rice in the bowl, water in the bucket— A rare treasure from Kunlun.
Sitting at the bottom of the abyss, a single mote of dust ascends and traverses Mount Sumeru. A clear-eyed Persian laughs and snaps his fingers;
as he laughs and snaps his fingers, a pure breeze rises upon the coral branches. (Yan Sisi of Donglin)
Chan Master Shao Yuan of Chengdu’s Zhaojue Monastery ascended the hall and said: "Melting the vases, platters, hairpins, and bracelets into a single gold;

stirring the cream, curd, and clarified butter into a single flavor. Thus, guest and host are in accord, the internal and external are at peace, the five ranks of ruler and subject are all penetrated, and the four kinds of discernment are strung together as one.
To let go is like fine rain falling in mist and the autumn wind blowing briskly. He held up [his whisk].

Abiding, it is utterly empty and void. Who would dare look directly at it with their true eye? Now tell me: is it better to let go for the sake of others, or is it better to hold fast for the sake of others?
At ease, it is just like the arrival of the autumn wind; unintentionally cooling others, yet people cool themselves. (Yan Sisi of Donglin)
The Venerable Jian of Huizhou went to visit Dahui Zonggao at Mount Jing. At that time, Chan Master Wanzhan Yan was serving as the Head Seat (Shouzuo).
One day, while leading the assembly into the inner room for private instruction, Yan asked: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven—no one with clear eyes can count them out.
Try counting them for me. The Master then gave a shout. Yan said, "Seven, six, five, four, three, two, one."
"What do you say to this? Yan struck him as the Master was about to respond, saying, "Do not speak recklessly.
At these words, the Master attained realization and immediately presented a verse: "Do not speak recklessly; my hair stands on end with cold.
I only knew the plum had ripened; I did not realize my nose was stinging. He then offered a verse on the story of Zhaozhou’s "The dog has no Buddha-nature": "Old Zhaozhou..."

Han [Hui] was utterly devoid of countenance; beneath his words, he deviated from the fundamental principle, causing the spirits to wail and the ghosts to weep (the six individuals above, including Yan Siji of Donglin).
Chan Master Mudian An Yong of Gushan, Fuzhou, was the son of the Wu family of Min County.
He became a monk at the age of twenty. Not long thereafter, he visited Lan’an Xu at Yunmen. One day, while entering the inner room for instruction, Xu said: "I do not ask about words that exist..."

He asked a question without speaking. The World-Honored One remained silent for a long while. [Zhaozhou] did not seek to understand from that state of silence; instead, he immediately let out a shout.

The Master (Nanquan) attained realization on the spot and prostrated, saying, "Had it not been for today’s question, how could I have lost this opportunity before my very eyes? Nanquan granted him his approval.
While residing at the rear hall, he took up his staff and said: "Linji’s little page has never spoken directly to my face.
Today, Mudan will put on a full display of feigned ignorance, wishing also for all of you to know that there is something more. He threw down the staff and descended from the seat.
A monk asked, "What is it like when one turns over and stands upside down atop Mount Sumeru? The Master said, "I have never seen the hair-tip star appear."
The monk said, "If that is so, then the torrents will overflow and the mountains will topple. The Master said, "Do not act recklessly. The monk then gave a shout.
The Master said, "The thunder is vast and loud, yet there is not a single drop of rain. (Xichan Xu succeeded him.)
Chan Master Nanya of Longxiang Baitang in Wenzhou ascended the hall and said: "Upon the summit of Mount Rui, beside the Phoenix Pavilion, we rely on each other with a bowl of plain congee;
a hundred ailments cover our heads as we sit in meditation. When the Second Patriarch prostrated three times and sat in his place, it was already too much of a fuss.
Old Dharma, that hairy barbarian, has exhausted his marrow and skin; what a mess! As for the rest..."
"Such a person—what is there to say? When Badang spoke thus, did he avoid the censure of the various quarters? He struck his meditation seat.
It was improper; it merely prolongs the imprisonment and increases the delusions [of those who study Chan] (Xichan Xu’s succession)."
Chan Master Tianwang Zhiqing of Fuzhou ascended the hall. Holding up his whisk, he said: "This thing cannot be covered by heaven, nor can it be supported by earth.
It pervades the world and pervades space; it forms a mass and forms a lump. Reaching this point, where can the Buddhas of the three periods of time search for it?
Where can the Patriarchs of the six generations grasp it? What about the monks of the world?"
Where can one find such a person? Only by attaining realization for oneself and verifying it within may one simultaneously practice both "knocking" and "singing.
Even so, this is not yet the place where a patch-robed monk walks. What, then, is the place where a patch-robed monk walks?
Entering crosswise into the sea of right and wrong, walking freely through the thicket of jackals and tigers. (Xichan Xu Si)
The Master of Anfen Hermitage at Jianmen in Nanjian went to visit Dahuai of Jing Mountain.

While traveling along the riverbank, he looked up at the imperial palace and heard the street patrol shout, "The Minister is coming! At that moment, he attained great enlightenment and composed this verse: "For years this matter has hung upon my breast;
I questioned all quarters, yet my eyes remained unopened. Now, liver and gall are both rent asunder— A single cry across the river!"
When the Court Vice-Minister arrived, [Dongshan] subsequently returned to Xichan. Lanan welcomed him and bestowed upon him the *saṃghāṭī* robe.
Later, he lived as a hermit at Jianmen, where his teachings spread throughout the regions south of the Ling Mountains (the four individuals above, including Xi-chan Xu).
Chan Master Miaofeng of Lingyin in Lin’an was the son of Liu [surname] of Wuxing. His great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, and father had all attained high office.
Although the Master was born amidst silks and fine fabrics, his natural disposition was lofty and pure. At the age of thirteen, he left home and received the tonsure.

Upon seeing a single passage from a sutra or treatise, he immediately grasped its essential meaning. While attending Fozhao Guang at Yunshan, he attained realization through the dialogue concerning the wind and the banner;
Fozhao certified this with a verse containing the lines: "Today I open a single thread for you; cut through the nails and sever the iron to revive our school.
He subsequently traveled through Heng and Xiang, then returned to Mount Lu, where he planted his staff beneath Miaogao Peak and sat facing a wall for ten years.

Scholars honored him as Chan Master Miaofeng. Later, he shared the teaching seat at Nengren in the Yanshan mountains; in his later years, he resided at Lingyin, which was close to the imperial palace.

Although the place was crowded with the constant arrival and departure of carriages and horses, the Master kept his door closed, neither welcoming nor seeing anyone off, even when high officials and nobles arrived.

Some saw him; he was merely indifferent to cold and heat. When the position at Tiantong became vacant, Zheng Qingzhi, who was then holding the helm of state, submitted a formal petition urging the Master to accept the invitation, exhorting him to go.
The Master said, "I am an old monk past my prime; would I still travel by night without rest? He declined and did not go.
At Lingyin, while ascending the hall for the discourse, he raised the case of Yunmen, who, while leading the work party in carrying firewood, threw it down.

Xia Chai-pian said: "The entire Great Canon of Teachings speaks only of this. The great and small Yunmens saw only the sharpness of the chisel’s tip, but did not see the squareness of the chisel’s head.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "Long-standing practitioners of high caliber have eyes that empty the four seas and nostrils that reach the heavens.
They see with intimacy; they speak with intimacy; they act with intimacy; and they employ it with intimacy."
"Disciples, it is simply that you do not recognize this old monk’s staff. Why? To build a mountain nine fathoms high, one must not fail to advance even a single basket of earth.
In the second year of the Duanping era, as the Master was about to pass away, he bathed his body, sat in the lotus posture, and wrote this verse:
"Coming is thus; going is thus. Coming and going are one and the same—a clear breeze across ten thousand miles. Having finished writing, he...

He passed away at the age of eighty-four, with seventy-one years of ordination seniority. Upon cremation, innumerable śarīra relics were obtained, which were interred on the western ridge of Lingyin (by Yuwang Guangsi).
Chan Master Tui Gu Yiyun of Jingci Temple in Lin’an was the son of the Huang family of Fuzhou. In his youth, he studied Confucianism;

after reaching adulthood, he attended the National Academy, where he gained insight through the study of the *Zhongyong*. After shaving his head and receiving full ordination, Fozhao Guang certified his realization.
While presiding over the assembly at Jingci, he ascended the hall and said: "A rushing torrent passes the blade; a swift flame outstrips the wind. The simultaneous act of pecking and striking."
"Ten thousand *li* to Yuezhou—what way is there? It is like a person learning archery: through long practice one becomes skillful.

Yet they fail to realize that even before the bow is drawn, hitting the mark already involves a circuitous detour. Setting aside for a moment Zhaozhou’s act of leaning his staff against Zhunyu, consider this:
when Elder Fu said, "The holy arrow is broken," what was his meaning? [The Master] let out a shout. If...
Do not sleep on the same bed. How could you know that the lining of the quilt is worn through? [The Master] ascends the hall and cites Shou Shan’s holding up a bamboo cane to the assembly, saying:

"To call it a bamboo cane is to offend; not to call it a bamboo cane is to turn one's back. What do you all call it? Ye Xian Sheng stepped forward, snatched the bamboo cane, snapped it into two pieces, threw them down the steps, and said:

[...]"* *(Note: The original text contains an ellipsis indicating an omission. The final line of the cited dialogue is "却曰" (and then said), which typically introduces the Master's subsequent response or a concluding remark.)*
"What is it? Shan said, "Blind. [Xuefeng] was enlightened and immediately prostrated himself. The Master said, "The Linji school has been swept away to its very foundations.
He passed away in the fifth month of the second year of the Kaiming era (1206). (Yuwang Guangs) succeeded him.
Chan Master Jingso Ju Jian of Beijian in Lin’an was a native of the Wang family of Tongchuan. Upon reading the records of Wan’an, he attained awakening.
Later, he studied under Chan Master Fozhao Guang, with whom his spiritual faculties were in accord; he followed him for a very long time.

He subsequently took up residence at Ba’en Guangxiao in Tiantai and later retired to the northern side of Feilai Peak. At that time, Grand Councilor Zhen Xishan served as the Regional Commander of Jiangdong.
This was brought about through the efforts of Donglin Yunju. The Master lay in high repose and would not rise. Later, he was appointed to Jingci by imperial decree. Entering the hall, he said:
"One who recognizes this single thing has all matters completed. A monk who has finished his affairs does not recognize a single character. Even if you were to act in such a way,"
It has not yet been fully brought forth. Where the power of Yu did not reach, the sound of the river flows toward the west. Ascending the hall, he raised the following case:
One day Zhaozhou entered the monks' hall and said, "Thieves! Thieves! Seeing a monk, he grabbed him and said, "The thief is right here! The monk said, "I am not the one.
Zhaozhou pushed him away and said, "It is indeed so, but it is simply that you are unfit to acknowledge it."
The Master said: "Zhaozhou’s gathering was too precarious; his letting go was too hasty. Jingci, however, is not like this: 'A house-thief is difficult to guard against;
the family wealth will surely be lost. [He] struck the meditation staff and said: 'One may only err in seizing, but one must not err in releasing.
[He] offered a verse on the story of the World-Honored One’s first birth: "A single cry of *wa*—then immediately *ta li*. Suddenly emerging, such a great *icchantika*."
In the spring of the *Chunyou* cycle year of Bingwu (1256), while residing at Tuxi Tianqi, he fell ill. He requested a brush and wrote a verse;
on the bottom of the paper, he further inscribed the six characters: "April 1st, take care. On that very day, he passed away as if awakening from sleep.
He was eighty-three years old and had been a monk for sixty-two years. His entire body was interred at the Chang Chan Temple in Yuetang.
Beside the master’s stupa, in accordance with his final instructions, the *Beijian ji* (Collected Works from the Northern Ravine) in nineteen fascicles was circulated in the world (by Yuwang Guangs).
Chan Master Zeweng Ruyan of Jingshan, Lin’an, a native of the Zhou family of Taizhou, ascended the hall and held up his staff.
Jiangshan calls this "a walking staff"; everyone else also calls this "a walking staff. Is there any distinction between the monastic and the lay here?
Though we lean on the same railing, we view the mountain scenery differently. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* Praise says:
Vimalakīrti manifests illness and displays his feigned ignorance; he adds to the full belly of doubts of the people of this age.
Were it not for Mañjuśrī’s personal penetration of him, who would have known of these underlying ailments? (By Yuwang Guangsi)
Chan Master Xingkong Zhiguan of Dongchan Monastery in Fuzhou ascended the hall and said:
Master Guo of Yanguan was once asked by a monk, "What is the Dharmakāya Vairocana? The Master said, "Bring me the pure water pitcher.
When the monk brought the pitcher, the Master said, "Return it to its original place. The monk asked again, and the Master replied, "The ancient Buddhas have long since passed away."
The Master said: "It is difficult for the blind to appreciate the beauty of colors and patterns; it is difficult for the deaf to appreciate sounds.

Since this monk failed to grasp the pivot of the National Teacher’s intent, the National Teacher’s teaching remained merely a hollow display. Yunmen said: "There are no tracks or traces"—this fails to support the National Teacher. Xuedou said:
"Even if one were to point with one hand toward heaven and point with the other hand toward the earth, how could that possibly support him? It would not support him.
The National Teacher did not rise; instead, he drew a single line with his whisk, severing all the preceding complications at once.
Now tell me, what is the Dharmakāya Vairocana? [He] threw down the whisk and descended from the seat. (Yuwang Guangs)
Chan Master Yixian, "Master Pugu," of Shangfang Temple in Huzhou ascended the hall. He cited the case where a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature?
Zhaozhou replied, "No. The Master offered this verse: "A dog has no Buddha-nature; This is the mark of a true man.
Though right and wrong enter his ears, A gourd hangs upon the wall. He then offered a eulogy for the image of Bodhidharma: "A single word—"

Once it has left, four horses cannot overtake it; thank heaven the Sovereign King let him go. Sailing across the heart of the Yangtze River with a reed for an oar—how does the crest of the wave compare to the peril of this question? (Yuwang Guangsì)
Chan Master Tien-niu Yin of Lingyin in Lin’an ascended the hall and said: He cited Nanquan’s address to the assembly, which said:
"Since I was young, I have raised a water buffalo. If I intend to let it loose to the east of the stream, it will inevitably eat the king’s water and grass;
if I let it loose to the west of the stream, it will likewise inevitably eat the king’s water and grass. It is better, therefore, to accept things as they are."
"Not so. In total, it is not to be seen. The verse says: "It is better to accept a little bit as it is; To call it an ordinary matter is already a mistake.
On the bank of the green grass stream, the horns are revealed; In the misty rain of a single straw cloak, to whose family does it belong? (Yuwang Guangsi)
Chan Master Kongsou Zongyin of Yuwang Monastery during the Qingyuan era was a native of Western Sichuan. He ascended the hall and said:

"Seizing the tiger’s head and grasping its tail—under the first phrase, the fundamental principle is clarified. Even if the fundamental principle were clarified under that phrase, what has been brought forth would still fall short by a hundred thousand miles.
Why? Because the Patriarch Dahui here hangs a goat's head while selling dog meat; so too did the Elder Fozhao."

Here, one who has assumed a borrowed name cultivates the fields of the state. A minor bhikṣu comes and sits, cutting off the lingering dust. How, in the end, shall he be established? [The Master] raises his staff:
"In my whole life I have possessed nothing; there is only this single branch of rattan. [Ascending the hall: "The Great Way is level and expansive;
it is free from names and free from forms. To weed it out is to lose its essential meaning; to establish it is to deviate from its source. Thus have been the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past."

The masters of the past and present have manifested great capacity and displayed great function; yet all of them were merely closing off the void and locking away dreams, their transgressions filling the heavens.
Did the Venerable Yin manage to avoid this by tearing his own face-skin? After a long silence, he struck the meditation seat and said:
"If one does not enter the waves that startle the world, it is difficult to encounter the fish that satisfies one's heart. (Yuwang Guangsi)
Master Xiu Yan Shuiren of Yuwang Monastery in Qingyuan ascended the hall and said: He cited Master Daowu, who said: "Exaltedness does not lie at the summit;
wealth does not lie at Fuyan; joy does not lie in heaven; suffering does not lie in hell.
Acquaintances fill the world, but how many can truly know one's heart? Master Dahui said: "Exaltedness lies at the summit; wealth lies at Fuyan..."
Yan: "Joy lies in heaven; suffering lies in hell. Who knows that beneath the straw hat is none other than the person of old?

"Assembly, it is not that these two great elders lacked the ability to apply themselves according to the capacities of others. However, as for the gate of the patch-robed monks (*śramaṇa*), they have not even dreamed of it.
But tell me, how is it within the gate of the patch-robed monks? After a long silence, he said: "If one is not a true knower, all labor is in vain."

On the occasion of the "Discourse on the Cold Season," he ascended the hall. He cited the case of Guankui’s study under Linji: when Linji seized him by the collar, Guankui said, “I understand, I understand.
Linji then let go. The Master offered this verse: After the rain has scattered and the clouds have cleared, Lofty peaks rise in their dozens.

Leaning on the railing, gazing again and again— To whom can I turn my head and share this view? On another occasion, he ascended the hall. He cited the case where the Great Master Huayan asked Baoci: “As for...”
"What is the Buddha-nature of True Suchness? Ci said, "Who does not have it? Huihua did not understand. He then requested further instruction from Huguo. Huguo said, "Who has it?
The Master said, "To say 'who has it' or 'who does not have it' is the total functioning of the Way. To turn one's body at these words is not clever enough;
even if you claim to act before the words are raised, you are mistaking a winnowing basket for an ironing board. A-he-he! If a person can understand this for themselves..."
Riding a donkey, one does not follow after others for a lifetime (Yuwang Guangsuo).
Chan Master Wujie Liaopai of Tiantong during the Qingyuan era ascended the hall and said: "Three and five, fifteen; the full moon faces the door."
Although it pervades the earth and fills the heavens, it nonetheless reveals not even a hair’s breadth. Facing the scenery, who can speak of this mind?

It makes one recall the son of Hanshan. Ascending the hall, he said: "In the twelve periods of the day, as you come and go, turn and pivot, bow and stoop, and exchange greetings, you cannot deceive Chong'en by even a single point. Right now, as you sit and stand with solemn composure—"
Host and guest intersect; face to face, they gaze at one another. Even Chong'en cannot deceive anyone by even a single point.
Since neither side deceives the other, why do you create obstacles for yourselves? (He lets out a shout. It is like fanning the fire with the wind;
not much effort is required. Ascending the hall, [he said]: "The Old Śākyamuni, from the past until this very day, has entered the Great Samādhi of Stillness. How laughable!"
Throughout the monastic forests of the world for over two thousand years, people have been like those who carve a mark on a boat to seek a lost sword;
they have labored in vain without ceasing. Today, Chong’en, without moving a single faculty of his divine mechanism, has twisted the nostrils of Gautama.

This was not intended to "strike the grass to startle the snake," but simply so that everyone may see one another. You all should each observe carefully; do not let this opportunity pass. He then joined his palms and said:
I am deeply perplexed, deeply perplexed (Yuwang Guangsì).
Chan Master Hai-men Shiqi of Tiantong during the Qingyuan era used to recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* orally.

When he visited the various halls to burn incense and returned to his quarters, he had already completed the entire scripture. He then went to the incense burner to inform the assembly, but none of them believed him. The Master then ordered—

There were eighty-one people, each holding a single scroll. When the Master ascended the seat and finished reciting one scroll, each of the eighty-one people heard him reciting the very scripture they themselves held.
Only then did they realize that the Master was an incarnation of the Bodhisattva Avataṃsaka appearing in the world (as recorded by Yǔwáng Guāngsì).
Chan Master Fanzong of Shu’an at Yunju in Jiangzhou ascended the hall. He cited the story of Baizhang and the Wild Fox and offered this verse:
Baizhang’s wild fox, The stone maiden has no husband. Once a tear falls, The vast ocean dries up. Ascending the hall for the Buddha-Bath ceremony, he said:
"How joyful it is that today the Sole Honored One has descended. At Shu’an, there is nothing to celebrate his birthday; we simply take this moment of fragrance—"
The morning dew washes the pure Dharma-body of the lake and mountains clear (Yuwang Guansu).
Master Guyun Quan of Yuwang Monastery, during the Qingyuan era, ascended the hall and said: He cited a monk who asked Xuefeng, "What is it like when the cold spring water flows in the ancient ravine?
Feng replied, "Staring with wide-open eyes, one cannot see the bottom. The monk asked, "And as for those who drink from it? Feng replied, "Not from..."

[The monk] entered. Again he asked Zhaozhou, "How is it when the cold spring water flows in the ancient ravine? Zhaozhou said, "Bitter. The monk said, "What of those who drink from it? Zhaozhou said, "Dead.
The Master [Zhao’an] said, "One person follows the waves; another cuts off the flow of all streams. Examining them closely, both are lacking in realization.
Today, if someone asks me at Yuyang, 'How is it when the cold spring water flows in the ancient ravine?'"
He replied only to him: "One must personally see Xuefeng. As for 'drinking,' ask Zhaozhou (Yuwang Guangsi). Chan Master Shiguan Zhengfan received the Dharma from Yuwang;
later, he returned to the shores of Lake Hong. He spoke this verse: "Birds do not startle in flight, the waters do not flow;
The azure abyss is vast and empty, coldly containing autumn. Upon the tip of a single thread there is no fragrant bait; The wind rolls [the line]..."
Reeds Falling, Flowers on the Fishing Boat (Yuwang Guangsi et al., fourteen people in total).
Zen Master Zongdai of Gushan in Fuzhou ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One said: 'One should know thus; one should see thus.'"
Understanding it thus, one does not give rise to the notion of dharmas. (He lets out a shout. "Jade is originally without flaw, yet it has flaws.
(This is the successor of Dongchan Yue. Chan Master Deqin of Jingshan in Lin’an, whose style name was Yuanan, was a native of Xinghua.
When he first took up residence at Jingshan, he reached the mountain gate, snapped his fingers once, and entered. (He is a successor of Dongchan Yue.)
Chan Master Zhishi of Shigan on Mount Gu at Fuzhou was asked by a monk: "Severing the clouds and mountains, the matter is already manifest;
alas, the wandering monks are lost in a vast expanse. Today, a single thread passes through the Stone Gate; he stands upright, wearing his brocade robes, and returns home."

"How do you sing the 'Song of Returning Home'? The Master said, "Rarely does one meet a true connoisseur. [The monk] asked, "As for that single phrase regarding not yet having stepped through the Stone Gate, how would you speak it?
The Master said, "In a hundred pieces. [The monk] asked, "And once one has already stepped through the Stone Gate, what then?
The Master said, "It remains, as before, a whole entity. [The monk] said, "It reaches the point where even the Great Peak nods its head, and Mount Guishan’s Lizi Peak..."

[The ground] shook. The Master said, "This is not beyond what is expected. [Yunmen] said, "Just now, National Teacher Yan clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, 'Fortunately, I have met the Master.
The Master said, "If you are not an old enemy, you will not meet head-to-head. The monk bowed. The Master said, "I grant you thirty blows.
[Later,] he ascended the hall for formal instruction. He said, "Speech is slander; silence is deception. Neither speech nor..."
He did not remain silent; his false fabrications increased further. With a shout, he cried: "The spring breeze blows down the peach and plum blossoms;
thin mist and scattered rain enshroud the green peaks. (The three masters above were successors of Dongchan.)
Chan Master Xiaoweng Miaokan of Yuwang Temple in Qingyuan was the son of the Mao family of Cixi. He studied under Chan Master Wuyong Quan at Tiantong.
Wuyong asked him, "Are you a wandering monk, or are you a mountain-roaming monk? The Master replied, "A wandering monk. Wuyong said:
"What is the matter of traveling on foot? The Master struck him with his sitting mat. Quan said, "This monk dares to come here to pull at the tiger's whiskers.
He then sent him to attend the hall. In the meditation hall, the Master constantly used the koan "The dog has no Buddha-nature" for instruction.
One day, as soon as the Master was about to open his mouth, Quan split his face with a bamboo staff. The Master responded with a verse, saying: Great...
The drum smeared with lethal poison roars through heaven and shakes the earth; it turns one’s brain and head, casting corpses ten thousand *li* away.

[The Master] accepted this in full. He immediately ordered his attendant to prepare incense. Shortly thereafter, Master Yue arrived to repay his kindness. He requested that the Master share the seat with him.

Provincial Governor Cheng invited him to reside at Miaosheng Monastery. Not long after, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Lingyin. Prince Wei, because of his great compassion and perfection, requested the Master to be the founding abbot (*kaishan*). And...
The King passed away. The Master was dwelling in a hermitage atop the cypress trees. Lord Chen, the Prefect of Taizhou, invited him to Ruiyan; before long, a summons from Jiangxin arrived.
Under the persistent pressure of Director Shi, he finally consented to rise. When the imperial decree for Jingci arrived, he requested leave to decline, but it was not granted.
A letter arrived from Grand Councilor Yu Gong, stating that one must not repeatedly disobey the sovereign’s command.

The following year, the Commissioner for Jinghu submitted a memorial requesting that monks and Daoists purchase purple robes and clerical titles, and that those holding such titles be permitted to serve as abbots. The Master [Daoyuan] considered this and thought:

"If this were allowed, then even the sons of wealthy families possessing thousands of gold pieces could preside over the Dharma; our Way would surely be in peril. He consequently submitted a memorial at the imperial court and presented a petition to the government ministers. His...

The proposal was subsequently shelved. By imperial decree, he was summoned to move to Tiantong, but he declined resolutely. He returned east to Cuoyan, where he built a dwelling to maintain the ancestral offerings.

When the seat at Yuyang became vacant, there was another edict to raise him up; he declined a second time, but being not permitted, he finally accepted the decree. Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly:
The dews fall in season; the rivers and mountains are as if washed clean. Solitary birds call from the lofty trees; the remaining petals drift with the flowing water.
How pitiable are those who are blind, deaf, and mute—they do not recognize the true essence of this teaching. [Postscript: Later, the imperial appointment letter arrived again from Tiantong.
Grand Councilor Zhao invited him again to preside over Jingci Temple, but he declined all such offers. Manifesting illness, he wrote his final memorial.

He then composed a letter to Zhang Gong, the Director of the Imperial Household, requesting that Zhang oversee his funeral affairs. When Cao Gong, the Regional Inspector of Yongjia, came to inquire after his health, they spoke at ease regarding their long-standing family ties.
After some time, [the Master] wrote this verse: "The mirror of karma hangs high; seventy-two years have passed. With one blow it is shattered: the Great Way."
He was composed; he set down his brush and passed away with serene stillness (according to Tiantong Quan’s record).
Master Shiguo Xiyi of Lingyin Temple in Lin’an ascended the hall and, citing the public case of the meeting between Langye Huijue and Fahua Ju, offered this verse:
"Hearing the name is not as good as seeing the face; Seeing the face is not as good as hearing the name. In this place there is no..."
Two taels of gold. A layperson purchased three *sheng* of wine. [The Master] ascended the hall. He cited Nanquan, who said:
"Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, last night at the third watch, gave rise to views of Buddha and views of Dharma; I give each of them thirty blows and expel them from the monastery.
Zhaozhou asked: "Whom does the Master’s staff intend for to eat? Nanquan said: "Tell me, where does Old Wang’s fault lie?"
[Zhaozhou] bowed and departed from his place. The verse says: The spring breeze blows down the emerald peach blossoms;
A single petal flows past a hundred thousand households. Who is at the painted tower where wine is bought? Inviting one another to come drink Zhaozhou’s tea. (Tiantong Quanji)
Chan Master Si Zhuo of Mount Pan in Youzhou ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he said: "Climbing mountains and wading through waters entirely depends on this man.
He threw down the staff and said: "It is easy to meet with one another; it is difficult to dwell together as a person.
Ascending the hall again, he said: "Silent yet alert is a dead man with breath; alert yet silent is a useless block of stone. Hehe! A cool breeze for carrying down."
Transmitted to Shui (Tiantong Quanji).

On the occasion of the Dharma assembly at Nan Chan Temple, Master Yebun of Xuedou during the Qingyuan era ascended the hall and said: "Though one seeks with every possible means, one will never see his face."
For a time, he paused. Wherever one encounters him, on the long continuous bed, he eats porridge and rice, taking satisfaction as his goal.

Now I ask you: how many times has a single grain of rice from the monastery treasury passed through his hands? Ascending the hall, he spoke with words that cut like nails and iron; truly eccentric and unconventional.
Leveling the high by following the low—this is the laughingstock of the monks. When Huangjue reached this point, there was no logic to be found.
I do not yet understand how you gentlemen would explain this (according to Tiantong Quanji).
Chan Master Liaozong of Xuefeng’s Mettang Hall in Fuzhou ascended the hall and said: "Empty and desolate; cold and ice-cold.
The principle of pure emptiness ultimately has no body. Why, then, are there so many mists and rains? Do you understand? If you understand..."
It is attained. There are seven kinds of offerings for all people; if one does not attain this in assembly, even a drop of water will be difficult to digest (as recorded by Tiantong Quan Si).

When the layman Qian Xiangzu, the State Councilor, was first governing Jinling, he once visited Baoning Temple to seek the Way from Master Wuyong Quan, through whom he attained a point of realization.
Later, in his hometown, he established ten guest-houses, all of which were dedicated to the Pure Land.

He named his dwelling "Le-yue" (Pleasure-Name) and established a hermitage as a place of rest. Since the Left Prime Minister resigned and returned home, he had diligently cultivated the Pure Land practice.
In the second intercalary month of the second year of the Jiading era, he contracted a slight illness. When anyone came to inquire after his health, he would say:
"I do not crave life, nor do I fear death. I shall not be reborn in the heavens, nor among humans; I shall only be reborn in the Pure Land. Thus he spoke.
[He] passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture (the above six masters were all successors of Tiantong Quan).
Master Qianyuan Zongying of Linzhou ascended the hall and, striking his staff, said: "A man of impatient temperament—there is nothing more than this single blow."
"Relying on the staff. A clever person does not need to be told again. Is there anyone clever here now? After a long silence, he said:
"To compare oneself to a mythical unicorn is to miss it even when it is avoided. (Xichan Jing was his successor.)
After Chan Master Biefeng Yun of Xinghua was certified by Xicuan, he first resided at Zhitu in Fuzhou, and later moved to Huayan in Fuquan.
He ascended the hall and said: "A thousand kinds of words and ten thousand modes of explanation are intended only to ensure that you remain forever undeluded.
But tell me, what is it that you do not delude? To call it a 'bamboo stick' is to offend it; not to call it a 'bamboo stick' is to turn your back on it."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Maitreya Bodhisattva entered the monastery in the morning and attained perfect enlightenment by evening.
If everyone were as dull-witted as he, what use would there be? Even if you could see Mount Zhidi and the Twin Peaks from across the mountains, you should still turn back immediately;
otherwise, I shall give you thirty blows right between your heels. (This was the successor of Xichan Jing.)
Chan Master Zhongji Wushan Licai of Fuzhou ascended the hall. He raised the story of Venerable Zhaozhou’s “Go drink tea” and offered this verse:
Zhaozhou meets people and offers them tea; Who would have known that when matters are urgent, one must leave the household?
He turns his hand to create clouds and rain, And with the wind, scatters earth and sand. This drew forth Dongshan, who lacked wisdom, Asking about the Buddha, to which he replied, "Three catties."
Ma ○ read this verse from the *Aṇa-yulu*: "A Persian from the South Sea holds secret mantras; Of thousands of words and myriad phrases, few people know them.
A spring breeze comes from nowhere; It blows down three or four branches of peach blossoms. (Xichan Jing and the three mentioned above).
Chan Master Huiqing of Yueku at He Mountain in Huzhou ascended the hall and spoke. He cited the story of National Teacher Yao of Tiantai’s first meeting with Fayan.
A monk had asked Fayan, "What is a single drop of water from the Cao source? Fayan replied, "It is a single drop of water from the Cao source.
Upon hearing this, Yao attained sudden enlightenment. His verse says: "A single drop of water from the Cao source— Even when scolding one another, it is still a connection."
[This bundle]. The quail, in its emptiness, chirps and squeaks; the steed Huaxiu has already traveled a thousand li (Huazang Yansi).

Dao-ren Wu Shisan of Mount Xianzhou in Jianning frequently sought instruction regarding his own spiritual practice from various masters of Chan, yet he remained utterly bewildered and found no way in.
Upon meeting Kainsan Jian, he attained the Dharma. Thereafter, he built a thatched hut to the left of the mountain and went to serve him.
On the eighth night of the third month in the Gengshen year of the Xiangxing era, [Zhao Mengfu] attained sudden enlightenment. He presented this verse: "Originally there were no seams or cracks;
Upon being touched, it immediately shines with brilliance. Since it is a treasure worth a thousand pieces of gold, Why need one use it to shoot at a sparrow? Shanda replied: "Excellent!"
At the moment of the "spit-down" breaking [of the staff], there is true joy and liberation; birth and death, ordinary and sage, all sink into equality.
Under Mount Xianzhou, he laughs aloud: "I have not betrayed the heart we pledged long ago. (Kaisan Ken’s Succession)
The layman Yan Bing asked about a monk’s citation of Nanquan’s story regarding the novice with a master.
The layman answered with a verse, saying: "Capable of grasping a single blade of thatch grass, And calling it the sixteen-foot golden body;
If one understands that every point is the Way, Then the pupil in the eye is the person before you. He then offered a verse on the story of Zihu’s dog, saying: "In my poor home, there is nothing..."
There was one who kept only a single dog; even if a Buddha were to appear, he would surely meet with a bite from it (Xuefeng Yan’s lineage).
Chan Master Miaozhi Congkuo of Yuyang Monastery in Mingzhou was the son of the Lin family of Changxi in Min.

From his youth, he was exceptionally brilliant and took delight in hearing the teachings of world-transcendence. At fifteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination. At that time, there were many men of the Way in Min.

He went to follow and study under them all. Later, he relied upon Dayuan (Dawen). Dayuan’s teaching style was solitary and austere; at first, [Zongxiao] encountered difficulties. After a long time, he attained a sudden and profound realization.
He served diligently for several years, until Dayuan took him under his wing, regarding him as his own equal. Subsequently, he emerged into the world to serve as the abbot of Yuyuang Monastery.
Emperor Xiaozong issued an edict for the śarīra to enter the imperial palace for veneration. Having personally witnessed its extraordinary excellence, he summoned the Master to the Bilin Hall.
The Emperor asked from where the śarīra had manifested, and the Master replied, "It has manifested from Your Majesty’s sacred mind. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
In his later years, the Master built a hermitage at Wushan, where he closed his door and withdrew from worldly contact. He passed away after manifesting slight illness. (Yuwang)
Puo was his successor.
Chan Master Xianan Daguan of Tiantong during the Qingyuan era was the son of the Zhao family of Yiwu. Initially, he studied under Ying’an;
next, he visited Wuan at Daochang; and later, within the quarters of Shui’an at Jingci, he attained realization through the teachings bequeathed by these two elders.
[He was] at Shouchu. With a single phrase he struck the mark and returned. Later, while serving as the First Seat at Longxiang’s Baitang, he successively held four monasteries.
By imperial decree, he was promoted to Lingyin. Ascending the hall, he cited the koan of the Second Patriarch asking Bodhidharma for peace of mind, and offered this verse:
"The night in Chang'an is deep and the snow falls thick; Seeking peace of mind, one becomes even more unsettled. Even if one could open it before a word..."
A living eye! How could he have known he had already been deceived by the Old Barbarian? (Jingci’s first successor).
Chan Master Jian’an of Qing, a successor of Yangshan of Yuanzhou, ascended the hall and said:
He cited the occasion when Great Master Bodhidharma one day said to his disciples, "The time has come; you should each speak of what you have attained. Finally, Huike stepped forward.
He performed three prostrations and stood in his place. Moxi said, "You have attained my marrow. The Master spoke in verse: "Rubbing one's eyes produces flowers; you stand there posing a question.
You have obtained his skin and marrow, yet you are deceived by him. A blind fellow like this can only cause trouble;
In the sixth month there is no frost, yet you say it is cold. (These two are the first successors of Jingci.)
Chan Master I’an Youquan of Huazang in Changzhou was the son of the Qi family of Qihua in Lin’an.
He received the full precepts at the age of fourteen and, at eighteen, went to pay his respects to Fozhi Yu at Lingyin Monastery. At that time, Wuan Quan was serving as the First Seat;
in the meditation hall, he questioned [Youquan] regarding the principle of "establishing all dharmas from the groundless root. After a long period, the Master attained realization.
The Master replied, "It is like threading a needle in the dark or blowing air through one's ears. Anke approved of this and secretly transmitted the mind-seal to him.

Once, while sitting in meditation until dawn, the Master forgot to spread out his alms bowl when the粥 (congee) server arrived. A neighboring monk touched it with his hand, whereupon the Master was awakened to realization.
He spoke a verse, saying: "A pitch-black K'un-lun man holds a fishing rod; The ancient sail is hoisted high as he descends the turbulent rapids. Amidst the shadows of the reeds..."

He played with the bright moon, drawing the blind turtle onto the fishing boat. Once, Fozhi asked him, "What is it like when the mind encompasses the vast void and its measure spans the boundless realms?
The Master replied, "The great ocean does not harbor dead corpses. Fozhi patted his seat and said, "This son shall one day occupy this very seat;
he will go on to revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs. The Master then became even more reclusive and concealed himself. He was seen again...
Ying’ān Huá studied at Guīzōng; Dàhuì Gǎo studied under him at Jìngshān. Later, when Chan Master Wú’ān Quán resided at Dàochǎng, he appointed the Master to share his seat.
**Ascending the Hall:** "Today, the mouth of the sack is tied shut. You clear-eyed monks, do not wander aimlessly.
When the movements of the mind cease, one can turn the body around; even a sneeze becomes the lion’s roar. In a sandalwood grove..."

Qingsheng Ruayan Jingmeng Chan Master was the son of the Shao family of Pingyang. At the age of thirteen, he shaved his head and studied the Tiantai teachings;

"A single shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function act simultaneously. "How does a single shout distinguish guest and host?

Among the works produced during his tenure, he completely excised the five generations following *Chuan-deng* (Transmission of the Lamp): Dan-xia, Zhen-xie, Zong-ju, Zu-an, and Ru-jing. However, since the *Chuan-deng* had already been included in the canon for a long time, [he] pointed to...

The work by Yue Cheng has circulated widely in the world. For many years, the editions of the *Dongzong Xudeng* (Continued Lamp of the Caodong School) and the various *Nian-song* (Verses on Cases) he compiled have been transmitted from generation to generation without any alteration or deletion.

Suddenly, however, a monk from Beizhi named Ta brought a "Stupa Record" from Qingzhou, which abruptly overturned the established records. It claimed that Tian Tong Jing’s successor, Lu Men Jue, was actually Jing Yin Jue, who had been a disciple of Fu Rong Kai. Now, it is well known within the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps) that Jing Yin succeeded Fu Rong;

his recorded sermons and dharma-words bear no relation whatsoever to those of Lu Men. To conflate these two individuals into one is an error for which I know of no basis. This has thrown the chronological succession of the lineage into disorder. I deplore this deeply. Recently, having read Master Gushan Pei’s treatise *Bianmiu* (Discerning Errors), I learned that the Qingzhou stupa record upon which Yue Cheng relied...

There are three points that mark this as a forgery. First, since this record of the stupa is a self-narrative, why is it so brief regarding the circumstances of his seeking the Way while being so detailed concerning his places of residence? As for the dates, they serve no other purpose than to provide a basis for his polemical arguments; this is merely its strength. This is the first point of forgery.

Furthermore, in recounting the origins of how he received the Dharma, he directly addresses his own master, his teacher’s teacher, and his teacher’s senior by their names, saying: "During the Zhenghe era, I studied under Zizhao of Lumen in Xiangzhou; Zhao sent me to see Furong Daokai."

While traveling through Dengzhou, he visited the site where Danxia Chun once stayed. These few words are the oral style used by elder masters and great monks when composing biographies for later generations; they could never be words of self-narration. They serve merely as a prelude to explain how Fuyong and Danxia changed Lukuan into Jingyin Monastery.

This is its second falsehood. Furthermore, regarding the account of his passing, it states: "On the eighth day of the twelfth month in the ninth year of Huangtong, he personally wrote the inscription for his stupa; at the hour of Hai on the twelfth day, he passed away. One must ask:

were these words written in advance before he died, or were they recorded again after he had already passed? This is its third falsehood. Since there are these three falsehoods, one who wishes to rely on them to prune the lineage of the five preceding generations and to borrow [their authority] for their own position—[is this not absurd?]

To deceive others while being unaware that one is, in fact, deceiving oneself. For drafting and polishing texts on behalf of others was a common practice during his tenure in office. For instance, he fabricated an entire set of *gong'an* (public cases) based on the "Opportunity for Discernment" from Qingzhou, and he interpolated the discourse on the ascent to the hall by Jue of Lukuan into the *Zhengyin-chapter*.

How could one know that he would not have altered the "Epitaph for the Pagoda"? If the epitaph were indeed composed of such fabrications, then even this record would be unworthy of trust; how much more so, then, his erroneous writings?
This compilation follows the chronological order established by the *Dīpamālā* (Lamp Succession) and the *Candrasūcaka* (Moon-Pointer), with no errors or discrepancies. May readers take note of this!
