[The monk] asked, "This refers to matters of the present; what about matters of the other side? The Master said, "Wait until you have exhausted the present, and I shall tell you.
[One day] he ascended the hall and said, "If one discusses this matter, it is like a person doing needlework—every stitch..."
It was just like this: suddenly seeing someone approach, he unconsciously lost his needle; he saw only the thread. He searched here and could not find it;
he searched there and could not find it. Then he said to himself, "If I cannot find it even nearby, how could it have come from afar?"
For a long time he searched but could not find it; his mind grew vexed and uneasy, and in a state of drowsy confusion, he pulled at his robes to go to sleep.

Just as he was settling onto his pillow, suddenly there was a sharp prick, and he said: "So, it has been right here all along! (Nan’an’s verse says: Through smoke and water across a hundred cities, he wandered in suffering;

though the gates of the pavilions were open, none would let him through. Only Sudhana saw for himself that Deven was not atop Mount Miaogao. [The Verse of Weizhong says: Out of pity for the bright pearl, how many times did he exhaust his compassionate heart amidst heaps of refuse! The brilliant light is stirred by those who seek it.)
To seize the dragon’s abode, there is no need to spend effort opening it. The Verses on the Five Ranks say: **Center within Deviation:** The moon locks within the deep palace before midnight.

Candles and incense fade as people fall silent; the vermilion steps grow cold. A single expanse of empty luminosity shines upon the azure sky. **Deviation within Center:** At dawn, the mirror of the Qin Terrace hangs not in the heavens.
The golden crow (the sun) has only just begun to emerge from Fusang; It is still faintly veiled by light mist. **Center**...
Coming from within: In the deep night, the cold plum blossoms amidst the snow. Its fragrant scent is unceasing; at every point of contact, there is not a speck of dust.
Reaching through both simultaneously: The great function is fully manifest without inhibition. Hand in hand, we proceed to celebrate peace; the scenery is joyous, forever extraordinary.
Arriving through both simultaneously: The subtle perfection transcends effort; it is not merely a clever artifice. The withered...
The wooden dragon roars, and spring fills the great earth; the numinous root emerges in splendor from the weeds of the cold crags (Puzhao).
Master Jue Chan, the Ten-Body Compassionate Cloud, appointed Puzhao as the senior monk (*upādhyāya*) within his quarters.

Bian posed one hundred questions to test the practitioners, yet at that time few were able to harmonize with the teaching. Only the Master’s responses were like water and milk blending together; I shall briefly cite seven of them.

Thus, one may see its general outline. A question was asked: "If realizing it before the sound falls into the present moment, and taking responsibility after the phrase is to mistake one's head for a reflection, what is the self prior to the empty eon? The Master said: "At midnight, the stone man has no shadow;
who can discern the source of their coming and going? A question was asked: "Not seeing a single dharma is still only half."
[The student] asked, "What is the principle of 'total presentation'? The Master said, "A stone horse gallops across a thousand mountains.
[The student] asked, "When eating one forgets hunger; when exerting effort one forgets satiety. Who is this person who exerts effort? The Master said:
The Great Spirit raised his hand but a little; he split apart the myriad layers of Mount Hua. A questioner asked:
"Even one who does not come in such a manner is still a matter for the descendants [of the patriarchs]. What is the person who goes beyond? The Master said:

"At midnight, a black chicken cries out in the snow. A questioner asked: "To practice the profound and embody the subtle falls into the present moment. To investigate principle and exhaust the source—"
"Ten thousand miles of mountains and passes—this is like one who does not yet know that [the Way] exists. How should such a person proceed? The Master said:
"The bed is narrow; lie down first. [The student] asked: "When lost, ten thousand scrolls are too few; after awakening, a single word is too much. Now tell me, what of the person who has awakened?"
"How does one practice? The Master said: "To go out, do not pass through the door; to sit, do not occupy the hall. A questioner asked:
"If you wish to stop at the bank, you must first pull in your oars; if a cart will not move, you must strike the ox. Now that you have struck the ox, has the cart moved yet?"
The Master said: "Who shall be entrusted with this boat that carries off the pure breeze?
(From the lineage of Puzhao Bian). Chan Master Tongxuan Yuan of Yuxi once composed the *Hundred Questions* to inspire his disciples. A summary of it says:
"Why is the bottomless boatman without outflows and firmly established? Raising his whisk, he said: "I have finished speaking the Dharma for you."
"How do you understand this? He then picked up his staff and said, "Is there anyone who can utter a turning word upon the tip of this staff?
He then drew a circle and said, "The Buddhas of the three periods and the six generations of patriarchs are all contained within this.
How do you understand this? Finally, he pointed a finger in the air and said, "Tell me, what about this one dot?"
He pointed and asked, "What matter does this clarify? He then held up a finger and said, "The monk Jueyi lets forth a great radiance and turns the Great Dharma Wheel right here.
Do you all see it? He further said, "A broken-legged cauldron is his livelihood."
Making a life out of the "pierced-heart bowl," he sits at ease within Tongxuan Hermitage. He pays no mind to the affairs before the mountain that are as numerous as hemp stalks.
But tell me, who is it that sits so at ease? (Puzhao Bian’s successor).
Chan Master Bao of Puzhao in Zhengzhou was the son of the Wu family of Cizhou. While he was building Yangshan Temple in Fuyang, someone suddenly inscribed a poem upon a pillar that read:
"People say the turtledove is clumsy; I say the turtledove is clever. With one or two pieces of firewood, one’s worldly affairs are complete.
Upon seeing this, the Master attained great enlightenment. He immediately retired to the Western Mountains, where he built a thatched hut to dwell.
He traveled extensively to visit various mountains before finally entering the chamber of Qingzhou. Later, he resided at Baoyan Temple in Hongyu.
One night, during a great wind that shook the earth, he passed away while sitting in meditative composure (these four, including Puzhao and Bian, were his successors).
Chan Master Wuyin Dazheng of Xuedou during the Qingyuan era was the son of the Shi family of Poyang. From childhood, he was exceptionally brilliant.
At the age of fourteen, he shaved his head, received full ordination, and went forth to travel. He visited various elders such as Jingshi Yan and Sigan Rui, but found no resonance with them.

Hearing that Master Yunwai Xu was propagating the Way at Tiantong, the Master went there to rely upon him. Upon entering the inner room for instruction, he attained realization. Thereupon, [the Master] appointed him to serve as the Librarian.
During the Zhizhi era, an imperial edict was issued to all those in the empire skilled in calligraphy to transcribe the Tripitaka in gold. The Master responded to this summons;

when the task was completed, the Emperor bestowed upon him a robe of woven gold *quxun* (linen). In the early years of the Taiding era under Emperor Ningzong of the Song dynasty, he returned south to Jiangzhe.
Chancellor Toghon Temür, who was presiding over the Xuanzheng Yuan, invited the Master to head Nan Chan Monastery in Quzhou, followed by Guangxiao Monastery.
Subsequently, both Cuiyan in Hongzhou and Zishan in Raoyang submitted official petitions from the Xuanzheng Yuan to invite him; however, the Master firmly declined on account of illness.
In the fifteenth year of the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty, he moved to Xuefeng Si. Ascending the hall, he said: "A thousand explanations, ten thousand explanations..."

If you meet face-to-face in a single glance: yesterday was the twenty-ninth; this morning is the first day of the seventh month. I inform you, you seekers of the profound mystery: time passes as swiftly as a flying arrow.
Those two eyes born of one’s mother, each as black as lacquer. Hurry! Hurry! Hurry! Turn your head and look upon the Buddha of True Nature.

After a long silence, he said, "What kind of face is that? He then descended from his seat and went on rounds to the hall for a meal. — From *Wumen Kuan* (The Gateless Barrier) (Note: The phrase "上" at the end indicates the conclusion of the case.)
The Hall. Sublime or not sublime? Most patch-robed monks have no nostrils at all. Mysterious or not mysterious? At the top of the banner-pole, there is no blue sky.
A man of resolve cannot bear to fold his hands; how could a fine steed wait for a whip? Completely transcending the staff and the shout, falling neither into the trap nor the net.
When the hundred birds do not come and spring has passed again, one wins the right to sleep late in the mountain hermitage. He resided there for four years before retiring.

At the Yuanming Hermitage by the waters of meditative concentration, he manifested parinirvāṇa the following year. During his cremation, his teeth and prayer beads remained unburnt, and his śarīra were brilliant and translucent.
His disciples erected a stupa behind the Yuanming Hermitage (Tiantong Xiu was his successor).
Continuation of the Record of Pointing at the Moon, Volume Four;
Continuation of the Record of Pointing at the Moon, Volume Five:
The Twenty-first Generation after the Fifth Patriarch.
Chan Master Xueyan Zuqin of Yangshan in Yuanzhou of the Linji school was a native of Wuzhou (the *Xudeng Cuncao* records him as being from Zhangzhou in Min).
Initially, he studied under Tianmu Li, who instructed him to investigate the story of Linji’s three blows of the staff. One day, as soon as he sat upon his meditation mat, he suddenly realized...

He had a realization. Later, he went to Mount Jing to attend upon Master Wuzhun Shanfeng. On one occasion, because the master was casting a bell, he ordered [the monks] to compose verses on the matter.
The Master presented this verse: "The entire body is but a single mouth; Rolled out from within the furnace of a hundred refinements.

After sending the setting sun back to its rest, It further urges the bright moon up onto the towers. Wuzhun immediately appointed him to serve in the office of the attendant. Whenever he entered the room for private instruction, [Wuzhun would test him].
He raised up the very nose of the monk and the fangs and claws of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; there was no further place for the mouth to enter.

After ten years, while walking before the Buddha Hall, he looked up and saw a branch of an ancient cypress tree. This triggered his realization, causing all that he had previously attained to fall away at once.
Only then did he see where the old man Wuzu stood. Later, he showed this to others, saying: "Right..."

"I would give him thirty blows of the staff. (Zhuo’an’s verse on this question says: "The tiger has no teeth; its claws and fangs are perilous. Not having yet penetrated the profound barrier, one only harbors secret doubts.

Is it not that one's heels must personally touch the ground? How many people can truly know this mind? ) Ascending the hall, he said: "Pure clarity, utterly free of a single speck—this is precisely the continuous flow of true permanence. Break the mirror open!"
It would inevitably result in a scene of utter disorder. It is better to eat when you encounter food and drink tea when you encounter tea.
At dawn, standing alone outside the empty courtyard, one idly faces several trees of cold plum blossoms. Ascending the hall [he said]: The waters of the sea cannot be measured with a peck;
space cannot be measured by a ruler; a pure ground cannot have sand scattered upon it; and one cannot set foot in thick mud. These are the four turns.
Speech. There is a point of falling at every turn. Tell me, where does it fall? Inside the Great Xiangguo Temple in the Eastern Capital, there is a plantain tree;
when the wind blows and the rain beats upon it, it is just like a tattered *kāṣāya* robe. [He circles his staff. Entering the hall: "A phrase, no phrase."
Like a rattan vine leaning against a tree: "A white heron descends to the field—a thousand dots of snow; a yellow oriole ascends the tree—a single branch of blossoms.
Having sold his cotton robe three thousand *li* away, he has come from no great distance. Why, then, does he set down his mud platter? He lets out a great laugh! *Hehe!*
Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon this long ago; until this very day, he has not attained the wondrous [fruit]. (Ascending the hall: Zen! On the tree above, there is clamor and noise;
at the gate of the Way, the wind blows vast and wild. To ponder this in cold silence is truly laughable. Laugh at what?
Casually picking up a pear from Suzhou, yet looking closely, it turns out to be a jujube from Qingzhou. (Ascending the hall: This matter is fundamentally accomplished.
Manifested, yet sought, it cannot be seen. A white jade disc originally has no flaws; it is through polishing that a blemish is created.
If you grasp it with substantial reality, lightning flashes within emptiness. To look upon it as something trivial is like adding a red thread beneath one’s feet.
If you are a student of the Way, observe this skillful means well. How so? Do not look at the immortal’s fan. — Elder Zhun.

On the anniversary of his death, he offered incense and said: "It is universally said that the former master died this day; Who knows that today is actually his birthday? If one does not know, what evidence is there?
Purple sandalwood and yellow sandalwood are burned together. A monk asked, "What is the essential teaching of the five houses?
The Master said, "Having a mouth is only fit for eating rice. The monk said, "If one does not pose a question, how can one reach the source?"
The Master said, "I do not yet dare grant you permission. [The monk] asked, "What is the lineage of Guiyang? The Master said, "The father is compassionate; the son is filial.
[The monk] asked, "What is the lineage of Linji? The Master said, "A thunderclap too swift to cover one's ears. [The monk] asked, "What is the lineage of Caodong?
The Master said, "At the third watch, one does not borrow the 'night-bright' curtain. [The monk] asked, "What is the lineage of Yunmen? The Master said, "The essence."
Lujin asked, "What is the Dharma-Eye School? The Master said, "The mountains are naturally clear; the waters are naturally green.

He asked, "I have received your instruction on the five houses of the patriarchal vehicle; as for the vehicle that transcends them, what is it like? The Master said, "The head touches the heavens; the feet tread upon the earth.
The Master resided at Mount Yang in Yuanzhou and was universally acclaimed as the foremost of the "Dharma Caves" (patriarchal seats). In the Jisi year of the Xianchun era, Emperor Yuan...

Bestowed with Honors and Reverence In the Dinghai year of the Zhizhi era (1347), [Wuzhun] sent a bamboo comb and a fly-whisk, along with the phrase "Green Waters and Blue Mountains," as a transmission of the Dharma to Gaofeng Yuanmiao.
He presented it with a verse of praise, saying: "The Great Master is now no more; Xueyan may be said to know the proper rites.
His empty fame has filled the universe; I entrust this to the attendant Yuanmiao" (who was the successor of Jingshan Fan).
Chan Master Duanqiao Miaolun of Jingci Temple in Lin’an was the son of the Xu family of Huangyan, Taizhou; his mother was Liu. She conceived him after dreaming of the moon.

At the age of eighteen, he shaved his head and went to Ruiyan to meet Guyuan Dao. Upon hearing the story of the "three catties of hemp," he harbored doubts and traveled everywhere to consult various masters.
One day, at Yunju, he visited Shantang while reading the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*; when he reached the passage concerning the mosquito...
Insects, moles, and ants have no speech, yet they are able to accomplish their tasks. Suddenly, he attained realization. He went to consult Master Wuzhun Shanfeng.
Wuzhun asked him, "Why does a dog have karmic consciousness? and commanded him to offer a response. He did so thirty times, yet none were in accord with the truth.
The Master asked, "Is there no expedient means? Wuzhun then cited a verse by Zhenjing: "To say that karmic consciousness remains..."

"Who says it is ultimately not deep? When the ocean dries up, its bottom will finally be seen. [The Master] said, "When a person dies, they do not know their own mind. He showed [this to him]. The Master stood in awe for a long while.

Suddenly, hearing the sound of the wooden board, he attained great enlightenment. (Jieguan Jin offered this verse: "A leaking roof meets a night of continuous rain; In summer, thick mists lock the rustic gate. Suddenly the clouds clear and the red sun emerges;

Layer upon layer, green mountains pierce the distant village. Yichu Yuan offered this verse: "One blow to the crown of the head, sweat like oil; He has been defeated, that old Zhaozhou of yore. By nature the Yellow River is turbid from bottom to top; With one sudden downpour, it becomes even more so.")

[The Master] ascends the hall. "In the Jingshan Mountains there is jade; he who obtains it does not find it within the mountains themselves. In the Red Water there are pearls; he who picks them up does not find them within the water itself.
A patch-robed monk has the 'True Person of No Rank'; he who realizes this True Person does not find him entering or exiting through the face-gate.
He suddenly grasps his staff and holds it crosswise. "Do you understand? A stone man crouches at the mouth of the Yangzi River in Youzhou. [The Master] ascends the hall.
Cimeng placed a basin of water in his room. Across the top of the basin he laid a sword, and upon the sword he set a pair of straw sandals.
Whenever a monk arrived, he would point them out; if the visitor hesitated even for a moment, he would strike him. The Master composed a verse on this:

"Leaping through the midst of a hundred flowers with the whip raised, How much effortless elegance there is! The unexamined scholar casts a furtive glance, His breast filled with helpless frustration."
"Old sorrows—what [are they]? [The Master] ascends the hall. Deshan lowers his head;
Jiaoshan nods his head; Jueyi raises a finger; Xuansha strikes his own toe. Holding up his staff, he says: "All of this does not go beyond the tip of my staff.
How can this be seen? He plants the staff on the ground and says: "A single leaf falls, and the whole world turns autumnal. (Master Mu Qian’s verse says: "A thousand wonders and... )

"A hundred monsters reside within a single hair-tip; remove the hair-tip and look at the frost-flakes—how cold it is in the sixth month! [He] ascended the hall and raised the case of Daguan Ying, who addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Seven Buddhas are subjects of nature; the myriad dharmas are slaves to the mind. But tell me, where is the master?

He then gave a shout himself and said, "From the Seven Buddhas downward, all have appeared. He then gave a nod himself and said, "Each attends to his own duties. The Master said: "Call forth the Seven Buddhas!"
To be a slave by nature means to regard all dharmas as the servants of the mind.

Even when a person of penetrating insight claims to have found the path of liberation, their own shouting and responding are still matters pertaining to the realm of slaves; how could the true Master have ever dreamed of them?
Do you all wish to see him? [He] sweeps once with the whisk and says: "A spring breeze stirs at dawn, opening up the gardens and groves everywhere."

When Master Yanghua was about to pass away, he finished his private instruction with the assembly, then requested a brush to write a letter bidding farewell to the various mountain monasteries and the Duke of Wei.
When the Duke sent medicine as a gift, the Master would not accept it. Furthermore, the Duke sent a messenger to ask, "The Master was born at Tiantai;
why do you die at Jingci? The Master replied, "The sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night. He then wrote a verse and passed away. (The lineage of Jingshan Fan).
Chan Master Yansou of Lingqu Temple in Taizhou ascended the hall and said:
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "True Suchness and ordinary or holy beings are all but dream-talk; what is true speech? Zhaozhou replied, "Oṃ phu liṃ pha. The Master said:
"Zhaozhou’s Chan resides merely on the surface of his lips. Look at him—doing so is like calling a bell a jar. Suppose someone were to ask Ling’ou:"
He replied to him: "When hungry, simply eat your rice. Now tell me, is this the same as the ancients, or is it different?
In the Western Heaven [India] it is called *Brahmā*, in this land [China] it is called *Táng* (Summer). Ascending the hall: Heat is heat; coolness is coolness. The Dharma is not a dual dharma;
there is no need for deliberation. Just as everyone’s nostrils are right on their faces, they certainly know that there is a self. Yet, even so, they ask further...
Do not let your fragrance drown in the lotus scent; how does it compare to the fragrance of rice in a deep village? (From the lineage of Fàn of Jìngshān).
Chan Master Bieshān Zǔzhì of Tiāntóng in Qìngyuán was surnamed Yáng and was a native of Shùnpíng in Shǔ. At the age of fourteen, he received full ordination.
Initially, while listening to a monk reciting the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, he heard of Maitreya’s tower and pavilion, which, once entered, would close behind one; he felt as if he had entered it himself.
Upon waking from his dream, he saw Wuzu at Xuedou. Zhiyan recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and treated him with ever-increasing severity;
at times, staff and shouts were delivered together, and not a single word was spared. Whenever the Master attempted to respond, he was suddenly silenced and unable to utter a sound.

Thereby, his intellectual understanding was entirely lost. He said, "All the skills I have cultivated throughout my life are but dead dharmas. Only now, meeting this old man, do I begin to walk the path of life."

Soon thereafter, when Fǎn moved to Jìngshān, he commanded the Master to share his seat with him. When Tiāntóng Monastery was destroyed by fire, the regional commander, Duke Wú, memorialized the Emperor regarding the Master’s spiritual conduct.

The Master received imperial edict and, carrying only a single bag and a single bowl, lived in a thatched hut. For a long time Ning Prefecture had suffered from drought; when the Master prayed for rain, it fell immediately.
Consequently, the people flocked to him, and within three years, the monastery was restored to its former splendor. One day, suddenly—

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The clouds are thin and the moonlight is fresh; the trees have shed their leaves and the mountains reveal their bones. Since heaven and earth first came into being, how many have had eyes that truly see?
When someone asked for instruction, the Master said, "It is too late to meet with me now; each of you must exert yourselves. Ten days later, he passed away.
During the night, he called his attendant and entrusted him with his final affairs; then, with palms joined, he passed away (the lineage of Fàn of Jìngshān).
Chan Master Huánxī Yī of Xuefēng on Mount Fúzhōu inscribed a eulogy for Pùtáihéshàng, saying: "Whenever meeting someone, he begs for a single coin;

Yet within his bag, he possesses the wealth of a rival state. It is not that his descent into this world was late; He simply detested being a Buddha and refused to become one. [The Master] raised the theme of "the very mind":
The Buddha then spoke in verse: "Mind itself is Buddha. Like arsenic and wolf-poison, it can raise the dead and restore life;
it requires not even a single dose. (Jinshan Fan Si)
After Master Ming of Yuepo at Tiantong in Mingzhou received the Dharma, he ascended to the abbacy of Tiantong.

He cited the case where a monk asked Yunmen, "What is it like when there has been long rain and no sun? Yunmen said, "Zha! The Master composed a verse on it: Yunmen’s single "Zha" Is a hair-splitting blade, its luster shining through the scabbard.
Were it not for Zhang Hua, It would be a vain exertion of blinking eyes. He further cited the case of Liangsui’s visit to Mazu.
The Verse on the Causes and Conditions of the Valley says: Carrying your hoe, you do not look back; you may as well go back at once.
Who would dare say, "You are a presiding master (of Mount Jing-shan, lineage of Fan)"?
Chan Master Zhizhi of Donglin on Mount Lu, in a verse sent to accompany a monk returning to Chengdu, said:
"Where wisdom does not reach, utter a single word; A single word that hits the mark, and you have arrived home. Before the Heron Pavilion, the wind stirs the willows;
Beside the city of Gansu, the rain hastens the blossoms. (Jingshan Fan, the successor)
Chan Master Xishou Shaotan of Xuedou, Qingyuan, was a native of Western Sichuan. He ascended the hall and said:
"To set forth a single mechanism that is alive, and to produce a single word that is appropriate—ten thousand miles away there is not a single cloud; the blue sky deserves a blow of the staff.

Without waiting for the spring breeze to intentionally cause it to bloom, the dark fragrance is already upon the plum blossoms. He then cited a monk who asked Nanquan: "The Master resides in the Dharma Hall; with what [will you teach]?"
Instruction: Nanquan said, "Last night at the third watch, I lost my ox; when I rose at dawn, I had lost my fire. A verse says:
"With servile face and cringing knees, he runs through the world; he would be ashamed to see one in sheepskin robes on the Qili滩.
Though Wen Shu is noble as the Son of Heaven, Zi Ling views him only as an old friend. ○ A gatha sent to Master Tiantong: "The old man [is eighty]..."
Ten times reborn sprouts; chewing the void until it is rotten, he spits out the seeds and scatters them toward the trees by the Linglong Cliff.
Branch after branch, leaf after leaf—these are all *tánhuā* (Dharma-flower) blossoms. (By Fàn Sì of Jìngshān)
Chan Master Ning, "Retired Plowman" of Lingyin in Lin’an, first resided at Chongsheng in Jiaxing and subsequently moved to Lingyin in Hangzhou.
He cited the following dialogue: A monk asked Zhaozhou, “What is your surname, Master? Zhaozhou said, “It is found in Changzhou.
The monk asked, “How old are you? Zhaozhou said, “It is found in Suzhou. The verse says: Suzhou has it; Changzhou has it. In the third month, the partridges cry in Jiangnan.
The Pigeon. How laughable is this man of many years but no virtue! When pressed by others, he tries to offer a forced explanation (Jingshan Fan’s lineage).
Chan Master Jue’an Keyang of Xuefeng in Fuzhou was the son of the Ge family of Ninghai in Taizhou. He cited a monk asking Caoshan:
"When snow covers the thousand mountains, why is the solitary peak not white? Caoshan said: "You must know there is that which is extraordinary within the extraordinary."
[The student] asked, "What is 'the extraordinary within the extraordinary'? The Mountain Master said, "Not falling into the forms of any mountain.
He then offered this verse: Within words, both self and other carry the profound mystery; Everyone seeks to discern the orthodox and the biased within speech.
Alas, they neglect the single imperial highway, Which lies vast and submerged before the bright moonlight. (Jingshan Fan)
Chan Master Xiyuan Liaohui of Tiantong during the Qingyuan era was the son of the Luo family from Pengzhou.

While still a young child with hanging tufts of hair, he would invariably play with groups of other children by kneading mud and sand to fashion Buddhist stupas and images. Upon reaching adulthood, he entered the monastic life and met Wuzhun Shanfeng.
When he presented his background and origins, Shanfeng scolded him, saying, "Go back to sleep! Subsequently, he was appointed as a non-administrative attendant (*shizhe*). One day, Shanfeng...
He said to the Master, "The place where one cannot see through lies right on the path of the nose-tip; the place where one cannot speak it lies not apart from the lips and skin.

To seek it is to travel a thousand or ten thousand miles. The Master raised his voice and said, "I thought there was so much to it! Later, when Zhuanxian became the Abbot of Yunguang Temple, the Master attended him as a servant.
He received instruction with composure and thereby mastered its essentials. When Zhuanxian moved to Mount Jing, the Master resided at the temple's head quarters.

The two seats [of abbot and guest] were established; from this point on, his reputation resounded throughout the monastic forests. When Zhao Guanwen, the Prefectural Commissioner for Ceremonial Observances, governed Suzhou, he appointed the Master as the Abbot of Foding Hui Temple.
On the occasion of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, the Master ascended the hall, held up his staff, and called out to the assembly:
"The Yellow-Faced Gautama was a fierce general of Central India. He took compassion as his bow and arrows, and wisdom as his halberds and spears, commanding a million heroic troops."
His troops were brave and irresistible; he deployed more than three hundred formations whose momentum was invincible.
Thus, for forty-nine years, he produced over five thousand scrolls of military treatises. Although these have circulated among mankind, not a single character has ever been leaked.
Because he had become an adversary and an enemy to the demonic armies of birth and death, he subsequently built a great [fortress] on the banks of the Vāḍī River.
The city is named Nirvana. Within that city, he first rewarded the soldiers with his body of purple-golden hue, allowing them to gaze upon it to their heart's content.
He repeatedly consoled and exhorted them, and furthermore, distributed eight pecks and four sheng of pearls.
His intention was no other than his desire to break open the formidable barrier of birth and death, so as to universally share [this liberation] with all sentient beings throughout the entire world.
One travels the path that penetrates to the heavens and brings life to the way; one must reach the state of great peace and security, the field of great liberation, and only then cease.
How could it be said that for over two thousand years, his aspirations have still not been fulfilled and his merit has yet to be proclaimed?

Since I, this mountain monk, know that his strength is exhausted and his schemes at an end, I cannot help but draw my sword to assist him. (He strikes once with his staff. The waves of the four seas are stilled.
The dragon sleeps soundly; the clouds of the nine heavens are clear, and the crane flies high. The Master once inscribed these verses upon the painted walls of the two corridors at Lingyin Monastery:
"Fortunately, the ten directions have no walls; who would paint the void with five colors? Within the eyes of Sudhana, cataracts have grown; one layer after another must be removed.
In his later years, he retired to Huanzhi Hermitage. As he was about to pass away, he gave these instructions:

When the administrative duties were concluded, he asked, "What time is it now? The attendant replied, "It is the second watch. Thereupon, he relaxed his body and passed away (at Jingshan, inherited by Fansi).

Chan Master Shi Shi Hui of Guangxiao Monastery in Yuezhou ascended the hall and raised the following case: An old woman in the eastern city was born at the same time as the Buddha, yet she did not wish to see him.
Every time she saw the Buddha approaching, she would immediately turn away to avoid him. Nevertheless, whenever she looked back, the Buddha was everywhere—both to the east and to the west.

She then covered her face with her hands, only to find that even within the ten fingers of her palms, the Buddha was entirely present. The Master offered this verse: Born together with the Buddha, She sought only to avoid his sight. Yet wherever she turned, The Buddha was there before her eyes. She tried to hide her face with her hands, But even within her ten fingers, The Buddha remained manifest. How could she ever escape him? How could she ever escape him?
In my whole life I never wished to meet the Buddha; yet on the tips of my ten fingers, his azure countenance appears.
After the wind and rain have passed through the peach blossoms along the road, where can horse hooves avoid the remaining red petals? (The lineage of Fàn Sì of Jìngshān, totaling twelve persons.)
Chan Master Yujie Hui of Jingci Temple in Hangzhou went to Lingyin Temple to study under Shitian Xun.
One day, while in the meditation hall, Xun raised the "Case of Yunmen’s Seven" (the *Nianqi* kōan) and presented it more than ten times, yet no one offered a word of response.

Suddenly, as a monk was just crossing the threshold, Xun abruptly said, "Xuefeng rolls the ball. The Master was standing by his side, listening with rapt attention, when he suddenly attained a profound realization.
Spontaneously, he spoke a verse, saying: "Yunmen’s 'Seventh Day,' Xuefeng’s 'Rolling the Ball,' White Freesias and Red Lythrum, the Bright Moon on a Lone Boat.
[The character ○ represents the seal. A Verse Sent to Zen Practitioner Ning: "When your mind was not yet at peace, I brought you peace for you. Falling petals and light rain brew a spring chill.
The broken bridge, flowing water, and the path to Mount Gu— Willow catkins brush against the painted railings. (Lingyin)
Master Xuewu Ke of Zhongzhu, Lin’an (the successor of Master Xun), ascended the hall and said: "The withered mulberry tree knows the wind of heaven; the sea water knows the cold of heaven.
But tell me, what does the patch-robed monk know? He knows that rice is made from grain. Even if you were to attain such realization, [Yama]..."

"Laozi Luo will have a day for demanding his rice money. Master [Wumen] took this as an omen that the Song dynasty’s cauldron had already been moved elsewhere, and he immediately resigned from his duties at the monastery.
At that time, Chan Master Moya Ya of Jinshan held the Master in high esteem for his spiritual conduct.
When the Yuan troops descended upon Jiangnan, Moya was coerced by General Bayan to join his staff and was taken with him to Wulin. There, Moya spoke to Bayan, requesting—
The Master was residing at Lingyin. Meng’an personally carried the invitation letter and knocked at the door. The Master pulled back the bolt, revealing half his face, and asked, "Who are you?
Meng’an replied, "I am an old acquaintance of yours, Reverend. The Master dropped the bolt and said, "I do not know you.
Although the Master lived beyond the secular world, he maintained himself with loyalty and integrity; thus, he did not deign to accept the summons from Lingyin. [End of Section]
Jiang En composed a poem that says: "Forty years have passed since the Snow House was lost; Its lofty spirit remains as stern as ever. Prime Minister Buyan bowed beneath its bed;
He refused to come for him to Cold Spring. (The above two individuals were Lingyin Xun and his successor.)
Chan Master Ruyong Xiangchuan Ruqiong of Yingwang Temple in Qingyuan was a native of Yongjia. His surname was Lin. From infancy, he abstained from eating meat.
At the age of fifteen, he left the household life; later, he shaved his head and received full ordination. He traveled to Mount Taibai to pay his respects to Tianmu Li, seeking to resolve his doubts.

When Li presented him with the kōan regarding "the *shui* bamboo shoots of Nanshan and the cuttlefish of the Eastern Sea," the Master attempted to offer a reply, whereupon Li struck him, and [his mind] opened wide.
However, there was one who attained awakening and, by imperial decree, was appointed to reside at Yewang Monastery. A monk asked, "What is the phrase that is transmitted outside the teachings?
The Master said, "It does not fall into the realm of the profound and subtle. The monk said, "In that case, one directly enters the stage of the Tathāgata in a single leap. The Master said:
"Wait a moment," he said. "Tell me, what is the place where a student of the Way practices? The Master replied, "From where did you just come?
The monk asked, "How can one repay the four debts of gratitude? The Master replied, "Just go back down the path you came.
[The monk] asked, "What is 'hearing again and the cataracts of the faculties are removed'? The Master said, "One is not established; two are not so. [The monk] said, "If..."
"What is it that, when the dust is cleared away, the awakening becomes perfectly pure? The Master said: "A leaking wooden ladle; a broken sieve. Ascending the hall, he said:

"The earth is great, the water is great, the fire is great, and the wind is great. If for a single moment there is no doubt, the earth cannot obstruct you. If for a single moment there is no attachment,"
Water cannot drown one who is for a single moment free from anger; fire cannot burn one who is for a single moment free from joy;
wind cannot blow one away. Such a person is a Way-man without dependence. The Buddha is born from non-dependence; if you awaken to non-dependence, even the Buddha cannot be attained.
Evening Assembly: The Shaoshi [Mount Shao] has no gates or doors; how can one pass through? Be patient and wait until the night is deep.

He stood up. "Listen as I speak of east and west. (Baoning Miao added: "There is the provisional and there is the real; there is the illumination and there is the function. It is simply that one must not understand it in such a way. Be careful! One day he said to the assembly:
"This old sick man is sixty-six this year. The day of my death is approaching. Would cremation be better? Or burial in the earth?
West Hall Weian said, "There is a patch of wasteland in front of the mountain. The Master immediately ordered stones to be piled up to form a stupa.
He further inscribed for himself: "Heaven has provided one cave to store my withered bones. When the bones decay, they become earth; the earth can produce life.
I shall form this gourd and hang it upon the wall of Zhaozhou, forever liberated from saṃsāra and transcending the Buddhas of the three periods. This was when he was about to manifest his passing.
He synthesized the essential teachings from various sayings. His writings include the *Three Assemblies Record of Sayings* (the lineage of Tiantong Li).
Chan Master Xing Gong of Shilin at Jingci Temple in Lin’an first resided at Shangfang in Anji, and later resided at Jingci.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "In a village of three households, when a cow wags its tail—how far removed is this from the whisking of my fly-whisk?
He threw down the whisk and added: "I almost stopped my imprisonment and let my wisdom grow. Ascending the hall, he said: "Xuefeng rolls the ball; Heyoshan beats the drum."
Bimā grasps his trident; Daowu performs a dance. All worthy sages have their distinctions based on the dharma of non-action.
(With a shout, he descends from the seat. (Tiantong’s ritual succession.)
Chan Master Binguo Yan of Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing ascended the hall and said: "How coldly blows the north wind, Blowing against those robes beneath the crags.
The family estate has long been overgrown with weeds; Why does the traveler not return home? In a hundred years of human life, how can one expect permanence?
Yesterday’s youth is now already old. I recall Han Shan once more: For ten years he could not return, And forgot the path by which he came."
(Tiantong’s lineage successor).
Zen Master Yun’geng Jing of Tiger Hill in Pingjiang ascended the hall and said: “If I were to truly proclaim the truth, there would be no place for you to set foot at the riverside pavilion.
For now, I shall temper my majestic light and accord with your capacities; I have not yet spoken of that which transcends the school.”
[The Master] said: "If you knew that Mount Huqiu is one hundred and thirty feet high, and that the Śarīra Stūpa was established during the Sui Dynasty, perhaps you might find a point of entry.
But if you are content to remain inferior, how can you blame this old monk? [On another occasion, he ascended the hall and said: "An ancient said:
'To interpret the meaning according to the scriptures is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three ages; to deviate from a single word of the scriptures is to speak like a demon.'"
Since both dependence and detachment cannot be found, what is it ultimately like? (He strikes the meditation staff. "The fisherman looks only at the fishing line;
he does not see the reeds facing the red smartweed. (Tiantong Li succeeded these four masters above.)
Chan Master Biantang Nan of Wanshou Monastery in Pingjiang ascended the hall and said: "If I were to explain it through for you, you would surely revile me later;
yet if I do not explain it for you, I fear you will let the opportunity pass by in negligence.
Suppose someone were to come forward and say, 'The Elder has fallen into a verbal trap! To him, I would simply say: 'It is the old monk's own fault. (Diao Yun)
Chan Master Chao’s verse says: People have long since reported that the Master has passed away, Yet I alone linger here, unable to resolve my doubts.
Since the nest is empty and the clouds have dispersed, In the depths of spring, the cuckoo still cries out. (Yunchao Yan was his successor.)
Chan Master Yì of Qīngxī at Húqiū in Píngjiāng sent this verse to a departing monk: "Ten thousand folds of Mount Tāi enter the brows, green;

Traveling together on the road, each hastens toward his own destination. At the clear dawn, the rooster cries by the moon over the thatched inn— Who is it that rises first to call out, 'Elder Brother'?
(Yúncháo Yán succeeded him; the two mentioned above.)
Chan Master Xuzhou Pudu of Jingshan in Lin’an was a native of Jiangdu in Yangzhou. His surname was Shi. As he grew older, he had no interest in worldly affairs.
Recognizing his resolve, his mother sent him to the Tianning Monastery in the prefecture to leave the household life. He then applied himself with vigor to traveling to visit various masters.
He first encountered the Seal of the Iron Ox at Lingyin. Thereafter, he traveled extensively throughout Jiangdong and Jiangxi to the east, and Hunan and Hubei to the south.
At the beginning of the Chunyou era, Zhao Xin’an, the Regional Commander, invited him to take charge of the abbacy at Banshan in Jinling.

During the Jingding era, the Grand Preceptor Duke of Wei, Jia Sidao, petitioned for his appointment to Zhongtianzhi, and subsequently requested an imperial edict for his promotion to Lingyin. This continued until the Zhizhi era of the Yuan dynasty.

In the year Dingchou, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing. Ascending the hall, he said: "When a person of heterodoxy speaks the True Dharma, the True Dharma is entirely heterodox.
When a person of orthodoxy speaks heterodox dharma, the heterodox dharma is entirely orthodox. He struck the meditation staff once and asked, "Is it heterodox?

Is it orthodox? He struck it again and asked, "Is it speaking? Is it not speaking? "If you can discern and distinguish within this point, then even a house made of gold would not be considered precious."
What glory is there in jade food and brocade robes? At the end of his life, he manifested a slight illness and requested a brush, writing in large characters:
"At eighty-two, I board the bottomless boat; having capsized it, I return home to a single sky of bright moon. He threw down the brush and passed away.
His stupa was erected at his native mountain (Huazang Tong succeeded him).
Chan Master Gaofeng Yue of Wanshou in Pingjiang composed a verse in praise of the First Patriarch, saying: "Unfurling his banner and deploying his array, he entered the realm of Liang;
Before even beholding the Emperor’s countenance, he had already surrendered. Though he possessed supernatural powers, they could not be displayed;
With a single reed boat, he sailed lightly across the Long River. (The Dharma heir of Jingci)
Chan Master Mengzhen of Jue’an at Chengtian Monastery in Pingjiang was a native of Xuanchuan. He became a monk at the age of eight and received full ordination at nineteen.

At twenty, he began his travels to visit eminent masters, yet he could not achieve definitive realization. Admiring the spiritual style of Wuzhun, he eventually ascended Mount Jing to seek an audience with him.
Every time he entered the master’s room, he was struck with trembling fear and could not even remember his meditation topic; from that point on, he would not leave.
He entered the room. Day and night he did nothing but practice *zazen*. One day, while walking along the corridor, he heard the fire-board strike and attained realization.
He rejoiced to himself and then entered the room. Zhun asked him, "Are you a monk who eats gruel and rice, or a monk who studies the Way through *chan*?"
The Master raised his voice and said, "A monk who eats gruel and rice. Zhun said, "One must eat until full before it is right. The Master replied, "Thank you for the Master’s offering.
From then on, he focused solely on the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature, yet he found no way to enter its depths.
He then went to Xuedou to see Daxie. Daxie asked, "What is the matter of birth and death? The Master replied, "The eyebrows."
Xuefeng placed it upon his eye. Xuefeng asked, "Why are the eyebrows placed upon the eyes? The Master said, "To speak of them makes one feel all the more unbearable.
Xuefeng asked again, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "From Mount Jing. Xuefeng asked, "What was the situation after the fire?
The Master said, "The five peaks still pierce the heavens as high as before. Xuefeng asked, "Has that matter ever been destroyed? The Master crossed his arms.
The Master reached out his hand and said, "Fortunately, it has not been disturbed. He then hung the portrait in the pagoda and returned to the hall.

The Master himself knew that he was not yet settled; his mind remained constantly restless and feverish. One night, deep into the night, as he raised his head and saw the crystal lamp, he attained a sudden and great awakening.

Everything he had previously acquired vanished all at once, like ice melting or a wall collapsing. The following day, he entered the room for private instruction. Xue asked, "What is [the meaning of] 'How is it'?"

"Buddha! A three-legged donkey prances about, pawing the ground. Before the sound had died away, the Master said, "Let it leap and bound as it pleases. Xie said, "Where do you meet Yangqi? The Master said, "You have missed it right before your face.
One day, while presiding over the assembly, the Master said: "To apply the mind in order to study the Buddha is to be drawn into the palace of Māra.
To direct the mind toward Zen inquiry is to fall into the realm of the five aggregates (skandhas). Even if you loathe the Buddha and refuse to become one,"
"Pierced through the skull by the staff. If you look at it this way, there is truly no place for the mind to function.
(He plants the staff. "Carry your poems and books back to your old retreat; wild flowers and singing birds are one and the same spring. (The *Yuan* era.)
There was a Dharma Master of the Xianshou school who petitioned for the famous monasteries of Jiangnan and Liangzhe to be converted into Huayan teaching temples.

By imperial decree, he was tasked with analyzing the commentaries and exegeses of various masters; [Xuedou] dissected every subtle detail as if pointing at his own palm. The Dharma Master was filled with remorse and realization, whereupon he paid homage to the Master and returned to report on his behalf (Xuedou Qian was his successor).
Chan Master Huoshan Zhao ascended the hall and said: "‘This very mind is Buddha’—the people of Jia, Mei, Guo, and Lang have a petition tucked in their sleeves.
‘Neither this mind nor Buddha’—the people of Jun, Yuan, Qian, and Ji have brushes stuck in their hair. ‘Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.’"
In Zhangzhou and Quanzhou, Fujian, the temple plaques are shaped like fans; one may hear of their fame, but cannot see them in person (Xuedou Xian succeeded him).
Master Xiangtan Yong of Huiran ascended the hall and raised the following case: When Master Wuzhuo arrived at Mount Wutai, he was having tea with an old man.
The old man picked up a crystal cup and asked, "Is there such a thing as this in the South? Wuzhuo said:
"No. The old man asked, "What do you usually use to drink your tea? He was unable to answer. The Master composed a verse:
Gazing longingly at Wutai, my thoughts linger; Under the bright sun and blue sky, I am bewitched by ghosts. The one thing most difficult to comprehend:
The crystal cup when drinking tea. (Xuedou Qian succeeded [to this lineage]).
The Chan Master Guān Pǔ cited the instruction of Mazu, wherein a monk asked Damei:
"Master, what did you obtain from seeing the Great Master Mazu that you settled here on this mountain? Damei replied: "The Great Master said, 'This very mind is Buddha.
I have simply remained here because of that. The verse says: "Using only Mazu’s lead blade, He tears asunder the vast iron mesh of the heavens. Bì...
"Night rain knocks upon lotus leaves in the marsh; to this day, poverty is lamented as having too much of a single body. (Xuedou Qian succeeded [to this lineage]).
A brief excerpt from the *Pǔshuō* (General Discourse) of Chan Master Zeshi of Xixizé at Guoqing Temple in Tāizhōu states:

"When superior practitioners who investigate the profound and eminent streams of the traveling monks reach a particular place, they immediately present their credentials for entering the gate—this is called 'giving birth' (*shēng*)."
The matter of death is great. Impermanence is swift, O brothers. Whether birth and death exist or not, from antiquity until now, there has never been a single person who could escape them.
If birth and death do not exist, what can one do about the birth and death right before one's eyes?
When birth and death are both existent and non-existent, yet neither existent nor non-existent—at such a time, is there anyone who slips through the net? Since they have already fled...
There is no door to penetrate. When the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month arrives before you, how will you ultimately manage it?

If you merely tread upon straw sandals, time will slip away like a fleeting dream; do not treat it with frivolity. You must exhaustively investigate until the place of departure is clearly understood.
Only when this accords with the manner of those who previously entered the gate can it be so (Xuedou Xian succeeded;
the five mentioned above). Chan Master Xutang Zhiyu of Mount Jing in Lin’an was a native of Siming. Within his quarters, he posed this critical phrase:
"For one whose own eye is not yet clear, why do they take empty space to wear as trousers? Why do they draw lines on the ground to create a prison? Why is it that those who penetrate this [are rare]?
This fellow is nothing more than one who enters the sea to count the sands. Why, then, does he stand with his feet raised upon the tip of a needle?

When the Master was eighty years old and entering his quarters at Jingci Monastery, while he was engaged in question-and-answer exchanges with his disciples, an imperial messenger suddenly arrived to deliver a decree.
The Emperor asked: "Why did Zhaozhou travel on pilgrimage for eighty years? Why did Xu Tang reside in the mountains for eighty years? The Master then cited the case of Zhaozhou.
Regarding the story of his travels to Linji, a verse says: "At eighty, Zhaozhou set out on pilgrimage; At eighty, he returned to dwell in the empty hall.
Possessing another faculty that expands upon the Buddhas and Patriarchs, He moved the imperial countenance within the nine-layered city.

The imperial envoy returned with this verse to the Emperor, who was greatly pleased. He specially bestowed five hundred *shí* of rice and one hundred bolts of silk. Later, [Zhaozhou] resided at Yuwang and Jingshan.
He was also granted generous rewards. The Master once cited the teaching of Dongsi to the assembly, saying: "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way.

The sword has long since departed, yet you are still marking the boat. He composed a verse on this: Yesterday, as I passed west of the bamboo courtyard, A neighbor’s young child cried out across the stream.
The mountains are cold and the waters solemn as half the leaves turn yellow and fall; Countless returning crows seek the trees for their roost.

The Master passed away and was interred in a stupa at the foot of Zhiling on Mount Jing. Formerly, when the King of Goryeo had requested the Master’s presence for his own offerings, upon hearing of the Master’s demise, he dispatched a Dharma heir to the mountain to sweep the stupa (the Dharma heir was Daochangyan).
Chan Master Shifan Yan of Tiantong in Mingzhou cited the case of Grand Councilor Lu Xuan, who asked Nanquan, "What is your surname, Master?
Nanquan replied, "My surname is Wang. The councilor asked, "Do you have any kinsmen? Nanquan said, "The four ministers are not obscure.

The councilor asked, "In what position does the King reside? Nanquan said, "Moss grows upon the jade palace. The councilor asked, "When moss grows upon the jade palace, what then? Nanquan said, "He does not reside [there]."
The Right Position. The Master’s verse says: The golden ducks have finished burning their incense, and the night-watch deepens;
In the silent jade palace, purple moss grows. The high heavens hold a moon that illuminates a thousand gates; On the Great Way, no one else is present—only walking alone.

[He] cites the occasion of Dadian banishing the Head Seat, and offers this verse: A single string of mani-jewels, confronting the situation directly. He deceived the Head Seat to death; he left Changli in doubt. Playing with...

Exhausting every last expedient, they fundamentally never knew the Spring and Autumn [Annals] (the two aforementioned masters, Daochang and Yan). Chan Master Shixi Xin Yue of Jingshan, Lin’an, a native of Meizhou, ascended the hall and cited a monk’s question to Jiufeng:

[The monk asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch coming from the West? Jiufeng replied, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. Shixi said: "If you can understand this one phrase, you will see that the Buddhas of the three periods have all descended upon the earth; if you cannot understand it, you will see that the patriarchs of the ten directions have all been cast into the sea."
"What is the student’s own self? Feng said, "Ask anyone else. The monk asked, "If one accepts it just like this, what then?
Feng said, "Sumeru must further bear Sumeru. He then offered this verse: "The cold and warmth of one's own house are known by oneself;
When the Patriarchal meaning has come from the West, who is there to ask? To accept it as the whole body is to be the whole body; It is like placing [a load] atop the summit of Mount Sumeru."
**Sumeru ○** [The Master] cites the karmic connection between Huitang and Huang Shan谷 (Shan Gu) regarding their dialogue on the "fragrance of the wood-apple flower.
The verse says: His home dwells in the land of white clouds; North, south, east, and west, the paths are vast and boundless. How many times he wished to return, yet could not;
Suddenly, he hears the secluded fragrance sent by the mountain osmanthus. [The Master] cites that Layman Pang had sons but did not marry them off, and daughters but did not...
She is married off. The verse says: Gathering the sentiments of mountain clouds and ocean moon, her nose is round and straight, her eyes and brows are horizontal.
With a whisk of tortoise hair and a staff of rabbit horns, she beats the void until it rings out with a *bò bò* sound. (Jinshan Kaishi)
Chan Master Long of Beishan in Fuzhou addressed the assembly, saying: "The mind is itself the Buddha—where there is water and bamboo, a hut is fine.
Neither mind nor Buddha—without socks and without a cap, the body is free. Neither mind, nor Buddha..."
It is not a thing. Leaning idly against the balustrade at the break of dawn, red banana leaves draw alongside the azure morning glory (Jing-shan Chong-si).

Master Shang-tang of Gao-tai-this-mountain Monastery ascended the hall and raised this case: Beside Da-sui Hermitage there was a tortoise. A monk asked, "All sentient beings have skin over their bones;
why does this sentient being have bones over its skin? Da-sui picked up a straw sandal and covered it [with it].
[The monk] was speechless upon the back of the tortoise. The Master offered this verse: "Do not insist on forcibly dividing skin and bone;
when the six viscera are obtained, let them remain as six viscera. With a single shoe, everything is completely covered; this monk has nothing left to contemplate. (Jingshan Chongsi)

Chan Master Jingweng of Tiantong in Qingyuan (added to the *Xu chuandeng lu*; erroneously listed under the twentieth generation, Wuzhun Shanfu) ascended the hall and, citing the story of Damei regarding "The mind itself is the Buddha," offered this verse:
"The husband’s heart is shallow, the wife is as pure as ice; The husband speaks of gold, but the wife does not respond.
Even if they should happen to share a single smile, Who would believe for half a lifetime that she keeps her solitary lamp? He then cited the story of Mañjuśrī.
He questioned the woman Āmrapālī: "What is the meaning of birth? The verse says: The question was clear and the answer was direct;
The one present before him saw his face and was not deceived. Birth and death, life and death, have no original boundary;
The moon rises over the green mountains like a single sphere of jade. (Jingshan Chongsi; the three masters above).
Chan Master Jieqing of Longyuan at Daochang Monastery in Huzhou was a native of the Wang family of Changxi in Fuzhou.

He received the full precepts from Chan Master Qi of Fazang at Yixing and traveled to Yuyang to visit Master Jichuang Zhao, with whom he entered the inner chamber and attained realization of the fundamental principle.
He was appointed as an attendant and further entrusted with the keys to the treasury. He appeared in the world at Shouguo in Siming and later moved to the Kaishou Monastery.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The three months of spring draw to a close; the foliage turns dark green and the blossoms grow sparse. Movement is turned by external objects; stillness is deluded by the Dharma. Do not be constrained by form, nor mounted upon sound.
Amidst the breeze, listen idly to the cuckoo’s cry. (Yuwang Zhao was his successor.)
Chan Master Xingyuan Huirang of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was styled Huanyin (Hidden Illusion). He was the son of the Xiang family from Huangyan, Taizhou.
Having left the household life, he first studied under Zhuyuan Dao at Xianju, and subsequently traveled to Jingshan to visit Yuansou.
Yuansou asked, "Have you come from the eastern ridge? The Master pointed to his straw sandals at his feet and said, "These were bought for three copper coins. Yuansou said, "Not yet."
While on the way to visit the Master, the student said, "I am just like this; I do not know how you, the Master, are.
The Old Man said, "Since you have come from afar, I shall let you off with thirty blows. At these words, the student realized the essential meaning.

After some time, he exhausted the depths of his realization and said, "As soon as one involves discursive thought, it is all merely superfluous dharma. On the day of the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, he ascended the hall and said, "Nirvāṇa and birth-and-death are equally emptiness."
"Flowers. "The Buddha and sentient beings"—these are all superfluous words. When people reach this point, how do they understand it?
After a long silence, he struck the meditation seat. One sees only falling blossoms carried away by the water;
one knows not where the spring within the cave flows out. In the hall, he gave a turning word, saying: "Last night, Lotus Peak was eaten away on one side by mayflies. Why do you not [see it]?"

Zhaozhou also said: "Setting aside for a moment the matter of Cold Spring Pavilion swallowing Hekurei Pavilion, when South Peak and North Peak clash forehead-to-forehead, what rank does this constitute as a kōan?
None among the assembly were able to reach a realization. Summer, the nineteenth year of the Hongwu era.
The Master was falsely accused and was about to be arrested. Some advised him to plan for his own safety early on, but he paid them no heed. With a serene countenance, he went before the authorities.
Before the interrogation had even begun, he recited a verse beneath the corridor and passed away while sitting upright. (Diansi of Mount Jing)
Chan Master Fanchi Chu-shih of T’ien-ning Temple in Chia-hsing was a native of Hsiang-shan. His surname was Ch’u.
From the time he was in his swaddling clothes, a divine monk saw him and said to his father, “This is a Buddha-sun; in the future, he will surely cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish.

At the age of sixteen, he became a monk. When Duke Chao Wei saw him, he recognized his potential and purchased a *seng-chieh* (monk’s certificate) for him, whereby he received ordination and the full precepts.

One day, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he attained a realization. As he subsequently surveyed various scriptures, it was as if they were long-familiar to him. He went to attend upon Master Yuansou Duan;

when Duan displayed his majestic power with a single shout, the Master was struck dumb with astonishment. One night, waking from sleep, he heard the sound of a drum and suddenly attained great enlightenment.
His sweat fell like rain, and striking the desk, he laughed and said, "Today, the nostrils of Mount Jing have fallen into my hands."

A verse on the causal accomplishment says: Outside the Gate of Revered Heaven, the drums roll thunderously; Suddenly, the void collapses upon the earth. Shide picks up a single speck of snow from a red furnace;
It is, in truth, the ice of the Yellow River in the sixth month. Duan Ying said with a smile, "I am glad that the Great Matter is now concluded.

He then appointed the Second Seat to serve as the one who receives inquiries and provides definitive resolution for those who come to consult him. [He subsequently] left his residence and went to Hangzhou.
[The Master] was serving his country. One day, High Chancellor Gao asked, "In Chan there are five schools, and in the Teachings there are three vehicles.
I do not ask about the Teachings; what is Chan? The Master replied, "It is precisely the time for the New Year’s banquet.

The Chancellor said, "Bodhidharma came from the West not to establish written words, but to point directly to the human mind, see one's nature, and become a Buddha. Where is the Buddha? The Master replied, "Amidst the mingling of pipes and strings."
[The official] entered. His crimson and purple robes were resplendent. The official asked, "Is this perhaps the Master’s own realization? The Master replied, "I dare not say so.
The official said, "We shall have the opportunity to discuss this on another day. The Master assented. One day, a Dharma Master came for an audience.
The Master asked, "What sutra are you lecturing on? The Master replied, "The Lotus Sutra. The Master said, "The sutra says: 'This is true diligence; this is called the true offering of the Dharma.'"
[The Master] asked, "Do you nourish the Tathāgata? Is this so? He replied, "It is. The Master said, "Offering is indeed not non-existent; however, what is the True Dharma?
He replied, "It is fully contained within the Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta. The Master said, "I took you for a golden-maned lion, but it turns out you are merely a member of the wild jackal's clan.
The Master then asked, "What is the True Dharma? He replied, "Have you not come from Tiantai? The Master said, "..."
"Yes. The Master said, "Mount Tiantai is eighteen thousand *zhang* high. How many people can stand upon its summit?
The host was speechless. The Master said, "Go drink tea. [Another time,] he ascended the hall. Juzhi held up one finger; Xuefeng rolled three wooden balls;
Shigong drew his bow and set his arrow; Huating had only a short oar and a solitary boat; Fengshan had no dharma to give.
He said, "It does not hinder one from sitting and cutting off [all attachments] in Hangzhou; yet within this, there is a point of excellence. What is excellent about it?
Four or five hundred flower-and-willow lanes, two or three thousand pavilions of pipes and strings. Entering the hall, he said: "The Great Matter has not yet been clarified."
"As if mourning one's deceased parents. The Great Matter has already been clarified: "As if mourning one's deceased parents. You say there is something to be gained or lost.
At the place where I usually see guests off, I recall the moment of parting from my family. Ascending the hall: To awaken to the Way upon hearing a sound—this blocks your ears.
To clarify the mind upon seeing form—this replaces your eyes. Sitting upright upon a thin mat, threading the needle’s eye.
A gust of west wind comes; two or three leaves fall. (Circle) In the *zhìzhèng* year *dīnghài*, the Imperial Preceptor bestowed upon him the title "Chan Master Fúrí Pǔzhào Huìbiàn.
This coincided exactly with the words of the divine monk from days past. He subsequently retired to Tiānníng Temple. Ascending the hall, he said:
"It is easy to swallow the mountains, rivers, and the great earth within a single hair; it is difficult for the mountains, rivers, and the great earth to swallow [the single hair]."
"A single hair is difficult. It is neither difficult nor easy. Spread out a tattered mat and sleep in the sun; even in the Tuṣita Heaven above, one could not expect such a day for warming one's back.

In the ninth month of autumn in the first year of the Hongwu era, an imperial decree was issued for more than ten eminent monks from Jiangnan to establish a Great Dharma Assembly at Mount Jangshan. The Master was commanded to ascend the seat and preach.
The Emperor was greatly pleased. In the spring of the second year, he again followed the precedents of the first year and summoned the Master to preach the Dharma.
He provided a vegetarian feast for him below the Wenlou Hall and personally received his counsel. As the Master departed, the Emperor bestowed white silver from the Inner Treasury as a gift.

In the autumn of the third year, the Emperor, considering that the manifestations of ghosts and spirits are profound and subtle and difficult to fathom, felt that the lost scriptures must contain clear explanations regarding them. He therefore summoned monks of broad learning...

Those well-versed in the Tripitaka questioned him. Thereupon, the Master, along with Mengtang E, Xingzhong Ren, and others, responded to the imperial summons and arrived at the capital, where they were lodged at Dajianjiesi.
The Emperor ordered the Ministry of Rites to provide them with hospitality and the Ministry of Food to distribute firewood and rice.
He then commanded that the questions be answered in detail and reported back. The Master cited the sutras and treatises to compose a work intended for submission; however, suddenly—
He manifested a slight illness. After four days had passed, he instructed his attendants to prepare a bath and change his robes. He then requested a brush and wrote a verse, saying:
"The true nature is perfectly luminous; fundamentally, it is without birth or extinction. A wooden horse neighs in the night; the sun rises in the west. Having finished writing, he said to Mengtang:
"I am going," the Master said. Daokai asked, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "I am going to the West. Daokai asked, "The Buddha is in the West; is there no Buddha in the East?
Thereupon, the Master let out a thunderous shout and passed away. This was on the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month in the year of Xinhai.

When the Emperor heard of this, he lamented for a long time. At that time, cremation was prohibited, but because of the Master, a special exemption was granted to follow the precedent of *jhāpa* (cremation).
The fire did not destroy his remaining teeth, tongue, or rosary; his *śarīra* were five-colored and interspersed among his skeletal remains.
His disciple Wén Shèng enshrined the bones and the indestructible relics, returning them to the western chamber built by the Master to erect a stupa.
Dūgōng Sòng Lán composed the inscription for it. (By Duānsì of Jìngshān)
Chan Master Yizhong Zhiji of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou was the son of the Gu family of Wuxian County in Suzhou.

From childhood, he left home to become a monk at Haiyun Monastery on Mount Qionglong. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he went to listen to Dharma Master Xianzong lecture on the *Huayan fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka).
Before the volume was finished, he suddenly laughed and said: "The single true dharmadhātu is perfectly identical to the great void."
"However, as soon as one engages in words and phrases, they become superfluous teachings. Even if one were to obtain a rain of precious flowers from the heavens, what benefit would that bring me?

Thereupon, he went to visit Xiaoyin at Jianye. Xiaoyin’s literary talent and moral virtue moved the entire world; when the Master slightly revealed his own literary brilliance, [Xiaoyin was deeply impressed].
At that time, they were mutually extolling one another’s reputations. A fellow practitioner, Master Yushu, saw the teacher and rebuked him, saying:
"With talent such as yours, do you not contemplate the responsibility of upholding the True Dharma? Instead, you are content to serve as a slave to the literary salon.

Regarding the verse from the *Wujinding* that says, "Yellow leaves flutter," I do not know what kind of understanding you have of it. The teacher was tongue-tied and unable to reply; he then returned to Haiyun.
His mind was so obstructed that for over a month his eyes did not close even for a blink. One day, suddenly seeing an autumn leaf fall into the courtyard, he attained a sudden realization.
He went to Mount Jing to visit Yuansou Yuan and there finally received the Dharma. The Chancellor of the Jiangzhe Provincial Administration, Dashihetumu'er, invited him to reside at Mount Jing.
Ascending the hall, he said: "At the beginning of the month of the winter solstice, sell the blanket and buy an ox."
At the end of the month of the winter solstice, one sells oxen to buy blankets. A year consists of three hundred and sixty-six days;

the four seasons and the year are established by means of the intercalary month. One cannot shift or alter it by even a hair’s breadth. At the eastern end, they buy at a high price; at the western end, they sell at a low price.
Where shall one put these worn-out straw sandals from thirty years ago? Ascending the hall, it was the third month; the season was Qingming.
It was neither cold nor warm, half-shaded and half-sunny. Fallen petals and crying birds—call after call.
Suddenly grasping his staff, he pierced the nostrils of Xie Kong and blinded the eyes of Bodhidharma. Treading through his straw sandals, he runs barefoot.
The fine mountains still remain upon the highest peak. A letter has arrived from Elder Tong Shànquán. Entering the hall for the discourse:

Since the time of chaotic confusion, for thirty years there has been no lack of salt and sauce. Only after the snowfall does one come to know the steadfast character of the pine and cypress. Let you be "neither mind nor Buddha" as you wish; I simply maintain that "this very mind is the Buddha.

It is only when faced with difficulty that the heart of a true man is revealed. Some might say: (Note: The text provided ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the source.)
"Jiangxi is where information is communicated. "The plum on Great Plum Tree has ripened. "Such is indeed the skillful means of Shanguan.
But as for Stonehead’s saying, "The letter does not arrive, and the message does not pass"—how will you all explain this?
Speak it directly right now; the adze has not yet reached you! [O] One day the Master entered the garden and saw the head cook cutting [vegetables].
Gua. The Master asked, "How many patriarchs' heads have you cut off? Gua said, "Thirty. The Master said, "Which one has blood under its skin?
Gua said, "Why do you, Reverend, repeatedly mock me? The Master said, "A good heart does not receive a good reward. [He] ascended the hall and said:
"Biting through the iron sour dumpling, all flavors are complete; it brings forth the Great Canon in a single phrase."

It penetrates everywhere. A three-legged donkey trots along, prancing its hooves; ten thousand miles without a single blade of grass. [Ascending the hall, he held up his staff: It startles the minds of those on the Ten Stages;
the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot fathom it. [He struck the ground with the staff: The son inherits the father’s trade—how many people has this deceived?
[The Master] leaned upon his staff and descended from the seat. ○ There was a man named Ju Fan, a scoundrel who lived off the daily offerings of the monks' meals.

An attendant criticized him for this, which incited his resentment; he then falsely accused the Master of corruption. The matter was brought before the provincial commissioner, who was not satisfied with the case and sought to frame the Master with a crime.
The Master ultimately refused to argue with him and showed no sign of anger whatsoever. After more than a year, the provincial government and the censorate informed the Master [of the outcome].
"Kuan! Furthermore, a formal letter was sent requesting that you reside once more at Mount Jing. Upon entering the monastery, the Master held up the letter and said:
'The life-force of the Buddhas of the past and the administrative regulations of the Buddhas of the future are both contained herein. It is as solemn as driving six horses with a worn-out rope;

it is as precarious as pulling three thousand *jin* with a single strand of hair. Were it not for the Great Chancellor who personally took hold of it and bore the full burden upon his shoulders, where else could it be found?'"
"Today has arrived. Have you all understood this thoroughly? A cart does not overturn when pushed sideways; there is no justice in a crooked judgment.

Having finished his formal address and the exchange of verses upon ascending the seat, he spoke again: "When departing, one must repay past debts; upon returning, those past debts are fundamentally empty. The carp on the mountain leaps and bounds;
the National Teacher of the Land smiles with open countenance. The Imperial Preceptor bestowed upon him the title "Enlightened Discernment of the True Lineage."
Master Guanghui: In the *guichou* year of the Hongwu era, ten monks of realized virtue were summoned by imperial decree to assemble at the Great Tianjie Monastery;

the Master was appointed as their leader. Due to illness, he was unable to attend the imperial audience, so he was granted leave to return to Qionglong. In the ninth month of the *wuma* year, he took up his brush to write a verse and passed away.
During the cremation, the flames were five-colored and a fragrant aroma pervaded the air; his teeth, jaw, and prayer beads remained unburnt.
The remaining bones were dark blue, like green lapis lazuli; the śarīra relics were interlaced.
He erected a stupa for them on the shaded side of his residence, and further divided some of the nail-clippings and hair to erect a stupa at Mount Jing (Jingshan Duansu).
Chan Master Yuanjing of Lingyin Puyin in Hangzhou was a native of Kuaiji in Yuezhou. His secular surname was Ni.
He received the tonsure under Master Li Hongjiao. Upon entering the presence of Master Yuansou Duan, Duan let out a single shout as resonant as thunder.
At that moment, the Master’s attachments and fetters were completely cast off; he immediately prostrated himself in homage, whereupon Duan appointed him to serve as his attendant.

The Master served as Secretary (Jishishi) and followed him for a long time, eventually receiving his seal of approval (*inka*). When the Master was summoned to the capital, he asked questions with composure;

having been granted an audience and provided with a meal, he withdrew. It so happened that the seat at Lingyin Monastery was vacant, and the various mountain monasteries collectively presented earnest invitations. He ascended the hall [to give a formal sermon].
Sound is not sound; this is the Samādhi of Avalokiteśvara. Form is not form; this is the Dharma-gate of Mañjuśrī. When sound and form are unimpeded, this is the realm of Samantabhadra.
[The Master] picks up his staff, draws a line, and says: "The Great Garuda spreads its wings, covering the Ten Continents;

the swallows and sparrows by the hedge chirp in vain. [Ascending the hall: "This very mind is Buddha" — the ox of Jia Prefecture eats the grain. "Neither this mind nor that Buddha" — [the ox does not eat the grain].
Yi Zhou Ma Abab said, "It is not the mind; it is not the Buddha. The world seeks a physician to apply moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig.
After a long while, he said, "To cry until one's blood flows is of no use; it is better to keep one's mouth shut and pass through the remainder of spring.
Before long, he was arrested and exiled to Shaanxi. On the way, at Baoying Ningguo Temple, he suddenly joined his palms, sat upright, and passed away. (Jingshan)
Duan Si). Chan Master Xingzhong Zhiren of Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou was of the Wu clan and a native of Fanyang. His father, Zhonghua, served as the Guangwen (Director of Education) of Jiangzhou.
When the Master was five years old, he was sent to Bao’en Temple in the prefecture to receive instruction from Master Chun of Zhemu.
As for his karma: at the age of seven, he received ordination. Once fully ordained, he went to visit Master Yuansou Duan.

Upon seeing the Master, Duan laughed heartily. The Master was at a loss and did not know how to respond; consequently, he failed to unfold his meditation mat. Duan rebuked him, saying, "Go to the hall!
One day, Duan saw the Master and asked, "Where are you from? The Master replied, "Fanyang. Duan asked, "How wide is Lake Fanyang? The Master spread out his hands.

Zuowang Qianshi said, "It is not so, it is not so. The Master said, "Shut that foul mouth! He then appointed him to serve as the attendant for incense and subsequently took charge of the secretarial office.
Zuowang once said to the assembly, "The Secretary Ren is one who has the wings of a tiger. Ascending the hall, he said: "The nature of Chan is unborn;
depart from the thought of Chan as being born. The nature of Chan is non-abiding; depart from the stillness of Chan as being abiding. On Mount Wutai, the clouds..."
Steamed rice. A dog’s urine on the steps before the Buddha hall. A frying pan atop the flagpole. Three monkeys winnowing coins at night.

At the beginning of the Hongwu era, the Emperor summoned the Master regarding matters of ghosts and spirits. The Master responded with a written composition based on the Buddha’s teachings, which greatly pleased the Emperor.
When Wei Gongguan of Pují served as the Magistrate of Suzhou, he visited the ruins of Wanshou Monastery.
