The site was desolate, yet he felt a profound sense of purpose to restore it. Hearing that the Master was residing at Tiger Hill (Hūqīu), he dispatched an envoy with letters and gifts.
After three rounds of correspondence, the Master finally consented. On the full moon of the third month in the fifteenth year of the Hongwu era, he manifested illness.

On the nineteenth day, his fellow practitioner Ruyu Zhongxun came to inquire after him and said, "Master, you are departing. Your disciples are here by your side; why not grant us a word as your final instruction?"
The Master said, "The Bhagavāns of the ten directions share one path to the gate of Nirvāṇa. [The monk] replied, "I have been close friends with you for fifty autumns;
after this parting, I shall go straight to the Pure Land to meet you there. The Master raised his voice sternly and said, "The entire great trichiliocosm is this very Pure Land;
where would we not meet? After a long silence, he wrote a verse with a white brush and passed away peacefully (Diansi Duansu).
Chan Master Mengtang Tanne of Xiangshan Ruelong was the son of the Wang family of Cixi. Both his grandfather and father held prominent official positions.
His mother was Lady Zhou. From childhood, the Master possessed lofty aspirations; as he grew older, he became widely versed in the classics and histories, and his literary talent flourished.

At the age of twenty-three, he informed his mother of his intention to leave the household life and went to follow Xueting at Changlu, whereupon he shaved his head and received full ordination. He was taught...
He studied all the various schools of thought, leaving nothing uninvestigated. After some time, Xueting moved to reside at Lingyin;

the Master again went there to attend upon him. More than a year later, Xueting passed away. Chan Master Jizhao Duan came to fill his position. Upon seeing [the Master] for the first time, they were in perfect accord.
He resided at Rulong on Mount Xiangshan. Entering the hall, he held up his whisk and said: "This very thing—when it comes to Linji, it is a great capacity and a great function."
In its application, it rolls out and gathers in, seizing and releasing, killing and giving life with total freedom. With Yunmen, it is solitary and perilous, towering and steep;

he upholds the teaching beyond the ordinary, making his decisive judgment prior to a word. With Caodong, the family style is dense and subtle; like a golden needle and a jade thread, light is cast and dark is met.
With Guiyang, father is compassionate and son is filial; they employ the matter of the sword’s edge and deploy the mechanism of the tiger trap. As for Fayan...
Then the arrow-points meet; the mind is empty and phenomena are understood. Sentiment is exhausted and views are eliminated.
Although the proclamations of the five houses possess the resonance of gold and jade, transcending the past and surpassing the present, they are all merely provisional arrangements of the gate.
A single direct phrase has never been spoken. But tell me, what is that direct phrase? [He] cried out in a loud voice: "Look beneath your feet! (O)

The Master ate but one meal a day and sat in meditation throughout the night until dawn. One day, he suddenly took a bath, changed his clothes, and brought out his belongings to distribute as gifts to his friends.
He gathered the assembly and spoke this verse: "I have a single thing; it has no back and no front.

You must see it clearly; look after my parinirvāṇa. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. There is a revised edition of the *Lidai gao seng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks Through the Ages).
Xingshi (Jingshan Duansu): Chan Master Fuyuan Fubao of Jingshan, Hangzhou, was a native of Ninghai, Tai prefecture. His clan name was Fang and his mother was surnamed Zhang.
He left the household life at Chongfu Temple on Liangzhu in Hangzhou. At that time, Princess Mei of Shihu was serving as the abbess of Jingci Temple; the Master went there to visit her.

Liu honored him as his teacher; he subsequently shaved his head and received full ordination. He went to attend upon Yuansou Yuan at Mount Jing, where Yuansou asked, "Where have you recently departed from?
The Master replied, "Jingci. Yuansou asked, "What brings you here? The Master said, "I have long admired your reputation for the Way; I have come specifically to pay my respects."
Duan asked, "When Zhaozhou saw Nanquan, what did he do? The Master said, "Heaven is above his head; he stands on the earth with his feet.
Duan asked, "What was it like after he saw him? The Master said, "When hungry, he eats; when tired, he sleeps.
Duan asked, "Where did you learn such empty talk? The Master said, "Today I have personally seen the Master. Duan nodded in approval. [At the beginning of the Hongwu era, he was invited.]

The Emperor summoned the śramaṇa Daohang. The Master traveled to the capital and was lodged at Tianjie Temple. He entered the inner court several times, and his responses were in accord with the Imperial will.
He remained there for three years before being granted leave to return. Later, while residing at Mount Jing, he ascended the hall and said:

"A single leaf falls, and the world turns autumn; A single mote of dust rises, and the great earth is gathered in. Who says that Northern Uttarakuru is not Southern Jambudvīpa? One simply rides the ox."
He went up to the hall again to give a discourse: "Speech is slander; silence is deception. Is there anyone who does not involve themselves in either? He struck the meditation seat.
This was enough to let the prisoner go free and allow wisdom to grow. One day he fell seriously ill. His attendant requested a verse.
The Master rebuked him, saying, "I still have three years of worldly life remaining. It was exactly so.
On the day of his passing, he suddenly clapped his hands and said, "A-he-he! O assembly, look at this! Thereupon, he entered final nirvana (Jingshan Duansi).
Chan Master Guding Zuming of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was the son of the Ying family of Fenghua. When Yuansou was residing at Lingyin Monastery, the Master went there to attend upon him.
One day, during a private interview, he inquired about the karmic connection between Huanglong and Ciming. Yuansou questioned him sternly, saying:
"As for Zhaozhou’s statement, 'The old woman of Mount Tai has been exposed by me,' Ciming laughed and asked, 'Is this an insult? What do you say?'"
"Regarding the application of these two old men, are they the same or different? The Master said, "A pair of unperforated iron hammers.
Xuedou said, "If one were to attain enlightenment directly beneath Huanglong, what then? The Master said, "It would still be like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky.

Xuedou said, "Not so, not so. As the Master was about to offer a word in response, Xuedou gave a shout. At that moment, the Master attained a state of vast clarity. In the seventh year of the Zhizheng era... Yuan.
The Emperor conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Huixing Wenmin Hongjue Puzhi.

In the year Wuxu of the Zhizheng era, as he was about to pass into nirvana, he left a letter entrusting his protection to the Chancellor. He further wrote a verse, saying: "Birth and death are pure and true; the great void is pure and full."
In the seventy-ninth year [of his life], the rope of his cradle snapped; he cast aside his brush and passed away.

During the cremation, his tongue, root, and rosary remained unburnt, and his *śarīra* relics were beyond counting. Stupas were erected for them at Mount Jing, Longjiao, and Putuo (Mount Jing was presided over by Duansu).
Chan Master Liaohan Falin of Zhuanquan at Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was surnamed Huang. A native of Ninghai in Taizhou, he attained awakening upon contemplating the words of Muzhou.
He then went to visit Master Yuansou Duan, who asked him, "Where have you come from? The Master replied:
The Old Man of Tiantai asked, "Have you ever seen Hanshan and Shide? The Master joined his palms and stepped forward, saying, "Today I have personally seen the Abbot.
The Old Man said, "You liar who speaks empty words! Go to the hall! One day, while they were reading the sutras, Cuiyan Duan asked, "Are you reading the sutras there?
The Master replied, "Yes. Duan asked, "With what do you read them? The Master said, "I read them with my eyes. Duan held up [his finger].
He raised his fist and said, "Why do you not say, 'Bring this here and look'? The Master said, "Drop your fist; with what will you look? Duan smiled.
The Master resided in the Meng Hall of Jingci Monastery for nine years without ever stepping outside the door.

When the Left Chancellor of the Provincial Administration, Duke Tuohan, invited him to preside over Wanshou Monastery, he was subsequently transferred to Zhongzhu. Upon reaching the Buddha Hall, he said: "Dust is brushed aside and the Buddha is seen—who [is it]?"
To know that even the Buddha is but a dust mote; rarely do we encounter those who pierce their ears, while many are seen as those who mark the boat after it has drifted.
Ascending the hall [the Master said]: "The Dharma is the eternal Dharma; the Way is the eternal Way. To break through the gateway of the face—pointing is not yet reaching it.
At Xuefeng’s place day and night, they did nothing but roll three wooden balls. When Zhaozhou saw people, he would simply say, "Go drink tea. Zhongfeng Jujian often saw his brothers.

When visiting one another, it is merely a matter of exchanging greetings of courtesy; they burn incense and join their palms. If one is a true offspring of the Golden-Maned Lion, even from three thousand *li* away, one will certainly resolve all contradictions.
At Lingyin, during an ascent to the hall, the Master raised the case of a monk asking Zhaozhou about the saying, "The myriad dharmas return to One.
The Master said: "Although Zhaozhou skillfully wielded the Great Black Sword to cut off this monk’s tongue, he could not avoid..."
To expose one's own family’s disgrace is not the way at Lingyin. Once, when a monk suddenly asked, "All phenomena return to One; where does the One return?

he simply said to him, "Today is as hot as yesterday. [He] ascended the hall. Within the jurisdiction of Old Hangzhou lies the famous mountain of Lingyin, first established during the Xianhe era of the Eastern Jin dynasty. Dharma Master Huirui was its first patriarch. Today, [he] ascends the hall...
It was the Yuanling Festival. Lanterns were being lit in various places. The administrative officers and the year-steward each took care of the lamps and candles, and then descended from their seats.

In the spring of the fifteenth year of Zhizheng, he contracted a slight illness. On the second day of the second month, he gathered the assembly, recounted the beginning and end of his life’s practice, and exhorted them, saying:
"The decline of the Buddha-dharma has never been more severe than it is today. You should each exert yourselves and seek [the truth]."
He wrote a verse with his brush, saying: "Seventy-two years; a wedge driven into empty space. The final phrase—unspeakable, unspeakable. He then passed away.
His entire body was interred to the west of the Songyuan Pagoda. At that time, an ancient cassia tree before the pagoda blossomed its flowers in the spring.
A fragrant aroma filled the road, and those who saw it marveled at its strangeness (Dìngshān Duānsì).
Chan Master Zhōngyóu Guī'ān of Tiānníng Monastery in Míngzhōu was of the Chén clan and a native of Yìnyīn. He received the tonsure and ordination under Chan Master Kuāng of Fózhi.
Having gone to Jìngshān to study under Jìzhào Duān, he attained the essential teaching. He ascended the hall and said: "If we were to discuss the primary..."
A single phrase: the Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot speak it; the six generations of patriarchs cannot speak it; the old monks of the world cannot speak it;
this mountain monk cannot speak it; the great assembly cannot speak it. [The Master] picks up his staff and asks: "Can this staff speak it?
Even if it could, that would still be the second phrase. [Ascending the hall: "This very mind is Buddha; neither mind nor Buddha."
The Buddha is not mind; he is not Buddha. On Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice; before the steps of the Buddha Hall, it is a "dog-urine sky.
At the tip of the banner pole, a hammer is being fried; three monkeys winnowing coins at night. (On the occasion of the Lantern Festival, he ascended the hall.)
Before the fifteenth day, the head and tail of the feet are golden lotuses. After the fifteenth day, white oxen and stray cats run about in packs.
On the very fifteenth day itself, above and below the pavilions, fire illuminates fire;
carriages and horses pass to and fro, and people look at people. Good assembly, tell me: where does this goodness lie? It is difficult for the eyes of the multitude to deceive (Jingshan Duansi).
Chan Master Yuzhong Shanru of Kaiyuan Temple in Suzhou was a native of Wujiang. He ascended the hall and said:
"The Buddha-body pervades the Dharma-realm and appears universally before all sentient beings. Why, then, did those residents of Hudu who followed the way of Huang-Lao [be reborn as fish]?"
When they went to welcome it, wind and waves surged in terror and the image immediately sank.

Zhu Yingdong of Wu County and the nun Lingbo requested it, whereupon the sacred form rose majestically and floated across the water on both sides; when they attempted to lift and carry it, it suddenly ascended into the boat.

These are the stone statues of Vimalakīrti, Vaiśravaṇa, and Kāśyapa currently enshrined at Kaiyuan Temple. Is this not proof that responding to conditions and manifesting for sentient beings is all-pervasive?
Yet he constantly dwells upon this seat of Bodhi. Nevertheless, even so: if you understand it in such a way, it is like a tiger watching a water mill;
if you do not understand it in such a way, it is like looking from Zhenzhou toward Changlu. When both "such" and "not such" are cast aside, what then?
In a world of peace and tranquility, there is no need for deceptive words. [The Master] spent his later years residing at Zhijin in Fengmen.
Zhian was known by the people as Master Zhizhi. As he neared the end of his life, he called his sons to bid them farewell;
then, sitting cross-legged, he passed away peacefully (Jingshan Duansu).
Master Wufa Benwu of Shangzhu, Hangzhou, was a native of Huangyan. He relied upon Jizhao at Zhongzhu and served as the monastery’s administrator (*gangwei*).
His maternal uncle, a venerable elder of the Buddhist academies (*jiaoxiang*), urged him to change his religious affiliation.

Consequently, he went to Yanfu to study under Zantang, where he devoted himself to the profound study of the scriptural teachings (*jiaobu*). Jizhao regretted his departure and sent him a verse, which said: "Entering Chan through the Teachings..."

In antiquity there were those who entered the Exoteric Teachings from Chan; in more recent times, there have been none. Although the gates of the "One Mind and Three Contemplations" differ, when the waters fill a thousand rivers, the moon remains but solitary.
Later, having become the dharma heir of Zantang, he nevertheless burned a single incense stick to honor Jizhao, not allowing the difference in their outward traces to create a duality in his mind.
When Jizhao passed away, he left a letter entrusting him with the vigorous propagation of the teachings of the Vehicle of Doctrine.
Gone. There is no other word for it. The Master, at the sacrificial banquet, offered incense and said: "The fifth transmission of Wuxi is the most brilliant flame;
Jizhao’s entire era is a gate of ambrosia. Casually touched, one’s liver and brain split apart; Frost and ice suddenly become the warmth of spring.
I think back to the day my nostrils were lost; What kind of breath remains even now? A celestial wind blows from the north as the year turns."
It was like evening clouds; a flash of lightning sought out the traces in the sky. At the end of his life, he passed away seated without illness (Dìngshān Duànsì).
Chán Master Zhīchún of Wànshòu Fó in Sūzhōu sent this verse for Attendant Zhōng:
“Níogē blew up the cloth-hair, and the attendant attained enlightenment on the spot. A pair of unperforated iron hammers, they peddle the livelihood of ghosts.”
If one is a sharp and discerning master, possessing a natural air of magnificence, expanding the original ground’s radiance, and manifesting the very core of the patch-robed monk—
drawing the great chiliocosm into the tip of a hair and containing Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed— one walks directly upon the crown of Vairocana,
such that even the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands cannot block the way. (With thirteen people, including Jingshan Duansu.)
Chan Master Wufang Zhipu, surnamed Long, was a native of Guiyang. He ascended the hall and said: "In the sixth month, travelers breathe smoke;
they toil only because they are dragged by profit and fame. How can they compare to the carefree guests beneath the forest trees?

With a single awakening, they sleep in their robes until dawn. [The Master] struck the meditation seat and said: "Ganming does not begrudge his verbal karma; for your sake, I have explained it all. The third day of the twelfth month."
When the tenth day arrives, Old Yama will demand from you the payment for his meal (Jiangxin Wansi).
Master Xiaoyin of Yunju in Nankang, the Great Chan Master, once spoke this verse to the practitioner Xin: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit;
it is like a medicine that, if effective, requires no great quantity. If you, O superior man, can directly realize and take this up, you are a Buddha."
"Ancestor An, what can you do about this? (The two aforementioned masters, Jiangxin Wan and Hansi).
Chan Master Daxin Xiaoyin of Longxiang Jiqing in Jinling was the son of Chen of the Yimen family from Jiuyang. He went to study under Huiji;
upon first seeing him, Huiji held him in high esteem and appointed him to oversee the secretariat. One day, Huiji asked: "Since Huanglong had already attained the essential meaning..."
At Letan, he led his disciples on a journey to travel among various teachers. Upon meeting Ciming, his spirit was drained and sweat broke out from him. [Ciming asked,] "Where does the fault lie?

The Master raised his voice and said, "Within a peach pit a thousand years old, what 'kernel' do you seek from the past? One day, Ji brought up the story of Baizhang’s wild fox and questioned him, saying:
"Falling away from cause and effect, one immediately falls into the body of a wild fox; not being deluded regarding cause and effect, one immediately sheds it."
"A wild fox body. [The Master asked,] "Tell me, where does the point of benefit or harm lie? As the Master was about to answer, the Master [Jianwen] suddenly struck him with a thunderous shout.

At that moment, the Master’s doubts were completely dissolved like ice melting away. In the first year of the Tianli era, Emperor Wen-zong established the Great Longxiang Jiqing Temple on the site of his former palace.
He selected men of renowned virtue to serve as the founding patriarchs. The Master was the first to be chosen for this honor and was bestowed the title Guangzhi Quan.

Chan Master Wudai was again summoned by imperial decree to the capital. He had an audience with the Emperor at the Quanzhang Pavilion, where he was granted a seat and questioned regarding the essentials of the Dharma.

When Emperor Shun ascended the throne, his treatment of the Master became even more honored. Later, seeking retirement due to old age and illness, the Master submitted a request which the Emperor declined with a gracious edict, ordering the local authorities to provide him with protection and supervision so that he might live out his final years in peace.
[At one time,] he ascended the hall and said: "In the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), the water birds and the forest trees..."
All of them were mindful of the Buddha. In the Tuṣita Heaven, the trees touch one another, preaching suffering and emptiness.
[The Master] held up his whisk. "This mountain monk’s whisk has pierced through all of your nostrils. Where will you all go to breathe? One day, the Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "I have come from traveling the mountains. The Master said, "Under your straw hat, you have crushed Lǔpǔ to pieces. [He continued: "Pervasive..."
"What is it that you have penetrated? The monk said, "Even before entering the gate, I have already presented it to the Master.

The Master said, "Why do you not bring it forth right now? As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him. In the fifth month of the fourth year of the Zhizheng era (1344), he manifested a slight illness.
He wrote a letter by hand to bid farewell to his friends and instructed his disciples to preserve the gifts bestowed upon him by the two successive dynasties.

He used gold coins to construct the Ten Thousand Buddhas Pavilion (Wanfo Ge) as an offering to repay the national grace. On the twenty-second day, he composed a verse, sat in meditation, and passed away.
Huang Wenxian Gong Qimin composed his stele inscription, and Yu Wenjing Gong Ji authored the *Record of His Practice of the Way*.
The Master’s works—including the *Pure Rules for Chan Monasteries* (*Chanyuan Qinggui*), the *Recorded Sayings of Four Assemblies*, and the *Pushe Ji*—circulate in the world. (Jingshan Xisi)
Chan Master Nianchang of Meiwu at Xiangfu Monastery in Jiaxing was surnamed Huang and was a native of Huating.

He entered the monastic life at the age of twelve and received the tonsure and full ordination at fourteen. When Fozhi Huiji moved from Baiyang in Jiangxi to Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou, the Master went there to attend upon him.
It happened that he encountered Fozhi ascending the hall, where he cited the story of Elder Fu of Taiyuan, who attained awakening upon hearing the sound of a horn.
On the causes and conditions of the Way, the verse says: Qinseng entered the vast ocean; Taishi traveled to famous mountains.
From then on, along the road outside the city of Yangzhou, strict orders were issued forbidding the gates from opening early. The Master attained sudden enlightenment beneath these words.

He went to the master’s quarters to present his understanding, and Fozhi nodded in approval, appointing him to oversee the record office (*jishu*). When Fozhi moved to Mount Jing, the Master succeeded him in that position.
He served as a leader for the entire assembly. Later, by imperial decree, he was summoned to take charge of the world at Xiangfu Temple.
His works include the *Fozu Tongzai* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) in twenty-two volumes (compiled by Xisi of Mount Jing).
The ancestral master Shi-shi Zu-ying of Xuedou in Mingzhou was the son of the Chen family of Wujiang. At the age of fifteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination.

Thereafter, he took up his staff and traveled to study under various masters. Initially, he followed Xu-gu Ling at Yangshan; hearing of the renown of Hui-ji at Jingshan, he went there immediately to seek him out.
Upon their first meeting, they were in perfect accord, and Zu-ying was subsequently retained to serve as the *jishi* (recorder). [He later] retired from Tiantong Ping.
In the verse for inquiring after the illness of Shidi, it says: "This body is without self, yet the roots of illness are deep; Out of shame and remorse, Mañjuśrī has come from afar to visit.
With the mountain flowers of our own tradition, we discuss non-duality; Facing each other by the blue lamp, we laugh and chant with joy.
The Dharma-body pervades all places; Whether eating food or eating emptiness, one attains freedom. Within the mist and rain of Mount Mao, Taibai, The bamboo sedan chair comes and goes."

Fengliu [Monastery]: In his later years, he contracted the ailment of flaccid paralysis (*viśvācī*). He constructed a small shrine called "Wooden Robe" (*mùduō*) and sat within it daily, withdrawing from worldly affairs.
In the third month of the *guīmǔ* year of the Zhèngtóng era (1363), he saw a woman in tattered clothing who prostrated herself, entreating the Master to take rebirth as a king.
The Master replied, "I have no desire to be born into the house of a celestial king. Seventeen days later, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
Huazhi’s verse at the time of his death says: "Fifty-three years of playing with cleverness have resulted in clumsiness. Treading through empty space, I walk barefoot;
the myriad phenomena and the host of beings laugh without ceasing. (Jingshan Xisì)
Chan Master Zhiguan Zhengkui of Zhongzhu in Hangzhou was a native of Fanyang. His clan name was Fang. He studied under Huiji at Jingci Monastery.
Huiji asked, "Where are you from? The Master replied, "Fanyang. Huiji asked, "How deep is the water in Lake Fanyang?"
The Master said, "Staring with wide-open eyes, one does not see the bottom. Ji said, "If that is so, then even the nostrils of a patch-robed monk will be soaked and rotted away.
The Master said, "I certainly do not borrow the Venerable One’s nostrils to breathe. Ji said, "In the end, whose nostrils do you borrow to breathe?"
The Master said, "I respectfully wish the Abbot ten thousand blessings. The Abbot approved his potential and appointed him as his attendant.

After more than two years had passed, he went to Mount Tianmu to study under Zhongfeng, and subsequently visited Yuansou of Mount Jing. At that time, Xiaoyin was presiding over Zhongzhu Temple and requested the Master to share the teaching seat with him.
Chushi Chongyin of Jinling was bestowed with the title "Buddha-Sun Universally Illuminating" (Jingshan Xisui) by the Imperial Preceptor.
Foyan Zhongfang, the Chan Master Tiantun of Ningbo, was the son of Zhang of Xiangshan. He went to visit Huiji at Jingci;
as soon as he entered the gate, Huiji said: "The lake mountains are misty and the lake waters shimmer; they soak and rot your nostrils and block them up."
"I am going to blind you! Why do you not understand? The Master said, "Throughout my entire being there is no shadow or image; at every step, all traces of form are severed.
Jiqi said, "That is not yet it; speak further! The Master shook his sleeves and departed. Jiqi then appointed him to the position of Attendant and later entrusted him with the keys of the storehouse.
The Master found their proliferation cumbersome and sighed, saying, "The age has declined and the Way has waned; the faculties of men have become frivolous and shallow.

Even masters of long-standing renown and great virtue, possessing vast knowledge and insight, are not yet fully trusted or accepted by students. This is for no other reason than that their inner and outer selves are not pure.

From then on, he was determined to erase all traces of his former ways. Hearing that the Peach Blossom Valley in Wuxing was secluded and remote, he went there to bind together thatch for a hut. One day...
While watering the garden, suddenly the clouds gathered over the four mountains; a torrential rain and fierce winds broke the trees and shrubs.
With a single clap of thunder, the doubts and obstructions within his breast were instantly dispelled. He then composed this verse: "Most marvelous, most marvelous, how truly marvelous!
I have overturned space and ride it upside down. A tiny gnat has swallowed the five Mount Sumerus! Previously, in the quarters at Nanping, he had repeatedly questioned the old Master.
Yet he ultimately refused to explain it for me. Had he explained it then and there, how could there be this day? Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case:
Once, when a monk asked Yunmen, "What is it like when long rains do not clear? Yunmen said, "Zha! The Master said:
"Yunmen’s single 'Zha'—the howling of monkeys in the Ba Gorges, the towering peak of Xiong’er, the slippery path of Shitou. In his later years, the Master selected a site to build a dwelling.
To the west of Fengtai was the Xianan (New Hermitage). As he was nearing his end, he said to Jingjue Tan, "I wish to trouble you with my final affairs.
What day is it today? Jingjue replied, "The twenty-ninth. The Master said, "This is the last day of the month; it is not appropriate to depart now.
Tomorrow is the first day of the fifth month; I shall go then. At dawn, he summoned his disciples to give them his final instructions. He made a gesture of farewell and sat upright.
[The Record of] Master Jiqing Hai of Tiantai Yiyuan, Yuezhou (Jingshan Xisi):
At the age of eighty-six, he went forth to reside at Tiantai Yiyuan. On the occasion when fellow practitioners arrived for the ascent to the hall, [he said:
"The scenery is cool and rustling; companions visit this desolate place. Brewing tea with water from beneath the mountain, burning..."
Chopping wood in Dingdong Valley: The ancients treated the communal property of the monastery as their own personal favors. Tianyi, however, was not like this:
he was too lazy to pick up flowers for the Buddha and too lazy to brew tea for guests. Do not resent his lack of formal etiquette; such frugality and simplicity is the way of the monk.
(The above six persons were from Mount Jing, by Xi Si.)
Chan Master Zhixi Zhiru of Zhongzhu Temple in Hangzhou was a native of Min. When the Yuan troops descended upon Min, he was seized by wandering soldiers and brought to Lin’an;
they then abandoned him there and departed. A wealthy man of the Hu family took him in as a foster child and ordered him to accompany his own son to study.
The Master stood at the corner and silently observed everything, noting it all without omission. The Hu family followed his lead.
Once he had grown up, they sent him to become a monk at Wuxiang Temple in their village. There, he studied under Yunfeng Hao of Mount Jing and attained the Dharma.

At the beginning of the Tianli era, Xiaoyin Yin of Zhongzhu was summoned by imperial decree to establish a monastery. When Longxiang Temple nominated three candidates to succeed him as abbot, the Emperor’s brush marked the Master’s name.
The Xuanzheng Yuan submitted a memorial requesting that the Master reside there (from *Jing Shan Gao Si*).
Chan Master Gu Zhi Zhe of Donglin, Jiangzhou, was a native of Duchang; his clan name was Chao. He ascended the hall and said:
"The Buddhas of the past have already spoken; the Buddhas of the future shall speak; the Buddhas of the present are speaking now. But tell me, what is it they are ultimately speaking?"
"What is it? [He] planted his staff on the ground and descended from the seat (this was the successor at Mount Jing).
The brief account of the general discourse by Chan Master Guaishi Qi of Tiantong Monastery in Mingzhou states: "Studying Chan is fundamentally neither difficult nor easy."
Provided one possesses great roots of faith and resolute determination, all worldly affairs shall cease; though a thousand sages appear, they cannot lead one astray.
Severs all conditions while sitting, and harbors not a single dharma. Like the vast void, it is utterly devoid of trace; like Mount Sumeru, it stands firm and unmoving.
Only then can one hope for the unsurpassed True Vehicle. It is further said: "This matter is like a person suffering from hunger and thirst who speaks of drink."
To speak of eating—how could that possibly provide healing? One must simply drink water and eat rice oneself; only then will there be real efficacy. (From *Jing Shan Gao Si*).
Chan Master Benyuan Shanda of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was the son of the Chai family of Xianju. He habitually did not set up a bed for sleeping.
At night, he would burn incense and light candles, sitting upright until dawn; this was his constant practice. Furthermore, his physical constitution was such that...
People differ. When encountering severe cold, he would wear fine linen; in great heat, he would wear silk and cotton.
He once used his alms bowl as the foundation for constructing the Dayuan Monastery on a mountain halfway along the eastern road to provide hospitality for fellow travelers.
One day, knowing that the time had come, he gathered the assembly, recounted the events of his lifelong travels, and then sat upright and passed away (his lineage was at Mount Jing).
The Chief Seat Dragon Rock Jin sang this song of delight in leisure: "The very mind is Buddha; no-mind is the Way. All matters simply follow conditions;
One naturally realizes that body and mind are well. I have never sought to dwell in a monastery; Even Buddhahood is not something to be attained.
I have never upheld the Vinaya, nor have I ever broken the precepts. Letting go or holding fast is entirely up to the person; To cling to the Dharma..."
The practitioner is like a donkey pulling a millstone: when he wishes to walk, he walks; when he wishes to sit, he sits. He is neither diligent nor indolent.
A single scroll of the *Three Character Classic* is his daily task. At times he walks the bottom of the deep sea; at times he lies atop the high mountain peak.
Having cultivated through many lifetimes to become a man of leisure, he refuses to be bound by empty fame. I...
I do not slight you. From others, one may receive spittle in the face; how much time can one truly gain even in a hundred years? Why must you insist on distinguishing between "yours" and "mine"?
Be poor, and there is no need for worry; be rich, and stop putting on airs. King Yama sends his invitation to all, regardless of kinship or distance.
Committing everything to a single mass of red flames, one gains mastery over oneself; one will never follow the wind and let the rudder drift. To patch what is torn and ward off the cold is enough;
with plain rice and coarse tea, pass the time as circumstances allow. I compose songs of leisure and sing them myself, singing and harmonizing my own tune.
It is not that I am a man of leisure who refuses to work; how many truly idle people are there in this world? (From Jìngshāngāo Sīyǐ)
(These were the five men).
Gōng Dūsì Liánjiè of Míngzhōu was upright and self-restrained. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* daily. Upon hearing the discourse from the hall of Tiějìng, he attained the essential point of the mind.
Once, while sitting in meditation at night, he composed a verse which said: "I have exhausted a single lamp of oil at my mountain window; the hearth stove has no—"
The fire crackled and hissed. "Leave this *huatou* to be raised again tomorrow," he said. The practitioner struck the bell and ascended the hall once more.
Because of this, Tiejing was specially praised upon his ascent to the hall. He passed away without illness; having changed his robes, he sat upright and expired.
During the cremation, his tongue-root remained unburnt (He-shan Ming succeeded him).
Chan Master Xuedou Zhutian Rulin was a native of the Wang family of Changguo. He received the tonsure and full ordination under Master Meijian Fu.
Having heard of the spiritual transformation brought about by Master Tiantong Jue, he went to attend upon him. Jue appointed him as his attendant.

One day, while in the meditation hall, Jue raised the koan of Zhaozhou’s “The dog has no Buddha-nature. At that moment, the Master attained a sudden and profound realization. Subsequently, he visited Master Yuetang Yin at...

At Lingyin, he was appointed to oversee the monastic utensils and tasked with the duties of the Record Secretary (*jishi*). Later, he traveled to Baiyang to pay his respects to Huiji, who subsequently ordered him to share the teaching seat.

He emerged from seclusion at Xuedou and later presided over Wanshou. In the fifth year of the Zhizhi era (1269), he manifested slight illness; having changed his robes and written a verse of farewell, he passed away.
His body was cremated, and five-colored *śarīra* relics were obtained. (Tiantong Jian was his successor.)
Chan Master Simin of Dayu in Daochang, Huzhou, was the son of the Zhang family of Xiangshan. He studied under Master Yin of Lingyin and immediately received his seal of approval.
Later, he went forth to reside at Baofu on Mount Damei. The Imperial Preceptor bestowed upon him the title "Buddha-Mind Mingmiao.
In the third year of the Zhishun era, the Guangjiao Prefecture appointed him as abbot of Shuanglin. In the second year of the Yuantong era, the Provincial Administration selected him to reside there.

At the Dharma Hall, he addressed the assembly: "This matter is like an iron wall or a silver mountain; it is like a great mass of fire. One cannot approach it, nor can one avoid it. How will you all deal with it?

(Xueqiao Xin’s verse says: "North and south, no gate, the road is blocked; for even a hair's breadth, the master is attacked by thieves.

Even if host and guest are both scattered like stars, it is much like willow catkins chasing the morning wind. Chaozong Ren’s verse says: "The moon has fallen, the frosty sky, the night is cold; the scaled fish pierces the net in a vast, surging wave. When will the pillow falling to the ground be awakened? This realization comes from what was before.")

[He was] deceived by his own awakening. He lived at Longxu for nine years, binding together wood to make a hut. Wind pierced it and the sun scorched it; through winter and summer he wore but a single robe.
Without a fan or a brazier, he daily pounded pine needles to mix with his gruel, merely sustaining his life.

In the spring of the Bingzi year of Deyou, when the great army reached Shuangji, the Master sat upright behind his closed door, unperturbed. Once the situation had settled, visitors arrived in crowds at his door; the Master packed his belongings into a cloth bag.
He fled under the cover of night and went straight to Lion Rock (Shiziryan) at West Tianmu. The rock rises a thousand *ren* from the ground, with cliff-stones standing like a forest.
The Master immediately established a small chamber about one *zhang* square within the cave and inscribed it as the "Death Barrier" (*Siguan*).

He completely discarded all attendants and finery; using a broken jar as a cauldron, he took but a single meal every two days. The cave was reached by climbing a mountain ladder, so that even his disciples rarely caught sight of him. Together they built...
The Lion Hall invited the Master to open the hall for formal teaching. At that time, Xueyan Qin had sent from Dayang a bamboo whisk and a fly-whisk to the Master;
the Master then took up the incense and ascended the hall. A monk asked: "The ten directions gather together as one; each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas;
with an empty mind, they return having passed the imperial examination. When Layman Pang spoke thus, was there still a way in which he benefited others?"
The Master said, "There is. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, which phrase is it? The Master said, "Ask from the beginning.
[The monk] asked, "What is 'the assembly of the ten directions gathering together'? The Master said, "Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary people and sages are mixed together.

[The monk] asked, "What is 'every single one studying non-action'? The Master said, "Mouth swallowing Buddhas and patriarchs; eyes overshadowing heaven and earth. [The monk] asked, "What is 'selection'?"

"Buddha-field. The Master said, "Ten thousand *li* from east to west, eight thousand from south to north. [The student] asked, "What is it like to return with 'passing the examination' through the emptiness of mind?

The Master said, "Moving one's countenance to reveal the ancient path; not falling into the mechanism of silent stillness. [The student] said, "If that is so, then every word reveals the ultimate truth."
"Every word flows toward the source. The Master said, "Where have you seen this? The monk gave a shout. The Master said, "This too is like swinging a staff at the moon.
[The monk] said, "Let us set aside this matter for now. But as for today at West Peak, where the ten directions have gathered and the Field for Selecting Buddhas has opened—"
“What ultimate auspicious signs are there? The Master said, “Mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the myriad phenomena stand in dense array.
Sentient and insentient beings alike all attain Buddhahood. [The student] asked, “Since all have already attained Buddhahood, for what reason do I, a student, not attain Buddhahood?
The Master said, “If you were to attain Buddhahood, how could you cause the great earth to attain Buddhahood? [The student] asked, “Ultimately, where does my fault lie? The Master said:
To the south of Xiang and north of Tan, there was a student named Huanxu who asked, "Is there no repentance? The Master said, "Prostrate yourself.
The monk prostrated. The Master said, "A lion bites; a Korean hound chases after clods of earth. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The realms of boundless lands..."
Self and others are not separated by even the tip of a hair; ten thousand ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from this very moment of thought.
It is just as when I, this mountain monk, dwell daily within Zhanggong Cave—lying down horizontally or vertically, sometimes singing and sometimes chanting.
Do you all know this? Every day, while you are in the field where Buddhas are chosen, walking east and west, sometimes angry and sometimes joyful, the mountain...
Does the Sangha still understand? If both parties understand, one cannot avoid being split into many bodies to be pounded in mortars, or having one’s tongue pulled out and plowed over.
If neither understands, take it for granted that Śākyamuni will fold his hands in submission and Maitreya will take refuge [in them]. Why is this so?
I do not see the Way. The single word "knowing" is the gateway to all calamities. [Ascending the hall: The entire world of the ten directions is this very alms bowl.
You people, when you eat gruel or rice, it is within this; when you defecate or urinate, it is within this;
walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—even a single movement or a moment of stillness—all are entirely within this. If you recognize this...
[He] attained [it]. Master Dharma would have served you as nothing more than a foot-washing slave. If you do not recognize this, with what will you eat your morning and evening gruel?
*Chan* (Investigation). Addressing the assembly: The mud ox at the bottom of the sea chews the moon as it runs;
The stone tiger before the cliff cradles its cubs as it sleeps. An iron snake drills into the diamond eye; Kunlun rides an elephant while a heron leads the way. This...
Within these four lines, there is one line that can both grant and take away, kill and bring to life. If a person can discern this, the task of their lifelong study is complete.

(The Master of Gunan said: "I, too, have four lines: At the fifth watch, the bell strikes and feet hit the ground; at the third watch, the board is struck and the dog barks; twice daily, the gruel and rice dampen the spoons and chopsticks;

at midnight, the session ends and frost sprinkles the covers. Among these four lines, one line is total function, one line is total essence, one line is total essence which is itself function, one line is total function which is itself essence, and one line is essence.)

"By means of dual forgetting, one proceeds freely and spontaneously; proceeding freely and spontaneously, one forgets. If anyone can discern this, then I invite you to return home and sit in peace. [He] addressed the assembly:

"The hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, the patriarchs of successive generations, and even the old monks throughout the land—all of them, by striking the meditation seat once with their whisk, have fallen into pits and ravines right here.
Is there anyone who can leap out? [He] struck it again. Three lives, six..."
Ten Kalpas ○ The Master once presented six questions for inquiry within his quarters. The first was: "A person who has attained ultimate penetration is fundamentally liberated from birth and death;
why then is their life-root not severed? The second was: "The public cases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are all but a single principle."
First: Why is there clarity and lack of clarity? Second: A great practitioner of the Way should follow the conduct of the Buddha; why then do you not observe the *vinaya*? Third:
When the bright sun is in the sky, there is nowhere it does not illuminate; why then is it obscured by a single fragment of cloud? Fourth: [Why is this so?]
The fifth [question]: Every person has a shadow that never leaves them for even a single step; why then can it not be stepped upon? The sixth [question]:

The entire great earth is a pit of fire; what samādhi must one attain so as not to be burned? If your response does not accord with the truth, the door shall be closed and no further reception granted.
Unless one possesses the eye that penetrates the barrier, few will not retreat in dismay at the precipice. —By Heisha Juti.
He traveled to Mount Ju to pay his respects and offered vast estates to support the assembly. The Master firmly declined and would not accept them.

Qu urged him to petition the authorities, whereupon a separate Chan monastery was established on Lotus Peak called Dajue. It was proposed that the annual income be used to provide for the permanent endowment, and that Master Zu Yong, the successor in the Dharma lineage, be requested to take charge of the temple affairs.
The Master had suffered from a stomach ailment for some time; just as Zu Yong came to visit him, the Master entrusted him with [his final instructions].
Regarding his final affairs: on the first day of the twelfth month of the Yizhi year of the Yuanzhen era, at dawn, he ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying:
"For thirty years at Xifeng, I have vainly discoursed upon Prajñā; my offenses fill the heavens.
Yet, in this final phrase, I dare not burden you all—I shall take it upon myself alone. He paused for a long while and said: "A hair’s breadth..."
There was a difference. Heaven and earth were as far apart as the poles. Between the hours of *chen* and *si*, he again spoke a verse:

"Coming, one does not enter the barrier of death; Going, one does not exit the barrier of death. An iron snake drills into the sea, Toppling Mount Sumeru. Then there was profound stillness. (Yangshan Qian succeeded him.)
Chan Master Xugu Hiling of Mount Jing was styled Xibai. He was the son of the He family of Yiwu.
Though his family was poor, he applied himself to study with great diligence and aspired to enter government service. One night, he dreamed that he entered the Hall of Arhats at Jingci Monastery;

having reached the southeastern corner, a Venerable One pointed to a poem between the lintel and the beam and showed it to him, which read: "A single chamber, vast and silent, opens upon the summit; several peaks are like a painting."
Green as moss. Having casually finished copying the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* from the *Pāṭala* leaves, he himself cut and tailored a cassock of a hundred patches.
From this, he developed the resolve to leave the secular world; at the age of nineteen, he shaved his head. Later, he visited Chan Master Gaofeng of Mount Yunfeng at Jingshan.

Their spiritual resonance and dialogue were in perfect accord, and Gaofeng held him in high esteem, appointing him to manage the library keys. Subsequently, he was appointed to share the teaching seat. He passed through various monastic appointments until he attained his position.
Yangshan was summoned for an audience by Emperor Yuan Shizu. His preaching of the Dharma accorded with the Emperor’s wishes, and he was granted the title Fojian.

Under Emperor Chengzong, his title was augmented to Dayuan; by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Mount Jing. Under Emperor Renzong, his title was further augmented to Huizhao. While turning the *Tripitaka* scriptures during a formal assembly, a monk asked:
"The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. This is the Thusness..."
"What? the Master asked. "A relative does not present a gift," the monk replied, and he prostrated himself. The Master said: "The Tathāgatas of the past have already perfected this gate;
the Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter into perfect clarity; those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this very Dharma.
Just as the past mind cannot be apprehended, the present mind cannot be apprehended, and the future mind cannot be apprehended—"

It can be attained. Since the three periods of time cannot be attained, upon what can one rely? If you know where to return here, your exhalation will not involve external conditions, and your inhalation will not dwell within the realms of the aggregates.
One constantly turns such a sutra as this, hundreds of thousands of ten-thousands of millions of scrolls.

Just as today, when the donor has invited the assembly of one thousand seven hundred at Mount Jing, that which is being turned over—does it exist within the hundreds of thousands of millions of scrolls or not?
If it exists therein, one grasps at the mark of dharmas; if it does not exist therein, one grasps at the mark of non-dharmas.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If one grasps at the mark of dharmas, one is attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span."
If one grasps at the marks of what is not the Dharma, one is immediately attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
At precisely what moment could there be anyone capable of definitively resolving this? If it cannot be definitively resolved, I shall come to you tomorrow to explain it.

On the twelfth day of the fourth month in the Renxu year of the Zhi Zheng era, he wrote these words by hand as a final entrustment, spoke a verse, and passed away. He was posthumously honored with the title "Dabian" (Great Discernment), and a stupa was erected for him.
He was called Baohua. His *Puyuan ji* (Collected Works from the Waterfall Cliff) and his recorded sayings (*yulu*) circulate in the world (he was a successor of Yangshan Qin).
Chiding Chan Master Iron Ox of Lingyun in Hengzhou was the son of Wang Shi of Panxi in Taihe; he was the ninth-generation descendant of the late Song Dynasty Minister Wang Zhi.
From childhood, he was austere, upright, and possessed aspirations beyond the mundane world. At the age of thirty, he went to pay his respects...
Xifeng Ken’an cut his hair and received the essential teaching of the separate transmission. He subsequently relied upon Xueyan Qin, serving in the fodder shed and practicing the dhūta austerities.

One day, Qin addressed the assembly, saying: "Brothers, when you practitioners apply yourselves to the work of cultivation, if for seven days and nights you maintain a single thought without interruption and yet find no point of entry, then chop off my head to make a dung-scoop! The Master remained silent.

He roused himself with diligent effort. Because he suffered from dysentery, he strictly prohibited all medicinal decoctions, tonics, and drinks. Maintaining right mindfulness alone, his eyes did not blink for seven days.
At midnight, he suddenly perceived that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth throughout the entire realm were like snow;

his own person was majestic and sublime, such that heaven and earth could not contain it. After a short while, hearing the sound of wood being struck, he attained sudden enlightenment, and his entire body...
Sweat poured from him, and his illness was cured. At dawn, he went to the abbot’s quarters and recounted this to Xuefeng Qian. Qian questioned him repeatedly, and subsequently ordained him as a monk.
One day, while Qian was ascending the hall, he raised the question: "When a deceased monk has died and been cremated, where has he gone? Qian provided the verse in his own place:
"Mountains, rivers, and the great earth / Fully reveal the body of the Dharma King. Upon hearing these words, the Master’s doubts were completely dispelled.

He immediately stepped out from the assembly, prostrated, and said, "Just now, when the Master expounded upon Prajñā, the stone lion in front of the Dharma Hall was so startled that it danced with laughter without ceasing.
Yunqin said, "Try to say something about it. The Master replied, "When spring returns beyond the kalpas, all things emerge from their withered state."
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—there is not a single speck of dust. How can one speak of the Dharmakāya’s transcendence?
It makes the blue-eyed barbarian of the Western Heaven laugh to tears. Yanguan Qin struck the sounding block and said, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—there is not a single speck of dust.
What is this? The Master made a gesture as if to overturn it. Qin laughed and said, "One win, two wins. Later, while Qin was making a circuit of the hall, the Master wrapped himself in a paper quilt.

He was lying down with his body stretched out. When invited to the Abbot’s quarters, [Deshan] spoke in a stern voice: "I was inspecting the hall when you were sleeping. If you can speak a word, I shall let you go;
if you cannot, you shall be driven down the mountain. The Master replied spontaneously: "The iron ox has no strength and is too lazy to plow the fields;
with its tether and plow, it sleeps amidst the snow. The great earth, all white silver, covers everything; Deshan has nowhere to find him."
He lowered his golden whip. Qin remarked, "What a fine iron ox! Consequently, he took this as his title. Among his contemporaries, there was none who did not respect and submit to him.
In the year of Renyin during the Dade era, as he was about to pass away, an attendant monk requested parting words. The Master said, "I have been leaving for a long time."
He passed away sitting peacefully. His entire body was enshrined in a ceramic reliquary. After three years had passed, his countenance remained as if alive; his nails and hair had both grown long.

Later, he was interred in a stupa at Satam on the north side of the monastery (Yanshan Qinsi [was his successor]). His disciple Bieliu Jing traveled to Zhejiang to visit the statesman Yu Jiji, seeking an inscription for the master’s stupa.

Yu asked, "Was there first the iron ox, or was there first the cowherd? Jing replied, "My late master personally saw Yanshan coming. Yu nodded and smiled, saying, "I shall try to sketch this out for you. Master Tianru composed a verse which says: "The iron ox—who came after, and who came before?"

"Previously, when the mouth was forever open, one lacked the single punch of a good text; having fashioned it into a mere sketch, it was wrongly transmitted as 'plowing the furrows and pulling the harrows'.
Chan Master Tieshan Qiong of Cihua in Yanzhou left home at the age of eighteen and first visited Master Xueyan Qin.
One day, while in his room, he brought up the karmic account of Prince Nalaka: "He split his bones to return them to his father; he split his flesh to return it to his mother.
He attained a realization and composed a verse, saying: "A single blade of grass manifests a jade tower; Awareness pierces the idle topic of past and present.
Lifting up the moon atop Mount Jiyun, I toss it before people like a hundred-flower ball. Qin Shen approved of this. [He then] visited Dongyan.
Dong asked, "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. Elder, how do you understand this? The Master said, "To cry out for injustice while clutching one's stolen goods.
Dong said, "It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, and it is not a thing. What is it? The Master said, "A hawk from Liaotian bursting forth between the eyebrows.
[He] ascended the hall and said: "If winter falls at the beginning of the month, sell the blanket to buy an ox. If winter falls at the end of the month..."
"Selling the ox to buy a blanket. Zuo strikes his staff. "Here there is no tail and no head; midway, all is brought to rest.
Walking, rest and rest; sitting, rest and rest; staying, rest and rest; lying down, rest and rest. When the eyes of sleep open wide, the five clouds manifest auspicious signs.
Radiant wind and clear moon reach everywhere. A plum blossoms on a withered branch by the ancient ferry; before the wind, it appears again and again."
A dark fragrance floats. Although one has arrived here, as for the upward path—ten thousand *li* to Yuzhou—how can it be seen? Relying on the staff.
Enough, enough. Later, he passed away and was interred in a stupa behind the Guanyin Pavilion (Yangshan Qin was his successor).
Chan Master Tianyin Muchuan Yuanzhi of Nengren Monastery in Jianchang was a native of Gaoyang. His surname was Yao; both his father and elder brother were distinguished jinshi scholars.
The Master aspired to the school of emptiness and, at the age of nineteen, shaved his head and donned the monastic robes. During the Yuanzhen era, he went forth to reside at Nengren Monastery.
Together with Fenggong Miaoxiu, he received the transmission and seal of approval from Yangshan. Among his writings is the *Muchuan Ji*. His "Parting Verses for Miaozhi" [are as follows]:...
The "Preface to Entering Zhejiang" states briefly: In the past, when Master Yue of Long’an led the assembly at Dongshan, he still considered his own realization of the Way to be incomplete.
He therefore concealed his identity and went out in secret to seek it amidst the common acts of eating, drinking, laughing, and conversing.
Upon hearing a single extraordinary word from Master Su, he humbled himself and lowered his status, walking alone to pay his respects with inquiries, never regarding this as a degradation.
This is called "displeasure. Yet, in the space of a single conversation, he was able to fulfill what [Sù] desired for the rest of his life.
How could this be merely the case with Yún'ān’s Way? It ensured that Sù would not have relied on Yuè to be known to the world;
had it not been so, the world would never have recognized what kind of person he was. For fame is the outward manifestation of the Way. Those of antiquity possessed this manifestation.
Thus, one should seek the substance to respond to it. Yet the scholars of today, on the contrary, allow the outward form to harm the substance.

Once they occupy a name, the power of their exalted status becomes so haughty that it cannot be bent; even if they inwardly measure themselves and find it unsatisfactory, how would they ever deign to lower their minds to seek what they have not yet attained?
Alas! This is why the ancients and the moderns differ, and why the Way has come to be as it is.
[He] declined. In the third year of the Daida era (Wuxu), he passed away at Mount Lu (the above five individuals were succeeded by Yangshan Qian).
Zen Master Zhuwu Jian offered this verse regarding the karmic conditions of the Elder Fu’s "Sacred Arrow": "Two green silk reins bit the jade-colored steed;
A pale white spring robe was encircled by a green sash. Returning at midnight beneath the flowers and the moon, The golden whip struck down [the blossoms]."
"Scattered red petals fly... It is also said: "Within the nine-layered city, it is not at all remote; shot through layer after layer, the arrows are doubly abundant.
Suddenly encountering the place where the three armies surround, there is clearly a road that leads straight to the heavens. He cites the *gong'an* of Linji visiting Pingtian and offers this verse:
"The path before one's eyes is as level as a whetstone; why do you not stride forth with dignity, arms akimbo? To provoke [the mind]..."
The old wife’s ox-nature has been aroused; she stands naked, enduring the blows—how pitiable! (Duanqiao Lun’s lineage).
Chan Master Juexiang showed the assembly, citing the time when Dongshan was unwell and sent a novice monk to Yunju to deliver a message.
He instructed him, saying: "If he asks whether the Master is at ease, you should simply say: 'The road to Yunyan is about to be cleared.'"
"It is cut off! You have spoken these words; you must step back and stand at a distance, for I fear he will strike you. The śrāmaṇera took his instructions and departed.
Before the sound of his voice had even faded, he was already struck with a staff by Yunju. The verse says: "The path to Dongshan leads through Yunyan."

At the point of utter severance, teaching penetrates; it is difficult for one to reach this state. Only when the living eye opens at the tip of the staff does one realize there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation.
[The Master] addressed the assembly, citing Master Tiance Huizhong: He asked a monk, "It has rained well these past few days; tell me, from where does the rain come? The monk had no reply.
Later, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he attained realization and composed this verse: "Travelers on the crossroads compete to gather [the flowers];"
Fragrance. Unaware that spring has passed before one's eyes. Last night, a sudden rain shower of falling blossoms;
the fragrance of flowing water fills over a hundred cities. (Lun Si of Duqiao)
One day, Chan Master Bao of Fangshan at Ruiyan in Taizhou hung up the sign for the private interview with the assembly.
He posed a koan, saying: "When Nanquan cut off the cat, what was it like? The assembly offered various responses, none of which were acceptable.
A servant standing nearby remarked, "The rat has grown too large. The Master laughed and said, "What an excellent turn of phrase! It is only that it should not have come from your mouth."
Regarding the needle-worker Ding Sheng from Li: Having long relied upon the Master’s presence, he hoped to clarify his fundamental nature.
One day, while trimming a crystal lamp, he attained realization. He composed a verse and presented it to the Master, saying: "Lift it up, lift it up! Let it go, let it go!

This single point of radiance illuminates heaven and earth. The Master rejoiced in the purity and simplicity of his practice and thus granted him certification. [The Master] then instructed him on non-seeing.
The verse says: The Wayman has managed to emerge from the mountains; He opens his entire heart to me.
Level and smooth as a mirror’s surface, Clear and profound, utterly free of even a speck of dust. Suddenly he finds a phrase for turning about; Rolling up his robe like cold clouds, he departs.
Upon the Eighty-thousand-fathom Flower-Crest Peak, A single laugh tears open the iron mask. One's own mountain.
Upon arriving, all thought ceases; one breaks off a withered vine to lean against the bamboo door. Buried within the manure and soil, the news is good:
when the taro is fragrant, it is the time when the Way is fragrant. (Duanqiao Lun’s Succession)
Master Yongzongben ascended the hall and presented the public case of Jia Shan’s visit to Master Chuanshi. He offered this verse:
"In laughter, he abandoned Zhulin Temple; I thought there was so much more at Huating. His wretched life was lost beneath the oar."
It appears that success or failure depends on Xiao He (the four individuals above, including Duanqiao and Lunsi).
Zen Master Zhong of Yueting at Mount Jiang in Jinling raised the following case: A monk asked Baiyun, "The old year has passed and the new year has arrived;
what is the meaning of 'non-transmigration'? Baiyun replied, "Eyebrows are above the eyes. The verse says: "Ceasing fishing, he returns..."
Coming, one does not moor the boat; when the moon sets over the river village, it is precisely the time for sleep.

Even if a night wind should blow it away, it remains only by the shallow waters among the reeds. Fallen leaves have already followed the flowing stream; the spring breeze has not yet released the hundred flowers.
The face of the green mountains remains as it was, spread out all day long facing the setting sun. (Wuxue Yuansi)
Chan Master Jianyan Zhuyuan Miaodao of Suzhou Kunshan was the son of the Chen family of Ninghai. In his youth, he suffered from an ailment in his right eye.
His mother took him to pray before an image of Avalokiteśvara; looking up at the image, the Master saw a small spider’s nest in the right eye of the statue.
He removed it, and the eye ailment was subsequently cured. His parents, believing that he had a karmic affinity with the Buddha, sent him to the Six... in Hangzhou.

Hezheng Yan received the full precepts. Yan ordered him to study the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas). The Master said, "If you do not study even a single dharma, how can you study the hundred dharmas?
He then went to visit Master Yongming Yunguang of Yuwang Monastery. Upon hearing the master cite the koan of "Dry Shit Paddle," he attained sudden and great enlightenment.
He immediately spoke this verse: "Yunmen’s dry shit paddle, its radiance illuminates the ten directions. As soon as I set foot upon Mount Mao, I have reached Qiantang in five days."

Tang Gong was struck with wonder and, looking at the assembly, said, "This boy is a man of rebirth. In the year Yichou of the Zhizhi era (1265), he went forth to preside over Ciyuan in the district, and later moved to Jianyan in Kunshan.
One evening, while gathering with the assembly for tea, he raised the story of when the Layman东坡 (Sūndō) visited Chan Master Shuiquan of Jiangshan.
The Master asked, "What is the noble surname of this great Confucian? The Layman replied, "My surname is Chéng. The Master said, "That is..."
"What kind of scale is this? the scholar asked. The Master said, "It is the scale for weighing the tongues of the elders throughout the world.
Jianquan then gave a shout and said, "Now tell me, how much does this one shout weigh? The scholar was speechless. The Master ordered the assembly to provide a response on his behalf.
At that moment, Biyuan suddenly rose and trimmed the candle. The Master smiled and said, "Master Biyuan trims the candle; one attendant coughs; one monk requests the Master [to speak]."

When his successor was appointed, the Master said: "It will not exceed this. Emperor Renzong issued an edict appointing him to Huangyan Hongfu Monastery and conferred upon him the title Dinghui Yuanming (Cultivated Wisdom Perfectly Enlightened).
Both Lingyin and Jingci monasteries vied to invite him there, but he declined both offers. He lived past the age of seventy.
Embracing the profound seclusion of the purple sheath, he then went there to spend his final years (Yuwang Hong succeeded him).
At the age of thirteen, Chan Master Gulin Qingmao of Baoning in Jinling became a full monk.
Upon hearing an elder monk cite the words of Master Ga’nan encouraging the clergy, tears fell uncontrollably from his eyes; he then realized the possibility of transcending birth and death.

A single stroke unites the sage and the ordinary person. With his resolve tempered, he traveled extensively to visit various masters. When Hengchuan resided at Yuyang Monastery, the Master went there to call upon him and received the Dharma.
He later stayed at Baoning Monastery in Jinling. Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked: "A hair swallows the vast ocean; a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru."
"This is a matter within the province of a patch-robed monk; this is not a matter within the province of a patch-robed monk. The Master said, "Remove that great mountain at the gate.
[The student] said, "When the whale swallows the ocean until it is empty, the coral branches are revealed. The Master said, "An iron caltrop behind the head of Vajrapāṇi.
[The student] said, "As for what is said in the scriptures: 'I have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention; among men, I am the foremost.'"
"What is the samādhi of non-contention? The Master said, "I give you thirty blows. The monk said, "Benevolence and righteousness are both severed where poverty lies;
worldly sentiments lean toward those with wealth. The Master said, "Those who recognize kindness are few; those who betray it are many. [Ascending the hall:
"If I were to speak of the Buddha-dharma as an offering to the assembly, your beards and eyebrows would inevitably fall out. If I were to speak of worldly matters..."
To offer the Dharma to the great assembly is like being shot by an arrow into hell. Departing from these two paths, what can ultimately be said?
"The tongue on one's three-inch head has no place to use; a pair of empty hands cannot form a fist.

[He] ascended the hall and, citing an occasion when Dongshan was eating pastries during a winter night, asked the Head Seat Tai: "There is a thing that reaches up to support the heavens and down to support the earth..."
Dizang said, "The ground is black as lacquer; it is constantly within the midst of activity, yet it cannot be grasped within the midst of activity.
Where does the fault lie? Tai replied, "The fault lies within the midst of activity. Shanshan then called for his attendant to remove the fruit table.
The Master said, "As for these words, throughout the various quarters today, whenever winter nights arrive, they have never failed to bring them up for commentary and explanation. However—"
Regarding the main text, not a single word has ever been spoken there. Some say, "Dongshan saw only the sharpness of the chisel-tip, but did not see the squareness of the chisel-handle;
why does he suppress and distort people? Others say, "The Head Seat Tai was unable to eat the fruit."
For now, those among the people of the great earth may all not eat it; those who complete it are few, while those who ruin it are many.
Little do they realize that Dongshan possesses the skillful means of shifting between the partial and the absolute (*bianzheng huihu*), a way of acting that does not err.

Even if the Head Seat Tai were to say, "It is not within the sphere of active function," one still could not eat his fruit. After a long silence, [Dongshan] said: "The flowing water and yellow leaves—whence have they come?"
At the dwelling, a cow and a flock of crows pass by another village. New Year’s Eve Small Assembly: Tonight, the year ends, the month ends, and the day ends.
Worldly affairs drift on endlessly; when will they ever come to an end? Tomorrow, the year is new, the month is new, and the day is new.

Amidst a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, all is seen anew. Therefore it is said: "When exhausted, there is change; through change, there is penetration. Casting the hook across the four seas, one seeks only the dragon.
Fierce dragons! As for the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices, you people certainly do not know them.

If you can achieve harmony between voice and resonance, each guarding the ancestral fields and gardens, and knowing that rice is made from grain, you will avoid extinguishing our lineage at the hands of blind donkeys.
(He plants his staff. No one has recognized the labor of past horses in sweat; we only wish to re-examine the merit that covers the ages.
The Master authored the *Continuation of the Essentials of the Chan School* (*Xu Zongmen Tongyao*), which remains in circulation. Later, he passed away at Baoning (succeeded by Yuyang Huiyong).
Chan Master Tianyi Dujiang Jue’en of Yuezhou was of the Gu clan of Cixi. In his youth, he relied upon Yunmen Guangxiao to receive the tonsure.
He followed the Dharma Master Wenhui of Yanqing to study the *Fourfold Ritual of the Teachings* (*Sijiaoyi*), mastering it thoroughly in seven days, to the great amazement of Wenhui.
Filled with admiration, he went to visit Master Yuyang. In the meditation hall, their spiritual resonance was perfectly attuned.

One day, while the assembly stood waiting in attendance, the Master suddenly leaned on his staff and said, "An old monk, hollow and weathered, leaning upon his cane; this clearly portrays Subhūti. He looked left and right and asked, "Do you understand?
After a long silence, he cast down his staff, leaned back against his meditation cushion, and passed away. (Master Yuyang Hong succeeded [to Dahui]; the four mentioned above are now complete.)
Chan Master Dehai of Dongyu in Lingyin, Hangzhou, was the son of the Chen family of Linhai, Taizhou.
At the age of fourteen, he left the household life and went to visit Shilin Gong at Chengtian Temple. Gong asked, "What is your own self? The Master hesitated.
Gong pushed him out. The Master immediately harbored a doubt. One day, during a period of private instruction, Gong asked, "The entire great earth is the true body of the Vajra;

where would you place the Venerable? As the Master was about to respond, Gong struck him. From that moment, he attained thorough realization. When Gong moved to Jingci Monastery, he appointed the Master to serve in the administrative office (*shisi*).
One day, in the meditation hall, Gong raised the story of the National Teacher’s three calls to his attendant. The Master said:
"It is not that you have lost the cat; it is certainly that you have lost the dog. Gong asked, "Is this a betrayal? Is this not a betrayal?
The Master said, "Deceiving others and deceiving yourself. Gong struck him with his bamboo staff and said, "The one who will carry on our lineage is Hai.
In the twenty-seventh year of the Zhizhi era (1290), he entered the world at Hanyan in Tiantai and later moved to Hanshan in Gusu, Kunshan.
Shandong Chan. Imperially bestowed with a golden-embroidered Dharma robe. In the second year of the Yanyou era, he was summoned by imperial decree to preside over Jingci Monastery.

Upon arriving at the mountain gate, he said: "The Pure Gate of Compassion; a single lake of autumn water. To enter or not to enter? A tiger bites a tiger; a snake swallows a turtle’s nose. He shouted, "Tou!
In his meditation hall, he gave this hanging word: "One holds a sharp sword in hand; for what reason does one [act] thus?"
The monkey does not die; it bites through the iron sour dumpling. Why, then, are there hungry people on the road? The Persian takes off his hat; he bites the sweet tip of the sugarcane.
Fish take water as their life; why, then, do they die within the water? When the assembly offered answers, none were in accord.
In the second year of the Taiding era, he moved again to Lingyin Monastery. In the fourth year, the Dingmao year, in the ninth month, he manifested a slight illness and summoned his younger brother.
Having finished his final instructions to his disciples, he passed away while seated in the full lotus posture. He was posthumously granted the title Chan Master Mingzong Huiren.
His recorded teachings comprise six assemblies. His stupa is located at the foot of the Rear Mountain of Yuwang (Jingci Monastery, Gong Sisi).
Chan Master Zhuyun Jingtan of Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing was the son of the Yan family of Putiang.
Having long relied upon Shilin, he later resided at Zhiping in Wuzhou, Beichen in Suzhou, and Tianning in Huzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "The golden crow rises in the east;
the jade hare sinks in the west. Clever monks search here and there. Suddenly, they smash through empty space, and for vast eons..."
Nowadays, Zhuo sets down his staff (Jingci Gongsi).
Chan Master Shouyong of Dongshan at Suzhou Huqiu sent this verse for a departing monk: "Movement and stillness have never involved entanglements;
why need one further penetrate that which precedes birth? Returning now to my old garden a thousand miles away—on land there is the journey, on water..."
The lay practitioner Zhang Yi of Yuozhai composed a verse on entering the Way, which says: A single blow of the bell reaches the ear-roots;
The ocean of three thousand worlds is suddenly darkened. The thief departs from the side of the bare flesh-ball;
Tomorrow, as before, it does not leave the gate. (Gong Si of Jingci; the three above.)

Chan Master Jingfu of Huarui at Mount Jinshan in Zhenzhou was a native of Huai’an. During the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty, he was summoned for an audience and presented an *gāthā* to the Emperor, of which the following is an excerpt:
“The Tathāgatas of the past dwell securely within the secret treasury; The Buddhas of the ten directions in the present have realized the Way and turned the wheel of Dharma;
All sentient beings are the World-Honored Ones of the future— This is due to the grasping of delusive appearances.”
Attached to the fetters, afflictions, hindrances, and entanglements, they wander in delusion through the bodies of the six realms, needlessly suffering the pains of the three miserable paths.
They think only of the Buddhas of the past and present, yet fail to revere the Honored Ones of the future; thus they harbor enmity toward the Buddhas.

Some even slaughter and cook living beings, failing to realize that the characteristics of sentient beings are entirely the body of *dharmatā*. In the past, there was one named Never-Disparaging who prostrated to all, saying, "I do not slight you."

"You! You all shall become Buddhas. If you can maintain mindfulness that both yourself and others are equally future Buddhas, your blessings and longevity will increase in this present life, and in birth after birth, you shall be born in the Buddha-lands.
Upon reading this, Emperor Shizong was greatly delighted and asked the Imperial Preceptor whether there were any among the sovereigns of past ages who had observed the precept against killing.
The Master replied, "In the past, Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty once said to his ministers: 'Last night I was very hungry and thought of eating a rabbit.'"

He had been burning sheep, but fearing the consequences for future generations, he subsequently established this as a permanent rule: "I would rather endure a temporary hunger than bear witness to endless slaughter.
The ministers all cried out "Ten-thousand-year Emperor! The Sovereign graciously accepted his advice and immediately received the precepts from the Imperial Preceptor (Du Si of Jing Mountain).
A monk came for formal inquiry with Chan Master Tanzhi of Tiantong in Ningbo. The Master asked, "From where have you come? The monk replied, "Jinge (Golden Goose).
The Master asked, "How high is Jinge Mountain? The monk said, "Its peak cannot be seen. The Master rebuked him.

One day, the Master ascended the seat and presented the koan of the World-Honored One holding up a flower. At these words, the monk attained realization. (The two aforementioned individuals were successors of Duzu at Mount Jing.)
Chan Master Baoye Yuanyuan of Dingshui in Yuezhou ascended the hall and spoke. He cited the case of the scholar Zhang Zhuo, who visited Shishuang.
Shishuang asked, "What is your surname? He replied, "I am your disciple, Zhang Zhuo. Shishuang said, "In this place, 'cleverness' (zhao) cannot be found at all;

from where does 'clumsiness' (zhuo) come? At these words, Zhuo attained great enlightenment. He offered this verse: "Advancing forward, there is a precipice three thousand fathoms high; Retreating back, there is a sheer cliff."
One hundred thousand layers of preciousness. The Great Tang’s Old Zhang Zhuo: “The seamless iron hammer dances in the spring breeze” (Yusi of Mount Jing).
Chan Master Xianji Yun of Tiger Hill in Suzhou long relied upon Master Xutang at Mount Jing, where he served as the First Seat.
One day, Baoye Yuan asked Xutang Yu about the "final word" of Deshan: "If one says it exists, how could Deshan have failed to understand?
If one says it does not exist, yet Yantou said that Deshan had not yet understood. I beg the Master’s compassion to provide instruction.
Yu said, "I do not understand. Go and ask the Head Seat. Yuan went to the master, only to find him out walking in the mountains.
