He returned and sought water to wash his feet. Huizhao hurriedly brought him water; he then prostrated himself for the Master to massage him. Thereupon, looking up, he raised the previous conversation to question the Master.
The Master then took some water and splashed it on him, saying, "What is that final phrase? Huizhao did not attain realization.
Again, he went up to see Yufu. Yufu asked, "How did the Head Seat speak to you? Yuan recounted the previous conversation.
Yufu said, "Na-na! I tell you, he has understood. Thereupon, Yuan was relieved and grasped the meaning.

[The Master] cites the karmic conditions regarding the exchange of value between Master Xinghua and Emperor Zhuangzong, and offers this verse: "The King’s treasure is naturally difficult to appraise; Xinghua..."

How could I ever have dared to borrow it? Since Heaven and Earth have impartially covered and sustained all things, they have remained until today to preside over the Central Plains (Yusi of Jingshan and the two aforementioned individuals).
The Chan Master Nansou Ma once cited the story of Master Yantou, who served as a ferryman on the shores of Lake Ezu.
He hung a board on each bank; whenever someone came to cross, he would strike the board once. Yantou would then ask, "Who is it?
If someone replied, "I want to go to the other side," Yantou would row out to meet them. One day, a woman carrying a child approached and said: "Present [this]..."
"I shall not ask about the pole-dancing oarsman; tell me, from where did the child in the old woman’s hand come?

Yankuan then struck her. The old woman said, "I have given birth to seven sons; six did not meet with those who understand them. As for this one alone, he is of no use either," and she threw him into the water. The verse says:
"The destitute ghost-child at the ferry crossing of E-zhu— His entire capacity was mistaken at the moment he tapped the boat's railing."
How about adding another turn of phrase to rescue the seventh son of the old woman? [The Master] cites the story of Jia Shan’s visit to the Boatman Monk, and offers this verse:
"Formless and flawless, he immediately turned his spear back; It was only because he lightly trusted the monk Zhi."
"If you do not return to Huating, what can a boat oar cast of iron do for you?
[Case] Layman Pang was selling his fish-trap fence when he fell down the bridge. Seeing this, his daughter Lingzhao also went and fell beside her father. The Layman asked, "What are you doing?
The girl said, "Seeing my father fall, I went to support him. The Layman said, "Fortunately, no one saw us. The verse says: Filial piety.
Conceal a rebellious child; do not hide a deformity before others. Those who are close kin in this life were enemies in past lives.
(By Jingshan Yue-si) Chan Master Dongsheng Deming of Yuyang, Ningbo, was the son of the Liu family of Yongdong. At the age of sixteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He studied under Wanjie Mi. Wanjie raised the question: "Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas; why did he emerge from the samādhi of the woman?"
"No. Wǎngmíng asked, "How did you manage to get out? The Master said, "The spring colors have no high or low; the flower branches grow long or short of their own accord.
Míqìzhī appointed him to oversee the treasury and later he took up residence at Yùwáng Monastery, where he was granted the title Fórì Pǔguāng (Sun of the Buddha, Universal Radiance).

He composed a verse on the "Boatman's Case" (Chuánzǐ Gōng'àn) which says: "In this vast, clear world, he occupies the vital ford; A single oar is his livelihood, weighing as much as a thousand *jìn*. At Zhūjīng..."
Few travelers pass on the road; the depths of the vast ocean cannot match the profundity of one’s own mind. Later, he passed away and was interred at Dongyun Pagoda (at Yuyang Monastery).
Chan Master Kongsou Xinwu of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was the son of the Niu family of Wuxian County in Suzhou. At the age of nine, he entered [the monastic order].
He received the tonsure at Longxing Temple in the prefectural city. Later, he went to attend upon Master Yuguan. When the Master questioned him, saying, "What is the essential meaning of Yongming?
the Teacher replied, "I am but a newcomer; I see only a lake. The Master approved of this and subsequently allowed him to enter his room.
At the time of his death, he wrote a verse: "At fifty-five years of age, I have trodden across the barrier of birth and death. At midnight, the sun rises."
At noon, the cremation took place. His tongue and his rosary remained unburnt. A stupa was erected on the eastern ridge of Lingyin (at Jingshan and his successor).
Chan Master Si Dao of Guangxiao in Changzhou—Dao Yan by name—was a native of Xiangcheng in Suzhou. His clan name was Yao; his childhood name was Tianxi.
At the age of fourteen, he left home to become a monk at Miaozhi Hermitage in his hometown. He studied under Yuanwu Keqin and Heshan Yuanhui of Jingshan.

Furthermore, he consulted and inquired about the essentials of Chan until he fully grasped its core essence. He held the records for three years before entering the world at Pukyeong Temple and subsequently moving to Tiantong.
He once inscribed his own portrait, saying: "Having seen through the plantain tree and the staff, I casually reveal my wind-and-flow elegance;
sometimes I shake the whisk made of tortoise-hair, until even empty space laughs and nods its head. During the Hongwu era, [he was honored by] the Emperor.

Chan Master Le was recommended to the court and served Emperor Wen at the Yan residence. During the Yongle era, he declined an official appointment on the grounds of his merit as a founder of the dynasty.
One day, the Emperor summoned him for an audience and secretly had someone clothe him in official robes and cap.

He was then promoted to the rank of Imperial Tutor (Taizi Shaoshi) and urgently ordered to announce his thanks. Reluctantly accepting the command, he nonetheless remained steadfastly unwilling to grow out his hair. He was frequently granted [gifts].
The two palace ladies could not refuse. After more than a month, she remained as pure as a maiden, so he summoned her back and no longer coerced her.
He kept a large rooster; whenever the rooster crowed, she would immediately rise and recite the sutras with clarity. Later, when the Master returned from his mission abroad, he fell ill on the road.
Upon reaching the city gate, he refused to enter and ordered his attendants to set up a tent, saying, "The Emperor is coming."
Having looked, the carriage indeed arrived. [The Emperor] treated him with the utmost courtesy and bestowed upon him a golden spittoon. He then asked what words he had to say.

The Master placed his hand upon his forehead and said, "What more could an ordained monk have to say? Thereupon, he entered nirvana. He was posthumously enfeoffed as the Duke of Rong, with the title of Posthumous Honor (Gongjing).
Later, he was accorded a place in the ancestral temple of Emperor Taizong. His remains were transferred to Daxinglong Temple for veneration. He was eighty-five years of age at the time of his death.
His collected works, the *Daoyulu*, circulate in the world. (Regarding the two masters above, Jingshan and Sisi:
Chan Master Nanshi Wenxiu of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was the son of the Li family of Kunshan. He left the household life at Shaolong Hermitage.
When Zhongren resided at Yunzheng, the Master went to follow him; their minds met like a needle and its eye. Initially, he resided at Pudu [Temple] in Suzhou.
[The Master] entered the hall. Next he moved to Lingyan, and later resided at Jingshan. He ascended the hall and said: "The ten directions have no divergent paths;

why then do you seek Tiantai in the south and Wutai in the north? Before one’s eyes there is no different grass; why then is the peach blossom red and the plum blossom white? After a long silence, he said:
"Break through the barrier of the Patriarchs, and it is all your own. [He drew a circle. Lingyan ascended the hall. To the full extent of the great...
The earth is oneself; from where do the myriad phenomena arise? To those who do not understand, I give thirty blows of the staff;
to those who do understand, I likewise give thirty blows of the staff. All quarters are thus. After the meal, he ascends the hall at Lingyan Temple;
after the session, they drink tea. Ascending the hall: Today is the first day of the seventh month; before the gate, the golden wind whistles.
Specifically beating the drum and ascending the hall, not a single word can be uttered. The pillar bows to Śākyamuni;
the lantern pays respects to Jizhí. Only the carefree monk remains, with eyes askance and nose straight as ever. I dare ask the assembly:
"Who is that monk of no affairs? After a long silence, he said: "Three feet tall. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Master Mazu said, 'Since the time of chaos, for thirty years there has been no lack of salt and sauce.
Here there is not even two ounces of gold; the layman buys three sheng of wine. A layman asked, "What is the business of the patch-robed monks? The Master said, "You are a layman."
"How can a mere man understand the affairs of the patch-robed monks' school? He asked again, "What are the affairs of the School of the Patriarchs?
The Master said, "I am busy today; I have no leisure to speak of the affairs of the School of the Patriarchs for you. As the scholar hesitated, the Master shouted him out.
As soon as the Master saw a monk enter the gate, he said, "You fellow who treads upon prefectures and counties—your heels deserve three blows!"
"Ten blows! A monk said, "I have not even asked a question, yet I have already received a blow. The Master said, "Wait until you open your mouth; what would that be worth?
The monk hesitated, and the Master shouted at him and drove him out. A monk came for an audience and spread out his sitting cloth.
The Master said, "In my place, there is no leftover soup or stale rice; there is no need to use up your worn-out cooking cloth. The monk said, "Out of compassion, O Master. The Master— [beat him].
It is said: "Laughing until he topples over the green stone pillar at the gate. The Master passed away at the age of seventy-something.

His disciples erected a *stūpa* to his left of Jizhao Pagoda. He authored the four-volume *Zengji xù chuándēng* (Continued Transmission of the Lamp with Additions), which remains in circulation. (Wanshou Rensu).

Chan Master Xibai Lijin of Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing was the son of the Yao family of Suzhou. He studied under Venerable Guding Ming, who presented him with the kōan concerning Deshan’s encounter with Longtan.

After a long period of practice, he attained realization. He subsequently took up residence at Ruiwang Monastery, where the Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the title "Complete Penetration and Universal Relief" (Yuantong Pujie).
Having lost his father in childhood, the Master lived in filial devotion, building a residence east of the city to care for his elderly mother who had no one else to rely on.
One day, he suddenly said to his attendant monk, "I have a karmic debt from a past life that remains unsettled; I must repay it. He subsequently manifested illness and passed away.
His stupa was enshrined to the west of the city of Jiaxing (the inscription for Mount Jing is recorded in the *Sishi*).
Chan Master Xiangyuan Renshu of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou was a native of Taizhou. One day, as he entered the gate, he cried out loudly, "The slaughter has arrived!
The slaughter has arrived! How will you evade it? He then sat down and passed away. (Jingshan Ming succeeded him; the two mentioned above are now complete.)
Chan Master Jueyuan Huitan of Tianjie Monastery in Jinling was a native of Tiantai. His clan name was Yang. At the age of sixteen, he became a monk and received full ordination.
Having heard that Master Xiaoyin Yun of Zhongzhu Monastery was presiding there, the Master went to visit him and inquire after the Dharma, detailing his earnest quest for the Way.
Xiaoyin rebuked him, saying: "That which enters through the gate is not the family treasure. The Way resides within oneself; why seek it from others?"
Qiu Ye withdrew and attained realization. One day, upon hearing the story of Baizhang’s Wild Fox, he was suddenly and greatly enlightened, saying:
"The Buddha-dharma has fallen into my hands! It is only because it was so extremely clear that what was to be gained was delayed.
Xing asked, "What principle have you seen? The Master spread his two hands and said, "Not worth half a coin. Xing nodded in approval. One day...
When the Master entered the gate, Xuanji asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from traveling the mountains.

Xuanji said, "When you were traveling everywhere under your straw hat, crushing through Luopo, what was that like? The Master said, "Before I had even entered the gate, I had already presented it to the Master."
Xin said, "Why do you not bring this forth right now? As the Master hesitated, Xin gave a shout. From that moment, the Master was suddenly liberated.
On another day, Xin spread out both hands and showed them to the Master, saying, "I have opened it wide with these eight characters.
Why are you unwilling to accept it? The Master said, "Do not try to weary me with such dullness. Xin said, "Come closer; I shall speak for you. The Master covered his ears.
He departed and resided at the Patriarch’s Hall on Mount Niu-tou. Ascending the hall, he said: "A single phrase—pitch black, without a handle, yet possessing a standard.
After a long silence, he asked: "Do you understand? The pestle pounds in the southeast; the millstone grinds in the northwest. Ascending the hall again, he said:
"The Sutras have masters of the Sutras; the Treatises have masters of the Treatises. Today, Longhe lets loose a single thread of the Way to divide the sections and arrange the chapters."
He held up his staff and struck it once. "Tell me, what verse or phrase is this? [Ascending the hall: "This is a ready-made case.
Among the assembly, there are many who have attained understanding, yet those who have misunderstood it are also not few. This is why gold and brass are not distinguished."
To fail to distinguish between jade and stone is a grave error; here in Longhe, we shall distinguish them directly.
"Venerable Zhang! Venerable Li! One has long arms, the other has large eyes. If it were all like the Dharma-school of Bodhidharma today, who would be able to shoulder the responsibility?
After a long silence, he let out a single sigh and descended from his seat. In the early Hongwu era, the Master went to pay his respects to the Emperor at Yuanyang.

Upon first seeing him at the gate, [the Emperor] sighed in admiration, saying, "Truly a monk of great merit. He appointed him as the abbot of Jiangshan. After more than a year had passed, the Longxiang Monastery was renamed the Great Tianjie Temple;
the Emperor issued an edict for the Master to preside over it. A grand memorial service was established, and the Master was commanded to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma.
The Imperial Carriage graced his presence, and the imperial favors bestowed were most abundant and thorough.

In the first year of the Hongwu era, he was granted purple robes and a golden-embroidered square cassock, along with an imperial edict conferring upon him the title of "Great Chan Master Who Propagates the Dharma, Benefits the World, and Exalts the Teaching.
He resided as the abbot of Great Tianjie Monastery and presided over the Buddhist affairs of all mountains. (3)

In the summer of that year, the court deliberated upon the fact that the Western Regions had not yet submitted. Since that kingdom highly esteemed the Buddha-vehicle, the Emperor specially issued an edict for the Master to go there.

Receiving this command, the Master set out on his journey that very day. From the ports of Min, through all the kingdoms and cities he passed, none failed to hear of his reputation and come to submit.
In the seventh month of the autumn of the fourth year, he arrived at the country of Harṣa (Hela), where he proclaimed the majesty and virtue of the Son of Heaven and was lodged in a guest house.

At Foshan Temple, the King treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher, attending upon him from the second watch of the night. The officials and citizens of the entire kingdom all came to gaze upon him in reverence.

In the ninth month, the Master manifested a slight illness. The king and his ministers all came to offer their condolences. After a short while, he bathed and changed his robes, saying to those around him, "My illusory conditions have come to an end;
I cannot return to life. He then passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Five days later, [the body was cremated].

The color [of the remains] was as if they were still alive. The King was filled with great reverence and admiration. He carved fragrant wood into a shrine and constructed an altar to perform the cremation.

The King and his hundred officials personally escorted [the remains] to the base of the altar. When the firewood and flames had been extinguished, the śarīras were beyond counting; the tongue, roots, teeth, and gums remained uncorrupted.
The sacred relics and the indestructible remains were collected and interred within the Śākyamuni Buddha’s stūpa in that country.

In the ninth month of the seventh year, the traveling companions returned and submitted a memorial; the Emperor sighed with grief and sorrow, and issued an edict to Zongle, the abbot of both Tianjie and Jiangshan monasteries, to receive the Master’s robes and bowl and construct a stūpa to his left on the Yuhua Terrace. Therein was established the Five-Assembly Dharma [Service].
Yuxing Shi (successor of Longxiang Xin):
Chan Master Quanshi Zongle of Tianjie Monastery in Jinling was the son of Zhou [family] from Linhai in Taizhou. At fourteen, he shaved his head;
at twenty, he received full ordination. He relied upon Xin of Zhongzhu. One day, Xin asked: "The National Teacher called out to his attendant three times—"
The attendant responded three times. "What do you think? the Master asked. Xing said, "How can you carve flesh to create a wound? The Master replied, "I took you for someone extraordinary;
it turns out you have nothing at all. The Master let out a shout. Xing prepared to strike with his staff, but the Master shook out his sleeves and departed. [Later,] he ascended the hall and said:
"When the Diamond King’s sword is brandished horizontally, a thousand demons vanish from sight; when the *śakāra* eye is pierced through, [all delusions are destroyed]."
Illumination. When the myriad things hide their forms, here it is that rolling up and unfolding rest with me; killing and giving life are applied according to the occasion.

It reaches the point where the *bèi* demon leaps within the Thousand-Year Rock, and the waters of the Qiantang River flow backward toward the Eastern Sea. Do you all know if this exists or not? Raising the whisk, [he says:
"Even the stone sprouts growing stalks in the courtyard allow one to see the phoenixes roosting on the high branches. [The Emperor] issued an edict summoning Jiang.
There were ten men from Nan Dao who traveled to the capital and held an extensive memorial Dharma assembly at Taiping Xingguo Temple, with the Master presiding at the head.

The Emperor observed the fast and purification; he composed a formal petition himself and personally arrived in his carriage, wearing a *pi-bian* cap and holding a jade *gui* tablet tucked between his girdle cords.

Facing north, he paid homage to the Buddha. The various ministers each donned their dharma robes to follow him. Previously, the Emperor had commanded the Master to compose musical pieces for offerings to the Buddha;

these were presented and received the Imperial seal of approval. The pieces consisted of eight chapters: "Benefiting the World," "Manifesting Faith," "Extending Compassion," "Dharma Joy," "Meditative Delight," "Universal Response," "Sublime Salvation," and "Perfect Achievement.
He decreed that the Bureau of Rites perform songs and dances to accompany them with rhythmic accompaniment. Furthermore, he commanded the Master to ascend [the altar].

He sat in meditation and preached the Dharma, exhausting the principles and perfecting human nature; he penetrated the fruits of the Dharma and its causes, and whether esoteric or exoteric, profound or shallow, there was no capacity for which he did not provide a remedy.

The Emperor was greatly pleased and appointed the Master as the Head of the Celestial Realm (Tianjie). The Emperor once wished to appoint the Master to office by ordering him to grow out his beard and hair, but the Master pleaded earnestly twice and was granted exemption.
Because the Master was implicated in the Hu Party, he was sentenced to a crime and dispatched to Chafeng in Fengyang to build a temple. After three years, he was summoned back.

The Emperor bestowed a poem upon him, which contained the lines: "When the Elder Le departs from here, who will inquire about Chan? Morning and evening, one should constantly contemplate that which is before one's eyes.
When Empress Gao passed away and her funeral was being held, a sudden storm with wind, rain, thunder, and lightning broke out. The Emperor was displeased and summoned the Master, asking him:
"Now the Empress Dowager is about to proceed to the tomb; please recite a verse for me to see her off. The Master replied at once: "The rain falls as heaven sheds tears;
thunder rolls as the earth raises its lament. All the sons of the Buddhas from the Western Heaven join in escorting the Tathāgata Māra. The Emperor’s mind was somewhat eased.
He was granted one hundred taels of white silver. Later, seeking retirement due to old age, he was granted leave to return to Chafeng Peak.
Crossing the river, he passed away at Shifo Temple in Jiangpu, saying to his attendants: "The birth and extinction of human beings is like a bubble on the water; as the bubble arises, it perishes."
"Returning once more to the waters—where is there that is not a place of quiescent extinction? Having finished speaking, he looked back at his attendant and said, "As for this...

The attendant was bewildered. The Master said, "Suffering," and then passed away. His cremation yielded countless relics, which were enshrined in a stūpa to the right of that of Xiaoyin Yun (the successor of Longxiang).
Chan Master Yongzhang Lanweng Tingjun occupied the seat at Zhongzhu Temple in Hangzhou.
Holding up his staff, he said, "If there were no one in this room who could realize the truth through the tip of this staff, I would swear that this staff would never be called a 'staff.

Is there such a person? He then shouted, "An imperial decree summons the flying dragon horse; a lame tortoise sticks its head out! On the anniversary of the Buddha’s Nirvana, he ascended the hall. An ancient worthy said: "Nirvāṇa..."
Behind the *pātra* is the mark of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). Śākyamuni has entered *nirvāṇa*; where, then, is the mark of a Great Man?
[The Master] drew a circle with his whisk and said, "Do you see it? His countenance was most wondrous and sublime; his radiance illuminated the ten directions.
I once made offerings to him, and now I come again to behold him in person. [He ascended the hall. "Lately, among the brothers in this assembly..."

Those who are intelligent and quick-witted are many; those who have attained thorough penetration are likewise not few. None of them fail to claim that they have grasped it within their hearts and manifested it through their hands.
When facing critical situations or encountering objects, they bring it forth with a lively, vibrant ease, without expending even a fraction of effort.
Upon arriving at Longfeng’s gate, [Longxiu] was just about to proceed from the beginning. He took up his staff and struck it once, saying: "It is like making a lamp or candle out of wax;
if one does not light it with fire, it will never shine. (In the first year of the Hongwu era, he stayed at Mount Zhong and passed away while sitting upright.
His cremation yielded countless relics, which were enshrined in a pagoda at Nanping in Hangzhou. [This concludes the lineage of Longxiang Yin.]
Chan Master Jie’an Yongzhenfu of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was a native of Wuxian County in Suzhou. He was a tenth-generation descendant of Fan Wenzheng Gong.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The single school of Bodhidharma has declined until it is nearly extinct. You must exert yourselves as if your hair were on fire.
The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable subtle meanings can all be fully understood within the tip of a single hair."
"I understand. Transform this great earth into gold; you should accept it without hesitation. Otherwise, there will be the shame of eating the bread of idleness—whom shall the blame fall upon?
Time flows like lightning. Regarding the matter of the higher path, I pray that each of you will look with urgency.

On the fifteenth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Hongwu era, he personally attended to his final affairs and said to those around him: "At the hour of the Snake (10:00 AM) tomorrow, I shall pass away."
When the appointed time arrived, he bathed, sat upright, wrote a verse of gāthā, and passed away peacefully. During the cremation, his teeth, gums, and tongue remained unburnt.
He established countless stūpas and enshrined [the relics] within the Guiyun Pagoda (the successor was Longxiang Yin).
Chan Master Chongyu of Lushan Yuantong was the son of the Chen family of Piling. He went to attend upon Xiaoyin, who questioned him with the koan of the "True Person of No Rank.
Without realizing it, the Master felt a sense of liberation and prostrated himself. Xiaoyin asked, "What did you see that you pay this homage?
The Master replied, "There is no second person. Xiaoyin said, "One who enters through the gate does not possess the family treasure. The Master...
He said, "Preceptor, be careful not to suppress the noble and degrade them to the base. Later, he resided at Nanchan, and subsequently moved to Yuantong and Yuyang.

In the autumn of the fifth year of the Hongwu era, an imperial decree was issued to summon eminent monks to hold a great assembly at Mount Zhong; the Master responded to the summons and arrived at the Private Audience Hall.

The Emperor asked about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma. The Master responded with a verse, and the Emperor was greatly pleased. He granted the Master food from before his own table. At times, the Master would nap;
when he snored, a neighbor sitting nearby drew back his legs to wake him. The Emperor laughed and said, "This old man has no artful mind; he is a true *kalyāṇamitra*.
Later, he passed away and was interred at Shier Peak (Longxiang Yin succeeded him; the five mentioned above are now complete).
Chan Master Gudong Mingde of Jingci Temple in Hangzhou was of the Zhu clan. At the age of seventeen, he received the full precepts and became a bhikṣu.
Carrying his staff, he traveled to visit various teachers; he first called on Zhuxi Tan, gaining realization upon hearing the words of his formal lecture.
He subsequently went to Jingci Temple to see Huiji. Huiji asked, "What thing comes like this? The Master replied, "Hū Zhangsan, Hē Lisi. Huiji—
He raised his staff. The Master shook out his sleeves and departed. He later returned to Shuanglin and met Mingji Jun.
When Japan sent an envoy to invite Jun, the Master escorted him as far as the seashore. There, he happened to meet the Venerable Zhutian Lin in Mingzhou.
Lin urged the Master to return to Xuedou and appointed him to the position of First Seat. One day, Lin ascended the hall and cited the story of Yishan’s “clay ox entering the water.”
The Sea Kōan: His voice was like thunder. Unconsciously, the Master’s many doubts were suddenly dispelled. He composed a verse to present to the Abbot.
Yun-lin said, "The Eye and Treasury of the Human and Heavenly Eyes remains resplendent even now. Later, when the Master manifested slight illness, he exhorted his disciples, saying:
"You all possess the one true, perfect nature; you are equal to the Tathāgata. The arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena are no different [from your own nature].

Like sparks from a flint or a flash of lightning, practice diligently day and night; do not give rise to regression. After my passing, you should follow the Buddha’s regulations and perform the cremation according to the Dharma;
do not dress yourselves in hempen garments and wail. Having finished speaking, he wrote a verse and passed away peacefully (Xuedou Lin was his successor).
Chan Master Tianguan Tieguan Fasou was a native of the Lin family of Pingyang in Wenzhou.
Having heard that Yuanweng presided over Shimen on Mount Xiuzhi, he traveled there to seek instruction. Yuanweng showed him the kōan of Nanquan’s “Three Nots.

After three years, one day he attained great enlightenment and composed a verse, saying: "Not mind, not Buddha, not thing; I have squeezed out the very bones of empty space. The golden-haired lion..."
"A lion cub—how could he cherish the den of a wild fox? He gave a shout. "Ho! Ho! Ho! Then he went straight to the abbot’s quarters.
The old man asked, "What are you doing? The Master said, "Nanquan has been caught and defeated by me.
The old man said, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. What is it? The Master said, "A set of bones for teeth; two pieces of skin for ears."
The old man said, “Not so, not so. Speak another way. The Master said, “The warblers sing and the swallows chatter; the magpies caw and the crows cry.
The old man said, “Wrong. The Master also said, “Wrong. The old man asked, “Where is Nanquan right now? The Master then gave a shout.
The old man said, "Setting aside that one shout, where exactly is Nanquan? The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
Later, he went to see Xuguleng at Dayang, but they did not reach a mutual accord. He then visited Haiyinru at Jianfu in Raozhou.
As soon as he entered the abbot’s quarters, Ru asked, "Who is it? The Master said, "I have come for a brief visit. Ru asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said—
Jiangxi. Yinyuan asked, "What has been happening recently in Jiangxi? The Master said, "The rattan vines beneath Jiyun Peak have been snapped by someone.
Yinyuan said, "Do not speak so loosely. The Master said, "If it were not for speaking so loosely, how could I have reached this place?
Yinyuan said, "Tell me then, what is the matter here? The Master stepped forward with his hands clasped and said, "On this day..."
"I respectfully wish that the Abbot, the Venerable Master, enjoys ten thousand blessings in your daily life. Yin asked, "Regarding the phrase 'not sand, not mud, not water'—how is it?
The Master gave a shout and said, "The wind follows the tiger; the clouds follow the dragon. Yin asked, "When a single shout does not function as a single shout, what is this?
The Master said, "Two earthen oxen fight their way into the sea; until this very day, there has been no sound."
Xiaoshi said, "Wrong. Yinyuan also said, "Wrong. Yinyuan called to his attendant, "Bring some tea. Xiaoshi said, "I do not accept offerings.
Yinyuan said, "If you do not accept [this] offering, what offering do you accept? Xiaoshi said, "Thank you for the Master’s offering.
Yinyuan said, "Whom have you ever met? Xiaoshi said, "I have never met anyone. Yinyuan said, "Since you have never met anyone..."
[The Master] asked, "If you have seen someone, where did you get this news? The teacher said, "If one has seen someone, then there is no such news.
Thereupon, he served diligently as the head of the purification duties. Yinzong once said to the assembly, "Attendant Shu of Yongjia is gold that has been thoroughly smelted.
Later, he traveled to Donglin and visited Zeshan Xian. He arrived just as the meditation hall was being opened for the assembly, who were being addressed by the master regarding the bamboo stick.
Before the words "causes and conditions" had even ceased, the Master snatched away the bamboo staff and stood to the left, asking, "What would you call this?
They all said, "A man who plunders the void. The Master struck them once with the bamboo staff, broke it in half, and walked out.

The following day, Xian again opened his room for instruction and raised the question: "For what reason did the Great Sage of Sizhou manifest in Yangzhou? He replied, "Clouds arise from the Southern Mountain."
"Rain falls on the northern mountain," the Master said, again seizing his bamboo staff. "Clouds rise on the southern mountain, rain falls on the northern mountain.
What is the meaning of this? Xuán gave a shout. The Master said, "This is the livelihood of one living in a ghost cave.
After all, what is the meaning? Xuán said, "A man who plunders the void. The Master struck him once with the bamboo staff and said, "I have heard that the flowers of Luoyang are like..."
Jin swept his sleeves and departed. Later, he returned to Shimen. As soon as Xìn saw him, he asked, "Where has Nánquán gone?
The Master said, "Forget about Nánquán; even Śākyamuni Buddha has arrived.
Xìn said, "It is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing—what is it? The Master said, "The sword was long ago cast away. Xìn said, "Zhàozhōu!"
"Is there not? The Master said, "A dragon gives birth to a golden phoenix chick; it breaks through the azure lapis lazuli. Xinxing said, "The ancients were like this—'Dao!
Dao! Dao! The Master gave a shout. Xinxing said, "Wrong. The Master shouted again. Xinxing said, "Wrong, wrong. The Master then prostrated himself.
Xinxing said, "I grant you thirty blows," and then he instructed him, saying, "Guard and maintain [the Dharma] well yourself. The Master then remained hidden among the assembly for ten days.

Five years later, in the *wumao* year of the Yan’yu era, he took up residence at Tianbao Monastery in Min. The Imperial Preceptor bestowed upon him the temple plaque and conferred upon him the title of Great Master Miaojue Zhenkong.
In the eighth month of the sixth year of Zhizhi, he manifested a slight illness and wrote a letter by hand, inviting all those with whom he had been close to enter the mountains.
When they arrived as scheduled, he fulfilled the requests of those seeking the Dharma according to their desires. At the end, he passed away.
Without showing any sign of fatigue, at noon he bathed and sat upright. He wrote a verse, saying: "Fundamentally there is no coming or going;
a single phrase is fully raised. Crimson clouds pierce the azure void; the bright sun circles Mount Sumeru. Having cast down his brush, he passed away. (Tianchi Xin was his successor.)
When Master Guyzhou Ji served as the First Seat under Master Yueting Zhong at Mount Jiangshan, Zhu Yuan went to visit him in the First Seat’s quarters.
Master Ji asked Yuan: "Monsan once said that the man who planted the pine trees did not grow from two conditions.
When Bodhidharma was buried at Xiongeri, his single shoe later returned to the West. Was this due to supernatural power?"
"Subtle function! This is the natural law (*dharmatā*). Yuan said, "Body and spirit are both subtle. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Not so.
You shall know this for yourself in the future. Later, when Yuan went to consult Wuneng, he brought up the Master’s words.
Wuneng said, "It was because you did not understand. At these words, Yuan was suddenly and greatly enlightened. (This is a case of a divergent lineage at Mount Meng.)
Chan Master Yongning of Longchi in Yixing, whose pen-name was Xuanhuazi, was surnamed Zhu and was a native of Tongzhou in Huaidong.
He traveled to Lake Tai in Huaixi to visit Wuyong Kuan. Kuan’s teaching style was stern and rigorous; as soon as the Master entered the gate, Kuan shouted at him in a harsh voice.
The Master prostrated himself outside the gate, and only after a long time was he permitted to enter and see him. Kuan asked: "What..."
When he was at Churen, the Master said, "Tongzhou. He asked, "How has the rise and fall been lately in Huaihai? The Master replied, "The waters drench the sun and flood the heavens;
not a single drop remains. He then gave a shout and drove him out. After the Master withdrew, he could not sleep all night.
One day, he heard Master Kuan cite the Yunmen story of Mount Sumeru. Before the sound had even ceased, he attained realization. He hurried forward, and Kuan struck him, saying, "Zhao..."
"Zhaozhou says there is no Buddha-nature—what does this mean? The Master suddenly replied: "Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature;

the myriad phenomena and the ten thousand forms all beg for their lives. An bottomless basket holds dead snakes; adding much or subtracting little leaves nothing behind. Kuān was struck with silent realization.

He served as an attendant at the Master’s side for three years. At that time, Yuanwan first took the portrait of himself that had been praised by Duanli, personally inscribed it, and presented it to the Master, saying:
"Your karmic conditions lie in the south; when you encounter a dragon, stay there. When you meet a pond, settle there. The Master then accepted this command and returned south.
In the year of the Water Pig (1323) during the Zhi-ting era, the Longchi Monastery in Yixing submitted a formal petition. The Master rejoiced that his name accorded with the prophetic record.

Nevertheless, he went there. Previously, at the summit of the mountain, there was a pool of unfathomable depth; whenever the dragon emerged, it would cause great floods, causing distress to the local inhabitants.
The Master conferred upon the dragon the Three Refuges and the Precepts, after which it never appeared again. Having lived there for some time, he returned to a remote peak and built a dwelling.
The cliffs stood as if carved by a knife; he fashioned wooden walkways and dwelt upon planks suspended in mid-air for three years, his feet never crossing the boundary.

The Emperor, having long been aware of the Master’s spiritual conduct, conferred upon him the title *Hongjiao Pujie Chan Shi* (Chan Master of Universal Salvation and Propagation of the Teaching). He was subsequently summoned to the capital, where he was commanded to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma in Longguang Hall.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered dharma robe, further adding the title *Foxin Liaoyi* (One Who Has Realized the Buddha-Mind).
[He] attained enlightenment. In the year Gengzi, he went forth to lead Shanquan. In the sixth month of summer in the year Jiyou of the Hongwu era, he manifested a slight illness.

He instructed his disciples to cut paper and prepare his inner and outer robes, saying, "I am about to depart. He ordered that his coffin be moved to a remote peak and requested a brush to write this verse:
"Seventy-eight years of guarding simplicity; A clear and bright scene of failure. The clay ox at the bottom of the sea..."

He turned over in his sleep. In the sixth month, amidst the scorching heat of midsummer, he flew through the air amidst falling snow. Having finished writing this, he passed away in auspiciousness. One month prior, the water in the pond had suddenly dried up;

when the Master entered *parinirvāṇa*, it gushed forth in an extraordinary manner. At that time, both monastics and laypeople were filled with longing and devotion, such that some even burned their heads or scorched their arms as offerings.
During the cremation, five-colored lights appeared; his teeth, jaw, and tongue remained intact, and his *śarīra* relics were without number.
Suan. His disciples divided his remaining bones and those that remained unfragmented, and enshrined them in stupas at five locations:
Longchi (Dragon Pond), Taiping (Great Peace), Qishan (Cypress Mountain), Ziyun (Purple Cloud), and Macheng (Hemp Hill). (Recorded by Taihu Kuansi.)
Chan Master Zhuyuan Shisheng of Miaoguo in Hangzhou was a native of Leping in Rao. His surname was Fan.
He visited Wuneng, from whom he completely cast off all mystical subtleties and intellectual understanding. Surveying all his previous realizations, they appeared to him like a single dream.

Wuneng patted the Master on the back and said, "In the future, you shall greatly propagate my school. Taking leave of Wuneng, he traveled east and lived in seclusion at Nan-chao during the Tianli era.
In the year Jisi (1279), he appeared at Miaoguo Monastery on West Lake. He once addressed the assembly, saying: "Those who study the Way must thoroughly penetrate the mind-source of all Buddhas.

When practice and understanding correspond, and through the long passage of years and months one possesses great fearlessness—like a moonflower reflected in water that does not scatter when struck by ten thousand waves and a thousand ripples—only then will one no longer be deluded by the demon of the aggregates of birth and death. Thus it was said.
Beneath his staff and whisk, with cliffs standing sheer before him, he made it his sole purpose to realize and awaken to the truth before he would cease.
Before long, he returned once more to Nan-chao. In the *dinghai* year of the Zhizheng era, he exhorted his disciples, saying, "The World-Honored One spoke thus:

'I now suffer from back pain and shall enter nirvana. This is my time. The Master struck him with his hand and rebuked him, saying, "What need is there for such verses? Sit upright! and he sat in meditation.
He passed away (leaving no one to carry on his lineage).
Chan Master Xueyan Man of Daming Temple in Cizhou of the Cao-Dong school first visited Puzhao Bao. Puzhao said, "Brother, you are young in years."
"It is precisely appropriate for you to come and consult me, old monk. In years past, I was constantly occupied with the Buddha-dharma.
The Master stepped back from his seat and approached, saying, "How is it now, Preceptor? Zhao said, "It is like being with an enemy born of one's own kin.

The Master said, "Had I not heard these words, I would have almost traveled a thousand li in vain. Zhao descended from his meditation seat, took the Master’s hand, and said, "An adept! (Come, let us be companions.)"

A verse by his companion reads: "The matter of masters meeting masters is a tangled mess; how can the Buddha-dharma be anything other than sand in the eyes? When medicine and disease are suddenly forgotten, there is not a single thing remaining; having trampled over clouds and moon, what house is there left? A verse on the "Seal of the Station" (位中符) says: "Pressed until the magnet stands firm, he urinates on the spot;
his sharp teeth and claws leave the youth envious. He holds the Wangshan seal upside down in his dream; for brewing tea with a cauldron, there is yet another kettle.

The Master practiced together with Shengmo. Once, he knelt to receive a scolding from him. When someone asked the reason for this, the Master said: "Nowadays, among the teachers, disciples, and dharma-heirs in all quarters, disputes and lawsuits are being incited."
[The Master] rebuked him, saying: "A master is like an insect that eats its own flesh. Although I am unworthy, would I dare again tread the path of those who have already failed?

Later, when he visited King Mountain [Tianhuang Daowu], he recounted the causal conditions regarding Dongshan’s seeing his reflection. The Master was greatly perplexed. Tianhuang said: "Do not doubt the words."

"This is a great illness. Since you have now fallen into doubt, the illness has flared up. Do you know that this illness is itself the medicine? One day, as the Master was reading the *Five Ranks* verses, he reached the line:
"In the final reckoning, one returns to sit within the embers. Suddenly he attained enlightenment and said, "Today I finally know that the illness is the medicine.
He went to present this to Xuansha (Titi). Xuansha said, "Your conjectures have no connection [to the truth]. The Master said, "Old man..."

"Master, this time you cannot deceive me. (Tianjie Sheng said: "A prescription from the head of the grass; by chance one encounters a physician and obtains one. He took up his staff and said, "Is there anyone who wishes to recognize this prescription from the head of the grass?
He struck the ground once with it and said, "I suspect they have no connection to it. He ascended the hall for the discourse. He cited Dongshan’s address at the end of the summer retreat:
"At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, brothers, whether you go east or west, you must head toward a place where there is not a single blade of grass. After a long silence...
[The Master] said: "If it is as you say—that where there is not a single inch of grass for ten thousand miles—then how does one proceed?
Shishuang said: "Stepping out the door, it is already grass. Taiyang said: "Even if one does not step out the door, it is still a vast expanse of grass. The Master said:
"These three old fellows, though they speak with different mouths but the same voice, cannot avoid bumping heads and knocking foreheads. Why? Because one man opens wide [the gate]."

One person’s mouth is closed and cannot be opened; another person has raised their foot high and cannot put it down; one person has bolted the door shut and cannot get out. Wángshān was not like this:
throughout the ten directions of space there is nothing external; it is entirely contained within a single mote of dust. Within that single mote of dust there is nothing internal;
that which pervades the ten directions is precisely the measure of that one mote of dust. One must exhaustively reach this limit.
It can be obtained. Where was the gate placed? Where did he enter the grass? Do you understand? Cease encroaching upon the mouth of the cave; the autumn grasses have just begun.
Please look at Shushan’s lotus in the twelfth month. A monk asked Master Ding of Gaoyou: "The golden fish that has passed through the net—"
"What do you take as food? He replied, "Dry dung. The Master heard this and said, "Thank you for the offering. (Fayin Hangnie says: What kind of person is this who sits so recklessly on the ground?
The Verse on the Five Ranks says: "Center within Deviation: Deep and profound, it is locked in dense, verdant mist. At midnight, the azure sky is clear as a mirror;
a bright full moon ascends the high peak. "Deviation within Center: As dawn approaches, thick clouds seal [the sky]."
A Landscape of the Wilds. In the snow-covered hut, spiritual clarity remains unawakened from dream; In profound stillness, it is as if a cold night stretches on forever.

Coming from the Center: The wooden man, carrying his staff, descends the steep heights. Moving freely back and forth, he does not tread upon the ground of the present age; Upon the stony path, auspicious lotuses bloom beneath his feet.

Simultaneously Reaching the Center: Lazily holding the wondrous seal, there is neither true nor false; one sleeps at will amidst the green *śaṣpa* grass, letting the flower-rain fall before the crags as one pleases.
Simultaneously Arriving: Lofty and abrupt, the three lights have never shone upon it; striking the void with a dream-hand, those who listen are few.
It stands far removed, not falling into the scales of *gong* and *shang*. (Wangshan Ti’s Succession)
Chan Master Shengmo Guang ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarchal intent? What is the meaning of the Teachings? The Master said, "Shaving iron on the tip of a needle;
stripping gold from the Buddha's face. The monk asked, "Is this the same as or different from 'when the rooster is cold it climbs the tree, when the duck is cold it enters the water'?
The Master said, "Passing along words and conveying messages is still too light a fault. The monk said, "In that case, thank you, Master, for your clear distribution of rewards and punishments."
The Master said, "You are throwing the lineage into chaos. He then said, "In my school, there are no words or phrases, nor is there any real dharma to give to others.
This old fellow Deshan has lost his teeth and cannot even chew; he has created this failure. If you wish to know the fundamental principle, you must first understand the phrase.
Old Yantou saw the jawbone behind the head—do not associate with him. These were the teachings proclaimed by that father and son. As for me, Master Shitou..."
In the place where light and darkness face one another, how is it that there is both mutual interpenetration and non-interpenetration?
Consider this today. A numinous tortoise comes in the night. I once raised the public case of Jiufeng’s refusal to accept [the transmission], and composed a verse on it:

"The primary seat is in vain, lost to a single stick of incense; Jiufeng was not merely suppressing a high worthy. If you take a single color as the succession, You will bring shame upon the Buddhas and Patriarchs."
The Former Master’s “Not Borrowing Conditions” for the Assembly: He cites the story of Magu shaking his staff and says: "There is no 'is' that can be affirmed;

there is no 'is not' that can be denied. Right and wrong have no master; the myriad virtues all return to the same source. Whether it be the owl or the cock, day or night, they are merely engaging in self-fragmentation.
I have no three inches [of tongue], yet the turtle can call out to the tortoise. Kāśyapa would not consent; let him frown as he pleases. The Verses on the Five Ranks (Zheng).
From the Center to the Partiality: Deep within the secret palace, auspicious clouds gather; at the end of night, amidst the autumn waters, all clamor ceases.

The azure moon is vast and clear, shining brightly upon the cold. From the Partiality to the Center: At dawn on the riverbank, the mist veils the scenery; deep within the reeds, the white-headed old man.
The red sun has reached three *gān* [heights], yet he does not wake from sleep. Coming at the very center, the jade dragon first leaps with a clap of thunder.

The ten directions harmonize together in impartial transformation; the stone shoot pierces through the moss of the ancient path. Reaching within the "both" (*jiānzhōng zhì*), there are no restrictive orders in the borderlands during this age of peace.
Farmers and fishermen sing their songs at will; the moon over the stream and the clouds on the ridge share a common spirit. Arriving within the "both" (*jiānzhōng dào*), there is no merit.
The wondrousness of the entire body is completely transformed; the flower crown is cast aside, acting differently within the midst of things. It vanishes into the great void and cannot be named.
(The two masters above, including Wangshan Ti’s successor, are thus accounted for.)
Chan Master Daming Quan of Cizhou had long studied under Master Heng of Renshan. By nature, he was fond of wit and laughter;
consequently, Master Renshan instructed his attendant Ding to constantly restrain him. The Master said, "Human life is but a dream; let us enjoy ourselves for a lifetime."
"A good dream is one that restrains oneself for a lifetime; an evil dream is one that does not. I would rather have a good dream.

The next day, the attendant removed his bedding and left, leaving only the Master and the junior monk behind. When the Prince Consort was traveling to his post in Nanjing and passed through Daming in Cizhou, he entered the hall and saw a monk sitting with his face against the wall.
The Prince Consort remarked, "What a fine, plain man! The Master replied, "Within the plainness..."
[The monk] asked, "What is that flavor? The Master said, "Today you have added salt and sauce to it.

(Ren-shan Heng-si) Chan Master Hong-xiang of Xi-chi at Da-jue in Zhengzhou was a native of the Wang family of Ningzhou. He studied under Qing-shou Heng for ten years before receiving his seal of certification.
He first resided at Da-jue and later resided at Qing-liang. One day after the snow had fallen, the road was steep.
The rocks were slippery. The Master was already advanced in years; his strength could no longer support him, and he slipped, tumbling headlong into a vast ravine.

His companions cried out in alarm, unable to save him. He fell straight down for several dozen feet before being stopped by a large tree. The assembly asked in astonishment, but the Master’s countenance remained unchanged.
He spoke slowly, "Having studied Chan for forty years, my heels have finally been tested by a stone. Those who heard this were moved.
Everyone was startled and laughed. His collected writings and recorded sayings were transmitted to the world (by Qingshou Hengsi).
*Continued Record of the Finger Pointing at the Moon*, Volume Six; *Continued Record of the Finger Pointing at the Moon*, Volume Seven.
The twenty-third generation descendant of the Sixth Patriarch in the Linji lineage,
Chan Master Mingben of Tianmu Peak in Hangzhou, was born into the Sun family of Qiantang. His mother dreamed of an unopened gate.
The old man was born into his family carrying a lantern. As soon as he left the swaddling clothes, he sat in the full lotus posture;

as soon as he could speak, he sang praises and chanted Buddhist hymns. In all his play, he invariably performed acts of devotion to the Buddha. At the age of nine, he lost his mother. At fifteen, he sought to leave the household life.
While reading the *Lamp Records of the Transmission* (*Chuan Deng Lu*), he reached the passage where the girl Āmrapālī questioned Mañjuśrī about how birth is clearly understood as non-birth.
[The Master] asked: "Why is it that principle itself is instead caused to wander through birth and death? He harbored this doubt and went to consult with Master Gaofeng Miao.

Miao was solitary, lofty, stern, and cold, never lending a word of courtesy or a trace of warmth to others. Yet, upon seeing the Master, he was immediately filled with joy and granted him permission to shave his head.

While reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* at the passage concerning "shouldering the Tathāgata," he attained a sudden and profound awakening. Later, while observing a flowing spring, he experienced further realization.

He went to visit Miaoxiu to seek certification of his insight, but Miaoxiu drove him away with blows. Shortly thereafter, a false rumor spread among the common people that children—both boys and girls—were being selected.
The Master asked, "If someone were to come suddenly and demand that you, Reverend, hand over a boy and a girl, what would you do? Miaoxiu replied, "I would simply ordain them."
Zhuhui Zhibi attained a thorough penetration of the source of the Dharma upon hearing [the Master’s] words. He then composed his own eulogy for his portrait and presented it to the Master, saying:
"My form is inconceivable; Even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot discern it. I grant my unworthy son alone The sight of half of my nose.

Muyun Men’s Verse: "When false words emerge, the ancient style sinks; A single question before one, the meaning is profound. Yet I laugh at the master lacking the power of the eye— Fine gold has been exchanged for counterfeit brass. ○

Someone asked about the relative merits of the various disciples of Miaoxin. Miaoxin said: "As for the Head Seat Yishou, he is certainly a mature, old bamboo stalk; yet it is like one that has been bent seven or eight times.
As for the Rector Wuben, however, he is like a fresh shoot from a bamboo grove on the upper part of the stalk; his future growth as a useful material is difficult to measure.
The Master had no fixed dwelling place, whether on a boat or in a hermitage, all of which he named "Illusory Abode" (Huazhu). Monks and laypeople alike...
People vied with one another to gaze upon him and pay their respects. He was hailed as an "Ancient Buddha of Jiangnan. Emperor Renzong sent envoys to summon him, but he did not go;
instead, the Emperor bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* and the title "Chan Master Foci Yuanzhao Guanghui.

The Master frequently rebuked students for valuing mere verbal expression while failing to seek genuine awakening, saying: "The reason why Chan practice today lacks efficacy is, first and foremost, that there are no people of the ancients."
First, one must possess genuine resolve. Second, one must not treat birth, death, and impermanence as anything other than a momentous matter.
Third, one must be prepared to relinquish habitual tendencies accumulated over kalpas and must possess a body and mind that are steadfast and non-regressive for all eternity.
Ultimately, where does the illness lie? It is truly because one does not recognize the root of birth and death.
Whenever he saw a student, he would invariably ask: "What do you call 'birth and death'? Some were at a loss for an answer;

others said that not knowing where one comes from when born and not knowing where one goes when dead constitutes birth and death. The Master said: "Even if you were to know it, that too is birth and death."
To know [this] is also birth and death. Furthermore, some point to a single thought suddenly arising as birth and a single thought suddenly ceasing as death.
The Master said: "Apart from the arising and ceasing of a single thought, there is also birth and death. These explanations are all merely branches and leaves; they are not the root.
Now, as for the fundamental source: its nature is truly perfect and luminous, fundamentally devoid of the marks of birth and death, or coming and going.

It is solely due to non-awakening that a deluded mind suddenly arises, causing one to lose sight of the original source and undergo empty cycles of transmigration. Therefore, when this Way is lost, birth and death begin;

when it is realized, saṃsāra ceases. One should know that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as light and darkness, form and emptiness, the five aggregates, and the four [elements]...
Great! As for the phenomena of movement and non-movement, these are all the very root of birth and death.

If one has not yet attained a sudden, transcendent awakening within the true Dharma, and instead establishes a separate livelihood apart from that awakening—failing to eliminate the habitual patterns of the mind—how could such a person possibly plant their feet upon the shore of birth and death?
Should even a hair’s breadth remain unexhausted, they will inevitably be deluded once more by superior and subtle sensory conditions.
Therein, various divergent thoughts arise; though one may claim to have attained clear understanding, in reality this is not yet the case.
Only those who take the great matter of birth and death as their own paramount responsibility can exhaust all thieving minds and then be capable of directly settling into the state of suchness.
Should even a hair’s breadth of views regarding good and evil, acceptance and rejection, love and hate, or continuity and interruption remain, then branches and leaves will sprout. Is this not so?
Be cautious. [This is] for the assembly: The sword of wisdom is held aloof in daily life; naturally, it has never required sharpening.
It makes spirits cry out and ghosts wail with terror; corpses lie scattered across the wilds, yet its blade is never revealed.
When the ancients spoke thus, they had already wounded their own lives. Little did they realize that within the treasury of our King, there is no such blade. — Buddha.

On the day of attaining the Way, he addressed the assembly: "The profoundest profundity is beyond all dependence; the most subtle subtlety has no support. It stands alone, revealing the true permanence;
it fully manifests the ultimate essence. It cannot be named; it cannot be described. Like snow and ice melting away until nothing remains, its principle is unimpeded and its phenomena are unimpeded.

The heavens are desolate and the earth vast; ten thousand miles of clouds have gathered at midnight. The stars shine brightly across the four quarters of the long sky. He has peeled back the skull of the time before Vipaśyin."
The Gate! Perfectly round, brilliantly shining. It blinds the eye of light behind the skull. Pure and naked, bare and stripped.

It restrains back the majestic mechanism of wind and thunder that rages through thirty thousand kalpas; it brings forth the drowsy words of the ocean-tide and massed clouds found within five thousand scrolls.
O Great Assembly! Śākyamuni the Old Man has arrived! He is right now within the eyes of all of you.
Looking up from within, one beholds the morning star; atop the crown of the head, one attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. Do you all perceive the movement of your eyebrows?
If you have not yet understood this, each of you is requested to return to the hall. A letter to Elder Dajue states:

Regarding the fact that the ancients so deeply clarified the lineage of their dharma heirs and direct transmissions, it was because the origins and development of the Great Dharma must not be misrepresented.
The world has grown corrupt and customs have become thin; there are those who offer gold to request a whisk and exchange their monasteries for a successor.
I have often felt deep pain over this. Although the Great Awakened One was the founder of this mountain, there are many venerable elders in the monastic communities throughout the ten directions.
To reject them all and insist that I preside over it—how narrow is such a perspective! It is not that I fear the position of abbot.
I truly fear that you would succeed to the Dharma from the Founder (Kaishan).

Therefore, I have withdrawn and earnestly declined, proposing instead that you yourself take Master Yishan as your teacher. How could one, following the ways of the world, change the one whom they serve?
If you were to follow worldly custom and change your succession, I, Taiding-ou of Da jue, would resolutely not associate with you for even a single day.

During the Huangqing era, he was invited to reside at Dajue Monastery. The Master declined the offer with great force, and Dingzou was nominated to accept the command. Dingzou had previously received certification from Master Wanshan Yishan; he later went to study under the Master (Dongyang Shancheng), who offered incense with the intent for him to succeed the Master. However, the Master rejected this in writing, instructing that he should instead succeed Yishan.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the Guihai year of the Zhizhi era, he spoke a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, saying: "I have one phrase."
He entrusted [his affairs] to the great assembly and asked once more, "How is it? Having no basis upon which to rely, he set down his brush, sat upright, and passed away.
A stupa was erected on the western ridge of his home mountain. In the second year of the Tianli era, an imperial edict conferred upon him the posthumous title Zhijue;

the stupa was named Fayun. By imperial command, Yu Wenjing Gong Ji composed the inscription for it. In the second year of the Yuantong era, thirty fascicles of his *Guanglu* (Extensive Record) were bestowed upon him.
The Master from the Zang [region], titled National Preceptor Puying (Gao Feng Miao’s successor), was Chan Master Duanya Liaoyi of Tiantu Mountain in Hangzhou. He was the son of Tang Qing.

At the age of seventeen, he heard a practitioner reciting Gao Feng Miao’s discourse on ascending the hall, which cited the words: “If you wish to exhaust the view of a thousand li, climb one more story higher. Thereupon...

He said, "This great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) will surely be able to pull out nails and remove wedges for people. He then went to pay his respects and attended upon Xuedou Chongxian at the "Gate of Death.
Xuedou instructed him to contemplate the koan, "The myriad dharmas return to one," and thus named him Congyi.

On another day, when Xuedou raised the koan of "the ox passing through the window lattice" for the assembly, the Master heard it and became even more doubtful. Day and night he investigated it, until one day, while passing by the Bowl Pond, he saw—

As snow fell from the pine branches, [Zhaozhou] attained a realization. He went to see Master Miaodao and presented this verse: "Without asking whether it is north, south, east, or west, the great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one expanse of snow.
Before he had finished speaking, Miaodao struck him with a severe blow of his staff. Unconscious, Zhaozhou fell over the cliff. The cliff was sheer and vertical; everyone thought he must have died.

His fellow students climbed up the vines and stepped across the ledges to rescue him. If the Master had not— (Note: The source text ends abruptly here. The standard version of this story concludes that the Master did not catch him, leading to Zhaozhou's death.)
He understood. He then made a vow to attain realization within seven days. Before the period had even ended, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.

He rushed back to Siguan (Death Barrier) and cried out, "Old Monk, today you can no longer deceive me! He further spoke a verse, saying: "The mountains and rivers of the great earth are a single expanse of snow;
The sun shines upon them once, and their traces vanish. From this day forth, I have no more doubts regarding the Buddhas and Patriarchs; There is nothing further to seek."

"North, south, east, and west," he said as he ascended the hall. "For over twenty years, this mountain monk has spread a net across the heavens to strike at phoenixes and snare dragons, yet I have never encountered so much as a single shrimp or crab. Today, however, there is a tiny gnat."
To have stumbled into the net is truly something that cannot bear to be seen. Thirty years hence, atop a solitary peak and at the highest summit, he will raise his voice and shout loudly.
But tell me, what does he call out? Raising his whisk, the Master said: "The great earth, mountains, and rivers—a single expanse of snow.
The Master said to his fellow students: "Throughout the entire world, if there is one person who awakens to the truth and returns to the source, everyone from the very beginning will know it."
Miaowen marveled at his brilliance and agility. Soon after, he returned home to visit his parents; he then escorted his mother to Shangbai in Wukang, where they lived in a thatched hut.
Seeing him mingling with the common folk, people could not fathom his intentions. Later, when he returned to the mountain to see Miaowen, Miaowen said:
Many people saw that you were dragging mud and water along with you. The Master said, "Two eyes facing two eyes," and subsequently shaved his head and gave him the name Liaoyi (Liaoyi).

After Miaojian had passed away, the Master further concealed himself, remaining dejectedly in a subordinate position. Although the fourfold assembly repeatedly requested him, he was only persuaded to reside at Shizi Zhengzong Chan Temple.
On the eve of the New Year in the first year of the Yuantong era, he said to his attendant:
He said, "There is one matter as vast as heaven; do you understand it thoroughly? After a long silence, he said, "Tomorrow is New Year's Day, the sixth day of the first month.
Go to the west of Fayun Pagoda and point to the empty space, saying: 'It would be better to erect another seamless pagoda here.
That evening, he conversed and laughed with the practitioners as usual. When the night was deep, he said, "Tomorrow, this old monk..."
"Tiantai is departing," he said. Another replied, "I shall follow my teacher. The Master said, "Even if you were to gallop like a horse, you would not catch up with me.

The following morning, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. On the day of his passing, thunder crashed and rain lashed down, such that the bright day was shrouded in darkness. By the time of the burial, [the weather had cleared].
Snowflakes fell in profusion, and the forest trees were draped in white. Several thousand people attended the funeral, their grief shaking the mountains and valleys.
Initially, when he manifested his passing at the summit, during the funeral feast, the Master said to the assembly, "Twelve years hence, there shall be another gathering for this old monk.

The assembly did not yet believe him deeply, but it was only now that the prophecy was verified. The Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title: *Fohui Yuanming Zhengjue Pudu* (Buddha-Wisdom Perfectly Enlightened Right Awakening Universal Deliverance).
Chan Master (Tianmu Miaosi). Chan Master Dajue Bunan Zu Yong was a native of Ninghai.
He attended Gaofeng Miaozhi for a very long time, personally performing tasks such as pounding grain and cooking.

His appearance was quite dark and emaciated; he was blunt and possessed little literary refinement. Later, when he led the assembly, his expositions were exceptionally outstanding. This continued until Miaozhi passed away.
The assembly invited Zhongfeng to reside at Dajue, but he declined with all his might, recommending that the Master take charge instead. His verse on mountain dwelling says:
"Building a hut by binding grass to trees, Weaving a fence from thorns beside a stream;
It was because this Lazy Zan lacked spiritual efficacy That the Imperial Edict came for him three times. Later, while at Guizitang in Zhongzhu, he wrote a verse and sat in the full lotus posture.

(Shi [Tianmu Miaosi]). Chan Master Kongzhong of Baiyun in Chuzhou received the Dharma from Gaofeng. He resided at Mount Baiyun, and when the reputation of his teaching spread, monks from all quarters came to visit him until their sandals filled the space outside his door.
In the summer of the *wuchen* year of the Zhizhi era (1276), one day he took up his brush and wrote this verse:
He said: "Earth, water, fire, and wind were predicted by the Buddhas of the past. To bury them deep after digging into the earth is the primary meaning.

Thus, the donor is spared the need for even a few pieces of firewood, and the criticism that there are no *śarīra* (relics) is avoided. Having finished writing this, he sat in meditation and passed away. (The four aforementioned masters from Tianmu Miaosi.)

Chan Master Shicheng of Shexue said to the assembly: "A person of resolve, taking advantage of the dry firewood and ready water within the community and the warmth of the Sangha hall, should vow not to leave the gate for three years; such a person will certainly experience great realization.
There are others who, as soon as they begin their practice and feel a sense of lightness and ease in their minds or perceive clarity before them, immediately abandon their efforts all at once."
To compose verses and hymns with a quick tongue and facile speech, thinking one has achieved great mastery—this is to have wasted a lifetime.
It is a pity that all the mental exertion previously applied has been abandoned midway. When the three-inch breath is severed, what will you have to rely upon?
Brothers, if you wish to transcend birth and death, you must practice authentically and realize authentically; only then will it be attained. (Lingyun was thus certified as his successor.)
Chan Master Zhuyuan Zhengyuan of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was a descendant of Ou-yang Wen-chung Gong. His family had resided in Nan-k'ang for generations.

At the age of twenty-seven, he shaved his head, received full ordination, and began traveling to visit various masters. He first called upon Hsü-k'u Ling, who presented him with the koan of Lung-t'an blowing out a paper candle.
The Master said, "A parched stone can break through layers of ice. Ling asked, "What is it like after it has been broken? The Master—
[The Master] said, "I have come to know it through investigation. Ling asked, "What is it that you have known? As the Master was about to respond, Ling struck him across the back with his staff.
Startled, the Master realized the essential meaning. He resided at Mount Jing and was granted the title Chan Master Fohui Cizhao Puying (Jingshan Ling was his successor).
Chan Master Shaodai of Baolin on Tongjiang in Wuzhou was the son of the Wu family of Yanzhou. His family had resided in Tongjiang for generations, and he took this as his monastic name.
He studied under Xugou at Mount Jing, where he received the seal of the mind (xinyin). He traveled extensively throughout the rivers and lakes of the realm.

One day, he sighed with profound realization, saying, "From this day forward, I know that the Dharma has no differing flavors. Thereupon, he ceased formal study and began to peruse the Great [Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra] with his own hands.
He lectured on the Tripitaka three times; both those within and outside the Buddhist school were thoroughly versed in his teachings.

In the *rénshēn* year of the Zhìshùn era, he went forth to reside at Wúlóng Monastery in the commandery, later moving to Bǎolín Monastery in Yúnhuáng. At one time, his Dharma assemblies were renowned for being exceptionally grand. One day, he manifested illness.
The bell was struck to assemble the congregation, who offered verses of gratitude for the Master’s departure. The Master took up his brush, threw it to the ground, and said:

"Even if writing were to continue until the descent of Maitreya, how could I ever leave this place? He then sat peacefully and passed away. Upon cremation, the *śarīra* relics were like deep-blue pearls, and his teeth and jaw remained unbroken.
(The above two individuals are successors of Lingyin Monastery.)
Chan Master Wumen Si Cong of Xiangyan in汝州 (Ruzhou) was a native of Xiangshan. Initially, he studied under Dufeng;

subsequently, he visited Wuneng Jiao of Huaixi, who assigned him the koan of the "Mu" (No) word. One day, while meeting with his fellow practitioner, the Venerable Jing, Jing asked, "In these six or seven years, what realization have you attained?
The Master replied, "Day after day, it is simply that before my eyes there is not a single thing. Jing said:
"You, you string of complications! From where have you come? The Master was at a loss. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, when one clarifies this great matter, how should one pay respect?
He replied, "Have you not heard it said: 'If you wish to know the essential meaning, look southward at the Big Dipper'?
Having said this, he departed. The Master was so struck by this that for five or seven days he could neither walk nor sit, remaining utterly bewildered.
For a while, he did not bring up the word "Mu," but instead focused solely on seeking the ultimate meaning: "The Northern Dipper faces south and looks.

By chance, he went to the head monk’s quarters and sat with the assembly; his doubt remained unresolved. After about the time it takes to eat a meal, he suddenly felt a lightness and clarity within his chest, and his conceptual thoughts shattered.
All people and things before his eyes vanished from view. Upon realizing this, sweat poured from his entire body. Thereupon—
Jianjing raised his fan and said, "Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The Master hurriedly replied, "It is clear as soon as it is raised;
how marvelous! A pure breeze pervades everywhere, penetrating one's breast. Within this, there is not much of a message; it simply brings forth joy throughout one's entire being.
From that time on, his speech and verses were entirely free of obstruction. However, when it came to the single path above, he was still unable to attain it.
He left and entered Mount Xiangyan to spend the summer retreat, single-mindedly upholding the "Mu" (No) koan.
One day, he suddenly felt that his body and mind were like a house whose four walls had collapsed; not a single dharma could withstand his scrutiny.
He then went to visit Master Tie Shan Qiong, who had returned from Goryeo and was staying at Shishuang. Upon meeting him, Qiong asked, "Where are you from? The Master replied, "Ruozhou."
Shan said, "What are the features of the patriarch Fengxue? The Master spent twenty years of effort explaining it all at once.
Then, [Zhao]qiong gripped his throat and asked, "What is 'Mu'? The Master replied, "I have recently come from Tanzhou;
I have not received news from Hubei. Qiong said, "Not yet. Speak further. The Master said, "When did you leave Goryeo, Preceptor? Qiong—
[Daowu] said, "Not yet. Speak further. The Master gave a shout and, shaking his sleeves, departed. Daoyuan said, "These brothers are all well;
they have only one great illness. I have now understood it. Upon hearing this, the Master was moved and inspired, and thus sought final resolution.
He entered the mountains of Guangzhou again, where for seventeen years he finally attained liberation. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The Dharma has no fixed characteristics."
Encountering conditions, one immediately takes up the fundamental principle. Grasping the Vajra sword, one swallows the *liji* thorn and cuts off the tongues of the monks.
Sitting upon the crown of Vairocana, one erects a single blade of grass as a sixteen-foot golden body, and takes that sixteen-foot golden body to be a single blade of grass.
Thus, one is made entirely free from even a thread of attachment; the moon is cold in the autumn sky, and the cold ashes burst into flame. Arriving at this point, call out—
If you treat it as the Buddha-dharma, you will enter hell like an arrow shot. If you do not treat it as the Buddha-dharma, you will likewise enter hell like an arrow shot.
O virtuous ones, how ultimately shall you understand this? Have you not seen the Venerable Boatman say: "Where the body is hidden, there are no traces;
where there are no traces, do not hide the body"? Although it is thus, when viewed with the True Eye, it is all—
"Idle furniture. On the level of a patch-robed monk, it has no connection whatsoever. (Tieshan Qiong’s lineage.
Chan Master Tianhu Shiwu Qinggong of Fuyuan, Huzhou, was a native of Changshu, Suzhou. His clan name was Wen.
He first visited Gao Feng, who presented him with the koan "The myriad dharmas return to one. He served diligently there for three years without achieving any realization.
Consequently, he went to Jianyang Hermitage to visit Master Xin, who asked him, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "Tianmu. Xin asked, "What instructions did you receive there?"
The Master said, "Study the phrase: 'The myriad dharmas return to One. Xinxing asked, "How do you understand this?
The Master was speechless. Xinxing said, "This is a dead word. What kind of person with a feverish illness would teach you such a thing?
The Master bowed and requested further instruction. Xinxing said, "Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell; where there is no Buddha, pass by quickly. The Master did not attain realization.
Xin said, "This is a dead-end. The Master did not notice and broke into a cold sweat. One day, while entering the room for instruction, Xin brought up the previous conversation again.
The Master said, "When you mount the horse, you see the road. Xin rebuked him, saying, "How long have you been here, and you still hold such a view?
The Master left in a fit of indignation. On the way, he suddenly looked up and saw a pavilion in the wind, and his mind was suddenly enlightened.
He had a realization and immediately returned. He said to Xìn, "Today I have grasped the 'living word' (huoju). Xìn asked, "How do you understand it?

The Master replied, "On this clear and bright season, the rain has just cleared; the yellow oriole on the branch sings clearly. Xìn nodded in approval. Later, as the Master was taking his leave, Xìn saw him off at the gate and said, "In days to come, we shall share the same reliquary stupa.
