—From the *Guangjiao Fu* (Records of Guangjiao) *Note: The term "living word" (huoju) refers to a teaching that is dynamic and directly points to one's own nature, as opposed to a "dead word" (siju), which is fixed, conceptual, or merely scriptural.*
A proclamation was dispatched inviting the Master to reside at Fuyuan in Danghu. The Master lay firm, refusing to rise. After he had been summoned back and forth twice, the Master finally consented.

Upon entering the monastery and ascending the hall for the formal address, when he held fast, not even a trace of his sharp edge was revealed; yet when he let go, the ten directions were laid out in纵横 (zōnghéng).
Meeting him in the depths of water and clouds, one finds him instead atop a thousand peaks; meeting him atop a thousand peaks, one finds him instead amidst the water and clouds.
In the depths. This morning, within Fuyuan Temple, I opened the hall to expound the Dharma; yesterday, by the side of Tianhu Hermitage, I broke the earth and tilled the smoke.

Therefore it is said: "The Dharma has no fixed form; wherever conditions meet, there is the source. Thus one may transmit the wind of true stillness and look up to assist the transformation of non-action.
At such a time as this, what is it? [He lifts his staff and strikes once. Ninety thousand miles.
As soon as the great Peng bird spreads its wings, the ten-thousand-year-old crane soars along. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:
"When one body is pure, many bodies are pure; when one world is pure, many worlds are pure.
Yet the foul stench from the latrine and the dust motes in the Buddha Hall—tell me, from where do they come? He covered his nose with his hand and said, "And yet another!"
A Dot: Ascending the Hall. That which is heard cannot be heard; that which is seen cannot be seen. Last night at the fifth watch, the wind blew down a petal of peach blossom.
Red clouds arise upon the surface of the gray moss; though the hundred birds do not come, spring is in full bloom.
During the Zhizheng era, the imperial court bestowed incense and silk, and the Empress granted him a golden-embroidered Dharma robe. There was one who heard of Tianhu...
Feng. Those who have chanted the poems of Tianhu have none whose hearts are not refreshed and spirits ennobled, considering them to have truly captured the legacy of the ancient masters.
One day, manifesting a slight illness, he gathered the assembly to bid them farewell. When the assembly requested instructions for his final affairs, the Master took up a brush and wrote this verse:
"The green mountains do not harbor putrid corpses; Once dead, what need is there to dig and bury? Look at me—I have nothing."
The fire of samādhi—its light cutting off what precedes and what follows—is but a single pile of firewood. Having finished writing, he cast aside his brush and passed away.

His cremated remains yielded relics of five colors, which were enshrined in a stupa at the source of Tianhu (Heaven Lake) and on the right slope below the hermitage stupa; thus, it truly fulfilled the prophecy of the "single niche.

The State Preceptor of Goryeo, Da Guyu Gong, once attended the Master and received his essential instructions. When the King heard of this, he felt deep admiration and longing, and sent an envoy to the court to express his devotion.

The court issued an imperial decree bestowing the posthumous title Chan Master Foci Huizhao. Furthermore, a formal document was requested to be sent to Zhejiang to invite the master’s śarīra back to the country for veneration (at the Daochang Monastery, inherited by Xin).
Chan Master Chulin of Pingshan at Jingci Temple in Hangzhou was the son of Wang Shi, a native of that prefecture.

At the age of seventeen, he received full ordination and took leave of his mother to travel to various regions for study. His mother prepared his traveling gear for him, but after several days, he returned again.

His mother admonished him, saying, "In the study of the Way, one must maintain a mind of non-retrogression. Why are you so hesitant and wavering? Thereupon, the Master severely chastised himself with words of exhortation.
He traveled upstream along the Tuo River to Jinhua to pay his respects to Xian of Jia'an Temple. Upon seeing him, Xian recognized his potential and kept him in his quarters as an attendant.
One night, Xian rolled paper soaked in oil to serve as a candle; holding it up, he asked the Master, "When Longtan blew out the lamp, what did you do?
Just as the Master was about to answer, Xian suddenly covered his mouth with his hand. From this, the Master attained awakening. Later, Xian moved to Daochang Temple.

He was appointed to the treasury and its keys. Before long, he took up the whisk and ascended the seat; his spiritual impact flowed like water from a jar, and the assembly was all struck with awe and submission.
Upon the passing of Daochang Xin, he went to rely on Xuguleng at Yangshan, where he served as the Second Seat. At the time of his death, he changed his robes and bathed.
He gathered the assembly to recite a verse before passing away. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Puhui Xingwu (the successor of Daochang Xin).
Chan Master Zhigang of Shimen Zhengjue at Luoshan in Wuzhou was originally a local resident whose family had lived at the foot of the mountain for generations.

Having received the Dharma from Master Xian of Ji’an, he returned to his hometown after completing his travels. The local people constructed a monastery on that very site and inscribed the lintel of its gate with these words:

One day, Huihai asked him, "Before your parents were born, what was your original face? From that moment on, he harbored this doubt within his breast for seven years.
During this time, he was particularly close with Yi Huan Shengfu of Cao’an. (Note: The text provided ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.)

Mojie went to pay his respects to Master Le of Quanshi in the Heavenly Realm. The Master said, "In years past, I once asked a teacher and friend whether the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings are the same or different;
he replied, 'The autumn tree sheds its yellow leaves; on a cold day, one digs a fire-pit in the ground.
Today, I ask the Master to provide a definitive judgment. Quanshi said, "This old man’s wrists have lost their strength in recent years; [he can no longer] hold his staff."
"Rest your head against the wall for now," the Master said. "There are those who would not agree with you speaking in this way.
Le took up his staff and struck him, saying, "Wait until the eyes of the pillar open of themselves; then I shall hurl an iron caltrop right in your face. The Master then bowed.
Later, he went out to reside at Puguang in Li Village. He was again commanded by imperial decree to move to Tiantong. Ascending the hall, he said: "On this day last year, I dwelt on Mount Laṅkā;
the fourfold assembly there rejoiced because one person was missing from this place. On this day this year, I dwell on Mount Foguo."
These four assemblies rejoice that there is one person missing from that place. He strikes the whisk: the single body becomes infinite bodies, and the infinite bodies become a single body.
When walking, he walks throughout heaven and earth; when sitting, he sits as all things. What need is there to speak of east, west, south, or north, of other lands or this realm?
Even if you examine it closely, you are still in the "transformed city. But tell me, where is the "Jewel Place"?

[The Master] said: "How is it? He then descended from his seat. [Another day,] he ascended the hall and said: "Greed, anger, and delusion; precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Precepts, concentration, and wisdom; greed, anger, and delusion.
Ignorance, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, and ignorance.

All sentient beings are all Buddhas; all Buddhas are all sentient beings. The moon has fallen, and the mountain has no shadow; the wind comes, and the trees have sound. The great trichiliocosm is without peer."
"Wait! The pillar is bustling in all directions. He gave a shout and descended from the seat. (Successor to Le of Tianjie).
Master Wenzhen Wuben of Lingyin, Hangzhou, was a native of Dinghai, Siming. His secular surname was Xie. One day, he manifested slight illness.
When Master Hong of Fantang visited to inquire after him, he encountered the Master gasping for breath. Hong said, "Zhaozhou said, 'All..."
"Ordinary people are driven by the twelve hours of the day; this old monk drives the twelve hours. "How about you, Master?
The Master straightened his body and said, "What do you call 'the twelve hours'? Hong said, "But what can one do about the urgency of the breath?
The Master let out a thunderous shout. He asked those nearby, "What date is it today? They replied, "The twenty-seventh day of the second month. Thereupon, he sought [to leave].
He wrote a verse with his brush, saying: "I am seventy-five years old; I have entered nirvana and do not fall into birth and death.
I turn my body upon the back of empty space and knock over the small cloud that flies toward me. Having cast aside his brush, he passed away in stillness. (Jingci Desi)
Chan Master Shiyu of Wushi Jiefeng Peak in Quzhou was the son of the Yu family from Xi'an in that prefecture.
He visited various great masters, including Guya, Shimen, Duanya, and Zhongfeng, receiving their dharma instructions. He resided at Nanping for three years without crossing the threshold of his room.
At that time, Master Cheng Zhiyan was propagating the Way at Daci; the Master went there to visit him again. Cheng raised the example of Nanyue...
"The spring is not the mind; it is not the Buddha; it is not an object. What is it? The Master was at a loss. Thereupon, he returned once more to Nanping.

One night, while listening to a neighboring monk recite the *Song of Realizing the Way*, he reached the line: "Do not eliminate delusive thoughts, nor seek the truth. Suddenly, he felt as if a heavy burden had been lifted.
He then said, "The Buddha-dharma has always been right before one's eyes; it is people themselves who distance themselves from it. He immediately composed [a verse]:
The verse says: From time to time we meet face-to-face, yet do not truly encounter one another. Having exhausted all the mother’s anger, our vital strength is spent.
At midnight, suddenly forgetting the pointing finger to the moon, The red solar disc bursts forth from the void. [The Master] ran to pay his respects at Cheng’s quarters.
As soon as Cheng saw him, he shouted, “Where have you seen gods or ghosts come from? The Master said, “Today I have caught the thief. Cheng said, “The stolen goods?”
"Where is it? the Master then shouted. Cheng said, "Neither opening the mouth nor closing the mouth is right; speak a phrase that goes beyond this.
The Master said, "The entire world is luminously manifest, with nothing concealed. Cheng took up his bamboo staff, and the Master overturned the meditation seat.
Cheng said, "You dare to come here and pull the tiger's whiskers! He struck him three times and immediately appointed him as an attendant.
Later, he moved from Wushi in Shizhou to Shixi in Guangde. On the day he opened the hall for teaching, a monk asked:
"Having left Wushi Ridge behind, you have come to Stone Creek Mountain. To reveal the path for humans and devas—how does one penetrate the Patriarch’s Barrier?

The Master said: "A dragon gives birth to a golden phoenix chick; it breaks through the azure lapis lazuli. The monk said: "If that is so, then we do not recognize each other face-to-face, even across a thousand li."
[The monk] said, "It is like the wind. The Master said, "Layer upon layer are the mountain passes and roads.

[The monk] asked, "Bodhidharma came from the West not to establish written words, but to point directly to the human mind, so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha. Since he did not establish written words, how is it that they have been transmitted down to the present day?

The Master said, "The official gate does not admit a needle, yet private paths allow for carriages and horses. [The monk] asked, "When you say 'pointing directly to the human mind,' which mind do you point to? The Master said:
"The opening of the mouth does not reside on the tongue. [The student] asked, "It is said that 'seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood.

Where is this nature? The Master said, "The Taihu Lake spans thirty-six thousand acres; night after night, the moonlight shines bright upon its waves. [The student] said, "I recall the Venerable Fu Dashi saying:"
"Empty-handed, one grasps a hoe; walking, one rides a water buffalo. A person passes over the bridge; the bridge flows, but the water does not flow. What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "One must by all means avoid missing it right before one's face. [The student] said, "If that is so, then when there is spirit, one adds to that spirit;
where there is no elegance, there is elegance nonetheless. The Master said, "A difference of a hair’s breadth results in a gap as vast as heaven and earth."
[The Master] said: "Let this matter rest for now. Do you remember what is said in the sutras: 'The great wealthy elder is none other than the Tathāgata'?

Does this refer to [the realization attained] over the course of many kalpas, or is it a realization attained in this very life? The Master replied: "The stream is deep where the flowers fall far away;

the mountain is high where the tree shadows stretch long. [The student] said: "Today, the lay practitioner Zhixin has donated his wealth to establish the Shixi Dharma Center and invited [you to preside]."
"Does the Master reside [here] as one with [the Dharma], or as something separate? The Master said: "When the lion roars, the fragrant grasses turn green;
where the elephant king walks, the hundred flowers turn red. [The monk] asked: "If it is thus, what karmic fruit is obtained? The Master said:

"Life after life, one returns to the Buddha-ground; age after age, one rejoices in the realms of humans and devas. In the twelfth month of the third year of the Hongwu era, he manifested a slight illness and wrote this verse:
He said: "Birth is fundamentally non-birth; extinction is fundamentally non-extinction. Letting go of the hand, one simply goes on—a single sky of bright moon.
He cast down his brush and passed away (Jiyan Chengsi).
Chan Master Nicui Zhishun of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou was the son of the Chen family of Ruian, Wenzhou. He entered Min Province to study under Venerable Tieguan Shu of Tianbao Monastery.
After more than a month of intensive investigation and inquiry, while using the toilet, he was triggered by the sight of a bitter gourd in the garden;
he suddenly realized that the entire earth had become level and still. He went to seek verification from Shu, who said, "This is merely entering the gate. As for what lies beyond..."
Once he had entered [the Way], it was as if he had traveled thousands of miles. Another half-year passed.
One day, he suddenly called out in an exhorting voice to Zhishu, saying, "The failure of Nanquan has now been seen. Zhishu asked, "It is not mind, not Buddha, and not things—what is it?
The Master replied, "The ground is paved with bricks; the roof is covered with tiles. Zhishu asked, "Where is Nanquan right now?"
[The Master] was at Chuchu. The Master said, "A hawk flies over Silla. Shu said, "Wrong. The Master also said, "Wrong. Shu said, "Wrong, wrong. The Master bowed and withdrew.
When Shu passed away, the Master succeeded him in leading the monastery's affairs. Not long after, he left and departed.

The imperial court bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* and conferred the title of Chan Master Foxing Yuanbian. In the early Hongwu era, an imperial edict summoned eminent monks of realized virtue.

Ten people gathered at Mount Zhongshan to establish a dharma assembly. The Master responded to the imperial decree and was commanded to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma. The Emperor visited in person, offering him the utmost consolation and support.
Upon returning south, he was appointed as the abbot of Jingci Temple. After six years, he was again summoned to the capital. Shortly thereafter, he manifested a slight illness;
having bathed and recited a verse, he passed away while seated (Tianbao Shu succeeded him).
Master Baokjin of Wutai Bifeng was popularly known as Jin Bifeng. He was a native of Yongshou in Qianzhou and belonged to the Shi clan.

He left home to become a monk at the age of six and subsequently traveled extensively among the lecture halls of various monasteries. Suddenly, he sighed and said, "The study of the Tripitaka is merely pointing at the moon with one's finger.
Thereupon, he changed his robes and went to visit Master Zhen Ruhai at Jinyun, where he applied himself with diligent effort day and night. Once, by chance—
Carrying a basket, he went to gather vegetables. Suddenly, he sat down and remained motionless. After three periods (twelve hours) had passed, he finally awoke.

Huizhen asked, "Have you entered meditative absorption? The Master replied, "Yes. Huizhen asked, "What did you see? The Master replied, "I have attained an awakening. Huizhen asked, "How is it that you have awakened?
The Master held up the basket to show him. Huizhen said, "It is not that. The Master set the basket on the ground and stood with his hands folded in reverence. Huizhen spoke again: "It is not..."
"It is so," [the Master] replied. The Teacher then shouted. Zhen lunged forward, seized him by the chest, and said, "Speak! Speak! The Teacher clenched his fist and struck him. Zhen said, "Not yet.
This was merely a temporary cessation of worldly toil. You must cut off the path of the mind and penetrate the Patriarchal Barrier; only then can the Great Dharma be clarified.
From that time on, the Teacher did not let his side touch the mat for three years. One day, hearing the sound of wood being felled, sweat poured from him like—
It rained. [Zhaozhou] then said, "The ancients said that there were eighteen instances of great enlightenment and countless instances of minor enlightenment;

how could they have deceived me? Only today do I finally understand what occurred before birth. He immediately went to see Xuanzhen to seek certification. Xuanzhen did not grant it. The Master overturned the meditation seat and left.
The following day he saw Xuanzhen again. Xuanzhen drew a circle on the ground; the Master brushed it away with his sleeve.
He went away. The master again drew a single circle. The master drew a single stroke within the circle and then swept it away.
The master again drew a single circle; the master drew a cross within the circle and then swept it away. The master again drew as before.
The Master drew a swastika at a corner of the crossroads and then swept it away. Then he drew thirty circular marks in total. The Master answered each one in detail.
The man laughed loudly and said, "Are there not those in the world who have attained realization through their studies? Yet, few are able to clarify the great function of the spiritual capacity."
"How many more people will there be? he asked, and was subsequently granted a prophecy. He was then commanded to go to Shuofang, where the Way would be widely propagated.

Previously, while in meditative absorption, the Master had seen a mountain of exquisite beauty, with multi-storied pavilions and magnificent towers resplendent in gold and green. Within it, various Bodhisattvas were practicing the Path.
One of them beckoned to the Master, saying, "This is Bimora Rock (Bimāśaila). You shall cultivate the Path here; why do you hasten to forget this?"

Later, while the Master was traveling to Mount Tai, he encountered a woman with disheveled hair wearing tattered garments of five colors, walking slowly barefoot with a black mastiff following behind her.
The Master asked where she was going; she replied, "Into the mountains. He asked, "For what purpose do you enter the mountains?
She replied, "I do not do anything at all. Having spoken, she vanished. When the Master questioned his companions, none had seen her. Or so it is said.
The Cloud-like Emanations of Mañjuśrī: The Master subsequently established the Lingjiu Hermitage on the mountain to await those who would come from afar.

Monastics and laypeople, hearing of his reputation, flocked there from a thousand li away; the crowds often numbered in the tens of thousands. During the Zhizheng era, he was summoned to the inner court.

One snowy night, a crimson light issued directly from the Master’s chamber, piercing straight through to the heavens. The Emperor was struck with wonder and admiration, bestowing upon him a gold-embroidered *kāṣāya*.

The following year, his prayers for rain were answered at once. He was granted the title of Great Zen Master Jikjo Wonyeom (Silent Illumination Perfect Clarity) and issued an imperial edict to reside at Haerin Temple.

At the beginning of the Hongwu era, he was summoned to the capital to reside at Daecheonhae Temple. His discourse on the Dharma accorded with the Emperor’s wishes, and the Emperor bestowed upon him a poem written in his own hand;

the honors and gifts conferred were most generous. On the sixth month of the Renzi year, he bathed, changed his robes, assembled the congregation to bid them farewell, and... [passed away]. His younger brother... [continued the funeral rites].
The disciple requested a verse. The Master said: "The Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are but old paper;
what is the use of my words? He sat upright and passed away. Upon cremation, his relics were formed in five colors, and his teeth and tongue remained unbroken. (Jinyun Zhen-si)
Master Wansong Xingxiu of the Cao-Dong school, whose posthumous title was Zhongdu Shuntian Ba’en, was surnamed Cai and was a native of Jie in ancient Henan.
At the age of fifteen, he earnestly sought to leave the household life; his parents could not thwart his resolve, and he paid his respects at Xingtai.
He took Master Yūn of the Pure Land as his teacher. Later, having received full ordination, he set out with his travel bag over his shoulder for Yanjing.

He visited Tanzhe, passed through Qingshou, and subsequently paid a visit to Wanshou Temple, where he studied under Chan Master Shengmo Guang. The master instructed him to contemplate the dialogue of Changsha regarding "turning the self back" and "the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
For half a year, he made no progress whatsoever. Guang said, "I wish you would understand this slowly. One day, the Master...
He reflected further on the saying, "Xuan Sha has not yet reached the ultimate. He requested instruction from Xueyan Muan at Daming in Zhi.

After only twenty-seven days, he suddenly realized that his intellectual artifice was exhausted. Muan said, "Whether walking or sitting, when no thought has yet arisen, raise it up with sudden force and look.
If you see, then you have seen; if you do not see, set it aside for a while. Act in this manner."
Exertion and rest do not hinder one another; study does not hinder rest, nor does rest hinder study. He then appointed him as a Record Keeper (Jishi).
When Master Heng of Tanzhe visited Daming, the Master went to his door at night and asked the attendant to burn incense and request instruction.
Master Heng immediately opened the door to meet him. The Master asked, "What is the living word? What is the dead word? Heng replied:
"Secretary, if you understand, the 'dead word' is also the 'living word'; if you do not understand, the 'living word' is also the 'dead word.
From this point on, the Master investigated with even greater vigor. One day, seeing a chicken fly, he attained great enlightenment and said:
'Today I have not only defeated the tiger of Sha, but I have also defeated the great tiger of Cen. He went to see Man, who approved of him and subsequently transmitted the Dharma to him."
The Verse on Robes. From this time forth, both the two rivers and the three provinces of Jin all revered the Master’s reputation. He constructed the Wansong Hermitage to dwell there in seclusion.

When senior monks earnestly requested him to open a Dharma assembly, the Master complied. Subsequently, he resided at Wanshou Monastery in Zhongdu. Emperor Jin Zhangzong issued an imperial decree for him to enter the inner court and ascend the seat.
The Emperor personally went out to welcome and honor him; upon hearing the Dharma, he was moved to realization and bestowed upon the Master silk brocades and the title "Great Monk."
Gaya. In the Ding-si year of the Cheng’an era, he was summoned by imperial decree to Qiyin Temple on Mount Dayu. Subsequently, he moved his staff to Baoen Hongji [Temple].
In the second year of the Yuan Taizong era, the Geng-yin year, he again received an edict to preside over Wanshou [Temple] in Zhongdu.

In his later years, he retired to Congrong Hermitage. Having successively occupied several great monasteries, he greatly revitalized the Dongshan tradition. Entering the hall at Liangong: [The text continues with: ...Liangong.
A special Brahma-palace has been constructed for practice; the sacred mirror awaits the imperial visit. After the rain, the waters are clear as birds float upon them;
with the dawn’s glow bright, the mountains are still, their peaks draped in brocade. King Tang once unfurled the vast net of Heaven; Lu Wang rarely cast his moon-fishing hook.
Let us inquire: what season is this splendor? A world of gold, the autumn of the osmanthus. *Small Sermon*:
Long ago, there was a man riding a donkey who asked a group of monks, "Where are you going? The monks replied, "To the site of practice (*dojang*). The man said, "Where is not the site of practice?"
The monk struck him with his fist and said, "This fellow has no sense of propriety! To enter the place of practice and not dismount from your donkey!
The man was speechless. The Master said, "Everyone says this fellow has a head but no tail; he can do it, but he cannot carry it through."
Little do they realize that this monk’s earlier words do not accord with his later ones.

Since you already know that every lifting and placing of the foot is a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), why do you not awaken to the fact that riding a donkey or mounting a horse is nothing other than the work of a Buddha?
Wansong wishes to settle this unjust case and shall further pass judgment upon it, saying: "A fellow of no luck who was struck by a fist; Maoguang and Du the Chan practitioner were already [caught]."
This is a failure to discipline oneself; how can one bear to wrongly blame others? "The site of enlightenment has but one;
the Buddha-dharma is fundamentally not many. I leave this for you, O *kalyāṇamitra*, to explain. On the first day of the intercalary fourth month, he ascended the hall and said:
"What is called a man of the Way does not know whether the months are large or small, nor does he know the extra days of the year’s intercalation. But I, this wild monk, am not like that. Now..."
The year consists of three hundred and eighty-four days. The previous month ended with a full moon; this month ends with a new moon.

It is now the first day of the intercalary fourth month, at the transition from the late *chen* to the early *si* hour. Suddenly, someone comes forth and says: "He is thoroughly unobstructed and sharp-witted; he knows the times and observes the seasonal rhythms."
"There is simply no scent of a person on the Way. The wild monk covered his nose with his hand and said, "Step back, step back!
Why is that? [The master] said, "The scent of a person on the Way is far too pungent! [Someone] asked, "Dongshan said, 'The dragon roars in the withered tree;

its strange resonance is hard to hear. What is this strange resonance? Dongshan said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "He understands the dragon's roar well—blind fellow! [Another] asked, "What about Quan? The Master said, "Blind!"
Zhen asked, "For thirty years, I have been unable to settle my deluded mind. I beg the Master for a skillful means. The Master said, "How long has your deluded mind existed?
I wonder whether, fundamentally, there ever was such a thing as a deluded mind. As for this deluded mind, how would you go about cutting it off?
Is it by cutting it off that it is [resolved], or is it by not cutting it off? Upon hearing this, Zhen experienced a state of vast, open clarity.

The Master said, "Only one who has realized the Way knows. The monk said, "Why do you, Master, meet me with such weapons?

"I know you do not have good intentions. While the Master was weeding, a monk asked, "When will this patch of ground be cleared of weeds until it is perfectly clean?

A monk asked, "If one holds the tiger’s head and grasps the tiger’s tail, what about the matter in between? The Master said, "He has attained freedom.
The monk asked, "As for the ancient saying, 'I too cannot bring it forth'—what is its meaning? The Master said, "Entering the water, you see the tall man."
Addressing the assembly: Now, those who act as patriarchal masters have no choice but to offer a word or a phrase;

Yet nowadays, those who occupy the seat of a master and instruct their disciples merely memorize texts and adorn their speech with flowery rhetoric to boast of their erudition.

Later on, as evil habits increased, they became unaware of the path by which they themselves had originally emerged. Like a tattered garment walking through a thicket of thorns, they could not move with freedom.
Thus, the school of the Direct Pointing of Shaolin fell to the ground; this is truly a matter for deep lamentation.

During the Chenchu era (the reign of Emperor Xiansong), Chan Master Jingxin Laifu of Dingshui in Cixi appeared. A native of Fengcheng in Nanchang, his secular surname was Wang.

The essential point is this: the true lineage of the Chan school transmits mind-to-mind, directly pointing it out by holding it up alone for those of superior capacity.

It does not involve verbal explanations nor the existence of conceptual understanding. It is like the spark struck from flint, like a flash of lightning—seeing is simply seeing, realizing is simply realizing;

This can be thoroughly investigated. If, however, one engages in discursive deliberation, involving acceptance and rejection or conceptual discrimination, all such acts belong to deviant meditation and deviant paths;

This requires no elaborate effort and is the most concise and essential method. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Worldly speech, the occupations for sustaining life, and so forth—all are not in contradiction with the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

The essence of mind: this is the place where the Buddhas and Patriarchs directly point out the way for others.

This is the season of peace and bliss. Formerly, there was a king who asked the Venerable Prajñātāra, "What is the Buddha?

The Venerable One replied, “When it manifests, there are eight such places. The King asked, “What are these eight manifestations?”

"Please explain this to me. The Venerable One replied: "In the womb it is called the body; dwelling in the world it is called a person. In the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing.

Manifesting everywhere, it encompasses all sand-grains of worlds; yet when gathered and withdrawn, it is contained within a single minute speck of dust. Those who recognize this know it to be Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit.

He relied upon Master Heng of Yunfeng for many years of inquiry and study, personally receiving his transmission and being entrusted with the robe and verse.
Subsequently, he visited masters of the Caodong school; later, he went to the quarters of Master Shen of Taiyuan, where he again received certification of his realization.
Afterwards, he traveled to the Great Wanshou Temple in Yanjing to visit Master Xueting. Xueting asked him, "Bring forth a single phrase that meets the occasion; try to produce one."
As the Master was about to open his mouth, Xueting said, "Your family estate has been confiscated by others; yet you still remain here crying out for injustice.
The Master clapped his hands and said, "Who can do anything with me? Xueting replied, "This madman! Within the Way of benevolence and righteousness, let me offer you one bow.

Thereupon, he attended the Master for ten years with his mendicant’s staff, received his instructions, and opened a hall at the ancestral monastery of Shaolin (at that time, those within Xueting’s lineage were known as...).
"Second is Tai Yi and Su Shi; they are the foremost among those I recommend. [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "The events of kalpas as numerous as dust motes reside only in the present.

Chan Master Zhitaie of Zhonglin at Ba'en in Taiyuan was the son of the Wen family of Yucheng in Fenyang.

"How can you confine yourself to such petty matters? At that time, Master Xueting was presiding over Wanshou Monastery. The Master went to rely upon him for several years.
One day, during a discussion on monastic affairs, the Master made a remark that offended Xueting. Xueting said, "A thing with a head but no tail—what connection does it have to anything else?

A monk asked, "What is the place where there is not a single inch of grass ten thousand miles away? The Master said, "This is not a realm within your reach, O *śrāmaṇera*.

The grass stretched out endlessly. The Master said, "To dwell upon it is an error. [A monk] asked, "How can one avoid being involved with movement and stillness?

The Master said, "Throughout the entire realm, all traces of red dust are severed; the whole body is devoid of shadow or image. One day, manifesting illness, he gathered the assembly and said, "My karmic conditions shall end on this day.
You must each protect and uphold yourselves well. You should cherish every moment and ensure that time is not spent in vain. Having heard this, [the monks were moved].

Zen Master Jing Su of Zu’an at Lingyan Temple in Taian was a native of the Zhang family of Yongping in Baoding.

Having thus departed, he retired to Mount Wuan and entered the monastic order under Chan Master Tianning Zhao. Through diligent practice, he attained realization and was appointed as a secretary.

The twenty-sixth generation descendant of the Sixth Patriarch in the Linji lineage,
Chan Master Baozang Puchi of Dengwei in Suzhou, studied under Master Wanfeng Wei and attained profound realization of the Great Dharma.
Weiyang entrusted him with a verse, saying: "The Great Fool’s ribs ache as he clenches his fist; The Three Essentials and Three Mysteries transcend both the orthodox and the biased.

A lion cub from the den of Linji— Lamp after lamp, flame continues flame, transmitted through ancient and modern times. The monk Huixian came to visit and related in detail the circumstances of his awakening.
The Master rebuked him, saying: "The Buddha-dharma is like the great ocean; the further one enters, the deeper it becomes. Where would you stop?"

Regarding this point, [Shicheng] remarked: "Although Master Baozang employed harsh tongs and hammers, his 'stinking air' was still too heavy. If I were Jin-su, as soon as his eyebrows moved, I would strike him across the spine, making him truly bare and clear, so that he might find lifelong joy.
One day, while in the meditation hall, Hui-xia stood in attendance. The Master asked, "Mind is not Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. How do you understand this?
Xia stepped forward, paid his respects, and stood with his hands joined. The Master rebuked him.
[The Master] said, "Having been here for all this time, you still maintain such a view. Chan-tai then applied himself with resolute effort in his practice.
On the second night, he suddenly attained thorough realization. He went to present himself before the Abbot, who looked at him and smiled, saying, "Even though it is so..."
"You must also skillfully protect and maintain yourself. When the time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself. Having received these instructions, Wutan Tianxiang stayed in the mountains;
the Master sent him off with a verse for his mountain retreat: "To see clearly is not Chan; advance further on the tip of the pole beyond the reach of words.
To propagate the ancestral Way, my school’s teaching, enter the mountains once more for twenty years. (Wanfeng Wei was his successor.)
Chan Master Wunian Shengxue of Jiu Peak in Wu Chang was a native of Ying Shan in Suizhou. His clan name was Chen.

At the age of nine, he left home to become a monk under Master Yuan of Bao Lin Monastery in his native prefecture. After receiving the tonsure and dyeing his robes, he could not recognize a single character;
yet he persevered in ascetic practice for many years. Later, realizing that the Great Matter remained unclarified and that scholastic study was of no benefit, he went to visit Master Wumen Shiwan.
"The Dharma returns to the One. To what place does the One return? Having spoken thus, he entered Mount Song to dwell in seclusion and studied with diligent heart.
One day, he attained a realization and composed a verse, saying: "For years at Dongshan, the mist hung thick; I leaned on the railing all day, awaiting a clear sky.

Last night, suddenly the moon rose in the frosty heavens; The myriad phenomena were fully revealed within a single mirror. Thereupon, he resolved to travel extensively to seek instruction from various masters. Later...
He arrived at Gusu and met Wansong Xingxiu at Dengwei. Upon being struck by a shout, he attained realization. Wansong then bestowed upon him a verse, saying:
"The Linji lineage has been transmitted through five branches; A single shout upon entering the gate reveals the full edge of the blade.
Out of her grandmotherly concern, she could not bear to be easy; Behold the mud snake transformed into a dragon! One day, Wansong raised the koan of "The Ox Passing Through the Window Frame."
He was instructed to look at a verse. The Master said: "Horns towering high, four hooves and hoofs; the entire body passes through the crevice as the moon sinks in the west.
If you can turn your body about when the opportunity arises, let out a roar and have no further doubt. Wei also verified this with a verse.
Later, he returned to Baolin, where his reputation for the Way spread far and wide. He subsequently resided at Jiufeng. In the fifteenth year of the Hongwu era, the Empress Dowager Xiaoci...

Later, after he passed away, the King of Chu invited renowned monks from various mountains to assemble at Hongshan. Upon seeing the Master’s dignified appearance, they were struck with wonder and amazement.

They specially provided him with lodging and entertained him, engaging in profound discussions on the mysteries of the Dharma. Their requests for instruction became increasingly earnest, leading them to establish a monastery and invite the Master to reside there.
One day, as he ascended the hall, the Master asked the assembly, "What is that single phrase of the direct pointing transmitted by Bodhidharma from the West? The assembly remained silent.

The Master spoke on their behalf: "Before the Five Milk Peaks, he discusses the Shaoshi [Patriarch]... In the seventeenth year of the Hongwu era, the August Emperor, admiring the Master’s exemplary conduct, summoned him to the private audience hall.
He granted him a seat, and the Master’s responses pleased the Emperor. The honors bestowed upon him were most generous.

The Emperor wished to retain him to preside over a capital monastery, but the Master declined with firm resolve. An imperial messenger was dispatched to escort him back to Jiufeng. In the twenty-ninth year, the August Emperor...
The Emperor personally composed a scroll of poetry and prose in praise of the monk Wunian, and enclosed within it pine nuts and pine flowers.

He further dispatched an imperial messenger to deliver these to the mountains, his words of consolation being most earnest and sincere. The Imperial Edict stated: "Previously, the monk Wunian’s observance of the precepts was as pure as the bright moon, and his concentration and wisdom were as stable as a towering mountain.
I came for a brief visit to see him; since he has departed, I have constantly harbored him in my thoughts. Having cherished this memory without ceasing, I now [bestow this upon him]."
A special envoy was sent to visit him, bringing offerings of pine nuts and pine blossoms, as well as poems and prose to honor him.
The Master also offered a verse in response, saying: "Below the myriad affairs, one investigates the true mystery; At the tips of the hundred grasses, lies the Zen of Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Every pore universally contains lands and worlds as numerous as dust motes; Upon the tip of a single hair, the sky of nature is revealed. Returning from meditation, I sit watching clouds stretch across the valley."
While enjoying a stroll and observing the stone spring, the monk beneath the trees—how shall he repay [the Emperor’s grace]? He offered prayers for the Sage’s longevity to endure ten thousand years.

The palace official returned and reported this; the Emperor was greatly pleased. On the twenty-ninth day of the third month in the third year of the Yongle era, he gathered the assembly and spoke a verse, saying:
"The World-Honored One lived seventy-nine; Wunian lived eighty. Treading upon the ocean of the Flower Treasury, I rely..."
The old waters joined the heavens; he passed away with serene composure. His entire remains were enshrined in a stupa at Shiziyuan, and he was posthumously titled Chan Master Qingfu Guanghui.
An official was dispatched to present silk offerings, and a court scholar was commissioned to compose the inscription for the stupa (Wanfeng Wei was his successor).
When the head monk of Guolín came for an audience, the Master threw down his meditation cushion and said, "Try to say something about this.

The monk replied, "This very message is fundamentally beyond words; upon this broken meditation cushion, earth bursts forth and heaven cracks open. The Master asked, "But tell me, what is it that cracks?
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him. (The above three were successors of Wānfēng Wèi.)
Chan Master Xizhu Benlai of Huanglong Shouchang in Jianchang was the son of the Pei family of Chongren in Fuzhou.
He left home to become a monk at the age of seven and, at thirteen, went to attend upon Yifeng Ning. He investigated the great matter of his own person with utmost intensity.

One day, he suddenly realized that his body was like empty space and his mind was beyond all boundaries; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he did not know who it was. Suddenly, he heard someone reciting the *Qing*.
The *Jing jing* (Pure Scripture) says: "Internally contemplate the mind; the mind has no mind. Suddenly he attained realization and composed a verse, saying:
"For many years I wandered abroad, losing my true soul; Today we meet, yet how utterly different! With a golden-haired stone lion as companion, I turn my head and swallow the Iron Kunlun.
He then went back to visit Neng, who gave him this instruction: "In the Sangha hall there is a Head Seat."
[Zhaozhou] said, "There is no Way, yet you speak as if there were. The Master asked, "How do you say it? Ning replied, "Empty-handed, holding a hoe," and so forth.
The Master said, "I understand this. Ning asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Empty-handed, holding a hoe.
Ning shouted, "This is the talk of one who has finished his work! How dare you speak such nonsense! He then grabbed [the Master] and said, "Right now—"
"Have you attained realization yet? The Master said, "The Way is natural; how could there be such a thing as 'attaining realization'? Ning said, "Go for now.
That evening, when they gathered at Pují, Ning said with a stern voice, "Just now, when I posed the question, what did you do?
The Master said, "I raised it quite clearly, but I did not speak to the Master. Ning shouted, "If it was clear, then why..."
"Extremely improper," said Master [Linji]. "I have already told you, Elder; why do you strike me so violently?
Linji pushed him down and left, shaking his sleeves. The next day, he saw him again. Linji said, "Under my staff, there is a step of practice.
If you understand this, even the Buddhas and Patriarchs can do nothing with you. You must go back and reflect thoroughly. If you apply your mind and yet do not attain this, it will be of no use."
From birth until death, it is simply like this. He then presented a verse, saying: Layer upon layer of green mountains, shrouded in misty rain;
The golden mane of the lion cannot be penetrated. I myself know that the time has not yet come; Of ten times I draw the arrow, nine times it goes empty.
The Master then went to Jiangdong in Guixi, where he established a hermitage to dwell. It was only after seven years that he attained enlightenment.
At that time, Huining had already passed away, so he went to Jinshan to see Cizhou Ji. Ji said, "I have heard that you were originally a dharma heir of Yifeng."
The Master said, "He deserves thirty blows of the heavy staff; the document has long been in his possession, and today he has come specifically to the Master to seek a seal.
Zouzhi pointed to the vase-flower and had him compose a verse, saying: "When the opportunity strikes, he shatters the very bones of heaven and earth;
His marrow spills across the void, pure and flawless. Startled, the pure vase opens its mouth to laugh, Constantly unfolding the four [realms] beyond the kalpas."
At that time, Huatong Jie said, "The Buddhas have not spoken it; the Patriarchs have not transmitted it.

Setting aside the flapping of lips and the drumming of tongues, the blinking of eyes and the raising of eyebrows, and the lifting of hands and the moving of feet—bring me back your words of arriving home. The Master remained silent.
Jie said, "The age since the Sage has grown distant, and the worthy sages remain hidden. Yet there is still this son; the dragons and devas shall bear great witness for me. From this point on...
"Go forth! Hold fast to the truth; return to that which is ultimate, so that you may attain great utility. If you were to treat this lightly and squander it, you would betray my entrustment.
The dragons and devas shall eliminate [those who oppose] me for you. The Master rose from his prostrations and said, "I respectfully obey your strict command. Ji spoke again:
"When the ancients reached such a state, they entered deep into mountain crags and valleys to nurture the sacred embryo (*āryagarbha*), remaining there for thirty years without..."

He was permitted to speak; his lips were so parched that a white film had formed upon them. Driven by the needs of humans and devas, he could not help but utter a word or two to support the final age of the Dharma.
The Master then took his leave with words of deep respect. He retired to live in seclusion at Shousheng Monastery on Sword River.

Later, when Prince Ning heard that the Master’s Way surpassed all others, he dispatched messengers three times to invite him. The Master did not go. Furthermore, the Prince presented a verse to inquire about the Way, to which the Master replied: [Verse omitted as per instructions] The Master answered: [Response omitted as per instructions]
On the essential points of progress and cultivation. In the fourth year of the Yongle era, while residing at Shouchang in Xincheng, he ascended the hall and said:
"The heavens and sun are bright and high, and the summer heat gradually intensifies. Pomegranate flowers erupt like fire, shining within the courtyard.

Within the eyes of the patch-robed monks, the true mechanism is revealed; the Unranked True Person is encountered face-to-face. If you know the point directly, hesitation creates a thousandfold barrier. To reach the matter of your own person," [he continued].
At the Highest Peak of Huanglong, he ascended the hall and said: "The flowers are in full bloom; the sun’s orb is crimson. The Dharma of the mind shines forth, penetrating everywhere.
Beneath the tip of the patch-robed monk’s nostrils, a vast spirit surges through the universe. With eyes emptying the four seas, he has no worldly concerns;
this very staff in his hand—where he wishes to go west, he goes west; where he wishes to go east, he goes east. He struck the ground with the staff.

[The Master] descended from his seat with his staff and gave a small discourse: "Clear, clear! A single expanse of sky, its light shining brightly. Rest, rest, rest! The clouds fly high and the waters flow on their own.
With eyes opened wide and the whole body pervaded, there is no front or back; throughout the ten directions and all lands, one may roam at will.
Later, when Shinkan Fukuden-ji Temple was abandoned, he was invited to restore it. As the work was nearing completion, one day he sat in meditation while burning incense.
He sat down, took up his brush, and wrote this verse: "This old beggar—when will his teaching ever end? Tumbling and toppling, he lets himself go with the flow;
Whether he is a sage or an ordinary person, no one understands. Hah! Come, come, come! Go, go, go! The ocean is deep and still, the sky is empty;
The wind is pure and the moon is bright. Having cast aside his brush, he passed away. His disciples enshrined his entire body in the Dharma Hall and subsequently interred his fingernails in a stupa.
Ha-eun (Jisi of Geum-san) was born at Chan-gi-ryeong, northwest of Sunchang, to the Mo family of Tonghyeon Town in An’gok, Shu. At the age of twenty, he left home;
having initially met no one who could guide him, he practiced the techniques of seated meditation and entering samādhi. Later, he resided at Nusan and sought out [the master] Cheong.
The Bodhisattva Qingju took up Zhaozhou’s “Mu” (No) kōan. At that very moment, the Master attained realization.
From then on, he relied upon this “Mu,” which was like Mount Sumeru; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he remained constantly in meditative concentration.
One day, while sitting, a brilliant light suddenly shone forth, and not a single atom could be grasped. He composed a verse stating: "Empty space cannot contain it."
Regarding the phrase "The great earth cannot bear it," [Zhaozhou] visited the ancient and rugged Master Jun.
During his prostrations, Jun said to an attendant, "This monk has the marks of merit. He then set down his staff, leaned back in his chair, and ordered the master to recount his travels.
The master recounted them directly. Jun said, "Go for now; I do not yet know such practice as yours. One day, he came again.

The Abbot [Zhaozhou] let out a thunderous shout and brandished his staff as if to strike. The Master threw himself forward to meet the blow. Zhaozhou said, "My staff has eyes; I do not strike such a dead man.
He then pulled his staff and went out. The Master stood with palms joined, remaining motionless.

Zhaozhou returned to his seat and suddenly asked, "When the great earth sinks away, where are you? The Master replied: *Note: This dialogue is from the *Biyan Lu* (Blue Cliff Record), Case 10, concerning the encounter between Zhaozhou and the Master Xuefeng.*
[The Master] fully revealed the body of the Dharma King. Yunjun said, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? He pressed him, saying, "Speak quickly!
Speak quickly! The Master said, "I do not speak. Yunjun said, "Why do you not speak? The Master said, "From antiquity to the present.
Yunjun said, "Setting aside for a moment that 'from antiquity to the present,' what thing is it that comes from Sichuan in such a manner? The Master remained silent. After a long while, Yunjun...
He said, "A mute person has a dream—whom would he tell it to? One day, Jun changed his name to Wuji (Boundless). The Master said, "If that is so, then even 'Boundless' is not yet it.
All the old monks of the world attain enlightenment here; all the patriarchs of successive generations attain Buddhahood here.
Let anyone who can speak of Buddha or speak of the Patriarchs come forward now, and I shall send them all away."
"Go out the door! It is better than this fellow here snoring away in his sleep. Jun laughed and said, "This fellow will not be deceived by others from now on.
The Master once had a verse regarding the "Running Horse Lamp" (Zouma Deng) which says: Rounding and rounding, it gallops without stopping;
There is no one with clear eyes to point out the way. Extinguish the slight fire within the mind, And the swords, spears, men, and horses [will vanish].

All at once, [the Master] paused. The monk Shanjian came forward and presented his practice, stating that he had reached the point where principle was exhausted and emotion ended, cutting off the ten directions, leaving no room for ordinary or holy beings, and that his mind was as profound as the Great Mystery (*tai-xuan*), such that not a single dharma existed—this being the Tathāgata’s ground of pure awakening.
"If this is so," he said, "then may the Master certify it; I do not seek the Master's instruction. The Master asked, "Which one?"
"This is the Tathāgata’s ground of pure awakening. A monk stepped forward, joined his palms, and said, "My own nature.
The Master said, "I find it difficult to provide you with proof. The monk said, "I am [it]. The Master said, "The Master says I am not yet [it];
this is the Master misleading me. I am not yet [it], yet the Master says I am; this too is the Master misleading me. The Master said, "Why do you not go elsewhere? The monk said, [silently].
"If there were anyone in the world who surpassed me, I would not have set foot through the gate of this old monk.
The Master said, "You are truly my son who has reached home. The monk did not look back. The Master said, "I grant you, I grant you. The monk still did not look back. The Master said:
"I grant you my approval. What more is there to doubt? You are thus; I am also thus. The monk stepped forward and performed three full prostrations.
The Master said, "Recite once more all the places where you have previously applied yourself to practice, as an offering to the assembly.
The monk then recounted his aforementioned practice of cultivation up until the point of seeing the Truth (*darśana-mārga*), after which he folded his hands and remained silent. The Master said:
The monk asked, "How is it that your realization of the Truth differs from mine? He spread out both hands and said, "This is nothing other than that.
The Master asked, "Does this still involve words and phrases? The monk replied, "In truth, there is not a single word.
The Master said, "At this very point where there is not a single word, I have already given you my certification. You may go to a mountain hut in the deep wilderness and eat when hungry."
He drank thirstily and wandered at ease as he pleased. An called him "Gu" (Ancient). "Ting" (Garden) is a term for ritual separation.
The Master said, "Son, you have reached such a place. Ting said, "It is a place where even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot travel.

The Master said, "Is it permissible for others to come there? Ting said, "It is level and unobstructed. The Master said, "Among the ancients of old, who possessed wisdom that transcended the Patriarchs? Ting said—
Yuanwu Keqin asked, "Do you see Huangbo? Xuedou replied, "Even if it were Huangbo himself, he would still have to be expelled.
The Master said, "You dare to speak such great words here in my presence. Xuedou said, "The true eye is impartial and without private bias.
The Master said, "Observing your insight, your wisdom surpasses that of your teacher. I now bestow upon you the robe and whisk. Be careful, be careful! Xuedou covered his ears and departed.
(Tianjie Junsu). Chan Master Xing Tianru Jiao of Hangzhou Hupao was the son of Zhou [family] from Siming. At the age of seven, he suffered from intestinal abscesses.
A physician was skinning a live frog for medicinal treatment. When the Master saw this, he was struck with alarm and said, "All things and I alike possess life;
how can you harm it? He snatched the creature away and released it. His parents marveled at this, saying, "He must surely be one of the Buddha-seed. They then ordained him as a monk.

Later, he went to visit the Venerable Guzhuo Jun, and upon pushing aside the curtain to see the moon, he attained realization. He exclaimed, "So this is how it has always been! The following morning, he hurried [to the master].

Upon seeing Jun, the Master let out a thunderous shout. Jun said, "Is it like a poor man finding treasure? The Master replied, "If you have not found the treasure, then what you have found is not the treasure.
Jun asked, "On what basis do you say this? The Master stepped forward to pay his respects, stood with his hands folded, and Jun said, "Bring me back that one phrase from above!
The Master then covered his ears and departed. He further presented a verse, saying: Midnight...
Pushing back the curtain, a crescent moon appears; gently, it steps through the gate above. There is no need to seek it elsewhere from others; simply maintain this joyful, smiling countenance.
(The verse "Jùn wèi zhùxǐ" [The Handsome One Assists with Joy] was written after he resided at Hupao in Wulin. At the end of his life, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"Literature and the Buddha-dharma are colors in the void; names, forms, body, and mind are mist upon willow trees. Only birth and death—"
"This is a truly great matter. Attend to it with earnest diligence; do not delay. "The assembly, tell me: how is it attended to?
After a long silence, he said, "I have no leisure now to explain it for you. Listen instead to the sound of the pines and the mountain stream. Having finished speaking, he passed away peacefully.
(The above two masters are Tianjie Junsu and his predecessor.)
The lay practitioner Tiansu’an of Yangzhou was by lineage a renowned clan of Jiangdu.

Having failed repeatedly in his attempts to pass the examinations as a student of the imperial academy, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), investigating it with fierce diligence. At that time, the Governor He Mimian was propagating the Way in the southeast.
The Master was a preeminent disciple who had entered the inner sanctum. After he had been refined through the hammer and tongs for a long time, [the Master] suddenly entrusted him with the mind-seal.
The Master then took up a bamboo whisk and examined the monastics; among those who came from all quarters to study, there were none who did not revere Suanan as a living ancient Buddha.

Throughout the nation, he was called "Great Being Tian" (Tian Dashi) rather than by his personal name. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Lately, those who are earnestly devoted to the practice of Chan are few. As soon as [the topic] is raised..."

As soon as one encounters this *huatou*, one is immediately bound by the two demons of torpor and distraction. Little do they realize that torpor and distraction are precisely the antidotes to the state of doubt (*yiqing*).
When the power of faith is deep, the state of doubt will necessarily be profound; when the state of doubt is profound, torpor and distraction will naturally vanish.
[The Master] addressed the assembly: "The great ocean does not harbor corpses; empty space does not cling to the five colors; a mass of fire does not conceal mosquitoes."
Within the dharma of non-abiding, there is no establishment of delusion or enlightenment. Those who practice Chan today merely cover themselves with the shadows and reflections at their own doors;
they enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow. Addressing the assembly, [the Master] raised the case of the layman Zhang Cheng (Jiucheng), who visited Chan Master Qing of Shanquan and asked:
"This matter is inherently possessed by every person and perfectly realized by each individual, is it not? Qing replied: "Indeed."
The scholar said, "For what reason do I have no point of entry? Qing drew a string of white prayer beads from his sleeve and showed them to him. The scholar looked up and down, unable to respond.
Qing tucked the beads back into his sleeve and said, "These are yours; take them. "As soon as you engage in discursive thought," he added, "they are no longer yours. The scholar was struck with awe.
That night, while sitting upright, he investigated the koan of the "Pine Tree" until he suddenly heard the sound of a frog. Immediately—
There is an entryway. Today I shall bring forth this matter. You practitioners who study the Way must not, by any means, understand it as a discussion of the profound or the marvelous;
nor must you understand it through conceptualization or intellectual calculation. When you reach that point of timing and season, you will naturally arrive there.
But tell me, how would you express the phrase "the season"? [The Master] drew a circle (○). A monk entered for an audience and asked about Potalaka.
The monk asked, "Which gate do you take to exit? The Master said, "Venerable, from which gate do you enter right now?
The monk said, "Why do you constrain me so? The Master said, "Watch where you step. The monk raised his head and took three steps forward;
the Master said, "Wrong. The monk then stepped back three paces; the Master said, "Tell me, was it you who were wrong, or was it I? The monk said, "Before you even raised [a finger]..."
[The Master] said, "I knew it was wrong beforehand. The layman said, "It is exactly right for you to receive a blow of the staff.
The monk remained silent. The layman said, "If you go to other places, explain this clearly [to them]. While a monk was reciting a sutra, the layman asked, "What sutra are you reciting?
The monk replied, "The Lotus Sutra. The layman said, "The Lotus Sutra has sixty thousand characters; which of those characters has eyes? The monk was at a loss. The layman then struck him.
As the monk entered the gate, he bowed. The Master shouted, "Walk quickly! The monk bowed again. The Master said, "What bowl are you looking for?
The monk shouted. The Master then struck him with his palm. The Master lived in a village of farmers outside the city, using his residence as a hermitage.

Monks from all quarters who came to seek instruction gathered daily at his seat. One day, while engaging in tea conversation with the assembly of Zen practitioners, he suddenly threw down his cup and snapped it shut.

Zhang. He departed from the assembly (The successor of Governor He was [He] Andian Zhong, Mingkan Yi, and Zhen; these three men each propagated the Dharma in their respective regions, yet the lineage of Master Zhen was the most flourishing.

His lamp passed through five generations, producing great figures. Before the Jiajing and Longqing eras, the lineage of the Yangzhou Great Being Tian was widely prevalent throughout the north and south of the Great River).
Chan Master Huan-yuan Fuyu of Bao-ying Temple at Shaoshi in Xijing of the Cao-dong school was a native of the Wang family in Ling-shi, Huo Prefecture.

He received the tonsure at Doushuai Temple in his home district and traveled extensively among the lecture halls, where his eloquence flowed like a stream. Having heard of Chan Master Tai of Shaoshi, he [went to him].
His insight into the Way was perfectly clear and bright, so he went to rely upon him for study. Daowei said, "I raise my whisk, and you immediately seek understanding from the whisk.

As soon as I remain silent for a long while, you immediately seek understanding within that silence. How will you ever penetrate this fundamental matter? The Master’s face flushed with heat and sweat poured down.
One day, he heard Daowei ascend the hall and say, "Be most careful not to seek it from others; it is far removed from me..."
The Commentary states: The Master was of keen intelligence; he immediately received the seal of approval and was secretly entrusted with the robe and verse.

A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The wind carries the sound of the spring to my pillow; the moon shifts the shadows of the flowers to my window.
The monk said, "This is still merely a matter within the gateway of sound and form. The Master rebuked him, saying, "You salt-smuggler!"
Question: "What is the Prince at Birth? The Master said: "Though he possesses the status of nobility, he is not a noble person.
Question: "What is the Prince Newly Born in Court? The Master said: "He does not rank as high as those on the golden register; in the end, he remains but an old court official."
[The student] asked, "What is the prince born at the end? The Master said, "Having exhausted all hardships and labors, one finally attains an audience with the Heaven of Yao.
[The student] asked, "What is the prince born by transformation? The Master said, "His essence is no different from his father’s; he temporarily wields the strategic authority beyond the borders."
[The student] asked, "What is it like to be a prince born within? The Master said, "Always dwelling deep within the palace, a mere foot and a half from the Dragon’s countenance.
[The student] asked, "As for the path that leads upward, how is that? The Master said, "The stringless lute has its melody; how could humans or devas hear it?
In the tenth month of the Gui-chou year of the Renzong Huangqing era, the Master passed away without illness. His disciples enshrined his entire body.
The pagoda was enshrined in the ancestral cemetery at Shaoshi (Shaoshi Tai succeeded him).
Chan Master Qiujiang Jie of Lingyan in Jinan was attended by the monk Xuexuan Cheng. The Master asked, "Where have you come from?
Cheng replied, "From Qingzhou. The Master said, "Did you bring the Qingzhou cloth robe with you? Cheng said, "I present it to the Master."
“[I] understand. The Master said, “Wait until you come back for thirty blows. Cheng shook his sleeves and departed. The Master said, “This disciple has attained realization.
He then sent him to attend the meditation hall. One day, Cheng suddenly went to the master’s quarters. The Master looked at him and said with delight:
"The golden lock of the mysterious pass has been opened. Cheng said, "Within a peach pit that is a thousand years old, what 'kernel' from the past can one seek?
The Master instructed him, saying, "This is something you inherently possess. Guard and maintain it well yourself. In days to come, you shall be able to propagate my Way."
It must have been you (the two aforementioned masters, Shaoshi Tai and his successor).
Chan Master Yongda of Boreng Moon-Rock [Temple] in the Western Capital was the son of the Liu family of Fenzhou.

He received the tonsure at Tianning Temple in that prefecture and constantly exhorted himself with the resolve to transcend birth and death. He traveled south to seek instruction and inquiry, and there he heard of Master Lingyan Su.
The Dharma-thunder shook far and wide; [Hui]su went there to attend upon him. Upon their first meeting, [Dongshan] Liangjie held him in high esteem as a vessel of the Way.

Having been in his presence for a long time, [Hui]su finally entered the innermost depths of his teaching, whereupon he said: "The words originate with the teacher, but the practice lies with oneself. He then departed for Taian to close himself in retreat.

When monastics and laypeople earnestly entreated him to emerge, he could not refuse and arose to reside at Baoying Temple. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Old Man of Lumeng says that the entire great earth is..."
For a student, a single scroll of scripture is the entire universe; it is the student’s own single eye.

With such an eye, one views such a scripture, without interruption for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas. Yet even so, the old man Wansong was ultimately driven to the end of his resources and exhausted of effort.
To say that this is not easy to see—do you all still think you can read it? You must know that this single volume of scripture belongs to everyone;
this one eye is complete in every person. If one wishes for it to be long, ten thousand billion kalpas would not suffice to exhaust it;
if one wishes for it to be short, a single kṣaṇa is enough to encompass it. Today, Baoying does not begrudge his own eyebrows as he brings this forth for all of you.
He stepped out, snapped his fingers once, and said, "Look! You have read it; do not let this pass you by. After a long silence, he struck his whisk and said, "From now on, one does not return;
yet if one returns, one attains it. Who can vie for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes?
He then threw down the whisk and descended from the seat. (Zu’ān Sù was his successor.)
Chan Master Fonglong Guyan Pujou was the son of the Liu family of Huyang.

He studied under Venerable Lingyan Su, who refined him further with the hammer and tongs of the fundamental teaching and entrusted him with the Great Dharma. When Fonglong earnestly requested that he emerge from seclusion to teach, the Master reluctantly accepted.
A monk asked, "What is 'falling into the category'? The Master said, "It is not one who wears fur and carries horns."
[The student] asked, "What is 'falling in accordance with'? The Master said, "It is not one who hears sounds or sees forms.
[The student] asked, "What is 'falling from nobility'? The Master said, "It is not one who cuts off sound and form. [The student] asked, "If that is so, how is it called 'falling'?

The Master said, "A wild goose flies across the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water. [The student] said, "An ancient said, 'The three falls are the illness of those who have finished their work. Since—"

"This is a man who has realized the ultimate truth. How could he have illness? The Master said, "Precisely because he has realized the ultimate truth. [The monk] asked, "When will this illness be cured?
The Master said, "Only when there is no body shall this illness be eliminated. Thereupon, he presented a verse: "The heavy golden locks have long since been struck open;
Tranquil and at ease, he comes and goes alone through the three realms. A wild goose flies across the vast sky, unattached; Its reflection sinks into the cold water."
He left them to their conjectures. Later, he returned to live in seclusion at Lingqi. Not long after, he manifested his passing.

In the sixth year of the Dade era, he was bestowed the title of Great Chan Master Miaoyan Hongfa. His stupa was erected on the southern slope of Fenglong Mountain (Zuanan Su succeeded him; the two aforementioned individuals are now complete).

Chan Master Xubai Huichan of Dongming Temple in Hangzhou, of the Linji lineage, was born into the Wang clan. His ancestral home was in Huguang.

His father served as a Vice Commissioner for Salt and Taxation in Danyang, where they subsequently settled. From his youth, he was exceptionally intelligent and did not resemble ordinary children. At the age of fourteen, he went to follow [a teacher].
Miaojue Zhanran was tending his duties one day when he asked, "What are you doing here? The Master replied, "I am slicing radishes.
Zhanran said, "You only know how to slice radishes. The Master said, "I also know how to kill people. Zhanran extended his neck toward him.
The Master said, "A surrendered general is not executed. Zhanran marveled at this. Later, when Zhanran moved to Shushan in Fuzhou, the Master heard only of him.
Anan was traveling to Songyin to seek the seal of its heart-mind. Upon reaching a small hermitage, he made a vow, saying, "If I do not achieve thorough realization now, I shall never return.
He then entered meditative concentration for six days. Only after emerging from samādhi did he raise his head and behold the pine trees.

Suddenly, he attained a profound realization. He applied himself with such fervor that he neglected both sleep and food.
