With a single blow, he shattered the great void; the ten billion Sumeru mountains left no trace. I ask you, who is the master within?
A single red orb surges forth from the eastern forest. Heshang laughed and said, "Though it is so, you must still guard and maintain yourself well.
When the time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself. Having received these instructions, the Master took his leave and went to Mount Pingshan at Tianmu.
In the Hall, he formed a group of companions and sat in meditation for a thousand-day long-term retreat. When the period was complete, he went to Zhaoqing Monastery to receive full ordination.

On one day, he traveled to the Ancient Dao Mountain in Anxi; seeing that its peaks and ridges were strikingly prominent, he conceived the resolve to spend the remainder of his life there. He resided there for thirty years.

His shadow did not leave the mountain, yet his influence spread far and wide; veteran monks vied with one another to seek refuge at his seat. He expanded the foundations and renovated the structures, establishing a great monastic complex.
In the year Yimao of the Xuande era, it was granted the name Dongming Chan Temple, and an imperial decree was issued to ordain monks to maintain the sacred offerings.
Offerings and alms had accumulated in abundance. The Master further diminished his remaining wealth to repair the Great Hall of Jingci Monastery.

On the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month in the sixth year of the Zhengtong era (the *xinyou* year), he suddenly assembled the community to express his gratitude and bid them farewell. When the assembly requested a verse, the Master said:
No one among the vast treasury of the Buddhist teachings ever looked upon him; what use, then, for these few idle words?

On the twenty-ninth day, at the hour of the dragon (7–9 a.m.), he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. His remains were cremated, yielding countless relics, which were enshrined in a stupa at Dongwu (succeeded by Baozangchi).
Once, while a monk was visiting the Chan Master in the Snow-Bone Assembly at Tianjie Monastery in Jianning, the Master asked, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "It fills the void; there is no coming or going. The Master said, "Since there is no coming or going, who is it that has brought this leather bag here?
The monk said, "Both inside and outside are empty; how could there be a leather bag? The Master asked, "What is the Patriarch?"

[The questioner] asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master replied, "When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, where will you go to find a place to settle your body and establish your life?
[The questioner] said, "With a step of faith, I tread upon and overturn it; heaven and earth are revealed alone. The Master then showed him with a verse:
"This is truly the golden-haired lion emerging from its den; The Wheel of Dharma turns back to enter the marketplace. A single cry suddenly reaches afar..."
An empty howl. Upon hearing it, the wild jackal’s skull split open (according to *Fútian láisì*).
Zen Master Deying Chéng of Dàgāng in Jīnlíng went into the presence of Venerable Wújì Wù of Dōngpǔ and attained realization.
As Wù was approaching his death, he spoke this verse of dharma-transmission: "I have no dharma to transmit; you have no mind to receive. There is neither transmission nor..."
Receiving the mind. What person does not achieve it? Master Ji-xi succeeded to the seat at Dongpu. There was a monk named Benshan who sought certification from the Master.
The Master said, "The Buddha-dharma is not like fresh fish that fears rotting. Day after day, he [the Master] struck east and beat west, secretly setting up examinations and tests.
One day, while Benshan was sitting with the Master in the garden, the Master said, "What have you been looking at lately?"
"What is the *huatou*? Wanshan said, "The word 'wu' (no). The Master asked, "What is the word 'wu'?
Wanshan said, "Looking at it now, it is just like the Vajra King’s Precious Sword. The Master asked, "What is the Vajra King’s Precious Sword?
Wanshan said, "Its cold radiance blazes forth, shining through antiquity and soaring into the present. The Master said, "Give me back the sword! Wanshan said, "If you try to move..."

[Zhaozhou] committed an offense against the other’s sharp edge. The Master said, "When you hold it crosswise across the gate, what then? Shouyan said, "Even if a Buddha comes, I kill him; even if an Ancestor comes, I kill him.
The Master said, "What about when this old monk comes? Shouyan said, "I will not spare you either. The Master said, "After killing, what then?
Shouyan said, "Fortunately, all under heaven is at peace. The Master said, "Ultimately, what is the meaning of the word 'wu'? Shouyan—
[Shanzhao] said, "The stolen goods and the thief are clearly identified. The Master said, "Setting aside the thief for a moment, bring me back my stolen goods.
Shanzhao said, "Six times six is thirty-six. The Master said, "That will not do; speak further. Shanzhao said, "The night is short and sleep is insufficient; the day is long and hunger remains."
The Master said, “When an ox passes through a window lattice, its head, horns, and four hooves have all passed through; why does its tail not pass?
Wu Jian said, “There is not a single dharma that stands before the mind; in a flash, the entire body is revealed in the open field.
The Master said, “Where do you now establish yourself and find your life’s sustenance? Wu Jian said, “Where would it not be called honorable? (Wu Jian succeeded to Wuji).
Chan Master Shaoqi Jingbi of Huan’ou at Touzi Mountain in Shuzhou was the son of the Lei family of Tang’an in Shu.
At the age of nine, he received his training from Xuanji Tong. He first visited Wuji, where one day he attained realization upon hearing the sound of the wooden board.
He subsequently traveled to consult various elders, including Yuexi and Haizhou, all of whom praised him. In the sixth year of the Zhengtong era, he returned once more...
Chan Wuji asked, "Where have you been living for the past few years? The Master said, "Vastly open and without fixed abode. Wuji said, "What have you attained?
The Master said, "Fundamentally there has never been anything lost; what is there to attain? Wuji said, "Is this something acquired through study?
The Master said, "Not a single dharma exists; from where could study come? Wuji said, "Do you not fall into emptiness?"
The Master said, "I am not even I; who falls and what is empty? Yiji asked, "Ultimately, what is it? The Master said, "When the water recedes, the rocks appear;
when the rain clears, the clouds vanish. Yiji said, "Do not speak so confusedly! Even if the Buddhas and Patriarchs were to come, they would not be permitted.
Even if you were to swallow the ocean of the Tripitaka from side to side and manifest hundreds of thousands of spiritual powers, here you still would not be permitted. The Master [laughed].
[Daowu] said, "Although you, Master, hold fast at the vital ford, it seems you have not spared yourself much mental toil. Daowu patted his knee once. The Master then shouted.
Daowu said, "One who can uphold the family must be one who can break the family; doing so to manage the household affairs is truly effortless.
The Master covered his ears and left. That evening, he summoned the Master again and interrogated him, saying, "Regarding the successive stages of your past realizations—"
"Speak and let me see. The Master answered truthfully and in detail. Yunju said, "Give me back the meaning of the word 'no'. The Master presented a verse, saying:
"The place where this monk asked was full of complications; How could Old Zhao have ever involved his thoughts?
A single word spoken offhand was fully revealed, Yet it turned out to be quite unnecessary, causing people to doubt. Yunju said, "What is your state of being without doubt? The Master said, "Blue."
The mountains are green and the waters clear; swallows chatter and orioles sing. Everything is distinct and clear—what more could one doubt? Jì said, "Not yet; speak further.
The Master said, "The head touches the void, while the feet tread upon solid ground. Jì then struck the bell to assemble the assembly and presented him with a *kāṣāya* robe and a whisk.
Later, when he took up residence at Tiānzhù, a monk asked, "What is the realm of Tiānzhù? The Master said, "A mountain stream..."
The vast clouds return at evening; the mountain is high, so the sun rises late. [A monk] asked, "What is it like to be a person within this realm?
The Master said, "Eyebrows beneath the forehead cover the eyes; ears on the cheeks reach the shoulders. [The monk] asked, "What is the house style of Tiantzhu?

The Master said, "Steaming pine powder in a cloud-bellied steamer; boiling moon-discs in an ice-cold cauldron. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The sea..."
Shen scattered forth a night-bright pearl. [A monk] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Mañjuśrī has lost his crystal cup. [The monk] asked, "What is the Buddha?
The Master said, "An iron weight for a scale. He asked, "What is the Dharma? The Master said, "A stone or a clod of earth.
He asked, "What is the Sangha? The Master said, "A black-lacquered staff. In the fifth year of the Jingtai era, he moved to Touzi.
The Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "Having left Mount Huanshan, you have come to occupy Touzi. With the assembly gathered before you, we request the Master to offer prayers for the Emperor.
The Master said, "The eternal seal within the cauldron; the ageless pine atop the peak. The monk said, "I have already received the Master’s direct instruction regarding the prayer for the Emperor.
As for the 'house style' of Touzi, what is it like? The Master said, "Carrying a water jar through the marketplace—one who passes through is not merely an oil-seller."
[The student] asked: "It is just as the Patriarch said: 'I do not permit traveling at night; one must arrive by dawn. Is this truly so? The Master said:
"Though there is sinew in the eyes, what can be done about the tongue having no bone? [The student] asked: "Zhaozhou said, 'I am already white as a monkey;
he is even blacker than a monkey. What was his meaning? The Master said: "If the arrows were not exhausted, he would not have consented to raise the banner of surrender."
Qi asked, "The Master is ascending the seat today to preach the Dharma; I wonder what auspicious signs there are? The Master said, "The qilin strides beyond the realm of painted colors;
the *utpala* flower blooms amidst fierce flames. Qi asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "When the snow melts, the mountain peak is revealed; when the wind passes, the treetops sway. Qi asked, "Before the precious sword has emerged from its scabbard..."

"How is it? the Master said. "The gods wail and the ghosts weep. [The monk asked: "How is it after [the sword] has emerged from its scabbard? The Master said: "The Buddhas and Patriarchs swallow their voices.
[The monk asked: "How is it when it has emerged and when it has not yet emerged? The Master said: "A lock without a hilt, shaking at both ends. The monk lifted up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*).
The Master then shouted. The monk hesitated; the Master struck him. Then he said: "Scratching an itch on the head of a venomous snake. "Mighty... [The text breaks off.]
To cast one's body across the tiger’s mouth requires precisely such a person. That monk just now was much like a seasoned warrior who dared to come here to seize the drums and snatch the banners;
yet, alas, his head was a dragon while his tail was a snake, and he perished beneath the blows of the staff.
Had he known how to turn back toward the path of life, he naturally would not have encountered the sharp edge of the blade. Therefore it is said: "To handle a snake, one must be..."
The Snake-handler. If one does not know how to handle snakes, they will bite and kill [the practitioner]. Master Faideng raised his whisk and showed it to the assembly, saying:

"I, this mountain monk, originally intended to hide deep within rock caves and pass my time in seclusion. However, because the Elder of Qingliang has an unfinished case, I cannot help but come forth to settle it for him.
At that time, a monk asked: "I do not yet understand—what unfinished matter did the Elder of Qingliang have?"
Having finished the *kōan*, Master Deng took up his staff and struck him, saying, "The patriarchs could not reach it; the calamity now falls upon their descendants.
The monk asked, "Where does the fault lie? Deng said, "The fault lies with me; the calamity falls upon you.

he would immediately shout, his eyes fixed and trembling, and strike them out with a succession of blows. O assembly! This mountain...

After a long silence, he said, "Everyone, take this clearly to heart," and then descended from the seat. The Master went to the vegetable garden and saw a winter melon. He asked:
The head gardener said, "This fellow has no mouth. Why then has he grown so large?
The Master asked, "Has the master of the house ever exerted even a little strength on your behalf? The head gardener replied, "I rely entirely upon his power.
The Master said, "Bring him here to meet me, old monk. The head gardener then prostrated himself. The Master said, "This one is still..."
"This slave and servant are here," [he said]. Turning his head, he picked up some rattan to bind a frame.
The Master then laughed heartily and, looking back at his attendant, said, "There are insects in the vegetable garden. During the Tianfu era, he returned from Mount Lu to Shu;
Han Duhou met him at Fushan and invited him to serve as abbot. On the fifteenth day of the third month in the ninth year of the Chenghua era, as he was about to pass away, the assembly...
"Please grant me the final phrase. The Master spread his two hands and said, "Do you understand? He spoke again:
"On this very day of this year, pushing a cart, he crashes into a wall; he shatters empty space. A thunderclap in the blue sky! Aha-ha!
The clay ox swallows the old dragon’s pearl; the tranquil ocean of nature stills its foam-flowers. Thus, he passes away in stillness. (Wuji Wu succeeded him.)
Chan Master Shanjian of Guting in Yunnan was a native of Kunming in his home prefecture. He first studied under Master Wujie Wu, who assigned him the koan:

"The myriad dharmas return to One; where does the One return? He applied himself with diligent heart to investigate this thoroughly, and only after ten years did he finally attain complete liberation.
Later, he sought awakening and certification from Wuzhuo at Longen. Wuzhuo asked, "In what way does your realization differ from that of this old monk?
The Master spread out both his hands and said, "This is nothing other than that. Wuzhuo nodded in approval. One day, as the Master was taking his leave, Wuzhuo asked, "Where are you going?
The Master replied, "I am going to the crossroads to revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs. Wuzhuo asked, "Will you return? The Master replied: "I will not return."
Without contradicting the venerable countenance of his *upādhyāya*, he paid his respects and departed. He first traveled to Jintai, where he stayed at Mount Dayong;
subsequently, he returned south to reside at Tianjie Monastery in Jinling, and later moved to Fushan in Wanshan, Anhui. Addressing the assembly, he cited Chan Master Wuye of Fenyang, who said:
"The ancient masters said that after one has attained the meaning, one dwells in a thatched hut or a stone chamber, cooking rice and eating from a broken-legged cauldron."
For twenty or thirty years, fame and profit did not occupy his mind, nor did wealth and treasure enter his thoughts.
He completely forgot the ways of the world and concealed his traces among the mountain crags and thickets. When kings summoned him, he would not come; when feudal lords invited him, he would not go.

How could he be compared to those like us who crave profit and love fame, sinking into the paths of the world like petty merchants who forget the great fruit for the sake of small gains? The Master said:
Truly profound are these words! We merely seize upon empty appearances and arrogantly exalt ourselves. The three poisons of ignorance remain secretly bound within our hearts;
when confronted by adverse conditions, we know no way to liberation. To speak according to reality:
set aside for a moment whether you are a learned master or not, and cast off all activity and stillness, speech and silence, and written characters. When birth and death arrive—what then?
Ultimately, how can one escape? One must not mistake a lifeless corpse for reality and indulge in deluded thoughts within its stillness.
One must not cling to a spinning wheel of existence and wallow in recklessness within its liveliness.

As long as there is even the slightest trace of dualistic perception or intellectual discernment—no matter how one’s backbone may be forged of cast iron, or how one’s eloquence flows like a cascading torrent—one cannot avoid the Lord of Death.
Laozi! He is cast into the *āpapa* and *āṭaṭa* hells; through the eight cold and eight hot hells, dying ten thousand deaths and being born ten thousand times—truly, truly so!

Human beings are fundamentally complete in themselves. As for written words, scriptures, and treatises, they have no place to be deposited. Lately, scholars from all quarters have been entirely buried by the tongues of the ancients;
unable to resolve their wills to break through, they allow the dust of emotion and intellectual views to settle upon every opening of their mouths.

Chan Master Xijing Tianqing Xianan Yirang was the son of the Li family of Zhending.
He shaved his head at the age of eight and traveled extensively to study under various masters of the school. Later, he went to Fenglong Mountain to consult with Master Jiu Gong.

He once composed verses on the "attaining the skin" and "attaining the flesh" of Bodhidharma, which Jiu praised, saying: "From the skin to the marrow of Bodhidharma, everything has been grasped by these disciples."

He addressed his attendant, saying, "What is my eye like? [The attendant] replied, "It is like the moon reflected in water. [Later], he went to reside at Tianqing.

Subsequently, he moved to Kongxiang on Mount Xiong’er, Lingyan on Mount Tai, and Songshao in Luoyang. A monk asked, "Regarding the 'merit of no-merit,' is there still a distinction between the partial and the correct?
The Master said, "The partial and the correct are clearly manifest. The monk asked, "What is the partiality and correctness of the merit of no-merit? The Master said, "The stone ox..."
He spat out the mists of the three springs; the numinous bird does not perch in the shadowless forest.

In the summer of the Gengchen year, he fell ill. He then instructed his disciples, saying, "This illness cannot be cured. I must depart. On the twelfth day of the fifth month, he gave his final charge.

When Chan Master Rong of Lingyan on Mount Tai first visited Wanfa Guiyi, he could understand the principle of "the myriad dharmas return to the One," yet he could not penetrate the words: "Where does the One return?
nor the statements regarding the "Qingzhou cotton robe" and "the patriarchal ancestors being exhausted by a single roar of the lion.

One day, while traveling with fellow practitioners up Mount Tai to Dayuan Peak, he suddenly recalled the saying: "Ascending Mount Dong, one sees Lu as small; ascending Mount Tai, [one sees the rest of the world as small]. At that moment, his previous doubts were resolved.
A story from the world: Suddenly losing his footing, he fell and fainted. His fellow practitioners helped him up, and after a long while he regained consciousness.
He cried out, "This is the single roar of the lion; it is the moment when both grandfather and father are utterly exhausted. Confucius and Mencius likely never reached such a state.
Thereupon, he went to visit Master Fenglong Jiu and presented his realization to him. Jiu said, "You must further know that there is a 'turning toward' [the source]."
Only when one has grasped the upper pivot does one finally succeed. The Master gave a shout and departed; Jiu Da-xi called out to him and received his seal of succession (Fenglong Jiu succeeded him).
Later, the Hermit of Jin-ning Heart-Nunnery would often raise his fist and say, "All the patch-robed monks in the world use only this to kill or give life."

Baibiao Chunan, the Abbot, frequently visited Xintiequan. A monk asked the Master, "What method do you employ to receive people?
The Master said, "Just use cold eyes to watch the crab; see how long it can continue its sideways crawl.
The monk said, "If that is so, then cold eyes and iron fists will be bound together in resentment throughout the world. The Master said, "Monastics are all too fond of chewing dung."

recorded by Chan Master Haizhou Yongci of Yishan at Jinling of the Linji School— the twenty-eighth generation after the Sixth Patriarch— it states that the Master...

He was the son of the Yu family in Chengdu, Shu (born in the Jiashu year, the twenty-seventh year of the Hongwu era). From the time he was a young child, he would always feel joy whenever he saw a monk.
One day, upon hearing a discourse on the matter of birth and death, he resolved to renounce the secular world.

He proceeded to Jingde Temple on Mount Daisui in Pengxian, where he prostrated before the abbot, Master Duzhao Yue, and received the tonsure and precepts. Later, he entered the Western Mountains to dwell in seclusion for eight years.

Resolving to travel abroad to seek instruction from various masters, he first visited Master Taichu to request guidance, and was shown the teaching regarding the state prior to the birth of one's parents.
He practiced meditation diligently. One day, Chū asked the Master, "Before one's parents were born, what is that original face?
The Master immediately walked from east to west and stood with his hands folded. Chū said, "That is not it; speak further. The Master replied:

Face-to-face with both eyes, what is there to conceal? At first he was greatly pleased; he composed a commentary and established his own practice hall. He then went to study under Master Wujie of Dongpu, but did not find resonance there.

Consequently, he left the gorges and traveled to the capital, where he received full ordination (in the second year of the Xuande era). He returned once more to Linggu Monastery in Jinling to register as a monk.
Master Xuefeng invited him to serve as the head seat (shouzuo), whereupon he composed a commentary and immediately proceeded to Gu Dao Mountain to visit Master Dong...
Chan Master Mingxia saw [the master] at once and asked, "Regarding the markless field-of-merit robe, what kind of person is able to wear it?
Mingxia descended from his seat and gave him a slap. The master said, "The four elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates do not exist.
How could you give me a slap? Mingxia gave him another slap. The master said, "One slap does not function as one slap; speak quickly! Mingxia gave him yet another slap. The master’s spirit—
His countenance did not change. [Dongshan] said, "The reputation of the Old Monk is not spread in vain. He then unfolded his sitting mat, prostrated three times, and stood up.
Chuan said, "I have dwelt on Mount Gudao for thirty years, and today I have seen only this monk. He then invited him to stay for ten days, intending to entrust him with his *kāṣāya*.
The Master said, "I have not come for the sake of robes," and firmly refused them. He then descended the mountain; from then on, his reputation spread.
At the Conglin [Monastery] of Niu’ou in Jinling, the Master was invited to lead the assembly for three years. He then withdrew to live in seclusion at Tianjie Mountain.
The Eunuch Yuan Cheng (whose Dharma name was Zhikai), admiring the Master’s virtue and wisdom, invited him to reside at Yishan Temple to open the mountain and preach the Dharma.
On the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month in the fifth year of the Zhengtong era (the Gengshen year), Master Tian left his final instructions to Mingbai An, saying:
"I have two things, clothing and the Dharma. Wait ten years, then deliver them to Mount Dongshan in Jinling for the Venerable Haizhou to receive.
Entrust this to him, saying: 'The characters are bestowed upon Cizhai Haizhou; when he seeks me, I shall have no reward. This shall be on the day after next year."
The west wind smiled and nodded its head. The following year, as expected, he passed away peacefully. Bai’an did not violate his final instructions;

on the day the period of mourning concluded, he invited the Head Seat, Fajian (on the twenty-third day of the eighth month in the second year of the Jingtai era), to carry the robe and bowl to Dongshan.
The Master offered incense and received them (Dongshan Chai was his successor).
According to the biography of Chan Master Dongming Haizhou Puci of Hangzhou by his seventh-generation descendant, Venerable Tiantong Wuzu, he was a native of Changshu, Suzhou, surnamed Qian.
His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations. He left the household life at Poshan Monastery.

When he first arrived at Huiri Temple to listen to lectures on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, upon reaching the passage that states, "There are only words and phrases; there is no real meaning," he remarked: "Words..."
He said, "Today my studies have increased even more. He then returned home and spent day and night reading the sutras and contemplating their true meaning;

his countenance grew increasingly haggard. A lay practitioner asked him, "Master, you look ill. The Master replied, "It is because I do not yet clearly understand the Buddha-dharma; it is not illness.
The layman said, "If you do not clearly understand the Buddha-dharma, why not go to Mount Dengwu in the prefecture to seek instruction from Wanfeng Wei?"
"The Master is leaving. Hearing this, the Teacher was delighted and immediately went to Dengwu to see Wanfeng. Wanfeng asked, "Where have you come from, novice?
The Teacher prostrated; rising, he said, "Changshu. Wanfeng asked, "What brings you here? The Teacher recounted the previous conversation and bowed twice, requesting instruction.
Wanfeng then struck him twice on the head, pressed down on his back with his foot, and kicked him twice, saying, "This very thing is it!"
Regarding the true meaning, the Master had an awakening. He rose and said, "Excellent! Excellent! You have truly expended great effort of mind and spirit, Preceptor.
Feng smiled and granted him approval, bestowing upon him a verse that said: "The hair of a tortoise is entrusted to sons and grandsons; The horns of a hare are brought forth to seek the ford.
A single shout leaves one deaf for three days; Within this, who may be intimate with the message? He further said, "You should conceal your traces and protect [the Dharma]."

He maintained this practice. He did not consider himself a teacher for others; yet, believing he had attained realization, he built a thatched hut in a valley of Mount Dongting and remained there for twenty-nine years.
One day, a monk arrived. The Master asked him, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "Anxi."
[The Master] asked, "Is there anyone from Anxi? [The monk] replied, "Venerable Xubai. His preaching of the Dharma is no different from that of Gaofeng.
[The Master] asked, "Whose disciple is he? [The monk] replied, "Baozang. [The Master] asked, "What sayings does he have? The monk cited the words used by [Xubai] to test people in his room, saying:
"Mind is not Buddha; wisdom is not the Way; the Tripitaka is not the Dharma. What is it? None of those who offered responses were in accord with the truth.
After he had finished speaking, he asked the Master, "Did you ever study under Baozang? The Master replied, "I studied under Wanfeng together with Baozang.
The monk asked, "What did you see on that day that led you to remain hidden here and never again go to study under another person? The Master said:
The monk asked, "This is merely words; there is no real meaning at all. Yunfeng then struck him. The monk said, "From this I have attained awakening.

The monk asked, "Please tell me the reason for your attainment. The Master said, "One simply needs to recognize that which knows pain and itchiness—this is the real meaning; this is the wondrous mind."
[The Master] said, "Your talk is nothing but skin and hair. The monk laughed and said, "According to this understanding of yours, you have not yet resolved the matter of birth and death;
how can you claim to have attained enlightenment? [The Master asked,] "Is it 'not yet' or 'not there'? Have you not seen the saying: 'Mind is not Buddha; wisdom is not the Way'?
The Master then became doubtful and asked, "Are there any among that assembly who are truly and profoundly enlightened? The monk replied, "There are none. The Master immediately—
Qi abandoned his hermitage and crossed the lake to go to Anxi, where he visited Dongming. It happened that someone had prepared a vegetarian feast;
when the Master reached the gate, he asked Dongming, "What is the flavor of today’s meal? Dongming replied, "One knows it only when it reaches the mouth; once described, it is far removed."

The Master asked, "What is it like when the flavor reaches the mouth? Ming immediately struck out the lamp and said, "If you can recognize where the light of the lamp has gone, that flavor will reach your mouth.
The Master was speechless. At dawn the following day, he sent an attendant to invite the Master.
When the Master arrived, Ming asked, "Have you seen anyone? The Master smiled and said, "I have seen only one person; I fear I would startle you were I to speak of him."
Renming said, "Even if one were to meet Śākyamuni face-to-face, he would still be just an ordinary fellow. What harm is there in saying so? The Master said, "Wanfeng.

Renming asked, "Is this to establish chronological precedence, or is it for the sake of the Buddha-dharma? If it is to establish chronological precedence, there are a thousand people under Wanfeng's guidance.
If it is for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, you old *jueli* (monk) have not even dreamed of the Buddha-dharma; why such alarm?"
"If you have seen them, it is as if you were seeing Ten Thousand Peaks face-to-face. But where are those Ten Thousand Peaks right now? The Master’s face turned red and he was at a loss.
Ming said, "If it is like this, you have never seen Ten Thousand Peaks. The Master returned to his guest quarters and for three days and nights forgot both sleep and food.
By chance, the cord of an incense lamp broke and fell to the ground; suddenly, he attained great enlightenment. He went before the gate to present the source of his realization to Ming.
[The Master] said, "Old *jueli*, you have inherited the lineage from Wanfeng. The Master replied, "Master Bai has brought me to full realization;
how could I merely inherit from Wanfeng? Ming then smiled. He subsequently gathered the assembly and, crossing the barrier, ascended the seat and said:
"Gautama had an intention for whom to transmit it; Kāśyapa opened a smile for no reason. Having reached this point, how can even the Seven Buddhas remain long? Even Mañjuśrī’s face turns red!"
Utterly bewildered. This morning’s amusing matter from Dongming leaves people drooling for a thousand ages.

Fortunately, Master Haegong forgot both self and other, so that the single thread of the Jeizan lineage continues unceasingly. Then, he cast down his staff and said: "The burden of a thousand catties is now fully entrusted;
the mysteries and essentials are now discussed by this staff. He struck three times with his whisk and descended from the seat. (A verse by Ingyon Gwi)

"I say: My body bears the scars of ten thousand peaks from the white staff; the Dongting Lake sways like a small universe. Suddenly, a gust of karmic wind arises, and waves strike my lone boat as it passes through the Haimen Strait.

The Master then entered the Abbot’s quarters to pay his respects. On the following day, the Abbot said, "I shall not remain for another month; I am leaving. On the twenty-seventh night, he took leave of the assembly. On the twenty-ninth day, he passed away.
The Master intended to retreat back to Dongting, but the fourfold assembly earnestly entreated him to stay. He thus succeeded to the Dharma seat.
Once, Xinghua raised up the case of asking the rector Kebin: "Before long, you will become a master of the liturgical chant.
Kebin replied, "I do not enter this community. Xinghua said, "Do you enter because you understand, or do you not enter because you do not understand? Kebin said, "There is no connection."
Hua-bian struck him and said, "Venerable Kebin, you were defeated in the battle of Dharma. You shall be fined five strings of cash and must provide a meal for the assembly.
On the following day, when the midday meal was prepared, Xinghua himself struck the wooden gavel and said, "Venerable Kebin, you were defeated in the battle of Dharma."

"You shall not eat your rice. He then immediately drove the head monk out of the hall. The Master [Zhaozhou] picked up the case and said: "If one is a descendant of the Jie (Linji) school, one must certainly understand the affairs within his house.

It was not until this very day that I realized it was I who was mistaken, not Wanfeng. Only upon meeting Master Dongming did I finally understand the meaning of the staff."

The same applies to words and phrases as it does to rewards and punishments. Indeed, while awakening resides within oneself, the Dharma relies upon the teacher. How could one say that awakening once is itself the final realization?
To claim that through a single awakening one possesses spiritual penetration and thus seeks neither teacher nor Dharma is precisely what is meant by "prior to the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranādin."
It may be said that there was no teacher; yet, from the time after the Venerable Wei-yin onwards, it is here that teachers have transmitted [the Dharma] one to another.
Thus, Ke-bin recognized his father-teacher’s bitter heart, exerted himself to clarify the pivotal mechanism of the higher realm, and thoroughly penetrated the matters within the inner chamber.

It cannot be expressed in words. To lose one’s money and receive a beating, to be punished and expelled from the monastery—were one’s bones crushed and body ground to powder, it would still be difficult to repay even a fraction of what Xinghua did for me;
how much more so when he beat me and expelled me? This is precisely why Elder Hai today did not succeed Wanfeng, but rather Dongming.
An ancient proverb says: "Only after raising a daughter does one know the suffering of a mother; only after fathering a son..."
Only then will you recognize your father’s arduous toil. Truly profound are these words! There is indeed a great matter within this; it cannot be treated with casualness.

If one is to extract the nails and pull out the wedges for others, sit upon the Lion’s Seat as a teacher of gods and humans, remove the cataracts from people's eyes, and succeed to the position of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one must penetrate each and every point.
By all means, do not mistake mere intellectual awakening for realization, nor cast aside the fundamental principles of the school.
"Kill! Set it aside and do not investigate it further. How is this any different from the celestial demons and heterodox paths? To be reckless and invite calamity and regret!
On the anniversary of Wanfeng’s death, the Master held up incense and pointed at the portrait, saying: "I nearly drowned you in a jar! Fortunately, it was Puci;
had it been anyone else, there would have been no saving you. I burn this portion of incense to repay your guidance. He gave a shout and said: "Only..."

I laugh at you for protecting your own shortcomings and failing to seek a teacher; you treat the Buddha-dharma as mere human sentiment. [The Master] spreads his sitting mat and prostrates. Again, holding up the incense, he says:
"This one portion of incense is offered to Elder Dongming. With a single heart of sincerity, he spurred me on, enabling me to penetrate the source of the lineage.
He gives two shouts and says: "How could a single word exhaust the heart of universal compassion? For a thousand ages, his descendants shall offer praise."
Repaying kindness. Again, he held up incense and said: "This offering of incense is for the power of my former teachers and monks who guided me.
Had I not been favored by my teachers, how could there be this day? When I return in the future, I shall have a share in receiving thirty blows of the staff;
this is sufficient to repay the kindness that cannot be repaid. He gave a shout and said: "Where the grace received is deep, that is one's home; only when there is milk does one know it is so."
Mother, rising from prostration, he spoke this verse: "The source-head resides only within the shout; The Three Essentials, the Three Mysteries, and the Four Hosts and Guests.
The five blows must be understood by the person beneath the words; The four patterns must be clarified within the phrase. The ultimate true function is the phrase of life and death;
The secret message therein lies in the lineage transmission. I shall shatter my form and grind my bones to repay the teacher's virtue; With this very body..."
He repaid the Buddha’s kindness with his heart and returned to the abbot’s quarters weeping bitterly. As he approached the time of his passing, he spoke this verse:
"For ninety-six years I have been in the world; For seventy-four years I have been a monk. How many contradictions and errors there were in between— Upon one glimpse of Dongming, they all dissolve."
Striking a circular shape with his whisk, he said, "From Śākyamuni down to me, there have been incalculable old monks.
Again striking a circular shape, he said, "Most of them find their resting place right here. *Du!* Then he cast aside his brush and passed away.

In the first year of the Jingtai era, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the left of Dongming. Twelve people attained the Dharma [from him] (Dongming Chai was his successor). [The Master composed this *nian*...]

One volume of these verses has been circulated in the world, with a preface written by Shen Guan, a disciple from Huacheng. Its summary states: "Among those who have succeeded Master Xian as a 'sea-voyager,' there has been no such person from the Buddha's time until now. One whose four marks of self and others are not yet fully exhausted cannot act as such a master;

he is truly an ancient Buddha reappearing in the human realm. Alas, the Master was advanced in years and of venerable seniority; his appearance in the world was brief before he entered extinction. Thus, while the winds of the school have not yet spread widely throughout the world, these one hundred verses on ancient kōans (gū jīyuán) shall cause the sun of wisdom to shine again, shattering the darkness for a thousand ages.

Some of these verses quote the lines of other poets, while others emerge from his own insight and perspective, aligning with the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. These were compiled by selecting and gathering [from various sources]. Regarding the underlying meaning within them, I dare not insist upon a fixed judgment of right or wrong."

One need only observe the Master’s conduct and character: for the sake of the Dharma, he forgot his physical form; he cast aside fame to preserve substance, never seeking self-satisfaction. As for his verses and *niandao* (critical appraisals), they were not produced through arbitrary conjecture or erroneous composition. Those with clear eyes will see them, investigate them, and put them into practice from this day forward.

Alas! In these times, demons flourish and the Dharma is in decline; the single lineage of the Plucking of the Flower is sparse and does not manifest in the world. True patriarchs and masters nurture their "holy embryo" within the hearth and mountain caves, awaiting the proper time and conditions.

Through these hidden streams and branches, they cause their descendants to propagate the ancestral Way, like clouds rising and rain falling to moisten the spiritual roots. Who else but the Master’s lineage could ensure that the flowers of the Buddhas and Patriarchs bloom and their fragrance wafts throughout China, so that all who touch or hear it may awaken and enter? At this time...

It traces the lineage starting from Śākyamuni through successive generations down to Dongming Xiàn, Haizhou Ciyún, Xī, and Yīng. Yīng and Baofeng Xuán were brothers. Based on this clear and authentic succession of the source and stream, it is beyond doubt that Haizhou Ci was the dharma-heir of Dongming Xiàn.

Chan Master Guoxi Juecheng of Gaozuo in Jinling was a native of Weizhou. He received the tonsure under Tiantong Tianhui Changyun and spent five years and six seasons reading the entire Tripitaka.

At Nanshan, there was a bountiful harvest. Later, while residing at Gaozuo in Jinling, he gave a small-scale *can* (sermon) upon concluding the retreat:
"Under three rafters, the body and mind are settled like dead ashes; yet from within the hearth, a spark of fire is struck out—a thunderclap that startles heaven and shakes the earth.
Is there anyone here who does not spare their eyebrows? Liang then entered and said: "Sometimes the Buddhas of the three periods..."

Returning with water on one's back and the moon on one's belt—if one realizes it here, it is possible for a mustard seed to contain Mount Sumeru, and it is also possible for Mount Sumeru to be contained within a mustard seed.
Viewed through the correct eye, there are two hearths; the Buddhas of the three periods of time are bound and confined therein.
Regarding the cloth shirt from Qingzhou, a single grain of mustard seed, and ten billion Mount Sumerus—these are all gathered back into the Hu-pie (sesame cake) of Yunmen.
As for the assembly of monks in the two halls, they can neither pierce it through nor bite through it. O Great Assembly, at such a time as this, what ultimately is to be done?
Do you understand? From between the eyebrows, the adamantine flame is squeezed forth; the lamp-stand and the lantern.
On the ninth day of the eighth month of the Gui-si year of the Chenghua era, he bathed, changed his robes, gathered the assembly to bid them farewell, and passed away while sitting upright.
After a short while, as the assembly wept, the Master opened his eyes again to comfort them, saying, "There is no need for this.
He then closed his eyes once more (Touzi Qi was his successor).
Chan Master Xing of Dayun in Xiangyang had long served under Master Qi of Chushan. One day, as Qi was returning from the prefectural seat, the assembly went out along the road to welcome him.
Qi said, "I have never descended the mountain, nor have I ever left the prefecture. Tell me, where have you come from? The Master replied, "The assembly has been standing for a long time;
we request that the Abbot return to the monastery. Qi asked, "Where is the monastery? The Master said, [pointing ahead], "Right there."
"The sound of the bell rings well," said Qi, laughing heartily. The Master then prostrated himself. Later, Qi bestowed upon him a verse, saying:

"In person from Xizhou, you have established the fundamental tenets; directly from Touzi, you have received the *kāṣāya*. In years to come, when you appear in the world, you shall uphold the essential principles."
"Not standing alone in peril is the mark of a master" (Touzi Qian was the successor).
Chan Master Jinshan Bao of Zhuozhou went to visit Master Chushan Qi. Qi asked, "Facing south, you look at the Big Dipper;
tell me, what matter do you clarify? The Master said, "Venerable Sir, you had better shut your mouth. Qi said, "Not yet."
The Master said, "You may get away with it when deceiving others. Qi asked, "What is the eye that penetrates the barrier? The Master let out a loud shout.
Qi asked, "As for the single pivot beyond, how is that? The Master said, "The sun at high noon in a clear blue sky.
Qi said, "I have not even dreamed of it yet. The Master said, "The wooden boy holds the jade thread; the stone girl passes the golden needle. Qi said, "A turn of the body..."
[Qingliang] said, "Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The Master said, "The rain adds luster to the mountain colors; the wind comes and the bamboo shadows shift. Qingliang took up his staff.
The Master then gave a shout and swept out of the hall with his sleeves. Qingliang said, "I grant you thirty blows.
The Master turned around, prostrated, and said, "I thank the Master for his compassion. Qingliang said, "Though you have waves that overflow the heavens, you still lack the clarity of still water."
The Master lowered his head and remained silent. Tanchi deeply approved of this (Tanchi Ch’i was his successor).
Later, Chan Master Zhan-yuan Yin of Tang-an went to study under Master Chushan Huan-sou Ch’i. He relied upon him for the longest period of time.
One day, during a private interview, Ch’i asked, "What is the single word of ultimate truth? The Master replied, "There are lips, but they cannot speak."
Qiji said, "The pine wind and flowing water—why do they speak? The Master said, "Because they have no mouths. Qiji said, "What do you say they are saying?
The Master said, "What did the Master ask just now? Qiji said, "As for that place where sound and echo are cut off—is there still speaking or not?
The Master said, "If there is, then certainly there is; it is simply that one does not hear it."
When [Zhao] Qi said, "As for 'hearing,' let us set that aside for now. Tell me, what did he say? the Master then raised his fist.
Qi asked, "Is there anyone else who can hear it? The Master pointed to the incense burner and said, "It is this one that hears.
Qi asked, "Why is it that this one hears? The Master replied, "Because it has ears. Qi said, "You also have [ears]."
"Both ears are there, yet you cannot hear. The Master said, "Even though you cannot hear, you cannot deceive him by even a single point.
Qi said, "I grant you thirty blows. The Master then bowed (Qi succeeded to Touzi).
While Chan Master Haiju Zuoyi was in retreat at Shijing, one day Master Chushan Qi arrived before the door, struck it once, and said, "I request to see the master within the retreat.
The Master stood with hands folded and body bowed. Qi asked, "What about Zhaozhou’s 'No-Character' (Wu)?
The Master replied, "It is precisely because of your earnest compassion that I lay my very heart and liver open to you."
Qī said, "What is it like when one does not involve oneself with existence or non-existence? The Master said, "At this point, I do not understand.
Qī said, "Wait until you pass through the barrier, and I will give you a beating. The Master said, "I am not even inside the barrier right now."
Touzi Qian pointed to the gate and said, "What can be done about this? The Master then gave a shout. Qian said, "The weather is sweltering;
please take good care of yourself. The Master then bowed (Touzi Qian was his successor).
Chan Master Changsong Daxin Zhenyuan was the son of the Zhang family of Sanchi.

He went to visit Chushan Qi and asked, "I pray that you, Master, will directly point out that place where the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past have not reached in speech and have not arrived in practice. Qi held up his staff and said:
[The Master] said, "Huh? The Master then gave a shout; Qi then struck him. The Master shouted again; Qi struck him again. The Master then bowed.
One day, while standing in attendance within the meditation hall, Qi said, "Speak a single word before your parents were yet born.
The Master said, "I cannot speak it. Qi said, "Why can you not speak it? The Master said, "He has no mouth. Qi said, "And yet you say he has no mouth? The Master—
It is said: "Thanking the Master for his response" (by Toudi Qi).
Chan Master Chongshan Tianzhi of Beidi in Songfan was a native of Peng County. His physical appearance was extraordinary.
At the age of twelve, he received instruction from Yueguang; after receiving full ordination, he resided in Songfan. One day, Master Chushan Qi...

He visited the master’s hermitage, where the master recounted the circumstances of his awakening. Qiji asked, "What is the meaning of the word 'wu' (no)? The master replied, "A drawn blade from its scabbard;
its cold light pierces the Dipper and Ox. Qiji asked, "Why did Zhaozhou say 'no'? The master replied, "A Persian chewing ice and snow; he does not realize his teeth are cold.
Qiji asked, "Having set aside both 'existence' and 'non-existence,' how can one find a point of entry? The master replied, "At night..."
"Who is it that holds hands with me? Let us stroll together along the Imperial Street. Qi asked, "What is the extraordinary phrase that transcends all?
The Master said, "The moon in every house on an autumn night; flowers everywhere when spring comes. A pair of clear and blind eyes—what need is there to scatter sand and mud?
Qi was immediately certified (and thus became the successor of Touzi Qi).
Chan Master Zutang Zu Yu of Shijing was the son of the Ju family in Chengdu. He had long studied under Chushan Qi.
One day, while Qi was reading a sutra, the Master approached him and asked, "What is it that you are looking at, Preceptor? Qi then gave a shout.

"What do you say it is? The Master also shouted. Qi held up the scripture and said, "A hundred thousand samādhis and immeasurable subtle meanings all flow forth from this single scroll of scripture. But tell me, from where does this single scroll of scripture come?
The Master snapped his fingers once, and Qi then withdrew. (Touzi Qi was his successor.)
Chan Master Sanchi Yuezhuang Changhui was the son of the Li family of Jianzhou.
He went to visit Chushan Qi, who asked, "I have long heard that you, Venerable One, have perused the Tripitaka; is this true? The Master replied, "Preceptor, do not slander me. Qi said:
"The white background is paper; the black background is ink. Ultimately, what is the sutra?
The Master said, "Preceptor, do not fail to take up the fundamental. Qi asked, "What is the principle of not taking up the fundamental?
The Master said, "The sutra? Qi said, "It is similar, but it is not yet correct. The Master then bowed (Touzi Qi was his successor).
Chan Master Changyun of Yishan in Zhongxi went to visit Chushan Qi. Qi asked, "What is your name? The Master replied, "Changyun.
Qi asked, "And what is your style (hao)? The Master replied, "Yishan. Qi asked, "Clouds are hidden within the mountains; why then do they emerge from the mountains?
The Master replied, "It is simply because last night a crane carried them over the mountain pass. Qi said, "Perhaps they will become rain to nourish the world."
"What is it like at that time? The Master said, "It universally moistens the entire realm. Qiji asked, "What is it like when it is suddenly scattered by a fierce wind?
The Master said, "It remains as before: blue sky and bright sun. Qiji laughed heartily (Qiji was a successor of Touzi).

Chan Master Cuimei Wugong was a native of Guansi. Having long relied upon Chushan, one day while entering the inner quarters for instruction, Qi asked him, "When the entire earth has been overturned and not a single inch of soil remains, what is the matter of thoroughly exhausting the source? The Master replied, "All stars bow toward the North;
no water does not flow toward the East. Qi asked, "Is there still any need for the function of practice and realization? The Master said, "Practice and realization."
"Then it is not non-existent; yet its functional activity cannot be apprehended. Qi said, "Even this very point of 'cannot be apprehended' cannot itself be apprehended.
What will you do then? As the Master prepared to offer a reply, Qi let out a thunderous shout. The Master said, "Your kindness is so great that it is difficult to repay."
[He] then paid his respects (Touzi Qi was his successor).
One day, while the attendant Zu Jie of Guian was ill, Qi went to visit him. He encountered the senior monk Xinxin arriving;
Qi looked at the Master and asked, "What is the mind? The Master replied, "Opening one's mouth admits no sentiment. Qi said, "Not yet. The Master turned back.
Guru Xin said, "Why do you not pay homage to the Master? Xin then prostrated once. Qi left it at that.
Later, when his illness became critical and he made sounds of pain, Qi asked, "At a time such as this, is the phrase upon which you relied during your daily practice still effective?
The Master nodded. Qi said, "If it is still effective, why are you crying out? The Master replied, "When there is pain, one cries."
When he felt itchy, he laughed. Qiji asked, "Suppose the three-inch breath were to be severed; where would you find a place to settle your body and establish your life?
The Master said, "The rain has passed and the sky is clear; the green mountains remain as they were. Qiji asked, "After we part from now on, will we be able to meet again?
The Master said, "Not separated for kalpas; how could there be any interval now? Qiji asked, "If that is so, then you have never been ill? The Master—
[Daowu] said, "Sickness and health do not concern one another. Qiji again took his hand and asked, "What is this?
The Master then pressed his palms together and said, "I must depart now," and with a vigorous movement of his body, he sat upright and passed away. (Touzi Qiji had twelve successors.)
Chan Master Xian-tong Da-wei Jing-lun of Wutai was the son of the Kang family from Yunnan. When the Venerable Gu-ting Jian resided at Fushan, the Master went there to seek instruction;
their interaction in the meditation hall reached a point of spiritual resonance. Later, he took up residence at Xiantong. [Ascending the hall, he said:
"An unperforated iron hammer is hurled right before your face; a black-lacquered Kunlun sits blocking the road. Is there anyone who can strike through it and grasp it?"
"Come forth and speak! A monk asked, "What is the realm of Mount Tiantai? The Master said, "It is neither sunny nor is it raining.
The monk asked, "Who are the people within that realm? The Master said, "Ten thousand bodhisattvas within the Vajra Cave."
[The student] asked, "I have not yet understood what dharma you usually teach. The Master said, "A clear breeze blows through the secluded pines;
the closer one listens, the better the sound. He asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "This year’s rains are timely; the farmers’ spring wheat will flourish.
He asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Wait for the Immortal of Mount Xian to turn his body."
I shall tell you at once: it has even happened that one took arsenic and made it into clarified butter (mṛtasaṃjīvana). Who is there who does not scatter pearls like shards of tile?
To climb a tree with eyes wide open is to needlessly lose one's entire body; to dream of ascending Tuṣita is likewise to broadcast one's own family shame.
Without stirring a thought, one transforms Māra’s daughters, turning them all into precious vessels of Bodhi; no effort of the wrist is required.
By the power of his finger, the Sahā world becomes the Pure Land of Abhirati. Longshui (Changshui) comes with deep peaks; Langya (Langye) departs as the ice melts.
With a step of faith, he overturns the lapis lazuli pit; in an instant, he shatters the coral branches. [Ascending the hall:
"The Three Sages (Sengsheng) let out a roar of awe and a shout, scattering sand within the Eye of the True Dharma. Nanquan brandishes his sharp blade aloft. Ancient...
The Buddha’s family style sweeps away the dust of convention; why insist on necessity or non-necessity? How could the probing pole be held by human hands?

From south of Xiang to north of Tan, the model of the pagoda is brought forth in its entirety. Spring returns upon the branch that never sprouts; a single snowflake flies amidst a mass of fierce flames.
One who possesses such a strategy may truly be called a man of realization. In whose well is there no sky? Everywhere, within the waves, there is the moon.
A Teaching for the Assembly on the Winter Solstice: The five peaks are heaped with jade and snow; the thousand pines have branches like pearls and gems.
All the springs, rocks, mists, and clouds of Mount Tai, along with the soaring towers and surging halls—all are but the true radiance of Mañjuśrī’s single eye of wisdom.
You people are constantly within it, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; yet do you know that you have never once stirred a single hair on his brow?
"Mao-ma. If you can see it in this way, then you will gather the great chiliocosm within the tip of a hair and expand the sands of Ganges River in the dharma-realm.
If this is not yet so, you must strictly avoid guessing here and there. For all of you, I, this old monk, give you a true report:
today is the winter solstice, and the first yang has arisen. Be careful. [He] addressed the assembly: "The mountains are high and the seas are vast; the moon is bright."
The wind is clear; the pines are verdant, the rocks are white. Summer is hot, winter is cold—thus it is distinct and vivid, each thing manifesting itself.
But tell me, within the realm of the patch-robed monk, what kind of matter is accomplished?
Is there anyone who can say it? If so, come forth and speak! If not, I, the old monk, shall speak for myself. (He raises his staff and descends from the seat.)
Addressing the assembly: Master Yuanzhu said, "There is a wondrous and extraordinary cause and condition; I shall present it to you all. If one wishes to speak of it, one is hindered by speaking;

if one does not speak of it, one is hindered by not speaking. Great Master Yuanzhu was much like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail—once a single word has fallen upon people's ears, how can it be hidden?
I, this old monk, also have one wondrous and extraordinary cause and condition; let me simply state it plainly.
Presenting this to the great assembly, he said: "As for those who lean against the door or peer through the window, each one stands like a thousand-fathom cliff.

He then descended from his seat. Addressing the assembly, he said: "In my place, I do not say that Li Daliang of East Village is too frugal, nor do I say that Wang Erjie of West Settlement is too extravagant.
I do not know how to call a hare by its horn, nor do I know how to add feet to it."
Painting a snake. In the morning, a bowl of white congee; in the afternoon, a cup of clear tea. Who cares for the tangled vines of years past?
A flower blooms in the cold stillness. He spreads his two hands and says: "You people, what dry wood-stumps are you seeking here? The Master has a poem on dwelling in the mountains:
"In my mountain hut, there is nothing to do, so the door remains unopened. On the earthen steps, the spring rain turns them green."
Moss grows. This mind thinks that no one understands it; from where does the solitary bird’s single cry come? (Ancestral lineage of Gu Tingjian).
Chan Master Ning of Yifeng visited Master Yuexi Cheng of Dagang. After a long time, he attained thorough realization. Yuexi bestowed upon him a verse, saying:
"From patriarch to patriarch, there is no dharma to transmit; every person possesses it inherently. You have realized the dharma of non-transmission; there is neither before nor after."

Regarding Wuhou (the Zangben [Tibetan Canon] edition adds two subsequent lines: "You have received the non-transmission of the Dharma; hasten to transmit it to posterity" [Ciyue Xi Cheng succeeded him]):
Chan Master Tianshen Dufeng Benshan of Hangzhou was originally from the Wu clan of Fengyang. His father traveled for official service to Leyang in Guangdong, where he was born.
At the age of seventeen, he left home to become a monk. He first encountered Master Yuanming, who showed him the koan of the word "Mu."
The Master immediately understood this and reported it to Ming. Ming said, "For twenty years I have been contemplating the word 'Mu,' like a mosquito on an iron ox.
Yet as soon as you begin practicing, you already possess such insights. He continued, "Observing your capacity, you are different from others;
do not let yourself be deceived by people along the way into becoming an abbot, for that would mislead you."

"This is a great matter. Having received these instructions from my teacher, I immediately made a vow to practice with single-minded devotion, swearing that in this life I would take awakening as my goal.
Admiring the boundless spiritual style of Master Wuji, I entered Sichuan to seek his guidance. Later, when Master Ji was summoned to the capital, I consequently closed myself in retreat.
I did not prepare a bed, but set out only a small stool; when drowsiness became heavy, I even discarded the stool. One day, upon hearing the sound of a bell, there was—
Xing composed a verse, saying: "Profoundly still and silent, all activity ceases; Touched upon, it roars like thunder without cause. A single sound shakes the earth, and all news is exhausted;
The skull shatters to pieces as the dream first returns. He went again to visit [Zhao] Ji, only to find that Ji had recently passed away.

He subsequently sought certification from the Venerable Monk Yuexi Cheng. Under Cheng’s words, he attained realization. Later, Cheng sent a letter summoning him to receive his formal entrustment (*kōshō*).

At that time, the Master was away on other business; however, as Cheng approached the end of his life, he ordered that his robe and whisk be sent to him. Having received the Dharma, the Master resided at the mountain.
For over forty years [he practiced]. At the beginning of the Chenghua era, he closed himself off in a stone hut; later, he resided at Tianzhen. A monk asked, "What is the master’s house style?
The Master said, "The tide is swift in the river ahead, so the fish move with difficulty; the peaks are high on the ridge behind, so the birds find it hard to perch.
A monk requested further instruction regarding the public address given by Master Gaofeng, which said: "The mud ox beneath the sea bites the moon as it runs."
"A stone tiger before the cliff sleeps while cradling its cubs; an iron snake drills into the Vajra-eye. A man from Kunlun rides an elephant; a heron leads the way.
Within these four lines, there is one line that can kill and can bring to life, that can let go and can seize.
If a person can discern it, their lifelong study of the Way will be complete. "I wonder which line it is? The Master said, "Wait until you have attained realization, and then I shall tell you."
"I have told you," [the Master said]. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Have you not heard it said: 'If you have a staff, I give you a staff;
if you have no staff, I take your staff away'? A brief general discourse says: "The precious sword is fully wielded within daily life;
with high brandishing and sweeping strokes, one is willing to remain composed. When it is withdrawn, souls and gall blanch before the wind."
Relaxed and at ease, skulls lie scattered across the ground. Through ten thousand deaths and ten thousand births, they have no regard for themselves;
with a single spear and a single horse, they achieve their purpose. Zhaozhou’s very life-force is clearly revealed here. Blades dripping with blood pierce the heavens, yet their edges remain hidden.

[The Master] sweeps once with his whisk: empty space is vast and transparent, without a trace of news. Ten thousand miles of cloudless sky, the Milky Way is azure. He presses so hard that Mount Sumeru is forced inside.
Lotus fibers—Maitreya and Śākyamuni both cry out in protest. Riding an iron horse backward against the west wind, they startle the clay ox as it emerges from the sea.
O virtuous ones, if you understand this as something extraordinary, you betray your own spiritual essence; if you do not understand it as something extraordinary, [you likewise betray it].

"Clutching his stolen goods while crying out for injustice. How will you understand this? Only when one knows how to conceal the whole world within the world does one first see the ram with its horns caught upon the treetop.
(Yuexi Cheng was his successor. On the *Ren-yin* year, he passed away at Tianzhen; his stupa was erected on the ridge of his native mountain.
Chan Master Wutai Puji Guyue Jingcheng was the son of the Zhang family of Xihe.
He first studied under Master Yuexi Cheng, who instructed him to contemplate the "Mu" (No) kōan of Zhaozhou. After three days, he attained realization; Cheng marveled at this.

Jingcheng subsequently traveled to Shu to visit Guangfu, who asked, "When a person who has died the great death comes back to life, what is it like? The Master replied, "The eyebrows lie across the eyes."
His nostrils were large and his head hung low. [A monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the word 'Mu'? The Master said, "The wind blows and the grass bends; the water reaches and the channel forms.
[The monk] said, "When the great earth sinks flat and empty space shatters to pieces, where will you find a place to settle your body and establish your life?

The Master said, "When the clouds vanish, the mountain peaks are revealed; when the sun rises, the heavens and sea are clear. In the first year of the Tiānshùn era, he returned to Qingliáng to serve as the abbot. [End of Excerpt]

The King invited him into the inner palace, where he questioned him and honored him with profound courtesy. By imperial decree, a temple was established in Huayan Valley, titled "Pujie" (Universal Salvation).
After the Master resided on the mountain, he once composed a verse on dwelling in the mountains which said: "Within the world, Mount Wutai alone is permitted to be high."
The True Person of No Rank is companionless and solitary; let the winds from all quarters blow as they will. With eyes ever empty, he gazes upon the clouds and the sky.
Content with poverty beneath the forest trees, his thoughts are far-reaching and serene. On a bamboo couch he sleeps high, with a stone for a pillow.

His life beyond the ordinary is settled according to his lot, for there is not the slightest seeking within his breast. He dwells by himself beside the red cliffs and green waters, completely free of—
Honor and disgrace, leisure and toil—the old monk does not understand the principle of returning to the source. Let the green mountains turn green and then yellow as they please.
Deeply hidden in the mountain crags, years are no longer counted; the snares of fame and the shackles of profit cannot pull him away.

The seven-pound robe, patched and mended again and again, grows ever more fresh under the scorching sun and the blowing wind. The rustling spring breeze blends with the lament of birds; its pure sound reaches [the heavens].
The sound comes to his ears; as he sits upright by the incense burner burning cypress seeds, he once again unfurls the remaining sutra by the moonlight.
(He later passed away at his home mountain. [The above three individuals are successors of Yuexi Cheng].)
Chan Master Wuyong Wenquan of Huguo Temple on Mount Chabai in Fengyang was the son of the Liu family from Shanghe in Jinan.
At the age of nineteen, he went to Lingyan Mountain to shave his head. Initially, he met Yuetian, who bestowed upon him the essential points of the Dharma.

Subsequently, he studied under Bietuan and attained realization. Bietuan asked him, "When empty space is pulverized and the great earth sinks flat, where will you establish yourself and take up residence?"
Ming asked, "Master, last night the earthen ox swallowed the vast moon; this morning the wooden horse breathes forth the clear wind.
Chuan said, "Where has that 'one' returned? The Master said, "Since the white ox returned to the snowy peaks, its tracks have not been seen until this very day."
Chuan nodded his head in agreement. He then went to Mount Jinshan to visit Wuji, who instructed him to see Bao Yue. Yue asked, "Do you have the money for straw sandals?
The Master replied, "The green mountains do not show their peaks. Yue asked, "What is it to manifest form in response to things?
The Master said, "The solitary light of the bright moon shines throughout the heavens; the myriad phenomena and the entire cosmos are fully manifested. One day, Yue passed away.
During a session in the hall, [Zhaozhou] called out, "Cold! Cold! The Master then moved the brazier forward. Yunyan asked, "What is the matter by the brazier?
The Master struck the brazier three times. Yunyan smiled and departed. Next, during a private interview, Yunyan held up his staff and said, "This is the staff;
tell me, where does the host reside? The Master snatched the staff away and threw it down.
Dizang stood with his hands joined in *añjali*. Yue said, "Look, you fellow! You have already struck down the staff.
The Master shook out his sleeves and departed. Later, he received formal authorization (*kṣānti*). He went forth into the world at Chashan. Ascending the hall, he raised an ancient saying:
"The fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens and strikes the nose of Śakra. A blow from the carp of the Eastern Sea brings rain like..."
The basin is overturned. Tell me, what is the meaning? The assembly was silent. The Master said:

"One does not recognize the true face of Mount Kuang-lu, precisely because one is within the mountains. Ascending the hall, he said: "Dharma does not arise in isolation; it manifests through conditions.
The Way is fundamentally wordless, yet it is revealed through words. Although this is so, it is still not the matter beneath the monk's robe. Now tell me—"
"What is the matter beneath the patched robe? A monk asked, "I do not ask about the Three Vehicles;
how is it with the matter of direct pointing? The Master said, "A crane perches on a tree atop the Double Peak; a bird sings among the flowers on Nine-Dragon Mountain.

The monk said, "The meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West has been pointed out by you, Master; what is the matter of its transmission here in this land? The Master said, "On the ridge there is a wind, beautiful for a thousand ages."
The flowing water by the mountain ravine remains clear for ten thousand years. [A monk] asked, "What is the realm of Bai-shui (White Water)?
The Master said, "A single expanse of wasteland stretches across the four fields; three thatched huts stand majestic among the mountains. [The monk] asked, "Who is the person within this realm?

The Master said, "The Imperial Temple stands at the head of the White Tiger; the royal foundation lies by the Black Dragon Pond. [The monk] asked, "When both person and realm are forgotten, it is like..."
"What? The Master said, "Su Wu did not understand the will of the blue ram; Seventh Younger Brother always regretted the white crow’s return.
The monk bowed. The Master struck the desk and descended from his seat. (Guangshan Tan succeeded him.)
Chan Master Chongfu Da-hui Juehua was the son of the Liu family of Weiyang. Initially, he attained realization upon meeting Haizhou;
he later studied under Baoyue at Fanchang and subsequently received his seal of approval. While presiding over the assembly, he ascended the hall and held up his whisk, saying:
"Beyond the limit of awe-inspiring sound, it is simply this very thing. Even now, before our eyes, it is also simply this very thing. If you call it a whisk, you are blind."
It blinds the eyes and faces of gods and men; it does not call this a whisk. It blinds the eyes and faces of gods and men.
O Great Assembly, in the end, what would you call it? If you can see it directly, then you will understand Kāśyapa’s smile and the Second Patriarch’s search for his mind.
"Utterly unattainable. He succeeded to the Tathāgata’s transmission of the lamp and continued the orthodox lineage of the patriarchs.
After a long silence, he said, "Not even a thousand sages can recognize it," and struck the incense table once with his whisk. (Guangshan Tan succeeded the two masters mentioned above.)
Chan Master Wuliang Cang of Baimu in Chuzhou addressed the assembly: "Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, follow the *huatou* while walking;
follow the *huatou* while standing; follow the *huatou* while sitting; follow the *huatou* while lying down.
Let the mind be like a chestnut burr, so that it cannot be swallowed or devoured by any sense of self and other, ignorance, the five desires, or the three poisons. Thus should one act."
In movement and stillness, the entire body is a single mass of doubt. Doubting and doubting on, one remains dazed and motionless all day long.
Upon hearing a sound or seeing a form, you may take it for granted that there will be a sudden "clunk"—a wordless realization (Yiguan Zhensu).
Chan Master Yonggang Zongruan of Mingzhou addressed the assembly: "In general, when practicing the Way, one must simply give rise to a great state of doubt and maintain right mindfulness.
A thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are but a single doubt. As soon as there is an interruption, one falls into emptiness.
Seeing that you have not yet reached the point of 'becoming one piece' after even half a month or a month of practice, how could it be otherwise?"
Go ahead and act! If genuine doubt truly manifests before you, shake it until it cannot move; then, naturally, you will have no fear of confusion.
Furthermore, you must not give rise to even a single thought of joy. As soon as there is the slightest heterodox thought, strike it down into two pieces.

The Venerable Chongxiang of Mount Qingxiang in Shaowu asked, "What is existence? What is non-existence?

This is self-nature (*svabhāva*). Self-nature is precisely Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). One does not calculate in terms of existence or non-existence; one alone manifests the self-nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

There is no further separate teaching: existence is illusion, and non-existence is transformation. When one does not calculate in terms of existence or non-existence, it is neither illusion nor transformation.
This is called "leaving illusion to realize awakening. Because one dwells in constant awakening without abiding, it is called the "wondrous mind of True Suchness" (*tathatā*).

To have [dualistic grasping] is evil; to be without it is good. When one does not calculate existence or non-existence, one is neither evil nor good. Because birth and death are forever severed, it is called *bodhi*.
Therefore it is called Prajñā; therefore it is called the Wondrous Dharma; therefore it is called the Wondrous Mind; therefore it is called the Buddhas of the three periods of time;

Chan Master Lanmu Zhanjue of Yuan Tong in Jingzhou, whose secular surname was Zhang and who hailed from Qujiang in Chang’an, had admired the joy of Chan since childhood.

This was Baopo. The Master [Baofu] was startled and broke into a cold sweat. One day, he fell gravely ill.

It is not that there is nothing; rather, throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, at every single location, turn the light back upon itself and reflect:
"Look—what is this? Do not fixate on it as being located in only one place. You must give rise to great doubt regarding all places.
Lower yourself from the high ground and follow the path of error; do not let even a single thread or a hair’s breadth slip away. When walking, look at that which walks.
Who is it that stands when standing? Who is it that sits when sitting?
Who is it that lies down when lying down? And who is it that sees when seeing forms? Look into this: who is the one who sees?
When hearing a sound, immediately look to see who it is that hears. When perceiving a touch, immediately look to see who it is that perceives.

When cognizing a phenomenon, immediately look to see who it is that cognizes. Even when speaking or remaining silent, moving or staying still, turning the head or shifting the gaze, defecating or urinating, putting on clothes or eating a meal, welcoming guests or attending to visitors, and in all your comings and goings—look at each and every one.
Look back. Day and night, do not grow weary. Should you forget for even a single thought-moment, look at who it is that has forgotten.
When delusive thoughts arise, look at who it is that is entertaining those delusive thoughts. You may say you do not understand;
yet, who is it that does not understand? Regarding your present doubts, look at who it is that is doubting. Thus...
Looking and looking further, it is not that each point does not stand forth alone; every phenomenon is fully manifest. Myriad objects cannot invade it;

various conditions cannot enter it. Gain and loss, right and wrong—there are no seams or gaps whatsoever. Brightness and darkness, form and emptiness—there is absolutely no distinction between self and other.
Mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sun, moon, and stars—all the holy and all the mundane—are, in their entirety, simply this one "Who."
No other thought arises; above and below there is no path, advancing or retreating there is no door. Mountains end and waters reach their limit; emotion dissolves and views are severed.
Suddenly, with a thunderous burst, one finally realizes that this is not something sought from another, and that it is not until the bones have been pierced by a single frost that one truly knows.

One day, the Master said to Kong, "I have a word I wish to say to you. Kong pricked up his ears to listen, but the Master merely smiled and remained silent.
After Kong had entreated him repeatedly, the Master smiled again. Only then did Kong assume the full ceremonial posture and prostrate himself in worship.
Kneeling down, he entreated him with deep sorrow. The Master then said, "The Patriarch came from the West to point directly to the human mind so that one may see their nature and become a Buddha.
The essential point lies in investigating this directly beneath you. If you truly have sufficient faith, you may cast aside all worldly concerns and investigate the phrase:
'Where does the One return? Empty yourself and look at this *huatou* until your mind is dead. He practiced this for three years. One day, upon hearing a cock crow, he attained realization.
He went to his teacher to seek certification. The teacher questioned him repeatedly and exhaustively. Later, he bestowed upon him the robe and whisk, and further presented this verse, saying:
"Neither dharma nor non-dharma; neither nature nor non-nature; neither mind nor non-mind. I have now completed the transmission of the Dharma of the mind to you. (Baofeng Jin succeeded him.)
