Ji’an’s teaching style was solitary and rigorous, yet the Master consulted and questioned him morning and evening. One day, upon hearing the sound of a *ghaṇṭā*, he attained sudden enlightenment.
He penetrated [the truth] thoroughly, and Chan Master An certified his realization. Before long, Chang’an’s Juewang Temple invited him to serve as the First Seat (Dìyīzuò).
When he held the whisk within the meditation hall, no one could match or approach the application of his spiritual power. At the beginning of the Jiāngjìng era, he resided at Ānyǐn Temple in Jīnlíng.
A monk asked, "What is the realm of Ānyǐn? The Master said: "Three mountains fall half-way beyond the blue heavens; two waters divide the white egrets."
A monk asked, "What is the ancestral style of the house of peace and security? The Master said, "The stone tiger fights before the mountain;
the clay ox sleeps at the bottom of the water. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "What is the use of understanding?

At the evening assembly at Jingyan Temple, the bell is struck within Jingyan Temple, and the drum is beaten atop the watchtower of the prefecture. Simultaneously manifesting great spiritual powers, they pierce through a thousand gates and ten thousand doors.
Does the great assembly hear it? If you say you do not hear it, how can you deny that the bells and drums are clearly sounding and that everyone has ears?
If you say you hear it, by what means do you hear? Now that the drum has ceased and the bell has faded, what is the nature of that which hears?
Try to say something! [He] strikes the staff: Gold naturally has its own price; one never sells it mixed with sand to others. —Lù.

The Layman said, "What is it like after the drawing is finished? The Master said, "Originally, there is not a single stroke. The Layman said, "There are currently sixty-four hexagrams;

"Whether discussing before or after the lines, or existence or non-existence, it has nothing to do with the Great Changes (*Da Yi*). Even if a single call and a single response make the hexagram lines distinct, it is still not the ultimate standard for a monk.

Was there originally a *Yi* before the lines were drawn? Why did this fellow from Tianning not call out 'Wutai' right off the bat? Master Xu’s verse says: *In a dilapidated wall and broken house dwelling deep in the dark forest,* *The back door and front gate stand open without being shut.* *Turning north and returning south, shadows and echoes meet;* *How pitiful—though only a few feet apart, they are separated by a thousand layers!* The first verse on the Primordial Beginning says:

*On the palace floor of the Yellow Emperor, they spoke with Paoxi;* *In the courtyard of Confucius, he destroyed the teachings of Zhongni.* *They lived together precisely because they did not know one another;* *Yet they caused the golden mallet to strike behind the head.* The Master asked again: "The Perfected Person has no dreams."
"Why is this? The Master said: "Ordinary people, regarding the illusory phenomena before them, discriminate among their perceived objects without realizing that their entire being is a dream.

They take these things to be truly existent and, with a deluded and conceptual mind, bind their consciousness to these wandering objects as if they were dreams—what is called 'dreaming while dreaming,' or dreaming within a dream. As for the person of realization, it is regarding the objects of their own mind.
One knows things as they truly are. Thus, regarding the illusory objects present before one, their wondrous function is coolly clear, penetrating and unobstructed;
even within sleep and dreams, one knows them with self-evident clarity and remains vividly awake. This is what is meant by "waking and sleeping being as one.
Therefore, the teaching that the Perfected Person has no dreams does not mean a mere absence of dreaming; rather, it means there is neither dream nor non-dream.
"Dreaming and non-dreaming are one and the same. The scholar asked again, "In a dream, how can one traverse ten thousand *li* in a mere moment?
The Master snapped his fingers once and said, "Ten thousand *li* and a thousand *li* are right here.
He asked, "Does a sage have deluded thoughts? The Master said, "No. [The scholar] said, "If there are no deluded thoughts, why must one be so cautious and vigilant? The Master said, "Vigilance..."
"Be cautious and vigilant; thus there will be no delusion. Question: "How can one govern without becoming weary? Master:
"Do not concern yourself with honor or disgrace, gain or loss, praise or blame, right or wrong. Simply empty the mind and act without doing anything.
Then you will have no weariness. Question: "One eats all day long; why is it that one never chews so much as a single grain of rice? Master: "..."
"The person who eats his meal. The layman asked, "Have you ever seen one?
The Master said, "Layman, try looking back at your own mind-capacity (*citta-pramāṇa*); does it have any limit? After a long while, the layman said:
"In truth, they are inexhaustible. The Master said, "The world is likewise so. The scholar asked again, "Do the hells truly exist?
The Master said, "When a person commits evil, they know it clearly within themselves. Though much time may pass, they remember it without forgetting; thus, the realm of karma is one's own mind.
Knowing their own evil yet being unable to release themselves from it—this is precisely because the ground of the Dharma King’s mind is not empty. The hells [exist].
Hell truly exists; yet if the mind realizes emptiness, hell follows that emptiness. [The Master] showed this to people with a verse:

"If your practice is uninterrupted throughout the four modes of conduct, When you hear the board or the bell, it is best to cast away doubt. Break through the face before it was born; Come then to the side of the furnace to undergo the tongs and hammer.
The Way is fundamentally non-action; how could it belong to cultivation? If there is cultivation, it is like placing a head upon one's own head. [The Master] said: "Empty space..."

If one were to add a handle to what is already heavy, the wild weeds and idle flowers would surely grieve. One might think there is a precious jewel within one’s garment, yet it is only when the garment is torn that one realizes the jewel is not there.
Last year there was still talk of the jewel being absent; today, even the talk of the jewel being absent no longer exists.
Not seeking within and not searching without, the great trichiliocosm is gathered within a single hair. Dust mote by dust mote, world-system by world-system, it is the Lotus Treasury World;
yet to cling to this is still to remain outside. In the hearts of every person dwells the Ancient Amitābha; among those in the age of the Dharma’s decline, many do not believe.
Moment after moment they seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere, unaware that every thought-moment is Amitābha himself. [Postscript by Bian]
In his later years, he retired once more to Tianning Temple. In the autumn of the Gengshen year, he manifested illness.
When someone requested that he speak a verse, the Master raised his hand and gestured back and forth before passing away (his successor was Jia’an Zu).
Chan Master Faju of Tianchi, Yuequan, and Yuzhi in Huzhou was the son of the Fu family of Jiahe.

As a child, he would frequently sit cross-legged upon the ground and fold blades of grass to recite the Buddha’s name. Everyone spoke of his parents, saying, "This child will surely become a disciple of the Buddha in the future.
Upon reaching maturity, he became deeply versed in the classics and histories. At the age of fourteen, he received formal instruction from Dharma Master Jian of Zisheng Monastery.

Having severed worldly attachments and received full ordination, he resolved his will upon the study of the Way, never flagging day or night. One day, while reading the *Platform Sūtra*, he attained a profound realization.
He went to visit Jiān Zú, but there was no accord; subsequently, he met Fǎzhōu Jì, from whom he received much inspiration.
By chance, he encountered the Duke Wáng Yánmíng amidst a gathering of scholars. The Duke took a key from his sleeve and asked the Master, "Do you see it? The Master replied, "I see it. The Duke—
He then withdrew it back into his sleeve and asked, "Do you see it? The Master replied, "I see it. The King said, "Not yet. The Master remained in doubt and could not resolve it.
One day, hearing a monk cite a question posed to National Teacher Dadian: "What is the seeing of nature? Dadian replied, "Seeing is itself nature.
At this, he suddenly broke into a smile of realization and composed a verse: "Leaning on my staff, the lake’s light extends for three thousand acres; The mountain colors unfold—"
The five or six peaks at the gate: whatever meets the eye is the manifestation of the original reality. The meditation cushion does not now refine a stubborn emptiness.
Later, while he was observing the retreat at Yunfeng in Louze, he suddenly remembered Master Xueyan’s question to Gaofeng:
"When one is fast asleep, with no dreams and no thoughts, seeing nothing and hearing nothing—where is the true master? At that moment, he had a realization.

He remained there, yet he had not attained complete liberation. One day, hearing a friend recite the verse by Chan Master Tiantong Xian, "In the temple at Mount Bifeng, there is a Tathāgata," he went straight to Bifeng.
As soon as he saw him, he asked, "Is there a Tathāgata in the temple at Mount Bifeng?"
"Is it not you, Master? Xian said, "Does the Senior Monk see [it]? The Master replied, "To see everything is like gold dust falling into one's eyes.
Xian said, "How long has this fellow been dead? You have come to beg for his life," and he then returned to the abbot’s quarters.
The following day, Xian ascended the hall and cited an ancient worthy who said: "Break open the Great Tang Empire and find someone who does not understand."

"There is no one at all who understands the Buddha-dharma. He further said, "I have traveled once through the South, yet with the tip of my staff, I have never struck upon a single person who understands the Buddha-dharma.
These two statements are highly enigmatic. Let me attempt to provide a response for them.
The Master said, "In front, it does not reach the village; behind, it does not pass the shop. Xian said, "That is not yet it; speak further.

The Master said, "If one does not meet a true connoisseur, it is but a vain labor to discuss the severity of winter. Xian said, "What is that phrase which provides real power? Try to bring it forth. The Master then presented two verses.
Xian said, "You have not yet escaped falling into others' traps. The Master asked, "How can one avoid falling into others' traps?"

Xian [suddenly] raised his palm and said, "Is this falling or not falling? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment; all that he had harbored in his past was completely dissolved like ice.

Subsequently, while attending Xian, they passed through Hangzhou and traveled to Nanping. Upon reaching Zongjing Hall, Xian ascended the seat and said, "This place is perfectly suited for preaching the Dharma.
The Master replied, "The preaching of the Dharma is already finished. Xian immediately descended from the seat and looked at the Master, asking, "Which one?"

"This is the fundamental Dharma I have taught," [the Master] said. Xian replied, "The sword has long since been lost. The Master nodded in approval, and Xian subsequently received his seal of certification.
Later, he retired to Tianchi, where disciples arrived daily until it became a great monastic center. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The Ultimate Way is non-action;
yet without action, one cannot penetrate its depths. There is learning beyond learning; yet without diligent study, one cannot reach its pinnacle. It is like..."
It is like jade within its rough stone or pearls within the deep abyss; were it not for cutting, carving, probing, and seeking, they could never be obtained.

Thus, [the Buddha] practiced austerities at Mount Snow for six years, and [Huineng] sat facing the wall at Shaolin for nine years. It reached the point where he severed his arm to seek the Dharma and carried stones on his waist to do the pounding of grain.
For thirty years, Zhaozhou did not allow his mind to be distracted by anything else; only after forty years did Xianglin finally become a single, unified whole. Diligent! Diligent!
Diligent and tireless, they neglected sleep and forgot their meals, desiring only to investigate and clarify the Great Matter; these were all models for those who practice Chan and study the Way.
Yet now, as autumn deepens in the monasteries, the Dharma-path has fallen into desolation. People pursue delusions and follow heterodoxy, no longer striving to uplift themselves.

They know only that the morning gruel and evening rice are provided for them, feeling no shame in consuming the faithful offerings in vain. Some even allow their minds to wander into alien studies, giving rein to their own whims.

Some are clever and ingenious, yet they merely exploit circumstances to pursue intellectual interpretations; all such efforts are but a waste of time and serve only to increase the consciousness of karma.
Like a destitute son who has lost his father, drifting about without a foothold—how lamentable this is!

If one is a man of true spirit, one must directly exert intense vigor at the very brink of birth and death. When a single thought is pure and true, not even a speck of dust can stand. It is like encountering...
Facing the enemy, one enters directly with a single blade, disregarding danger or death; like falling into a deep well, every thought is focused on nothing else but seeking an escape.
If one can possess such a profound mind, one will surely reach home one day.

A monk asked: "When the Golden Body first descended, the nine dragons spat forth water. Now that the birthday celebration is encountered once more, what auspicious signs are there? The Master said: "Gold..."
The phoenix bears blossoms, manifesting auspicious colors; the brocade oriole turns its tune as it perches upon the new bamboo.
It is said that by pointing and looking about in every direction, one reveals the true mechanism. How do you manifest this message today? The Master picks up his staff and says:
"This staff reaches upward through the thirty-three heavens, striking the nostrils of Śakra Devānām Indra; it reaches downward through the eighteen layers of hell, shattering the realm of King Yama."

From the crown of his head, he looked down to respond to the myriad capacities of beings; the ten thousand phenomena, as vast as the forested heavens, all bowed their heads to proclaim Prajñā. The great earth, mountains, and rivers listened with bated breath.
A monk asked, "If that is so, was it not the same as the time of Vulture Peak in the past and this day at Tianchi? The Master said, "A single beam of divine light illuminates the universe;

do not compare the distant and the near across past and present. He then descended from his seat. —Lu Wutai* *Note: "Lu Wutai" (陸五臺) is likely a signature or the name of the scribe/annotator of this record.*
The layman asked, "Where are the one thousand seven hundred *kalyāṇamitras* (spiritual friends) of the Eastern Land now?
The Master pointed to a cicada chirping on a tree in the courtyard and said, "There is one here. The layman asked, "Is it the sound itself?
The Master replied, "To call it 'sound' is already to miss it. The layman then pointed to a rock and asked, "Regarding 'insentient things preaching the Dharma,'..."
"How can this be described? The Master said, "What do you call this, Layman? The Layman replied, "Stonehead.

The Master said, "And yet you say it cannot be described. On the nineteenth day of the fifth month in the Gui-chou year of the Jia-jing era (1553), the Master entered nirvana (his successor was Tian-tong Xian).
Chan Master Jingqin of Shuangfeng on Mount Jianning was the son of the Cai family from Jianyang in his native prefecture.

From childhood, he was exceptionally outstanding and unconstrained by convention. He would often sigh, saying, "In this world, all seeking leads to suffering; it would be better to seek a way out as soon as possible."
At the age of twenty-five, he shaved his head at Dongfeng. Initially, upon meeting Dachen, he received no inspiration. Next, he visited Xingkong, the abbot of Guanzhuang.
One day, while sitting below the seat, he saw the venerable elder Jinghuang reading the *Recorded Sayings of Old Mei*.
In it, there was an account of a monk who went to the abbot’s quarters and said, "I have a point of entry. Mei struck him out. The monk entered the quarters again, and Mei [struck him once more].
Daguang laughed and said, "This monk truly has a place of awakening; it is simply that he has not yet clarified the Great Dharma.
Upon hearing Daguang’s words, the Master rose, performed a prostration, and requested instruction on the essential points for entering the Way.

Daguang said, "Although Buddha-nature is inherently present in every person, if one does not cultivate and transform it through wisdom, one remains merely a common worldling. Now, if you wish to accomplish this matter, directly..."

One must completely sweep away all entanglements and branches. Taking only a single "meaningless" *huatou*, one should doubt it oneself, question it oneself, press upon it oneself, and constrain oneself;
one must refuse to seek someone else to explain it for one, and refuse to rely on intellectual interpretations or forced analysis.

One must resolutely sever the life-root and realize it through direct personal experience and awakening. In this manner, throughout the three watches of the day and the three watches of the night, one must drive oneself forward with urgency. After many years and months have passed in this way—
Suddenly, the flower of the mind blossomed with clarity, like the sun appearing when the clouds part.

Every ancient *gong'an* was thoroughly understood; for the first time, he realized there is no Chan to be studied and no Buddha to be made. Everything is realized in every instance, and everything is penetrated in every object.

It is like a person who has reached home and no longer asks the way. Having received this instruction, the Master applied himself to study with life-and-death intensity, contemplating: "The myriad dharmas return to the One. The One—
He returned to the place where he had spoken [of his departure] and traveled further south to visit Shoutang. Upon reaching Jiumingtan, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
When he met Shoutang, they were like a needle meeting its eye; he immediately received the seal of transmission and retired to live in seclusion at Shuangfeng. (The year was Zhengde Renshen.)
He moved to Ruiyan and addressed the assembly: "A student of the Way should sever all external conditions and stifle miscellaneous thoughts.

Holding up the original koan of one's own inquiry alone, one must not let it be forgotten at any time—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or amidst suffering, pleasure, adversity, or favor."
Whatever good or evil objects and conditions one perceives during periods of stillness all arise from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).

It is simply because when sitting in meditation with eyes closed, the mind lacks vigor and the consciousness flows along with external conditions, remaining in a state between dreaming and waking. Or, by craving the state of stillness, one causes various visions to appear.
If one is a practitioner of the Right Cause who is applying effort, they should sleep when it is time to sleep and wake immediately upon awakening.
Rise up and rouse your spirit. Rub your eyes; clench your teeth; tighten your fists. With single-minded focus and right mindfulness, press on with earnest diligence.
As you oscillate between doubt and inquiry, reach the moment when the water runs dry and the mountains end.
Suddenly, the mass of doubt bursts apart, and you instantly perceive your own original ground and its natural radiance. This is not obtained from without. Upon reaching this state—
Regarding the timing: as soon as one is said to have entered the gate and attained the ground, one must still seek out a master of clear eyes to undergo decisive discernment;

one must not stop short of this. If there is even a single dharma that is not understood, it must be clarified; if there is even a single principle that is not penetrated, it must be thoroughly mastered.
Even if, after awakening, one cannot penetrate the gates of transformation, the ancients called this "sitting atop a hundred-foot pole," unable to reach the destination.

Within the ocean of all-knowledge, let go from the precipice; if you are willing to take responsibility for yourself, you will revive after death—this cannot be faked before the Honored One. Be careful! (Shoutang Songsi).
Chan Master Wansong Huilin of Jingshan in Hangzhou was the son of the Shen family from Renhe County.

He followed Pingxu of Tianmu and obtained the essential teachings of the mind. Later, while traveling to Jinling, he heard a monk reciting the words of Chan Master Danxia from his formal lecture hall.

He then attained great enlightenment. At that time, Chan Master Konghuan Jiao of Funiu was residing at Guangde. The Master went to visit him and presented his realization; he immediately received the master’s seal of approval. Later, he went to Mount Jing.
One day, he took leave of the assembly and wrote a verse, saying: "For seventy-six years, my life has been like a drifting weed—what reliance can there be?
Fundamentally, there is no coming or going; I have merely responded to conditions. Having finished writing, he passed away (Jin Tai Jue was his successor).
Zen Master Gikun Kiben of Manshu-ji on Mount Song in Xijing of the Cao-Dong school was a native of Yuanqu in Pingyang. His clan name was Wang.
He received the tonsure under Dharma Master Musō of Jūshō-in and, after a long period of study, traveled to visit various masters, eventually meeting Zen Master Keijun Kagen.
At Mount Song, he requested an instruction on the essential point of the mind. Daokai said, "Tell me one phrase before Bodhidharma had not yet come from the West.
The Master was unable to respond and felt deep doubt within his heart. One day, seeing a *huai* tree planted by the Qin dynasty, he attained sudden and complete enlightenment.
He went straight to the abbot’s quarters, intending to present his realization; just as he was about to speak, Daokai suddenly said to him, "Qibin has attained Chan. The Master then—
[The Master] shouted. [The other] changed his words, saying, "What was that shout for? The Master said, "How can you, Reverend, falsely accuse another of a crime?
[The other] said, "Zhaozhou exposed the old woman; where was the old woman's point of failure? The Master said, "A pair of iron hammers without holes."
Ran said, "But what was Zhaozhou’s intention? The Master said, "Amidst a thicket of brambles, one further adds a pitfall.
Ran said, "Shitou’s letter could not be delivered, nor could the messenger reach him. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "A thousand miles away, the same wind blows.
Ran said, "As for Qingyuan’s lowering of his feet, what was that? The Master said, "A disaster! A disaster! Ran said, "Dong..."

The preceding point lies secretly within your own person. In the fourth year of the Jingtai era, while presiding over the ancestral temple (the Chan monastery), a monk asked, "What is the matter prior to the empty kalpa?
The Master said, "A tortoise facing the fire. [Yuan'an Yu] said: "This is a futile attempt to evade; it has nothing to do with the matter.

Tell me, where does the fault lie—is it with the host or the guest? Only when you can clarify this can you be permitted to understand the matter prior to the empty kalpa. If you cannot clarify it, then simply look at 'the tortoise facing the fire. [Longtang Zhu] said: "If one proclaims it in such a manner, does that suffice as the matter prior to the empty kalpa?"
"The weather is getting late; each of you should return to the hall and seek [the truth] for yourselves. [Question: "What is 'the partial within the central'? [Master:
"At midnight, a black hen sleeps amidst the snow. [Question: "What is 'the central within the partial'? [Master: "An old man cradles a stone tortoise.
[Question: "What is 'coming from the central'? [Master: "A blade drawn from its scabbard—its coldness pierces the heavens. [Question: "What is 'the simultaneous'?"
[The Master] arrived at Zhong. The Master said, "Gongsun’s Sword Dance is inconceivable. [The monk] asked, "What is 'reaching within the synthesis'?

The Master said, "A black dog with silver hooves—nowhere to be found. [The monk] asked, "Since I have received the Master's instruction on the five ranks, what is the matter of the Direct Pointing of Shaolin?
The Master said, "There is no oil in sand; there is flour in wheat. A monk asked, "What is the Lord? The Master said:

[The student] asked: "Who can fathom the depths of the ninefold palace? The Master said: "How is it that the subject serves the sovereign? The Master said: "Ten-thousand-li mountains and rivers are but traces of ink.

[The student] asked: "How is it that the sovereign turns toward the subject? The Master said: "The light of the jeweled hall contains the renewal of myriad transformations. [The student] asked: "How is it that the subject serves the sovereign? The Master said:

"At the jade steps, the celestial retinue draws near to the Dragon Countenance. [The student] asked: "What is the relationship between sovereign and subject? The Master said: "The Sovereign and Subject."
The Way was in accord. The Master said, "With dignified composure and non-action, the world is at peace. A monk asked, "Is there anything further beyond this?
The Master said, "Only by being careful, O *jiaoli*, will you succeed. The monk bowed, and the Master smiled, saying, "Today this mountain monk has not hit upon the right opportunity.
He then descended from his seat. In the *Ren-shen* year of the Jingtai era, the Master passed away and was interred in the western valley of Shaolin (Nengran later changed his lineage).

The Thirty-First Generation Descending from the Sixth Patriarch.
Chan Master Wumen Juexue Zhengcong of Longquan in Suizhou of the Linji school was a native of Guanzhe in Shaowu. His clan name was Xi, and his mother was surnamed Wu.
He entered the monastic life in his childhood and received full ordination at the age of twenty. He studied the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. One day, there was...

An elderly monk questioned the Master, saying, "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.

What was the meaning of this? The Master answered according to the literal text. The elderly monk ridiculed and rebuked him, then departed. From that point on, the Master was spurred to exert himself;
doubt arose within him all at once, and he found no peace whether sitting or lying down. After six years had passed, one day he heard the sound of a horse neighing.
He attained great enlightenment. He then went to see Master Tianqi Rui; as soon as he prostrated himself, Rui struck him.
The Master said, "I was somewhat hasty just now, and I have offended you, Reverend. Rui said, "Today, this old monk has been seen through by you, Senior.
The Master said, "The Reverend forgets the world while in the world, and forgets thought while in thought. How could I possibly have seen through you? Rui said:

"How is it to be in the world yet forget the world? The Master said, "To realize that things are not things. [The student] asked, "How is it to have thoughts yet forget thoughts? The Master said, "To have no mind within the mind.
[The student] asked, "What is it like when both mind and things are forgotten? The Master said, "Mount Hua rises abruptly; Mount Tai is towering.
Rui nodded in approval and subsequently received the seal of certification. After taking up residence, he ascended the hall for a discourse. He cited a monk who asked Yunmen:
[The Master] asked, "What is the teaching of the one lifetime? The Gatekeeper said, "It is spoken in response to each. Longquan, however, was not like this.
If someone were to ask me, the mountain monk, "What is the teaching of the one lifetime? I would strike them across the spine. [The Master] said, "Shut that dog’s mouth!
A monk asked, "What is the original face? The Master said, "The Stone Incense Pavilion. [The monk] asked, "If I go away just like this..."

"How is it? The Master said, "He has lost it already" (Xiaoyan Bao added: "To let go is perilous; to pull back is too fast. He offered this verse: *At the peak of Ancient Yunfeng, people find it hard to glimpse; / Suddenly caught by the wind, it reflects the evening clouds.

/ Before the hundred birds have returned, the day is already late; / Deep into the night, as always, they roost among the reeds.* Shi Che Cheng added: "Although Master Cong did not fail the monk who came with his question, he laid everything out on the table.

Yet that monk relied on the words to produce an intellectual understanding. If I were asked, 'What is the original face? I would strike him across the spine. When that monk asks, 'If I go thus, what then? I would strike again and say, 'A hundred thousand miles and eight thousand more. Now tell me, how does this compare to the ancients?")
[Try to examine this briefly. A monk asked, "Today is the eighth day of the fourth month; the monasteries throughout the world all celebrate the Tathāgata’s birthday.
I wonder where the Tathāgata was born? The Master drew a circle on the desk and showed it to him. The monk was speechless.
(Xiaoyan Baoen bowed and said, "The entire realm gazes upon it everywhere. One day, the Master suddenly vanished, and no one knew where he had gone. His disciples...
After a long time, no trace of him could be found. Two years later, the Master returned to the mountains. On the evening of the first day of the seventh month, the Master said to the assembly:
"Because my mind was not yet fully realized, I traveled abroad again. The mountains and rivers of Wu and Yue are vast and distant;
with a single staff I carry the sun and moon. At Longquan Temple, the talk was especially long. Having finished this verse, he cast his staff to the ground and sat in the full lotus posture.
[The Master] Shi (Tianqi Rui Si) passed away.
Zen Master Ji of Guyan in Mianzhou had become blind in middle age. The monk Xiangyan Bao went to visit him.
The Master asked, "Where have you come from? Bao replied, "I have come directly from Guanziling. The Master asked, "Is your elder brother Wumen well? Xiangyan said:
"Good," said the Master. "In what way do you see it as good? Yank said, "I am robust in my old age. The Master said, "How do you know you are robust?
Yank said, "I put on my clothes, eat my meals, sit, lie down, and walk about. The Master said, "If that is so, then you have not transcended ordinary circumstances."
Yan said, "In any case, ordinary people cannot fathom this. The Master looked up and laughed heartily. The next day, Yan entered the room.

The Master said, "Old brother at the mountain pass, our late teacher once granted you his seal of approval; your realization penetrates to the very bone. It is only that you are too simple and lack extensive learning."
Yan said, "Is the Master widely learned? The Master replied, "I am not widely learned either. Yan said, "If that is so, then we are the same.
The Master said, "There are also points where we differ. Yan asked, "In what way do we differ? The Master said:
"He has eyes, but I have none. Yan said, "If the Master has no eyes, how can you see that there is nothing to be learned?
The Master laughed loudly again and instructed him, saying, "Your capacity is extraordinary; you should take deep root and establish firm foundations, bringing vast benefit to others.
Who else but you could do this? It is a pity that I am old and infirm and shall not live to see it. Yan bowed in thanks and departed. (Tianqi Rui was his successor.)
Chan Master Daxiu Shishi of Fu-niu Ji-’an was the son of the Li family from Xinzheng. From his early childhood, he suffered from chronic illness;

when he was only a few years old, his parents, fearing he would not survive, sent him to receive instruction under Baozhu. At the age of twenty, he visited the veteran master Guxin, who presented him with the koan:

"All dharmas return to One; where does the One return? He subsequently entered the meditation hall and attained awakening upon being struck three times. He then composed this verse: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
The verse says: “The Dharma-body is fundamentally without marks; The characteristics of dharmas are originally empty.
Those who realize this through subtle communication Reveal their family style everywhere. Later, he went to pay his respects to Master Tianqi Rui.

On the way, he encountered two Chan guests, Tianzhen and Yueyin, and they traveled together to Guanzilizheng. Tianqi asked, “Are you three on the same path? The Master replied, “Although we are on the same path,” and so forth.
Their origins were different. Qī asked, "What is your original face? The Master replied, "Take care. Qī said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master gave a shout.
Qī asked, "Before your parents were born, what was there to shout at? The Master was speechless and departed.
Thereafter, he presented several more displays of skill, but Qī did not approve of any of them. One day, while attending Qī at Cheng...
Tianqi asked, "Where the body is hidden, there are no traces; where there are no traces, do not hide the body. How do you understand this?
The Master said, "If one does not sit upright in the hall, how can one respond to the dualistic promptings? Tianqi expressed his appreciation.
Later, when he ascended the seat, [he declared: "Sumeru dances, the ocean waves surge, dragons and elephants mingle, and devas and humans gather together."
The earth, mountains, and rivers all together proclaim the wondrous phrases; the three levels of worthies and the ten stages of sages jointly realize Bodhi.
A jeweled sword emerges from between the brows, casting a cold light; a golden mallet is hidden in the sleeve as one executes the true command.

Illuminating killing and bringing to life, manifesting the golden mechanism—raising the whisk, is there any clear-eyed monk who, disregarding danger or ruin, can step forward and shoulder this burden? [He] then descended from the seat.
Seng Xiyuan Bao attended the Master for training. He asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

The Master held up his whisk. Bao said, "Is there anything further to be pointed out beyond this? The Master threw down the whisk. Bao then prostrated. He then recounted his inquiry regarding the story of Guanziling.
The Master said, "I knew it was because you had personally met a master. Bao then gave a shout. After a short while...
The Master asked again, "It has been forty years since my old brother last visited; I wonder how his nostrils are today.
Baoshou said, "They are just like the Master’s nostrils. The Master said, "Does the Sengzuo see this old monk’s nostrils?
Baoshou said, "I do. The Master asked, "Where do you see them? Baoshou said, "Below the two eyes and above the mouth. The Master—

Visiting him morning and evening, although he deeply believed and knew that [the Way] existed, he was unwilling to rest until he had personally realized it for himself.
He visited various elder masters, including Dachu, Yuezhou, Guchun, and Guzhuo. Later, he went to Guanziling to attend upon Master Wumen Cong.
When asked, "The Ten Sages and Three Worthies have already fully perfected holy wisdom; why do you say they did not understand this principle? Wumen then spoke sternly.
Sheng said, "The ten sages and three worthies you already know—what is the meaning of this? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!
The Master offered a dozen or so successive turning-words, none of which accorded with the truth. He then became despondent, abandoning both sleep and food.

One day, carrying a basket to the edge of a stream to wash vegetables, a single leaf fell into the water and spun around; though he tried to catch it, he could not hold it. Suddenly, he attained realization and returned with his basket.
Overjoyed, he returned home. Zongli stood beneath the eaves and asked, "What is that? The Master said, "A basket of vegetables. Zongli said, "Why not say something else?

The Master said, "Please ask me something different, Reverend. That evening, when they entered the inner quarters, Zongli brought up Xuansha’s saying, "I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the end.
The Master said, "A thief enters an empty room. Zongli said, "This koan cannot be [dismissed as such]."
"Roughly done. The Master gave a shout, shook his sleeves, and went out.
He subsequently visited the various venerable masters Ji’an, Guyan, and Dajue, all of whom held him in high esteem. Later, he ascended Guanziling and again attended upon Master Cong.
One day, during a cold rain, Cong ordered a brazier to be lit. The Master then asked: "Everyone has their own original parents; what about your parents?"
“Where is it now? The Master said, “A single fire has consumed it. [The monk] asked, “In that case, do you have no parents?
He replied, “I have them; it is simply that even the Buddha-eye cannot see them. [The monk] asked, “Do you yourself see them? He replied, “I, too, do not see them.”
[The Master] said, "Do you not see them as well? [Cōng] replied, "If I were to see them, they would not be my true parents. Cōng said, "Excellent! The Master then presented a verse, saying:
"The original true parents Have never been apart throughout kalpas. In rising and sitting we rely on their power; In cold and warmth we share their knowledge.
Meeting yet not seeing one another, Seeing yet not recognizing one another— I ask: where are they now? He then divided [the verse].
He presented it clearly to the Master. When Cong read it, he was greatly pleased and said, "So it is, so it is!
This single verse alone is worthy of succeeding to my school. He then spoke this verse: Your mind is my mind; My mind is fundamentally no-mind. No-mind is identical to the Buddha-mind;

The Buddha-mind is not my mind. (Muchen Meng’s verse says: Picked up from the water and burned in the fire, emerging above the heavens, one is naturally carefree. Reflecting back on what was not yet understood, there is a point before the mechanism that strikes.)

"Haoh! This is a true hero! Muyun’s Verse says: Having traversed a thousand mountains, my straw sandals are worn through; I pass my good years with effortless ease. The ground is secure through steady deliberation; At Mount Ling, the life-essence of wisdom hangs by a single thread. Ruan’an’s Questioning Verse says: A single stalk of vegetable leaves suddenly flows away;
Returning with joy, I repay my parents with my very being. My whole body is red and raw on the ground; Only this blind donkey can truly uphold the ancestral tradition.

He further said: "The Buddha is like a Wheel-Turning King; the Buddha-dharma is like the King’s command. A son of the Buddha raises the banner of the Dharma, able to transform the heterodox into the orthodox. Thus he entrusted [the teaching].

He said, "Receive and uphold this with careful attention. When the conditions for those to be saved ripen, both the wise and the foolish shall be delivered. To continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom, one must wait for such a person.
Having received this prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), the Master attended [his teacher] for over a year until the latter reached an advanced age, at which point he took his leave.
He subsequently resided for several years in places such as Jinghai, Niu’ou, and Gaozuo in Jinling. He then returned to Jintai, initially dwelling at Yuantong and later moving to Nan...
At the Si-lu-yuan, Ci-guang, Shan-guo, and other monasteries, on the occasion of the Dragon Boat Festival, the Master ascended the hall and said:
“Master Dahui once ascended the hall and said: ‘Today is again the fifth day of the fifth month. The great ghosts clap their hands and the little ghosts dance.
Suddenly they run into the Tao Fu deity; both hands beat upon their chests as they cry out in grievous suffering. The Master said: “Old man Dahui was very much lacking something.”
Regarding methods for exorcism: when facing the blue sky and the bright sun, one sees gods and ghosts. Xiaran, however, is not like this. This very day is the fifth of the fifth month.
Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. This mountain monk wishes to gamble a wager with all the great sages and ordinary people present here.
Reaching out my hand, I pluck from the tips of the hundred grasses: the sweet is sweet, and the bitter is bitter. (He raises his staff.)
Suddenly emerging is this one single thread that pierces through all the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past. You people here before me possess everything in a hundred ways;
why then is you alone lacking this one thing? Suddenly, there might be someone who, seeing this meaning, acts with heroic resolve.
He spoke forward with indignation: "Preceptor, do not force the noble into the lowly. If one were to discuss this single matter, I dare say that every person lacks nothing by even a hair's breadth.
He set down his staff and said: "You truly do not know. What harm is there in adding a point to an arrowhead, or piling more earth upon a mound?
[On another occasion,] he ascended the hall and said: "A man of spirit may indeed harbor ambitions to pierce the heavens, yet none surpasses—"
Let it flow down from the head; let the skull wither away completely. Yet, he causes the eye of death to suddenly open wide.
[The Master] ascends the hall and cites National Teacher Nanyue Huairang. One day, the Teacher asked the assembly, "Has Daoyi yet preached the Dharma for people?
They replied, "He has already finished preaching the Dharma for the assembly. The Teacher said, "But no one has yet brought back a single word of news."
He then secretly dispatched a monk to scout, instructing him: "When he ascends the hall, go out and ask him, 'What is it?
Observe what words or phrases he utters and remember them for me. The monk went and acted exactly as instructed.
Mazu said, "Since the time of the rebellion, for thirty years there has been no shortage of salt and sauce. The monk returned and reported this; Master Shang deeply approved of it.
He said, "In my place, for thirty years, I have never seen so much as salt or sauce.

What kind of bowl are you all looking for here? With his staff, he drove them all away at once. [He] ascended the hall and said: "A single arrow at the gate; those who come must observe the skillful means.
If you intend to step forward and ask 'How?', it will pierce right through your skull. [He] ascended the hall, held up his staff, and said:
"Is there anyone? Is there anyone? At that time, a monk came forward and prostrated. The Master struck him across the back and said, "Why such a garrulous mouth?
The monk replied, "I have not yet uttered a single word; why do you call me garrulous? The Master struck him again and said, "A second offense will not be tolerated.

Han Yue Zang’s *Nian* (Commentary): "Exceedingly clever indeed, yet he cannot avoid being in a state of haste. Verse: "No need to understand guest and host; Come directly and personally seize the divine mechanism. The path of men is cut off. In the snowy night, the plum blossoms [nod]; In the early spring, the fragrant grasses fill the garden—none know it."
[New] ○ A monk asked: "When a single word has exhausted the Way and there is no further room for speech, what then?

The Master said: "The cuckoo cries by the banks of the Wuling Stream; ten li of peach blossoms are crimson with blood. [Yuan’an Fang’s Verse]: "The cuckoo calls by the banks of the Wuling Stream; Ten thousand words and a thousand phrases have no other sound.

If one turns their head and knows that returning home is best, All travelers from the ends of the earth will turn back their steps. [Lü’ān Yue’s Verse]: "Whose peaches and plums vie in their fragrant beauty? The du-yu cries out, calling the traveler to return. Have you ever trodden the banks of the Wuling Stream?"

The spring colors within the Pànlu Cave differ from those of the human world. Tian’an’s verse says: Words exhausted and principles fully realized, the tongue goes dry; Coral in the ocean bottom supports the moon. Amidst the cries of the cuckoo, the fallen flowers are red— How much has this master fully revealed?
Ascending the hall, he said: The dew wets the courtyard, the moss on the steps is slippery; The climbing vines entangle the mountain path, causing one to lose their way.

Zen practitioners often inquire about the meaning of the True Patriarchs; Last night, I took my sandals and returned alone to the West. He raised his staff and pointed, saying: "Look, look! Look! The Patriarch...
The Master had also come over the mountain gate. He called for an attendant boy and said, "Give me [the staff]," immediately casting him out.
After a long while, he said, "This is for your own sake; you must not take such things lightly.
A monk asked, "What was the matter that brought you benefit in years past? The Master held his whisk upside down and looked at the monk, saying, "Do you understand? The monk said, [No].
"Venerable Sir, I already know where the Preceptor has been at work. The Master said, "Tell me, when Huang Siniang of Jingzhou prostrates before the Buddha, what does she seek?
The monk was speechless. The Master then struck him out. (Shiche Cheng commented: "The monk asked for benefit, and the Master swept him away; both sides were clearly manifest.

Who knew that at the final squeeze, he would fall into a ten-thousand-fathom abyss from which he cannot rise even to this day? He calls to the assembly: 'Can you save him yet? Do not say it is like drawing a bow after the thief has passed. Yundian Chi commented: "Huang Siniang finished her prostrations.")

In the end, what was he seeking? He then uttered a long sigh and said: "The tracks of birds in the sky were originally unseen; the sound of wind on the leaves is as if heard. A monk came for an audience and asked:
"From the time of the ancient masters of the seventeen hundred [cases], I have today strung them all together on a single thread to present to you, Master. I humbly request your judgment."
At that time, the sound of a dog barking was suddenly heard outside the gate. The Master immediately looked back at his attendant and asked, "Go see what kind of guest has arrived.
The attendant went out to inquire about the matter, but the monk was at a loss for words. The Master asked, "What did you ask just now, Senior Monk?

As the monk prepared to repeat his question, the Master struck him with a continuous blow of his staff and drove him out. A monk asked, "What is the Samādhi of Universal Vision of Mañjuśrī? The Master said, "Death."
[The Master] said, "The human eye. [A monk] asked, "What is the Samādhi of Universal Hearing of Avalokiteśvara? The Master said, "The ears of a dead man.
[The monk] asked, "What is the phrase that exhausts the bottom of the single path? The Master said, "The mouth of a dead man.

A monk requested instruction on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* passage regarding being "held in contempt by others. The Master said, "Do you have any doubts? The monk said, "I have doubts. The Master said, "If you have doubts, then..."
The monk was held in low esteem by others. Without doubt, he should have fallen into the evil realms. The monk hesitated. The Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "Bring forth that which you do not understand and let me see it. The monk said, "Since I do not understand, what could I possibly bring forth?
The Master said, "Your karmic offenses are instantly extinguished. The monk rejoiced and prostrated in gratitude.
[The Master] asked, "Regarding Xuansha’s ‘not crossing the ridge’ and Baoshou’s ‘not crossing the river,’ to which level of spiritual capacity do they belong?
The Master said, "They both fall into the second level. [The student] asked, "What is the first level? The Master said, "Xuansha does not cross the ridge; Baoshou does not cross the river.
[The student] asked, "Ultimately, what did they obtain? The Master said, "Truly so! Ultimately, what did they obtain?"
Question: What is "taking away the person but not taking away the environment"? The Master said: "A single copper coin; a large fried cake. Question:
What is "taking away the environment but not taking away the person"? The Master said: "It has already been eaten into the belly, and one is immediately joyful.
Question: What is "taking away both person and environment"? The Master said: "You do not have a single copper coin, yet you would willingly endure hunger."
[The monk] asked, "What is meant by 'neither person nor environment being taken away'? The Master said, "Cloud Gate’s sesame cake; Niu-tou’s golden ox rice.
Coming with an empty stomach, one returns with a full belly. A monk asked, "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different?

The Master said, "Willow shadows stretch across the pond as fish climb trees; locust-tree shade covers the earth as horses mount branches. The monk said, "If that is so, then form and shadow are both—"

[The monk] said, "Right and wrong will reveal themselves. The Master said, "I have never eaten my fill of the rice of Luling; you merely take your meditation cushion and mistake it for the Dharma-realm.
A monk came to inquire, saying, "I have heard that the Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition.
I ask the Master, what is this 'one great cause and condition'? The Master said, "Dressing in robes and eating food; defecating and urinating."
The monk refused; he did not prostrate and departed. The Master called him back and showed him with a verse: "The Buddhas appear in the world Only for the sake of a great causal condition:
To defecate and urinate, To eat when hungry and sleep when tired— These are the urgent matters before one's eyes."
People desire only to ascend to heaven; they discuss the profound and speak of the wondrous together. Yet when they encounter calamity, they must pay fines.
The monk, feeling ashamed and anxious, bowed and departed. One day, two officials were touring the mountains. Upon entering the gate, they recited: "Lush pines and tall bamboos.
Looking back, they saw the Master and asked, "What is the style of a man of the Way? The Master replied, "Lush pines and tall bamboos. The officials said, "We have [seen it]."
"What is the underlying meaning? The Master said, "It is not enough for you to observe within your own house; I have left it for you, the guest, to look at.
A scholar read the Master’s verses on the Pure Land and asked, "When the Buddha preached this sutra, the Buddhas of the six directions extended their broad and long tongues as a witness.
Now, when my Master speaks these verses, what special witness is there? The Master said, "The tongue of a layman like you is also not [limited]."
[The Master] said, "Short. He asked again, "What is inconceivable merit? The Master said, "A person on the street ahead calls for his dog; a person in the alley behind scolds his cat.
He asked again, "Teacher, how old are you this year? The Master said, "In terms of years, I have not seen a single bit of meat."

"Why do you not wither away? [The Master] drew a circle. A monk asked, "Everywhere one enters the Dharma-realm; in every thought-moment one beholds Vairocana. What is Vairocana? The Master said, "One need not defecate on clean ground. [The Master] cited Zhaozhou Zen Master’s question to Touzi: "When a person who has died the great death comes back to life, what then? The Verse says: All thirty-six things have been reduced to ashes, Leaving behind only a pair of withered eyes.

Placed upon the nine-fold thoroughfare after the deep night, They act as a light in a place where there is no light. The Verse on the Patriarchal Case of the World-Honored One Holding Up a Flower says:
The wondrous resonance between teacher and disciple is like a mustard seed meeting a needle; like the ocean or a mountain, it has no place to be sought.

Only when one casts their eye into the flash of a flint-stone does one first know that the Buddhas and Patriarchs have no "mind" to transmit. Regarding the title of the Sūtra, the character "Mi" (米), the verse says:

Before black and white were distinguished, one had already fallen into pervasiveness; how much more so when one attempts to deliberate and exhausts oneself in research? The sages and worthies of the Western Heaven and this land—lift up their nostrils!
The Master was completely covered in holes [from being pricked by thorns]. He presented a verse to the Head Seat:
Carrying a hoe everywhere to sell one’s labor, A few copper coins are enough to sustain oneself. Though one clears the fields of others, One’s own field remains utterly overgrown with weeds.

He addressed the monks: "The profound subtleties within the Dharma are the physician for the eyes; The ultimate mystery above is but dust upon the realm. At the edge of the black lacquer bucket, apply the binding."
The Son’s Severance. A free person within the realm of Great Peace sits in stillness upon a cold crag; this illness is difficult to endure. How could a man of spirit willingly deceive himself?
A single step taken turns back—there is not much more to it. Only then does one believe that the dust contains the vastness of the Dharma-realm.

The Master once gave this instruction in his room: "Before the Buddha appeared in the world and before the Patriarch came from the West, there was originally neither the Buddha-dharma nor the worldly dharma."
The name [of this teaching] stands far beyond the ghost-cave of the Black Mountains. How would you say it? Again he said:

"Since the Buddha appeared in the world and the Patriarch came from the West, the Dharma of the Buddhas and the worldly dharmas have been established in mutual relation. Without violating the gate of transformation, bring forth a single phrase. Again he said:
"The Buddha arose within the realm of dualities between ordinary beings and sages; the worldly dharmas and the Buddha-dharmas are merely names and phrases established by force."
Set all that aside for a moment. Try to speak the single phrase that is the fundamental portion of a patch-robed monk (śramaṇa).
[He] said again: "Ordinary speech and dialogue are most simple and yet most inconceivable. Yet, as soon as someone asks, 'What is this Buddha-nature that you inherently possess?
why do you instead turn your eyes upward and remain speechless? [He] said again: "Since you have already become..."
"O Son of the Buddha! You have set your will upon the stage of Buddhahood; for what reason do you find even the single word 'Buddha' most unpleasant to hear?
In his later years, the Master retired to live in a lane of willows in the capital city. On the sixteenth day of the first month of the *xin-si* year of the Wanli era, he manifested *parinirvāṇa*.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa outside the Xiaoxi Gate (succeeded by Wumen Cong).
One day at dawn, Chan Master Baoying of Longshu on Mount Tai arose and, upon beholding the morning star, attained realization.

He composed a verse, saying: "The sun rises from the eastern mountain; The moon sinks behind the western ridge. Yesterday and today— They have never been two different things. (Tianqi Rui and Dachuan Hongsi)

Master Chufeng of Mount Tai lived alone on Bimoya Cliff for over ten years. Subsisting on wild fruits and drinking from mountain streams, others could not endure such hardship, yet the Master remained serene and unperturbed.

One day, hearing the sound of a firecracker exploding, he attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: The firecracker suddenly bursts forth; In an instant, it returns to its original source. If you wish to know the meaning of this, Look at the bright moon in the sky.
The eyes protrude like dead firewood; a majestic divine light illuminates the four continents. Manifesting in every place, people do not comprehend it;
how many times has spring passed and autumn returned? (Daechon Hong Si)
A monk asked Master Yudang, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Look beneath your feet. The monk asked, "How should one practice it?
The Master said, "Go straight ahead. (The above three masters are from Dachuang Hongsi.)
Chan Master Wuhuan Guzhan Xingchong of Chexi, Suzhou, was the son of the Zhang family of Xiushui. Initially, he visited Chan Master Wuqu in his lay attire and subsequently attained a realization.
He soon left the household life to follow Wuqu and received the tonsure. One day, Wuqu asked the Master:
"Jingshan’s verse on the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials says: 'To utter a single phrase that penetrates to the very bone and marrow—the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials.'"
"Absolute obstruction and protection. Regarding these two phrases, I, this mountain monk, wish to take one phrase as the Dharma.
Which one do you think is better to take? The Master said, "Which one did you ask about just now, Reverend? Qiu narrowed his eyes and scolded him, saying, "How can you be so lacking in discernment?
The Master said, "It is precisely because you have penetrated to my very bones and marrow, Reverend. Qiu said, "Not so. It is for the sake of you alone."

“I have already attained it. “Then what of the great assembly? The Master said, “I do not decline to take it; yet I would betray the former sages and lose my future followers. Wuqu said, “So it is, so it is.
The Master went to Mount Jing to build a thatched hut and compiled the *Recorded Sayings* (*Yulu*) of Wuqu.
One day, he returned to pay his respects. Wuqu asked, “What have you been doing lately? The Master replied, “I have bought a piece of land.”
Tian received the original deed and requested that the Master sign it; he then presented the compiled copy.
Yuanqu took it and examined it, saying, "This is mine. What about yours? The Master replied, "Master, you must not encroach upon another's path or seize their market.

At every land is the wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom; in every dust mote he can save the suffering of the world. The Master [resided at] Longchi, Tongxuan, Jinsu, Huangbo, and Yuyang.
At Tiantong, he presided over six monasteries for more than thirty years, causing the school’s teachings to flourish greatly. Those under his guidance numbered over thirty thousand.
Eminent monks from throughout the land who had long led disciples and managed monastic communities all turned toward the Master’s reputation and took refuge at his feet.
In the *Xinsi* year of the Chongzhen era, the imperial relative Lord Tian brought purple robes into the mountains on behalf of the Imperial Noble Consort.

He requested that the Master ascend the seat. Having again received the Master’s consent, he invited him to reside at Ba’en Temple in Jinling. The Master declined firmly on the grounds of his advanced age.
In the spring of the Renwu year, he took up his staff and returned to Tongxuan. On the third day of the seventh month, he manifested a slight illness.

On the fifth day, he wrote a letter by hand to the Dharma-protector, Imperial Censor Qi. On the sixth day, a monk arrived from the capital to inquire about the meaning of the shout as a shout and the staff as a staff.
"Regarding the 'Hitting with a Staff' assembly: entering hell is like being shot by an arrow. Ultimately, how do you understand this? The Master struck him. The monk bowed.
The Master said, "A thousand phrases, ten thousand phrases—all are understood from within oneself. If you do not understand yourself, you will never finish receiving blows.
At dawn on the seventh day, he inspected the craftsmen as usual. At noon, returning to his quarters, he told his attendant monk that he was extremely weary.
After ascending his bed for a short while, he rose to sit in the full lotus posture and passed away peacefully. He was seventy-seven years of age.

His entire body was enshrined in a stupa and brought back to Tiantong, where it was interred on the right ridge of Huanzhi Monastery. His *yulu* (recorded sayings) were requested for inclusion in the Tripitaka for widespread circulation (as recorded in the *Longchi Chuan-si*).
Chan Master Tianyin Yuanxiu of Qingshan in Changzhou was the son of the Min family of Jingxi.

Having lost his father at a young age, he sold vegetables to support his mother and constantly recited the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Upon reaching the age of twenty, he listened to lectures on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which states:

Realizing that [all things] are not true, he was subject to the cycle of rebirth. Trembling with urgency, he recognized the great matter of birth and death, and subsequently went to seek ordination under Master Huanyou Chuan at Longchi.
At twenty-four, he received full ordination and took up the koan of "the state before one's parents were born. For a long time, he made no progress.
One day, while following Chuan to transport bricks from a kiln, a fellow practitioner spoke of the four great sacred mountains and the Bodhisattvas.
Xuanchuan appeared; his spiritual powers were vast and great. It is said that he remarked, "There are not a few here.
The Master stepped forward and asked, "What are the spiritual powers here? Xuanchuan replied, "Quickly bring me some bricks! At these words, the Master attained realization.

One day, while casually unfolding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the passage where the Buddha rebukes Ānanda, saying, "This is not your mind. Suddenly, he lost his original point of inquiry and attained enlightenment under Xuanchuan.
He traveled north. The Master closed himself off at Longchi, where he studied the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients. Furthermore, regarding the Yunmen koan of the "fan," he could not let it go;

he investigated it with great effort for two years until, suddenly hearing the braying of a donkey, he attained great enlightenment. He then said: "Suddenly hearing the donkey cry, / The person of the moment is startled awake and laughs.
/ Ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences / Are neither sound nor form, yet they clamor. Thereupon, he broke through his seclusion and went to join his fellow practitioners.

Chan Master Yu Fengxiao Yuanxin of Jingshan, Hangzhou, was the son of the Zhu family of Ningbo. At the age of nine, he heard the *Amitābha Sūtra* being recited;
hearing that even the waterfowl and the trees were all chanting the Buddha’s name and the Dharma, he conceived the aspiration for enlightenment from that moment.
He left the household life at the age of twenty-nine. Once, afflicted by a fever, he nearly died; in a dream, a deity told him, "You will recover tomorrow," and he drank cold water.
His sweat broke out and his illness was cured. He immediately set out on a pilgrimage, often lamenting to himself: "Now that I have left the household life, what should I be doing?

Every day I am dull-witted; my food and clothing are mostly neglected. In the depths of winter, my bones are exposed. When I encounter those without trousers, I immediately take off my tattered ones and give them away.
For seven days and nights I remained naked; the cold air assailed my belly with such pain that it was unbearable. He continued in this state for two years, suffering without end.

At Ruzhu (or Qiangshi), [the master] returned to lay life, drank wine, and ate snails. After one month, a large golden arm suddenly descended from the sky and snapped off his nasal bridge, yet he did not reform. Several days later, another large arm descended and pulled out several inches of the tendons from within his throat; his pain was nearly unbearable.

He felt the knot of tendons on his neck, which had formed into a mass, and immediately rolled up his clothes to cross the river; only then did the mass disappear, though the scar remained. Ascending Qinwang, he visited the mountain master Miaozhen.

The master related that in the past, there was a monk with the power of *paracittajñāna* (knowledge of others' minds) who resided on the mountain. He encountered a monk from Shaolin who wished to test him.
