"Not borrowing conditions. Why have you come here? The Master said, "Because of not borrowing conditions, I have therefore come here.
The Book [of the Layman] asked, "Regarding the single phrase 'not borrowing conditions,' what do you think it means? The Master said, "The colored phoenix soars through the wind with body at ease;
the iron ox gallops and bellows with mind ever at leisure. The Book said, "Excellent. The next day, he took his leave. The Book presented him with a verse, saying: "You shall surely become a person."
The Celestial Lord said, "You should consider the autumn at Shaoshi. The Master asked, "Who is Changrun? How would I dare to presume such a thing?

He wrote a note of instruction, saying, "My Way has long been in decline; how can you fold your hands and do nothing? The Master responded with agreement. When the letter was delivered, Changrun had already entered nirvana.

The assembly deliberated that the seat must be succeeded by none other than the Master. Although the Master steadfastly declined out of humility, refusing even after being invited twice, the community then recited the verse of entrustment.
The Master suddenly shed tears and said no more; he then retired to Shaoshi Mountain. The Master’s physical presence was robust and dignified, and his voice was like a great bell.
He shared in the simple frugality of the students, yet his character was broad and expansive, exerting himself with single-minded devotion.

He bore the great burden of the Dharma, remaining diligent morning and evening without the slightest hint of weariness. Those who entered his chamber to offer incense numbered two hundred and seventy.
On the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month of the Wuli year of the Yiyou cycle (1605), he wrote a verse and passed away. (Recorded by Zongjing as his successor.)

Chan Master Changzhong Yunkong of Lingshan in Jianchang was a native of that province. While he was still a layman, he had frequently lectured on the school of "innate knowledge" (liangzhi) at Yao River.
One day, while traveling as a guest to Helin in Zhenjiang, he visited an elder named Guxi, who told him of the monk Yuezhou Tan.
Thereupon, Changzhong shaved his head and left the household life. When the elder fell ill, he said to him again:

"Once you have left the household life, you should go and consult various spiritual friends. The Master then traveled to Central China. Hearing of the reputation of Master Shushan of Xiao Shan, he went to visit him immediately.
Shushan asked, "For what purpose have you come? The Master replied, "I seek the Dharma for liberation from birth and death.
Shushan said, "Where is birth and death? What do you want me to liberate you from? The Master was speechless. Shushan said, "Go for now and attend to your duties."
[The Master] was staying below. One day, the Master asked again, "How can one see one's nature and become a Buddha?
Xuefeng said, "Have you even eaten yet? The Master said, "I have already eaten. Xuefeng said, "The tongue is in your mouth; do you see it?
The Master asked, "Ultimately, how does one become a Buddha? Xuefeng said, "A Buddha is a dried-up shit-stick. Can you bite through it? As the Master was about to speak again—

The questioner shook his head and said, "Not it, not it. The Master grew increasingly suspicious; he then took leave of Shu and traveled extensively to visit renowned masters throughout the various regions.
After some time, he attained realization and thoroughly understood Shu’s pedagogical methods. Consequently, he returned to Mount Song. Just as he arrived, Shu had gone out on a journey.
The Master went to meet him and asked, "Where is Bodhidharma’s 'wall-gazing'? Shu pointed and said, "A..."
At that dark blue-black spot, the Master said, "Why point east and talk west? Xuefeng said, "In the south, there are fabricated Chan practitioners as numerous as hemp and millet.
The Master said, "Be careful not to bewitch the men and women of others' households. Xuefeng picked up his staff and struck him;
the Master prostrated himself, and Xuefeng then departed together with him. Later, having thanked the Master for the matter of Shaolin, Xuefeng went to reside at Zongjing in Beijing.

The Master followed him, serving him diligently for three years and deeply grasping the profound essence of the teachings. Whenever he transcribed [the texts], he would cross-examine them with the Master, never yielding in the sharpness of his intellectual sparring.
One day, as the Master was preparing to take his leave and return home, Shu presented him with a verse, saying: "Under the Mirror of the School, ten thousand pine trees stand;
For ages they have held the white clouds in their embrace. In the world, no casual acquaintance is permitted; Yet one branch has burst forth, smiling at the spring breeze. The Master returned home.

In Jianchang, at a secluded spot by his paternal aunt’s house, he would always sit in a solemn, upright posture. When people asked him about it, the Master would shake his head and say, "You do not understand;
go away. Someone might say, "Master, please explain this to me for a moment. The Master would reply, "Is this not itself 'not understanding'?
Everyone laughed at this. Later, having traveled to Mount Fuchuan, he visited the old sites of Grand Master Shaolong and composed a poem on the Xiaoqu Peak.
On the wall of Fengjing’s chamber it says: "The overturned boat deceives Xuefeng; he has no birth or death, for the great void is empty.
The sound of the jade flute ceases and the thousand mountains grow cold; who listens to the cries of the monkeys in the night moon? This was clearly a profound expression of his realization.
Twenty *li* from the city of Xunjiang lies Lingshan, where the scenery rises majestically on all eight sides; the Master traveled there and took delight in it.
He lived in a thatched hut for twenty years, never associating with others. Although many local gentry and old friends came to visit him, he would do nothing but sit in silence.
When the two gentlemen Luo Jinxi and Deng Qiangu discussed the study of nature and destiny (*xingming*) with him, they both transcended the limitations of emotional perception.
However, when it came to the "upward matters" (*shangxiang shi*) of the Chan school, most people were unable to grasp them.
Wuming addressed Master Jinggong, saying: "Your reputation for the lofty and austere practice of the Way is well known, yet you specifically seek to leave the household life and receive the precepts.
The Master said: 'To leave the household life, one must leave the house of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Wait until this matter is clearly realized, and even then it will not be too late.

To take refuge in the precepts, one must take refuge in the Dharma of one's own mind; why must the three platforms of ordination be necessary to achieve perfection? Do you know how the sixteen novice monks continued the lamp and attained Buddhahood? "
"To leave the household life in this manner is to be a true man. The Sūtra then asked, "What is the essential method for entering the Way?
The Master said, "If you can simply be diligent and not deceive yourself, you will be able to penetrate from beginning to end.

One day, after Jingxing had discussed the meaning of the *Vajracchedikā* with his fellow practitioners to great satisfaction, the Master heard of it and laughed, saying, "If the eye of the school is not clear, it cannot be considered ultimate. Jingxing [was taken aback].

Greatly startled, he then asked, "What is the Eye of the School? The Master shook out his robe and rose. Jingyi remained in doubt. One day, he brought up the previous conversation and questioned the Master.
The Master said, "I am not as good as you; you should go see for yourself. Later, Jingyi went into seclusion on Mount Emei.
Upon hearing the words "a truly great mountain," he attained great enlightenment. He went to Nangsan and presented a verse to the Master. The Master said, "It is not that you lack awakening;
however, you must further attain its practical application. If you do not attain its practical application, you will merely be using 'mercury-silver' Chan."
He then cited the story of Master Nanyuan Wang selling himself to test [the student], saying: "Try to tell me, what was Nanyuan’s state of mind?
He continued, citing the Sutra: "This old fellow has no sense of propriety; he waits for your head to emerge before he strikes. He further asked about the lay practitioner Gan-zhi:
"When he requested that Nanyuan recite the scriptures, Nanyuan broke his cauldron—what was the meaning of this? He replied, citing the Sutra: "He brushed his sleeves and left."
He then cast a baited hook, and the lad broke the cauldron; its jade was flawless. The Master marveled at him and said, "In the future, you shall propagate the ancestral Way;
I am not your equal. Throughout his life, the Master’s conduct and speech were as refined and dense as fine jade within its ore;
he would refuse to see anyone who was not a person of true realization for the Dharma. When he saw someone discussing their realization at a certain place, he would acknowledge it.
"Wu! [The Master] suddenly roared in protest and rebuked him, saying: "What have you seen that you dare to cite this as proof for others?
Since the Great Ming Dynasty was established, how many people can be found who have truly engaged in inquiry and authentic investigation?
You dare to utter such great false speech, claiming awakening where there is none and claiming realization where there is none? He then composed several *niansong* (verses on cases).

It was transcendent and extraordinary; he kept it secret and did not reveal it to others. (Master Deng, who had been acquainted with the Master for the longest time, once sent him a poem which said: "The mud ox has entered the sea and its tracks are lost; at Longshan, the family style is most fully revealed.

Who knows there is another profound meaning, whose tone emerges anew and differs from that of Xinfeng? When the Master saw this, he laughed and said: "You may be said to have understood half of this mountain monk.
One day, the Master, being without illness, suddenly addressed the assembly, saying: "I have one matter that remains unresolved. You all must know it. The assembly...
He remained silent. He then ordered that he be bathed and his robes adjusted; subsequently, he sat upright and passed away.

During the cremation, his cranial bone did not decompose, and it was enshrined in a stupa at his home mountain. Later, the layman Huang Duanbo, serving as a judicial official, together with the monk Shouchang Mi, relocated the stupa to the foot of Ling Shan (as recorded in the *Zongjing Shu Siji*).
Chan Master Rujin of Yinan Hermitage at Mount Daipi in Weibo was a native of Yongnian in Guangping. His clan name was Chen.

Having received the Dharma from Master Shu of Xiao Shan, he cultivated the Way at Xingguo Temple on Mount Daipi. For several years, his shadow did not leave the mountain and his feet did not step across the threshold.
He did not permit nuns or women to enter the gate, nor did he allow them to have an audience with him face-to-face. After a long time...

When he ascended the hall to preach the Dharma, his spiritual resonance was like rolling pearls and his eloquence like a cascading river. Monastics crowded shoulder to shoulder and heel to heel, seeking audience with him as if driven by madness.
One day, accepting an invitation to travel north, he stayed overnight at the Sanjiao Hall (Hall of the Three Teachings).

The presiding monk approached him and said, "In the past, there was an image of the 'Mad Bag' (Hán Bùdài) enshrined on the western wall. Later, when Daoist practitioners resided here, they placed a double topknot upon its head."
They changed his title to "Immortal Zhongli" and moved his offering-tablet to the eastern wall. From time to time, those in black robes and yellow caps vied for precedence over his position.

To this day, the consumption of meat and wine and the performance of licentious sacrifices have brought calamity to this region; it is truly a strange matter. [The petitioner] requested that the Master eliminate them.
The Master pointed at the image with his staff and said: "This lump of clay has manifested many strange transformations. Failing to abide by its own nature, it causes vexation."
They throw the human world into chaos: shaven-headed Buddhas and patriarchs, and top-knotted immortals, displaying their eccentricities and exposing their shame.

They bewitch the common folk, inciting one another with mischief, moving hither and thither, giving rise to false joys and angers, and acting with the recklessness of "four in the evening and three in the morning.

Had they not encountered this old monk to execute the True Command, they would have remained entangled in cold indifference for many years. Now that the four elements have each returned to their place and they have reverted to their original source, from this point on—

"As soon as you have finished the *Zhiwulun* (Discourse on Equalizing All Things), I shall immediately send you up to Chang'an. Heh! Heh! [With] a continuous blow of the staff, [all shall be] ground to powder;
thus shall the heterodox and the malevolent be solemnly cleared away from this point forward. (From the *Zongjing Shu*)
Longgang Dafangru Xian was the son of the Li family from Qishan County in Fengxiang, Shaanxi.

At the age of seventeen, he paid his respects to Master Wuzongben of his native prefecture to become his teacher. He first visited Master Yue’an Xi, who conferred the full precepts upon him and pointed out the path of the Ultimate.
Subsequently, he entered Mount Qingfeng to dwell alone in seclusion, whereupon he attained a realization. He then went to visit...
Dazhangshu visited Master [Xuefeng] in the courtyard where he stood in the snow; he subsequently remained there as a dependent disciple.

Day and night he entered the master’s room, refining his understanding through the karmic conditions of the ancestors, until he finally received formal certification (*inka*). He applied himself with tireless diligence day and night, like threading a jade needle with a silk thread or taming an iron ox at the bottom of the sea.
A Record of the Master’s Entrustment to Yi Bo: When the Master arrived in Huaqing, Prince Zheng Ryang renounced the throne and cultivated pure deeds in seclusion.
Hearing that the Master had arrived, he constructed a hermitage at Longgang and invited the Master to dwell there in tranquil stillness.

The Empress Dowager Cisheng bestowed upon him the Tripitaka and a protective imperial edict inscribed with the four characters "Dafabaozang" (Great Dharma Treasure Storehouse). Upon arriving at Longgang, the Master founded a temple there to enshrine and offer worship to them.
Later, the Master passed away while sitting upright without illness; his stupa was erected to the right of the temple (as recorded in the *Zongjing Shu*).
The Chan Master Tongxuan of Yugufeng in Ye was a native of the Wang clan of that region. At the age of seven, he paid homage to Master Damiao and received the tonsure.
Upon reaching maturity, he traveled south to seek instruction, traveling with Jin of Pishan to visit Chan Master Shu of Xiaoshan. From the moment they first met, [Shu] directly...
The dragon and elephant [of the Dharma] were expected to appear. After a long time, he finally transmitted the robe and the Dharma to him.
Later, hearing of the imperial court, he received an edict to open a hall at Śarīra Temple in Zhending. He was invited by the Prince of Dai to propagate the Dharma in Datong, Shanxi.
A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Why do you not ask about yourself? The monk asked, "How is it that one's own self is the Way? The Master said, "Everywhere."
"The green willows can tether the horse; every house has a road leading to Chang'an. A monk asked, "Is there anything further above this?
The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is the matter above this? The Master said, "When the green mountains appear low, one sees the vastness of the sky;
when the red lotuses bloom, one smells the fragrance of the water. Not long after, he took his leave to return home, where he supported his parents like Chen Puhui and made a vow.
King [Wang] retired to the hermitage to spend his final years. Later, he passed away sitting upright without illness; his stupa was erected beside the hermitage (from the *Zongjing Shu*).
Chan Master Tianran Yuanzuo of Que Mountain in Shunde was the son of the Fan family of the district. Together with Dafang Qian, he...
He visited Master Shoushan Shuheshang at Shaoshi Mountain, where their karmic affinity was realized; the master ultimately entrusted him with the robe and bowl.
Returning to his hometown, he lived in seclusion at the Shihe Hermitage on Mount Penglue. Whenever there were requests for him to preach the Dharma, the Master declined most firmly.

However, when Lord Wu, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, led the fourfold assembly in repeated invitations, the Master then ascended the hall. Holding up his whisk, he drew a circle and asked, "Do you understand? This is the one path that leads upward."
"Transmitted by no sage among the thousands, scholars exhaust their bodies like monkeys grasping at shadows.

Unless one forgets form and discards intellect, loses duality and ceases mental activity, and personally arrives at the state of empty lucidity and unclouded awareness—the ground where there is constant, clear knowing—one will find it difficult to perceive the meaning of the Flower-holding and the essence of the Wall-facing.
This is much like counting another's peaches and plums from outside the palace walls; in the end, they do not belong to oneself."

"There is. Do you people still wish to know the message of the Buddhas and Patriarchs' direct pointing? [The Master] then struck the desk with his whisk and said, 'Just now, I have already announced it.
He then descended from the seat. A monk asked: 'What about raising the mallet and brandishing the whisk?'"

Citing the past to clarify the present—all such things are merely yellow leaves used to stop a child’s crying. What, then, are the gold coins? The Master said: “One sees only the thunderbolts issuing their commands;

who knows that the stars and constellations illuminate the literary patterns? [The student] said: “The Master himself is walking with a torch; what does this have to do with this student? The Master said:
“Sitting with eyes closed on the Mid-Autumn festival, one instead complains that the moon has no light. —By Wu Zhu of Pengyan.
Shi asked, "What is the essence of prajñā? The Master said, "Quiescent and unmoving.
He asked, "What is the function of prajñā? The Master said, "Responding and thereby penetrating all things. He asked, "Where is the place where one applies effort and gains power?
The Master said, "When the formless reaches it, the light is brilliant. He asked, "What is the place where one does not gain power? The Master said, "The waves where Li Lou walks."
[Tao] Tian said, "If that is so, then there has never been any difference between Confucianism and Buddhism. The Master pointed to the empty space and asked, "Is this Confucianism?
Is it Buddhism? Are they the same? Are they different? The official performed a prostration and said, "Thank you for your instruction.

In the tenth month of the year Wuli Yiyou (1605), the Master, foreknowing that his time had come, bathed and then passed away while sitting in meditation. (The above six individuals are recorded as the successors in the *Zongjing Shu*.)
Continuation of the Record of Pointing at the Moon, Scroll 18;
Continuation of the Record of Pointing at the Moon, Scroll 19;
Thirty-Fifth Generation Below the Sixth Patriarch.
Chan Master Wufeng Ruxue of Mount Guiyang in Tanzhou of the Linji school was the son of the Ren family from Lintong in Guanzhong. He studied under Master Miyun Wu.
One night, during a conversation over tea, Wu suddenly extended his leg and asked, "What will you do? The Master [responded] with his own leg.
He kicked him. Wuzhuo laughed and said, "Not yet! Not yet! The Master said, "Venerable Sir, speak! Wuzhuo lay down on his back. The Master said, "It is simply that you are tired.
Wuzhuo said, "And you have gone off like that again! The Master then bowed. In the winter of the Bingyin year, the assembly at Jin-sul numbered over five hundred.
Wuzhuo then appointed the Master as the West Hall Attendant. (Lin Gao Yu saw the Master in the West Hall quarters and asked...)

The Han Head Seat asked, "What about Master He? He said, "I do not know. Yu said, "A patriarch possesses the eye that discriminates between dragons and snakes; why do you say you do not know? He said, "Where is your eye, brother? Yu then gave a shout.

He remained silent. Yu shouted again. He said, "Why do you not shout once more? Yu said, "Excellent! You do not even know pain or itch! He then ceased. One day, as the Master was departing, Wuxue grasped his whisk and said, "To call it a whisk is to encounter resistance;
not to call it a whisk is to turn one's back on it. One may neither pick it up nor set it down."
"If you can give me a word, I will not remain silent; but you must not speak erroneously. If you do not speak erroneously, I shall entrust this to you.
The Master then leaped twice in succession, saying, "No, no! Wuzhuo said, "This is still just shouting and leaping about.
Try raising [the question] again. The Master turned his body and said, "I am going. Thereupon, Wuzhuo was entrusted with the lineage seal and the whisk. (Chongzhen era)
On the day of Gengwu, Wuzhu resided at Huanggai. The Master was in the West Hall quarters when the monk Yinyuan Qi came to pay his respects.
Pointing a fist toward the Master, the monk said, "If one recognizes this, the world is at peace; if one recognizes this, the world is in strife. How do you resolve this? The Master struck him.
The monk shouted again, and the Master struck him once more. The monk shouted twice in succession, and the Master struck him twice. The monk—
He then presented what he had attained. The Master said, "This boy has penetrated it. He then called him into the quarters and said, "You have reached an awakening; try to speak of it.
The monk said, "To speak of it is not difficult, but I only fear startling the crowd and disturbing the assembly. The Master said, "What harm is there in simply speaking?"
The monk performed a somersault and departed. The Master said, "A true lion cub; he knows well how to roar.
In the year Guiyou, he left Mount Guiyang for the Jintuolin Monastery in Jinling. He suddenly passed away, and his remains were returned to a stupa.
His work, *An Account of the Five Schools*, was shown to the monk Guying of Hengzhou. Later, Huanglong Mufu had it carved into woodblocks for circulation (Tiantong Wu was his successor).

Chan Master Fancang of Han-yue at Sanfeng in Suzhou was the son of the Su family of Wuxi. At the age of seven, while attending the local village school, he encountered a sudden surge in the lake waters;
though his family searched everywhere and could not find him, he had mounted a large tortoise and emerged through the surging waves. The villagers regarded this as a divine marvel.
He left home to become a monk at fifteen and received the full precepts at nineteen. He devoted himself to the study of the Buddhist scriptures and mastered the subtle analysis of Confucianism.
Shu once said to others: "Throughout the ten rivers and nine Luo, the total mastery of the Buddha’s teachings must be sought where there are no words.

He then composed commentaries on the Four Books, the Five Classics, and the *Cantong qi*. One day, he sighed deeply and said: "As for the matters of the *zongcheng* (the core vehicle), one must personally investigate and comprehend them.
Even if one comprehends them and can explain them, if this one matter is not yet resolved, one cannot face birth and death."

He attained [realization] and subsequently resolved to travel as a wandering monk (*paryaṭaka*). He went to consult on the koan "The myriad dharmas return to one," visiting renowned masters everywhere, yet none satisfied his mind.

He then went into seclusion at Sanfeng Peak on Mount Yu, where he lived in a thatched hut with walls of vines, providing neither bed nor seat. One day, two monks outside the window were leaning against a fence, snapping a large bamboo stalk;
its sound was like a sudden clap of thunder, and he attained great enlightenment. While he was in retreat behind closed doors, he suddenly pushed open the window and saw them.
When the yellow plum fell to the ground, he finally attained thorough realization. He then took up a bamboo staff and, day and night, developed his disciples;

at that time, they were known as the "Furnace and Bellows of Sanfeng," and his reputation was esteemed throughout the monastic communities. In the autumn of the Jiazi year of the Tianqi era, he paid respects to Master Wu at Jingu Temple.
When Master Wu ascended the hall, he cited the story of Huangbo’s visit to Baizhang, and Baizhang recounted the circumstances of Huangbo’s second visit. Huangbo...
Huangbo involuntarily stuck out his tongue. Baizhang said, "In the future, will you not take up the lineage of Mazu? Huangbo replied, "Not so.
Because of you, Master, I have been able to perceive the great function of Mazu’s awakening; yet I do not recognize Mazu. If I were to succeed Mazu, my descendants would later lose themselves.
Baizhang said, "So it is, so it is. When one's insight is equal to the teacher's, one falls short of the teacher."
"One who possesses half-virtue cannot receive the transmission; only one whose insight surpasses that of the teacher is fit to inherit it. You possess an insight that greatly exceeds your teacher’s;

thus, when Linji asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times, he was struck three times. Later, when Linji appeared in the world, he used only the staff and the shout to guide people.
He would not accept 'how' or 'what,' valuing only direct entry with a single blade. When you stepped out from the assembly and shouted, Wuzu said:"
"Excellent shout! The Master shouted again. Wuzhuo said, "Try shouting one more time and see. The Master bowed and returned to his place.
Wuzhuo then cited a monk who asked an ancient worthy, "When the bright moon is suspended in the sky, what then? The worthy replied, "He is still a man standing on the steps."
The monk said, "I request the Master to lead me up the steps. Deyi said, "We shall meet after the moon has fallen. [The monk] asked, "Tell me, how do you meet after the moon has fallen?
The Master then left the hall. That very day, he was invited to occupy the First Seat. The following day, Wuxue ascended the hall.
The Master addressed the assembly gathered like clouds, saying, "The compassionate rain falls everywhere. I do not ask about leaping forth and soaring aloft; how is it otherwise?"

"This is the phrase that drives the thunder and flashes the lightning. When Wuzhuo [Wu] was about to strike, the Master said, "If it is so, then the golden grain flowers have bloomed and the fruits of Baolin have ripened.

Wuzhuo struck again. The Master bowed and returned to his place. Not long after, wishing to take his leave, Wuzhuo personally wrote out the lineage seal of Linji and bestowed upon him the whisk and a letter.
At An-yin Monastery in Hangzhou, the Master was invited to ascend the hall. He ascended...
Before the striking of the wooden gavel had even finished, the Master held his staff across [the assembly] and said: "The thousand Buddhas could not open their mouths;
the patriarchs have suffered a total defeat. Today, I bring this forth directly: it remains as bare and stark as ever.

This matter is like the Ganjiang and Moye swords—when both wrists are applied together, it is like an icicle flower or a flame; it lies beneath the faculty of speech within the realm of retribution and transformation."
"Cut it off! It would be just right to melt down weapons to forge plows; such a life would be a joy beyond compare. Is there such a man today? It would not be out of place for him to meet An-yin.
(Initially, An-yin requested that Chan Master Yunmen Cheng serve as his head seat. Cheng said, "I am advanced in years. If you request Sanfeng to be the head seat, I will come.

The assembly went to Sanfeng and informed him of the matter. The Master joyfully consented. However, by the day before Cheng was to arrive, Cheng passed away. His final instructions were: "The Head Seat Han is a master of our age; in his understanding of the Buddha-dharma and his learning, he surpasses me tenfold. You should invite him to preside over the community. The assembly followed his advice.

In accordance with his final instructions, he invited the Master to expound the Dharma. ○ Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like a sudden clap of thunder piercing the crown of one's head;
there is no time to cover the ears. It spews forth a pure breeze—a single blade of tempered steel. With one blow upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, one passes through beneath the Diamond Mountain.
One rolls back the void and stands as a sheer cliff ten thousand fathoms high. Only those who are the true bone-and-son descendants of Linji can understand this."
Striking the teeth within the lion’s mouth; probing the bones upon the back of the black dragon. Host and guest interchange; throughout the entire body, one grants and seizes.
Emerging from within the final phrase, living one's life before King Bhīṣmagarjitanirghoṣa. Is there anyone who possesses such a path of practice?

"Come forth and meet the old monk. (An-yin addresses the assembly: "The phrase prior to the trigger is where you all find your place of rest; the first move of the initial opportunity is where you all establish your life-force.

Moving left or right between them, extending or contracting, is where you all set foot; the final phrase is where you all emerge. [This Dharma discourse has been transmitted and recited by all quarters, titled 'The Five Decisive Points of Sanfeng.

Da'an's verse on the Green Peak says: 'Spread out both hands for you to behold; penetrating the trigger prior is truly difficult. Sentient and insentient are both sent off; gathered together, they are buried in Tongguan. For seven hundred years..."
The old master scatters and gathers them to test dragons and snakes: "Though you may have the bold strategy to enshroud the world, how can you dare to bare your fangs when you reach this point?

Ascending the hall, he said: "The azure sky above is as if it might drip; White clouds beneath my feet stretch for ten thousand feet. A staff in hand, a gourd at my waist— Going and coming, there is neither compliance nor resistance.
This is good news: Treading through the grass, my sandals are worn away and my feet are bare. Three heads, eight arms, and eyes on the back of the head."
Meeting daily yet not recognizing one another. Ascending the hall: Unable to climb further, suddenly turning back, he breaks through the ultimate barrier of our school.
Left with only a pair of destitute hands, he finally knows there is no dharma to direct toward the world.
The Dharma seat is prepared; ascending the hall: A majestic lion throne surges from within the hall. The old monk, donning his robes, sits in the emptiness of the Dharma. Striding beneath—
The lion suddenly leaps and tosses about; with one roar, its majestic power is revealed. He gave a shout and said:
"When the lion crouches on the ground and roars, the Buddhas and Patriarchs flee headlong. Looking out from beyond the heavens, there is only the Old Man of Ten Thousand Peaks.
(He gave another shout. Within his quarters, he would often pose three questions to test the monks. The first was: "When the house is broken and the family is lost, who is the master?"
The second [question] says: "Even if one lets go of the wedge and the staff, what is the underlying intent? The third says: "When rolling up the mat and hanging up the whisk, why do they not remain?

Few have been able to accord with the pivot of these questions. (Liu Daozhen of Xichu entered the mountains to inquire about the Way. Having attained realization, he offered verses in response to the Master’s three questions. First, regarding "The House is Ruined and the Family is Lost":

O worthy ones, since there has been such a vast and magnificent tradition from of old, why not push aside that father of yours from this secure and secret field, and let forth his own true head? Grant it to me!
How can one directly take it up? At this very moment, what is the single phrase for the continuous transmission?
He struck his staff and said: "The heavens are high and the myriad forms are upright; the seas are vast and the hundred rivers flow with the tide. He ascended the hall and said:
"Last night, Mount Nanyue and Mount Kuanglu debated the Buddha-dharma. One mountain said: 'The Master Nanyue Huairang was [a disciple of] Cao...'"
"One Mountain says: 'The son of Xuedou. The Way of Mount Yi. "Master Qingyuan Si is truly the orthodox lineage of Baolin," One Mountain says.

"I think of the Great Master, National Teacher Huairang of Mount Nanyue. He could not have avoided going from here, in our Lingnan region.
I, this mountain monk, suddenly struck him on the head with a blow of the staff from Mount Luofu. Tiantai then pressed his palms together and said, 'Excellent!
This one blow struck by the Master penetrates to the very top and the very bottom; it is truly exhilarating. Thereupon, I let out a thunderous shout and said, 'Huh!'"
"Retreat with your heads tucked in! Thereupon, the four mountains each withdrew with embarrassment. Holding up a corner of his *kāṣāya*, he said: "Do you see?
Since Old Lu gathered it back in, one must believe that everyone possesses it. Ascending the hall, he said: "What Lingyun saw, everyone shares;
peach blossoms in the second month are red everywhere. Do not needlessly seek this from the outside."

"In my old garden, there are many fine fragrant clusters. Zhashang (Zhaozhou) said, "Look, look! He threw down his staff and said, "If you try to fix your eyes upon it, you fall into a thousand divergences.

Winter (The Imperial Audience and Dharma Discourse are seen separately in the *Zhisheng Zoudui Ji*). ○ Addressing the Assembly: True Suchness, ordinary beings, and sages are all but dream-like words;
the Buddha and Nirvana are both merely figurative designations. What, then, has this mountain monk been proclaiming throughout this winter at Wanshan Hall?
Only the pure breeze comes upon the mats; no idle words fall into the human world. Sweeping the ancestral stupa of Master Xiaoyan: golden skeletal chains and jade-like tinkling bells.

Ji died at the age of seventy-nine. His works, including the *Records of the Nine Assemblies* and the *Northward Journey to Baicheng*, were published during his lifetime (he was a successor of Tiantong Wu).

Chan Master Shiqi Tongyun of Xuedou, Ningbo, was born with the secular surname Xu. His family was poor; he left the household life at Nan Guang Temple. Having seen Zhongfeng bestow his instructions, [Shiqi] wrote:
"There are those who stumble and fail to follow their foolish companions; I fear that through procrastination, I too shall fall into the wind."
The Dust-Verse: In the past, I dwelt in seclusion at Mount Yu, where I drew blood to transcribe the sutras. Later, I studied under Master Wuzu of Jinsu.
One night, as I was walking out into the darkness, a monk struck me across the face and broke my nose; through this, I attained realization. I presented this verse:
"This fellow is thirty-two years old now; Until now, he has made his living in a ghost cave. Suddenly, when the tip of the nose was smashed— But..."
Seeing fresh blood flow and fill the ground, he attained awakening, yet he did not yet nod his head in agreement. Later, beneath the staff, he suddenly cast off all lingering doubts and obstructions.
At that time, he followed Xuewu to Yuwang and Tiantong for thirteen years. When he encountered Muchun Men, they departed the mountains together.

He received the transmission of the robe and whisk, which were entrusted to him with these words: "There is not a single pair of broken chopsticks; there is not a single dog. This is your place of dwelling. (Dwell here.)
At Vulture Peak, he ascends the hall: "The great forge is wide open, smelting Buddhas and patriarchs; saints and ordinary people alike are forged by the fierce tongs and hammers.
This time, do not regard it as something ordinary. The assembly must raise their eyebrows high; do not shrink from the furnace; see what is right and act with courage."
To see through this clearly is truly extraordinary. Who else possesses such total, elegant freedom? [He suddenly raises his staff and says: "Do you see?

Holding fast and letting go—all returns to oneself. Should it be otherwise, this mountain monk cannot help but point it out for you repeatedly.
Do you understand thoroughly? The staff has eyes as bright as the sun; to recognize true gold, one must look within the fire.

When the ancient masters spoke thus, it was much like being atop a solitary peak, waiting for someone to arrive. “Assembly, tell me: whom does he wish to wait for? [With this, he] struck with his staff.
The Incense Table says: Do you understand thoroughly? Dīpaṃkara beckoned from afar at Jīn Dizǔ; Zhìzhě nodded his head in the dark at Jianglíng. Xuědòu ascended the hall and said:
"A single move facing the sun stands alone, revealed without concealment. It is brilliant on all eight sides and open throughout the ten directions.
With clear eyes as witnesses, how could one dare to hide it away? It reaches even to the jade palaces and towers, right down to the tips of the hundred grasses."
The Supreme is fully revealed: the thousand-fathom Reward Body suddenly appears amidst heaps of rubble;
in every atom, in every world-system, the True Person of No-Station stands forth, clarifying this ready-made koan.

Even if all the Buddhas of the three periods and the ancient masters of successive generations were to arrive, each would have no choice but to step back. At such a moment, what is it like? Water returns to the great ocean.
The waves and billows of the sea are stilled; clouds reach the misty air of Cangwu. Ascending the hall for instruction:

In the second month, the spring breeze is vast and serene. Mountain flowers like brocade before the green cliffs. Having come today to this deep ancient temple, Truly there is nothing like the Zen of the Patriarch.

In the *Xinchou* year of the Shunzhi era, the Master returned to Nan’guang and said, “I am old; I must not forget my origins.

Chan Master Tongmen Muchun of Gunan in Jiaxing was the son of the Zhang family of Changshu, Suzhou.

At the age of twenty, he entered Mount Podong to take ordination under Master Muncheng; his original name was Qimen. He applied himself with vigor to investigation and inquiry, and soon attained a realization.

To attain this is the second-grade capacity. As for the first-grade capacity, not even a single old monk in all under heaven has ever grasped it;

At that time, he took his leave of Tiantong and came to Helin Shouzhuo. In his daily life, he had no practice other than the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha.

He spoke in verse: "A single pond, frogs drumming, clamor all night long; Clear and distinct, it reaches the very edge of my mouth. I announce this to the guests beneath the forests of the Five Lakes:

Changwu said, "It is not so, it is not so. The Master said, "The Abbot himself is not so. He bowed and departed.

(In Dun Village, Baen Temple welcomed the Master and bestowed upon him the temple plaque. "Before the Hall of the Bright Moon, jade dew hangs down; within the Palace of Crystal, pearls are scattered. Ascending the hall, he said:

the assembly must all at once take this up and carry it forth. Tiantong ascended the hall and said: "He is fundamentally a man of immeasurable capacity; nothing can fully depict him."
From the moment of emerging from the mother’s womb, one has mistaken the wrong for the right. Joining his palms, he said: "Does the great assembly understand?
I do not dare to look lightly upon you; you shall all become Buddhas. A monk asked: "If it is not a single frost that pierces the very marrow of one's bones..."
"How can one obtain the fragrance of plum blossoms that strikes the nose? The Master said, "You are still a guest greedy for bait; you have not yet become one who seeks nothing.
The monk asked, "What is it like to be one who seeks nothing? The Master said, "The patched robe covers the head, sleeping in the deepest slumber;
at such a time, this mountain monk would mostly not understand. A monk asked, "What is it like to take a secret step and behold the flying dragon? The Master said, "Passing through the thorns."
Thorn Forest. Only then can one be called a skilled hand. Question: "The Buddhas of the three periods have all been swallowed by me in a single gulp;
where else could there still be sentient beings? [The Master] provided his own verse in their stead: "How many dead people are there on level ground?
The Master habitually used the kōan of Mazu’s single shout and Baizhang’s three days of deafness to test his students. He further offered this statement: "The report."

"When the World-Honored One was first born, he immediately understood how to point to heaven and point to earth. You people here—what kind of bowl are you still trying to beg from this old monk?

It was the time of the summer retreat. Verdant trees cast their shadows; clear waters flow through emerald ravines; birds warble in the secluded forests.

Everything is distinct, without confusion or overlap; it is clearly not two people. Thus, the National Teacher Shao of old said: "At the summit of Tongxuan Peak, it is not the human world. Outside the mind there is no dharma;
before one's eyes are green mountains. Our former teacher also said: "At the summit of Tongxuan Peak, it is something else entirely."
People, it is only because they fail to realize this that they mistakenly identify with the green mountains.
These two venerable elders have expressed themselves in such a manner, and I, this mountain monk, have likewise proclaimed it; it is much like being unable to forget what is familiar.

No need to display it again: the jade bamboo rises high, sweeping away the torrential rain; the willows flutter about, dancing in the emerald mist. *Hè!* (A shout).
He plants his staff on the ground and descends from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "The successive patriarchs who appeared in the world each had their own way of presenting the Dharma.
Holding up his staff, he said: "How can it compare to this monk’s staff? He struck the desk and said: "With a casual stroke of the hand, he opens the gate of non-duality. He then raised another case.
He summoned the assembly and said, "This is the mountain monk’s staff. Tell me, where is the Gate of Non-duality?
If you can discern it here, you may as well pull up your straw sandals; if you cannot discern it, do not say that the terrain of Tongxuan Mountain is steep—for ahead of us lies an even higher peak.
[Ascending the hall, he said: "The primary truth is utterly beyond contrivance."
The moment one attempts to offer an explanation, it becomes an obstruction. Therefore it is said: "If the mind does not differ, the myriad dharmas are of one suchness;

if the eye does not sleep, all slumbers are naturally dispelled. If you are a man of brilliance who, upon hearing the mountain monk speak thus, directly takes up this burden before the patterns of words have even appeared, you will be somewhat ahead of the game. To avoid being trapped by the tracks of the road. As for the phrase, "Without traversing the path," how would you say it?
"The single breath speaks not, yet it contains all forms; where do the myriad spirits go to thank its impartiality? [Ascending the hall: Twenty years ago, this mountain monk...

One day, while on cold ground, I gathered the lives of all sentient beings within the three thousand great thousandfold worlds and contained them within a single minute speck of dust, such that not a single person knew of it.

This is what is meant by "hiding a mountain in the sea" or "hiding a boat in a ravine"—when a strong man carries it away at midnight, those who sleep do not perceive it. Today, this mountain monk proclaims it universally to you all.

Huijing opened his mouth and immediately asked people, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
At that time, why did Mazu step forward one pace and say, "Wait until you can swallow all the water of the West River in a single gulp, and then I shall tell you"?

The Master said, "I have a verse. Xiu asked, "What is your verse? The Master presented the verse: "Not associating with the myriad dharmas—for whom? No one is established, yet from the start I am intimate with him.
If you have intention and seek him out, you become increasingly estranged; If you are without mind, you recognize him and there is no contradiction.
Xiu said, "I do not ask about 'not associating with the myriad dharmas. I want you to understand how to swallow it all up in a single gulp."

"Xijiang Water. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment; he then shook out his sleeves and departed. Thereafter, whenever there were inquiries or challenges, he never yielded on the spot.
Yuanzhe deeply approved of him. The Master closed himself in retreat at the banks of the river in Rongcheng.

When Yuanzhe moved to Ba’en Temple in Wukang, he sent a series of letters urging the Master to come, saying: "I, this old monk, am at Ba’en Temple; my spirit is daily failing compared to before. You should..."
"Know that I shall not remain in this world for long. Upon receiving this letter, come at once; there is a most essential matter to entrust to you.

When the Master received the letter, he broke through the barrier and went to Xiu. He did not prostrate, but approached him with palms joined and said, "In the realm of a mad child, even his father cannot pass beyond this peak.
Is this still the dwelling place of an old man? Xiu said, "Stand your ground for a moment; I shall give it to you."
"Way! The Master suddenly overturned the incense table and left. Xiu called out loudly, "Bring me the staff! The Master responded from afar, "The sword has long since departed.
The next day, Xiu ascended the hall. As the Rector was about to strike the gavel, the Master shouted to stop him, saying, "Wait until I have finished my discourse, then strike the gavel.
He then asked: "In the Great Tang of old, there were no Chan masters; but now..."
"Is there anyone else in the monastery? Xiu raised his staff, made a gesture as if to strike, and said, "Look at this stick! The Master then gave a shout; Xiu also shouted.
The Master shouted once more, turned around, and said, "It is not that this wild child has much spirit; it is simply because he has already passed through the highest barrier.
He then departed. Xiu gave a shout; the Master also shouted. From afar, he heard the rector striking the gavel again. The Master—
Then, raising his voice, he said: "Alas for the breath of death! [He then ascended the hall for the *bào'ēn* (repaying kindness) assembly. Holding up his staff, he said:
"A wondrous and extraordinary cause-and-condition must be brought forth by an extraordinary person. A sentence that startles the multitude must be proclaimed at a place that startles the multitude.
Today, having encountered an extraordinary person and an extraordinary occasion, this is truly a place that startles the multitude. But tell me, what is this sentence that startles the multitude?"
The Master raised his staff and called out to the great assembly, saying: "The Great Stone Buddha of Wuzhong shows the assembly.
He then cited the karmic conditions concerning how Daowu always carried a wooden sword, saying: "Barking at the sky and chasing clods of earth—Han Lu the hound has bitten into it.
This fellow, half-awake and half-drunk, will ultimately not escape rolling in the grass with everyone else. Had Daowu, as soon as this monk was about to take up his sword, simply kicked him once—"
He kicked it over. Had he known his error, not only would it have caused him to suddenly change his skin and fur, but he himself would have been upright from head to tail;
how could one fail to show him the fodder of his own true portion? The wooden sword has ended up as nothing more than a toy. Addressing the assembly:

To penetrate and escape the final barrier—Yun’an was right to scold for that. To thoroughly understand the fundamental principles of the successive patriarchs—Miaoxi still rebuked for that. You all...
People who aspire to this Dharma-gate must be extremely careful. "The water in the front stream is swift, so the fish move with difficulty;
the wind on the rear ridge is high, so the birds find it hard to perch. Addressing the assembly, he cited the karmic conditions regarding the birth-pangs of Aṅgulimāla, saying:
"Tell me, what principle is contained in these two words of the World-Honored One? How can they be so efficacious as to save a family?"
Regarding the difficulty of childbirth: [The Master] suddenly lets out a shout and says, "Do not dream! For all of you, I shall provide a parable.
It is just like someone coming to buy ginger, yet the World-Honored One gives them a large handful of ginseng. At that time, they take it away and treat it as if it were ginger;
this brings trouble upon others who bite and chew it wildly, swallowing it so they cannot spit it out, and even when they try to spit it out..."
"You cannot swallow it. If anyone here can emerge without chewing it up, I will give them thirty blows of my staff.
Why? Because the World-Honored One lost his capital that year; today, I am giving him a profitable return.
Addressing the assembly, he raised the case of Chan Master Cizun of Dacheng in Tangzhou, who said while ascending the hall: "Those who come up have not asked; those who go down..."

Furthermore, he did not doubt it, nor did he know whether it was so or not. That it is thus is truly marvelous. The Master said: "At that time, the immeasurable multitude all attained the Way at once.
A monk asked about the story of Jiupeng looking after the Head Seat. The Master said: "The wealthy man laments that a thousand mouths are too few;
the poor man regrets that a single body is too many. A monk knocked on the door and presented a verse. The Master said: "You cannot even enter through your own gate."
"How do you present your verse? The monk replied, "I have already presented my verse. The Master did not open the door; the monk stood for a long time, feeling abashed, and withdrew.
A monk asked, "I am unclear about birth and death. The Master said, "Do not speak nonsense. The monk replied, "I beg the Master for instruction.
The Master said, "Do not engage in deluded thoughts. A monk asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the environment'?"
The Master said, “Within the red gate-bar at the front of Hongwu Gate. The student asked, “What is ‘seizing the environment but not seizing the person’?

As for the final phrase, what is it? The Master then gave a shout. A monk asked, "What is having a staff?"
The Master gave him the staff. The Master said, "The wind and moon of Chang'an penetrate both past and present; which child walks along groping the wall?
The monk asked further, "What is 'giving the staff to one who has no staff,' and how does one take away the staff from one who has it?
The Master said, "How many people starve to death right beside their own rice baskets? [The monk] asked, "What is 'having the staff' and giving the staff? The Master said:

The Master said, "Of the hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, none could find a way.

[The Master] said, "This has terrified me! He asked the Hall Attendant, "How many Bodhidharma eyes are there inside this rice bucket?
The attendant was at a loss for words. He then asked the Kitchen Head, "Do the Buddhas of the three periods of time truly preach the Dharma within the flames?"
The monk was at a complete loss for words. The Master pointed to a monk standing nearby and said, "Only this monk can answer the question. He then returned to his quarters.
The Master asked a monk, "What is it like when the trees are stripped bare and the leaves have fallen? The monk stepped forward and said, "Not separated by so much as a single hair's breadth.

Sheng. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said, "A hunter pursues the deer in the forest;

Sheng was the Elder Yue-shan. He also recounted the history of the mountain. The Master said, "Jia Dao has a poem for you. The scholar asked, "What does the poem say? The Master said:

At the head of the stream, he eats his daily meal with the descendants of kings; at the parting ways, he utters "Dudud," filled with great alarm. The old woman with her white eyes acts with such vigor;

[The Master] said, "I wish that my descendants may see one another well for generations. Yao Ju bowed in prostration.

Chan Master Zhitong of Ciluo Mountain on Mount Nanyue was the son of the Li family from Tongzhou in the region of Hanguang.

When he was a child, his father met a physiognomist who said, "The skeletal structure of this son of yours is too ethereal; his years will likely not be long. Thereupon, the father relinquished him to the monastic life. At first...

He went to visit Master Wuzu from Jinsu Temple, who upon first seeing him asked, "When the guests have dispersed and the hall is empty, what is it like? Wuzu said, "What kind of occasion is this? The Master then gave a shout.
Wuzu struck him. The Master shouted again. Wuzu struck him again. The Master prostrated and said, "From today onward, I shall rise and move together with you."
Shang went up to Qingshan to attend Master Xiushan. He asked, "In the past I heard of your reputation; today I meet you face-to-face.
Regarding this one phrase of meeting face-to-face, I ask the Master to grant me its transmission. Xiushan said, "Try saying it yourself. The Master then bowed.
Xiushan said, "That still does not suffice. The Master turned around and departed. One day, Xiushan asked, "It is just like when Baizhang [responded] to Mazu’s shout."
[Zhao] asked, "What did he get? The Master said, "If there were something gained, that would be a failure to do justice to Mazu.
Xiu said, "He said, 'For three days his ears were deaf'—what does that mean? The Master said, "I cannot allow you to continue with the understanding of a wild fox spirit.
Xiu then ceased questioning. One day, Xiu asked, "An ancient said, 'There is a phrase; there is no phrase. How should one understand this? The Master said, "A rock."
"Long-rooted weeds grow; the mountain hides the unmoving clouds. Xiu said, "It is like a vine leaning against a tree, isn't it? The Master said, "I have always been earnest about this.
Xiu said, "When the tree falls and the vine withers, what then? The Master lowered his head and left the abbot’s quarters.
One day, Xiu raised the four types of "concealing the point" (zangfeng) and asked, "What is 'concealing the point within'? The Master said, "The Liang [Dynasty]."
The Emperor said, "I do not understand the Way of the Palace. What is 'concealing the point within the event'? The Master replied, "Today the rain falls, and the steps before the hall are wet.
The Emperor asked, "What is 'concealing the point in both principle and event'? The Master replied, "Walking, one does not leave the door; sitting, one does not occupy the hall."
"What is it like when both principle and phenomenon are not involved, and the point is kept hidden? The Master said, "An octagonal millstone rolls through the void.
Xiu said, "These four turning words can carry on the legacy of the former awakened ones. Nevertheless, they are still a jumble of seven and eight.

Li Sili Huang Duanbo invited the Master to reside at the ancestral temple of Dongming. The Master said, "I have heard that you, Layman, had an awakening at Kaixian. You have toppled [the old barriers]."
The Layman asked, "Is Mount Lu there? The Master said, "Do you see Mount Lu? The Layman said, "Wait until I have helped it up.
The Master said, "An adept, an adept! The Layman then withdrew. After a short while, the Layman asked the Great Master, "Where have you been staying all this time?
The Master said, "Layman, tell me where I am staying right now. The Layman—
[The Master] said, "One cannot exit this gate. The Master asked, "Layman, can you exit this gate? The Layman hesitated. The Master said, "In fact, it is you, Layman, who cannot exit this gate.

[Later,] while ascending the hall, he raised the case of Cuiyan Zhen Dianxiong, who used to revile Yunju Shun Laofu for preaching the "Wordless Zen" (wuzi chan). Shun thereupon composed a verse which says: Yunju does not understand.
"Zen. Washing one's feet and going up to bed to sleep. The winter melon is straight and blunt; the gourd is curved and bent. The Master said, "I, this mountain monk, also have a verse:
'East Ming does not understand Zen; he has lived in these remote mountains for many years. In the morning he cooks white congee; the firewood produces smoke that fills the hearth.
Now tell me, is this the same as the ancients, or is it different? [He] resided at Lùluó and ascended the hall. Mountain...
Monks, here we do not discuss the mysterious, nor the subtle, nor Chan, nor the Way.
We only require that you break through the mind of birth and death. If this mind of birth and death is not broken, you are right before Old Man Yama.
The Public Notice for Consuming Iron Sticks. Therefore it is said: "Investigation must be real investigation; awakening must be real awakening. King Yama does not fear much talk;
do not trouble yourselves by standing for long. Be careful. While staying at Nanyuan, he addressed the assembly:
"In all quarters there is the Zen of mysterious subtlety, the Zen of nature and principle, the Zen of fine detail, the Zen of daily progress, and the Zen of resting."
Cease this "Chan. There is the Great Dharma Chan and the Small Dharma Chan; these are for people to deliberate upon and for people to chew over.

In my own place, there is none of such manifold Chan. I have only a single blunt iron hoe left to me by our distant ancestor, the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang, which I require everyone to use every day.
If you can use it until it is thoroughly mastered, and when you reach the point where [effort] is exhausted—
Forget yourself; let the hand forget the mind. Before your eyes, there is no field to be opened; beneath your feet, there is no ground to stand upon.
Suddenly, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are overturned by the hoe and shattered into a hundred fragments, revealing the two eyes of the person right here and now.
"O Assembly, at this very moment, in whose hands does the handle lie? He suddenly hurls down his staff and says: "Right here!"
Yang held it up for everyone to see. A monk asked, "When one who has died the great death returns to life, what is it like?
The Master said, "Call him here and let him wash the mountain monk’s feet. "How is it when the student turns his body?
The Master said, "Quickly prostrate three times. "What is the student’s intimate phrase? The Master said, "Take this clearly to heart. A monk asked, "The ancients..."
[The Master] said: "When meeting people three thousand *li* away, I do not know what kind of person I am meeting. The Master said: "It is no one else.
In the *wuyin* year of the Chongzhen era, the Master ascended Mount Nanyue and, admiring the excellence of Mount Zhurong, stayed beneath Peak Zhibo and built a thatched hut to dwell.
It was, in fact, a tiger’s den, yet he paid it no mind. When King Guilin heard of this, he marveled at him and went in person to inquire.

The King sent palace attendants to escort him, with no break in the procession along the road, wishing to welcome him into the palace. Bodhidharma firmly declined, refusing to comply, and would simply depart in secret.

The King was displeased; he burned the hermitage and made a vow before a pomegranate tree in front of it, saying, "If this monk from the South truly possesses the Way, let this tree bear fruit in winter.
Before long, the tree blossomed and bore fruit. Thereupon, the King’s respect increased all the more.
Xìn visited the place where the Master had planted his staff and, humbling himself, traveled three hundred *li* on foot to see him. He further built a hermitage for him and provided offerings.
In the spring of the Jiǎshēn year, bandits ravaged the Three Chǔ regions, and food became scarce in the mountains.

To stave off hunger, he gathered wild *wéi* roots, but mistook them for wild celery; two people who ate with him both sought remedies to counteract it. The Master said, "Why must you do this? and then [ate it].
Shi (successor to Tianyinxiu).
Yangshan Songji Yinzhongshou Chanshi was the son of the Yan family of Wucheng. At the age of seventeen, he left the household life at Daochang Mountain.
Master Xiu showed him the "Puppy" koan (*wugouzi*), and after investigating it with great effort for a long time, one day he heard [the sound of] someone painting eyebrows.

Shengda attained great enlightenment and subsequently received the Dharma. He succeeded [his master] on the seat at Qing Shan. Ascending the hall, he said: "The gate faces a thousand peaks; a clear stream flows along a secluded path.

If you seek further for the profound and mysterious meaning, it is like stirring the ashes to search for bubbles. Thereupon he descended from the seat. The Master was by nature inclined toward quietude and withdrawal.
Because his responses were so intricate, he departed shortly thereafter and lived in deep seclusion at Yangshan in Suzhou.
A monk asked, "What is the place where you, Master, have attained awakening? The Master said, "One cannot deceive others. The monk asked again, "What is the place from which all Buddhas emerge?"

The Master said: "A magpie crows at the corner of the hall. Regarding the karmic occasion where a monk asked Xuefeng to ascend the seat and rolled out a wooden ball, and Xuansha seized it and placed it back in its original position, the Master said:
"Yangshan would have no objection to rolling it again," and he immediately entered the abbot’s quarters.
Regarding the public case of Zhaozhou’s question, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? to which Zhaozhou replied, "No," the Master said: "Zhaozhou..."
This "no-word" of the State—ten people, five pairs—are all caught in doubt. Piteous indeed, their own lives are devoid of understanding; they still seek what is not right from the side of a dog.
The Verse on the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials says: The First Mystery: A clay ox treads through the water, and the heavens overflow.
A thousand stars and ten thousand constellations are all thrown into chaos at once. With clear eyes, how can one distinguish the orthodox from the biased? The Second [Mystery]...
Xuan. The blazing sun crosses the stream, white as a spring. Laughing at those who climb trees to catch fish, he pays no heed as they rush to set their traps.
Third Xuan: Sitting and watching the void as it carries an iron boat, one need not inquire about the ferries of north, south, east, or west;
it sends forth the wind while still being pulled by a lotus fiber. First Yao: The crescent moon of the night shines upon the face of the stone woman, a private affection. Not...
It resembles an ordinary countenance. Second, one requires the roar of the dragon and the howl of the tiger; it startles the child within the dream, causing him to repeatedly call for his mother.
Third, there must be a single tune of non-arising; were it not for a true connoisseur, who could recognize its subtle wonder?
The summary verse says: "The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are the barriers of the Patriarchs; Limitless Zen practitioners find it difficult to reach them.

If you ultimately ask me for the meaning of these mysteries and essentials, The clear stream flows with a murmuring sound from Qingxi. The Master lived in a deep and secluded mountain retreat, so those who sought the Way rarely had the chance to see him.
After Attendant Ze took away his robe and whisk, he would no longer admit even a single person. Throughout the land...
Gaozhi (the successor of Tianyin Xiu; the five aforementioned masters).
Chan Master Yunfeng Hengshi Jun of Jianning, Fujian, was the son of the Pan family of Qiantang. He traveled extensively throughout all quarters.

Whenever there were those with whom he shared a long-standing affinity, he would ultimately not accept their invitations. He later visited Fofu Fang, from whom he profoundly attained the subtle instructions of the Dongshan lineage.
Fang was on friendly terms with Yuanhu Yong; as Yong suffered from many ailments in his later years, he worried that he would have no successor.
Fang, following the precedent set by Daowu and Jiaoshan, directed the Master to attend upon Yong at Puming. There, the Master’s realization became thoroughly penetrating and perfectly constant.

The thirty-fifth generation descendant of the Sixth Patriarch in the Cao-Dong school was Chan Master Fangan Cizhou of Beijing Dajue Temple, whose courtesy name was Qingliang. He was a native of Tang County and belonged to the Yang clan.
At the age of ten, he made a firm vow to leave the household life. He went to the Elder Guangde Daci of Jintai to receive the tonsure.
Reflecting that the matter of birth and death was of great importance, he received full ordination and traveled to various regions to study.

Initially, he frequented lecture halls to extensively investigate the fundamental principles of the Xing (Nature) and Xiang (Characteristics) schools under the guidance of the Dharma Masters Xian and Li, serving as their chanting master. Upon reaching the section on the "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Locations" in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he suddenly realized that all things arise through conditions and lack inherent reality.

Cánjìng Jiāojiào Āogǔ Miàoyín Chánshī was the son of the Máo family of Hándàn. From birth he possessed extraordinary features, appearing exactly like a monk from India.
His parents knew he was no ordinary person of the secular world, so they sent him to Dùjiā Ān in his native district to receive the tonsure.
One day, while looking at Tiantong’s verse on the occasion concerning Linji and Sansheng—“The Eye of the True Dharma must not be extinguished”—it was said:

Chan Master Wuming Huijing of Huanglong Shouchang in Jianchang was the son of the Pei family of Chongren in Fuzhou.

He was tall in stature and possessed an ancient, dignified air. At the age of nine, he entered a local schoolhouse and immediately asked, "What is this 'vast and unyielding breath' (*hao-ran zhi qi*)?

The schoolmaster marveled at his precocity. Later, he followed Master Zhong of Lingshan to renounce the household life. He constantly harbored doubts regarding the four-line verse of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, feeling certain that it must have a definitive basis.
By chance, he encountered a verse by Master Fu Dashi which read: "If one discusses the four-line verse, It should not be separate from the body."
Suddenly feeling a sense of liberation, he took his leave of Lingshan and went into seclusion on Mount Emei. Once, while ascending the summit and gazing about, he composed a verse:
"Having stepped upon the first peak above the clouds, The vast expanse before my eyes is but a small void. At that time, I wished to see [you], yet had no way to meet;
