One night, while conversing with Fo-jue and Huidang, the Master was then twelve years old and stood attending them by their seats. Furi said, "I, this mountain monk..."
Coming from the south, he carried his staff such that it did not even brush against a single person who understood the Buddha-dharma.
The Master [Yunmen] joined his palms and stepped forward, saying, "This is simply because your staff, Reverend, is too short. Yunmen was greatly startled and said, "I beg you to accept this man;
let him continue my Linji lineage. The Master replied, "How could there be two—Yunmen and Linji? Yunmen praised him incessantly. [The Record of] Jinshi.
The Emperor went to the Hall of the Auspicious Image of Sheng’an and asked the Master, “Is it right to prostrate? Or is it not right to prostrate?
The Master replied, “To prostrate is to show mutual respect and honor; not to prostrate is for each person to claim their own dignity. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
After receiving the Dharma, he resided at Yansheng Monastery and addressed the assembly, citing Dongshan: “At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, brothers may go east or west. Directly...

"One must go to a place ten thousand *li* wide where there is not a single blade of grass. He asked again, "But as for that place ten thousand *li* wide where there is not a single blade of grass—how does one go there?
Shishuang said, "Stepping out the door, it is already grass. Dayang said, "Even to say directly that one does not step out the door, it is still a vast expanse of grass.
The Master said, "Now tell me, what is the phrase beneath the feet of you all right now?"
"If you say that on the Way there is not a blade of grass, I allow you to have seen Dongshan. If you say that as soon as one steps out the door it is grass, I allow you to have seen Shishuang.
If you say that even when one does not step out the door, it is still a vast expanse of grass, I allow you to have seen Dayang.
If you cannot say any of these, I allow you to have seen Yansheng. Why? Because there is only the fine breeze."
As he came to the banquet, there was no idle talk regarding the human world.

Emperor Gyeongjong of the Goryeo Dynasty sent an imperial messenger with a sheet of paper inscribed with the two characters "Heart-Buddha" (心佛) and asked Master Hyon-woo Yum, the State Preceptor, "What characters are these? At that moment, Won-tong was seated in the assembly and replied instantly.
He replied, "It is not the mind; it is not the Buddha. This pleased the Emperor. On the following day, the Emperor bestowed upon him a long-short poem (chángduànshǒu) which said:

"If one can only achieve purity, what need is there to inquire about the causes and conditions of the myriad dharmas? In daily life, remain non-active; throughout the twelve hours of the day, harbor no further doubts.

One must always maintain self-mastery; recognize that from the beginning there has been nothing to obstruct. Buddha after Buddha, mind after mind—if a Buddha relies on the mind, even that is but dust."
The Master replied in thanks: "Non-action and non-effort—yet to cling to non-action is still bondage. Illumination and function are simultaneous;
even 'swift as a flash of lightning or a falling star' is already too late. Neither mind nor Buddha—yet to call it 'neither mind' is still the Buddha.
When both person and environment are empty, the myriad phenomena are contained within a single realm."

The lay practitioner Zhao Wenru of Mount Huang was a disciple who entered the inner chamber of Yuantong. After receiving his formal prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), he often composed this verse:
"Delusive thoughts are originally nothing other than reality; To try to eliminate them is to raise yet another layer of dust.
In speech and thought, movement and stillness—who provides the power? If one looks closely, there is no one else."
When Master Ding of Gaoyou first visited Master Xuanwu, the Master posed a question from the records:
"A monk asked Xuansha, 'What is the pure Dharma-body? Xuansha replied, 'Dripping pus. At these words, the Master attained realization.
Later, a monk asked, "What does the golden fish that has passed through the net eat? The Master replied, "Dry dung."
Chan Master Taichu of Mount Gui was styled Ziyu. A native of Wenling, his family had been Confucian scholars for generations. The Master was unconventional and possessed great ambition;
his poetry and prose were all extraordinary, earning him the high esteem of many scholar-officials. One day, he abruptly abandoned his worldly life.
He chose the path of Buddhahood through the Most Victorious [Dharma] and disciplined himself according to the Vinaya, completely abandoning the habits of worldly extravagance.

After traveling beyond the mountain ranges to visit various monasteries, he gained a great reputation. After some time, he ceased his travels and returned to Min. At that time, the seat at Baon Monastery in Nanjian was vacant;
the Prefect, Chen Fu, having heard of the Master’s fame, appointed him to lead it. Not long after, Zhen Dexiu, the Layman of West Mountain, invited the Master to preside over Dayue Monastery.
For over twenty years, he attended upon ten thousand disciples daily. The Master’s exposition of the Dharma was versatile, profound, and vast, not yielding to the ancient patriarchs.
Once the Western Mountain [Master] retired from official service, he frequently visited the Master and discussed the Way at leisure; there were none who did not become intoxicated with admiration.
For the most part, the Master received others with sincerity and simplicity, and thus he was held in high esteem by scholars of all ranks.
Chan Master Zhongguan Zhao was the preceptor under whom Haiyun Yinjian received his training. He constantly instructed Haiyun, saying:
"What you desire is merely words and language; from now on, cease them all and cause your body and mind to undergo a great death."
"Do not retain any residual energy. When that time arrives, you must have a sudden moment of self-reflection; only then will you be able to meet with me.
Later, he was captured by the Yuan troops along with Haiyun and escorted north to Shuofang. The Emperor of the Yuan dynasty conferred upon him the title of Master Ciyun Zhengjue.
When the Master was about to pass away, the immortal Yang Zhishen requested a verse, and the Master commanded him:
The attendant who was recording the words wrote a verse, saying: "Seventy-three years have passed like a flash of lightning; As you depart, I shall open a single thread for you.
A clay ox flies across the sea from the east, Seeking it in heaven or among men, one finds it not. The guest asked, "When will the Master depart?"
The Master said, "Three days later. This was the twenty-seventh day of the fifth month; on the first day of the sixth month, he indeed passed away without illness.
Chan Master Xuefeng Qiaoyin Wuyi was the son of the Nie family of Huai'an. He repeatedly sought instruction from renowned elders before finally attaining the Dharma.
Regarding Chan Master Fohai of Xuefeng: the provincial governor appointed him to reside at Xuefeng for seven years, after which he retired to the Western Hermitage.

In the second year of the Huangqing era, he was again summoned by imperial decree to reside there; he was granted the title "Fozhi" (Buddha-Wisdom) and remained for six years before declining the position.
In the second year of the Taiding era, he again received an imperial decree to resume his former seat; he remained there for another seven years.

During his three tenures at Xuefeng, the Master restored all that had fallen into ruin, creating a great and flourishing event for the Dharma gate. He once composed a preface to the *Xuefeng Lu*, in which he wrote:

"After Old Zhenjue’s 'single blow from Deshan' caused the bottom of the bucket to fall away, he attained a state where the moon was cold over the fisherman's shop and the snow cleared atop Elephant Peak. He grasped...
A single ladle of *amṛta* (the finest essence) reveals its great function through three balls; it is like the thundering of ten billion peals of lightning beneath the four heavens.
For several hundred generations, the true sound has grown ever more magnificent. All that was bestowed as instruction flowed from his breast, covering heaven and earth.
Once the single performance of the *Gao-ling* melody on the small strings has been played, the vulgar tunes of the *Xia-li* can no longer be heard. —The second year of the Yuantong era.
He entered nirvana. His stupa was erected beside the Fohai Stupa.
Later, when the Great Master Yuanfan Huihong of the Tiele Monastery on Mount Wutai was reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the passage: "When one person gives rise to the true [mind]..."
Shifang Xiaoyin suddenly attained awakening. He then went to see Chan Master Wen of Heshuo and presented his realization to him;

Wen approved it. His verse at the time of death read: "Sixty years of springtime, plus eight more years; The floating clouds have cleared away, revealing the blue sky. As I depart, I kick over Mount Sumeru;
In the night that follows, the moon atop the mountain is perfectly full. He changed his robes and passed away while sitting upright.
Chan Master Huikong Yuemo of Jiangshan in Jianning was the son of the Su family of Gutian. He practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and those far and near took refuge in him with devotion.
One day, while wandering through Jiangshan in a state of samādhi, he arrived at the site of the former Chan Master Xuangiang’s practice hall.
An old man came forward to greet him, saying, "I have guarded this mountain for five hundred years. Having finished speaking, he transformed into a black dragon and departed.
He departed. Upon waking, he said, "I shall return to this mountain. He then went to his thatched hut. One day he told the assembly, "My work for the sake of others is now complete;
I shall enter parinirvāṇa immediately. He further spoke a verse: "For over forty years I have dwelt amidst the dust of the mundane world;
Now, at last, I manifest the Honored One within this very midst. A night wind has risen from the east on Yantou Peak, Blowing the flowers open until they fill the air."
The Spring Tree; an iron boat with neither rudder nor sail. It is steered into the sea of the nature-lotus.
This final mechanism is now revealed: white clouds never depart from the vast sky. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are surveyed until no trace remains;
empty space is shattered to see the ultimate point. Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon one’s head, the perfect luminosity of one's original nature is never lost.
He spoke again: "The third patriarch of the Western Heaven, the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, dwelt on Mount Gajaśaila and manifested the Dragon’s Agility Samādhi (*nāga-vikrīḍita-samādhi*).
There he preached the Dharma to subdue the various non-Buddhists, and subsequently transformed himself into fire and incinerated his own body.
I shall now go before the Elephant Trunk Rock and act in the same manner. He then entered the Dragon’s Agility Samādhi; at that moment, clouds and mist rose up from all sides, and thunder—
A heavy rain fell, followed by a transformation into fire that consumed him from within. The assembly gathered his sacred remains and enshrined them in a stupa to the west of the hermitage.
Chan Master Daowu of Puzhao Foguang Temple in Zhengzhou was the son of the Kou family of Lanzhou. Once, while staying overnight at Wanzi Inn, he encountered this event.
Hearing the neighing of a horse, he attained sudden and great enlightenment. Returning home, he told his mother, "I picked up something on the road. His mother asked, "What thing?
The Master replied, "Something I have not seen since beginningless time. His mother struck him with her palm and said, "What joy is there in that?

Thereupon, he took leave of his mother to travel to various quarters. His mother asked, "Where will you go? The Master replied, "Water flowing must reach the sea; a crane emerges from atop the white clouds."

He went to visit Chan Master Baiyun Hai and subsequently received his seal of certification. In the twenty-fourth year of the Taiding era of the Yuan dynasty, he emerged to take charge of Puzhao Monastery.
Clad in white robes, riding a yellow calf, and blowing a short flute, he roamed through Luoyang. He once said:
"If you say I am an ordinary person, I have come from the rank of the sages. If you say I am a sage, I have gone back to the rank of the ordinary. If you say...
"Am I neither ordinary nor holy? he asked. He then retreated to the summit of Mount Vairocana, where he had a distinct place of practice. In the fifth year of the Taihe era, he entered nirvana.
At Lohan Temple on Mount Yan, the senior seat-holder Zheng was blind; yet his vision of the Way was clear and bright, and every morning he personally swept the grounds.
Someone asked, "Have you swept this patch of ground clean? Zuo held up a broom to show him.
The person asked again, "In the realm of true purity, there is originally not a single speck of dust; what is there to sweep? Zuo likewise held up the broom to show him.
He once composed a verse on Mount Jiuniu, which says: "For how many years have they lived in herds of four or five? Coming in spring and departing in autumn, they are well-fed."
Wind and smoke; though there is water in the clear stream, when have you ever drunk from it? Though the green fields are unplowed, you sleep forevermore.

Every single one has his heels planted firmly on the ground; every head and nostril reaches toward the heavens. You usually dwell atop a thousand peaks; when people of the great earth come, how can you lead them away?
Chan Master Seng’an Si of Lingyun in Wenzhou was a native of Ninghai in Taizhou. Of four brothers, he was the eldest. They all simultaneously resolved to leave the household life.
He distributed his grandfather’s inherited estate among his relatives and traveled extensively to visit various teachers throughout the land. Later, he emerged from seclusion at Lingyun;
there, for the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said: "The Great Perfect Enlightenment, the horns of oxen, and the horns of horses—these shall be my monastery."
[The Master] ascended the hall while carrying a melon basket and a vegetable basket. He raised the koan concerning Zhaozhou’s “The dog has no Buddha-nature” and offered this verse:
“The dog has no Buddha-nature; The dog has Buddha-nature. When the monkey worries, it pulls its head back; When the dog runs, it shakes its mouth.
In his later years, he retired to the front mountain of Lingyun. In the year Jia-shen of the Zhi Zheng era, Kongshi went together with several monks to pay their respects to him.
At that time, the Master was over ninety years old; with long, white eyebrows and hair, he stood tall and dignified as he stepped out wearing his sandals.
As he walked, he asked, "Where have you come from? Kongshi replied, "From the center of the river. The Master asked, "How many fathoms deep is it? Kongshi replied, [silently].
"You cannot deceive the Old Monk. The Master said, "Sit for a moment and drink some tea.
The layman Huang Min, courtesy name Jinqing, was a native of Yiwu in Wuzhou.

At the beginning of the Tianli era of the Yuan dynasty, an imperial decree summoned all monks and literati skilled in calligraphy throughout the empire to assemble at Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou to write the *Tripitaka* in gold ink.
The scholar was also included among them. Whenever he ate, he insisted on being in the company of the assembly of monks;

if separate preparations were made for him, he was displeased, even to the point of reviling those who served him, refusing to eat, and departing. Once, he inscribed a poem on a hanging cliff in the style of orchids in ink, saying:
"Fluttering in the spring breeze, all are blown alike; Resting upon a high place, what can one possibly do? Let others harbor their own inverted thoughts; One must see the precipice for oneself."
At the moment of letting go, he inscribed a eulogy for the portrait of Dongpo, saying: "The Fifth Patriarch, a man beyond the world, Has long since severed the causes of birth in this Sahā world.
Who could possibly depict with a hand that sketches empty space? Go and behold his body beyond bodies in years to come.
He inscribed a eulogy for the portrait of Huang Shanggu, saying: "I laugh at old Huìtáng of those days; When they met, he bluntly said, 'The fragrance of the osmanthus. Unfurling the scroll..."
His face and features remain exactly as they were; how could his nostrils ever have been long or short?
Master Yangbei’s surname was Jiang. It is unknown where he was from. At the age of fifteen, he had read through the classics and histories;

his speech was concise and profound. With disheveled hair and a soiled face, his conduct was unrestrained. At the beginning of the Zhizheng era, he arrived at the family estate of the Shen clan in Songjiang.
He often inscribed this poem: "Ten thousand purples and a thousand reds are all but spring; What need is there to use flowery words to ask the Lord of the East?
A mute man has a dream—whom can he tell it to? Raising an empty fist, he points at the white clouds. He also said:
"Neither leaning nor biased, one stands in the center; Not clinging to the West, not clinging to the East. Transcending the realms of East, West, South, and North, Upon the tip of a single hair..."

He "hooked the Azure Dragon. One day he said to the assembly of monks, "My work of transformation is nearly exhausted. You all must exert yourselves. As soon as he finished speaking, his physical form was cast off.
The attendant Chang of Xuedou during the Fenghua era was not versed in literary texts but specialized exclusively in the practice of dhyāna; his peers called him "Chang."
Dharma said: "The verses he composed are perfectly integrated in both principle and phenomenon, and their prosody is harmonious and flowing. His verse on the Iron Ox says:
'Rolled out from within the hundred-fold smelting furnace, Its horns and head are towering, its body free of dust.
Struck, it does not move; pulled, it will not budge; This time, it truly shall not enter a womb. His verse on the Sea Gate says: 'The winds of karma blow up waves like mountains...'"
The Mountain: How many fishermen find it difficult to set foot there? Only by risking one’s life and casting away the body can one force one’s way in;
only then does one know that the jade door has never been closed. A verse on bitter bamboo shoots: Purple robes stripped away, white as silver;
Twisting one’s body within the boiling cauldron. Those who have endured such bitterness will not believe this; But when chewed upon at ease, the flavor is entirely true. —Also by Xian’an.
The verse says: At the top of a hundred-foot pole, cease asking for the way; on a solitary peak, at its very summit, nourish a life of leisure.
Although the dilapidated hut lacks any covering, it is difficult to explain one’s private possessions to others.
Lady Ding of Haotou in Huangyan, Taizhou, whose Dharma name was Juezhen and whose style name was Zhuxin, first encountered Juetian while tilling fields on Mount Weiuyu.
Upon attaining realization, she abandoned her home and built a dwelling for herself.
She then went to consult Yongquan Guyu, who asked, "Why does a daughter of a noble family run hither and thither? Lady Ding replied, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master."
Shangquan said, "There is no room for you here. An then clapped his hands once and said, "That which has been used for thirty years has been caught out this very day.
Quan then withdrew. Later, he went to visit Wuji at the Chunyu Hermitage on Mount Yan.
As soon as he entered the gate, he said, "The spring rain is like a balm; travelers loathe its mud. Wuji said, "Not so, not so."
As An was about to offer some words of greeting, he was shouted out by Baizhang. In his later years, An established a reception hall beside Mingyin Temple in the town.
A monk entered his quarters directly with his pack and hat; An asked, "What is that? The monk replied, "I am a wandering monk.
An suddenly pointed to the monk's feet and said, "Your straw sandals' strings are broken; why do you not know this? The monk was speechless. An then took the pack.
Dropping his straw rain hat out [the door], he said, "In this place, there is no footing for you. One day, Chan Master Mingyin Kui went to pay his respects.
An said, "I have heard it said that you, Elder, fathered a son last night—is this true? Ming said, "But tell me, is it a boy or a girl?
An said, "A rooster runs off with a lamp; a turtle bites a fishing rod."
Qingyuan Yuwang Mian, the Attendant, saw off a fellow monk traveling to Tiantai and Yandang with this verse:
"When Niaoke blew on the cloth-hair, The attendant was enlightened at once. Though it did not involve verbal explanation, It had already become a public proclamation.
Clouds atop the ridges of Tiantai, Trees within the mountains of Yandang— As you go forth, deliberate well; Do not offend the taboo that stands before you. His verse for the end of life says:

Birth is fundamentally non-birth; death is likewise not death. When Baima held up his staff and Jueyi raised a finger, the hair-puller Zhang Dedao—a man from Xiashui in Jinyi—once encountered heavy snow.
A novice monk had formed a Buddha image out of the snow, and everyone composed verses to praise it. Dedao followed suit with this verse: "A single flower is held aloft."
The Tathāgata’s sixfold emergence: his round, smiling face opens wide. Recognizing that the skull is originally water, he did not enter the womb in Māyā’s palace.
Yongfu Lingjiang Haoshou served under Gulin at Yongfu in Raozhou; he occupied the position of the First Seat and established...
In summer, Xiang held the whisk. A monk asked, "What is it like when taking a step forward? The Master said, "Bumping into walls and crashing into barriers.

The monk asked, "What is it like when taking a step back? The Master said, "Falling into pits and dropping into ditches. The monk asked, "What is it like when neither advancing nor retreating? The Master said:

As for the late Senior Seat Master Tien-li Lao-su, throughout his life there was one profound and hidden barrier that few were able to recognize. A monk obtained three verses on "Expressing My Feelings While Dwelling in the Mountains" which he had written:
"Having finished reading the *Transmission of the Lamp*, my hair has already turned white; yet in the pursuit of merit and achievement, we still compete over a few [strokes of the brush]."
Lakṣa. Having risen from my midday nap, dust covers the desk; half a eave of slanting sun sets upon the courtyard flowers.

This pointed-roofed hut is not built too low; above it are long forests, below it lies a pond. Through the long night, startled winds sweep across yellow leaves, just like when the rain falls beneath a thicket of reeds.
The light of this floating world is naturally short; I compose these verses merely to respond to the passing years.
This morning, I was beneath the tall pines; facing the west wind, I watched a flock of crows in flight.
Yuan’an Huì, the Abbot of the Zang Hall at Jingci Monastery, a native of Lin’an, composed a verse for the Nirvana Hall, which says: "The single path to nirvana has been overturned;
The practice of every moment is not difficult to see. While washing one’s face, one suddenly touches the nose; The eye of the embroidered needle."
Lihao Zangshan. The Chan Master Kaian of Tiantu Mountain in Hangzhou was a native of Suzhou. By nature he was quick-witted and proficient in both Buddhist and secular classics.
He was a close friend of Pingshi Di and dwelt among the cliffs and valleys, avoiding contact with the world. There was only [the monk] Hong... at the foot of the mountain.

He was the son of the Hong family. Members of the family would frequently come and go to provide offerings for him. One night, the wife of the Hong family dreamed that the Master arrived at her residence riding in a palanquin.

Upon waking, she gave birth to a son. The following morning, she went up the mountain to await him; indeed, he had already passed away. Consequently, the child was named Yingkui (應魁) and styled Shiyuan (士元).
In his youth, he studied and entered the local school. He married and fathered a son. At the age of thirty, one day, he suddenly became resolute.
[He] reflected [upon this] and subsequently abandoned his home. He tied together thatched grass at the summit of the Eastern Peak and practiced the Way with diligent application day and night.
One day, Master Kōshitsu, while fleeing from bandits, passed by his hut on his way from Mount Jingshan.

Seeing that his deportment was serene and elegant and his responses were composed, he inquired into the reason for this; thus he came to know that he was the reincarnation of Yishan. Thereupon, he said to him: "Sir..."
In a previous life, you and Elder Master Pingshi were inseparable friends. This year, you are nearly ninety years old, yet your ears and eyes remain sharp and clear.
Why have you not sent word? Is it that you see one dream within two awakenings, such that the dream and the awakening are as one?
The Master joyfully took up his brush and composed a verse to send him, saying: "Send my greetings to the old man of Tiantong, Pingshi: A single thought is not of this present age."
Nor is it the past. One wishes to hear the midnight bell of Hanshan; the Wu River remains as ever, its waters merging with the azure sky.
Chan Master Juezhao Hui of Shouchang, Wenzhou, once sat out the summer retreat in the eastern latrine quarters of Jingci Monastery.

On the wall there was a water-and-ink image of the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara). The Master worshipped it morning and evening, his earnest prayers most fervent. One day, he suddenly beheld the Pure [Land]...

Water gushed from the wall into his flask; his entire body was filled with joy and clarity. From this point on, his wisdom and discernment grew daily more brilliant. He once composed a verse that said:
"Before my efforts have reached the ground of perfection, How many times have I leaned upon the railing in solitary grief? Today is the third day, tomorrow the fourth;
The snow and frost easily settle upon one's head."
The verse sent by Chief Seat Xuan’an Shi of Yuyang Monastery in Mingzhou to the Hermitage Master Wo-yun says: In the golden garden, horses gallop side by side;

A mere inch often provokes the suspicion of a drawn sword. When the moon shines upon a thousand trees of plum blossoms like snow, It is the moment one awakens from a dream upon the pillow of cloud-dwelling.
The verse by Zhuan’an, the former Head Seat at Tiantong in Mingzhou, for paying respects at the stupa of Ying’an: A slumbering tiger, its stripes glimpsed through a tube;
He took Mount Zhongfeng as his mountain to lean upon. Had he not possessed that single broken sand-pot, It would have been difficult even for his descendants to seek their livelihood.
The Xutang Yongchan of Muzhong at Tiantong in Mingzhou composed a verse on silkworms that says: "The mulberry trees are bare and the *zhè* trees are exhausted; only then does the mind find rest.

Through the diligent work of dense threads, a single cocoon is gathered. Even if one must enter the furnace coals and the boiling cauldrons, for the sake of others, it all depends upon that single strand."
The verse "Listening to the Rain" by Chanshi Fulong of Yixing says: The dripping from the eaves is most distinct;
Deluded sentient beings call it sound. I, too, have for many years followed after external things; On this spring night, a single pillow makes sleep difficult to attain.
The verse of the passing of the Senior Seat-holder Shou of Jiufeng in Ruizhou says:

"Seventy-two years, here and there, Eating the food of the ten directions, Studying the Chan of Bodhidharma. This morning, with one cast, I turn over and depart; My laughter shatters the half-smile of the onlookers."
Chan Master Wujin Zudeng of Yunfeng on Mount Tiantai was the son of the Wang family of Siming.
He went to Tianning Temple to study under Master Rixi Yong and asked, "The matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift; I beg you to grant me some instruction.

Rixi said, "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, investigate this closely and secretly. When you suddenly strike upon it, come back and ask again. The Master raised his voice and said, "There is none!"

"Always swift! The matter of birth and death is great. Before he had finished speaking, the Master gave a shout. The Master immediately prostrated himself. Xī said, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate yourself so?
The Master replied, "To open one's mouth is already an error. Xī nodded his head in approval. Thereupon, the Master departed to visit various teachers throughout the land.
He then sought out a place to plant his monk’s staff atop Yunfeng Peak, where his shadow never left the mountain for fifty years.

On the eighth day of the second month in the second year of the Hongwu era, he manifested a slight illness. When the night was nearly half over, he looked toward his attendants and asked, "Is the sky beginning to brighten? They replied, "Not yet."
Someone asked, "What would you say, Master, at such a time as this? The Master smiled and said, "Formerly, when Deshan was ill, a monk asked him, 'Is there anyone who does not fall ill?
Deshan replied, 'There is. The monk asked, 'Who is this one who does not fall ill? Deshan said, 'A-ya, a-ya.
After a long silence, the Master said, "Can such a thing be called being ill? The assembly remained silent. The Master said, "The physical body..."

"Impermanence! I have long sought realization; the time has come and I shall depart. When the attendant held out paper and requested a verse, the Master said, "I will certainly not leave without a verse;
would it not be improper to die [without one]? As the attendant's request grew increasingly insistent, he wrote:
"Birth and death, coming and going, Are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. Five Sumeru Mountains are toppled; Vast and open, there is neither back nor front. He then threw down his brush.
He passed away while seated.
Chan Master Jiefeng Ying of Mount Jing was a native of Jinhu. Initially serving as the Head Seat (Shouzuo) of Mount Jing, he returned to Ningbo.
Chushi Qi composed a verse to see him off, which said: "The first seat atop Lingxiao Peak; the Mahāyāna Dharma is all clearly penetrated."

He has completely transcended the hundred negations and the four propositions. "White snow and spring sunshine—dare anyone dare to harmonize with them? Ascending the hall, he said: "The conduct of a patch-robed monk is by no means ordinary.
Drawing the blade from its scabbard, it leaves nothing hidden. Seizing the food and driving the plow, the true command is fully exercised;

east and west, there is no longer any room for ghosts to divide the spoils. Furthermore, he spoke in verse: "In this peaceful world, the arms have been laid down. Yet one cannot help but register the young children."
How extraordinary! Casting a straight hook at a rapids on swift waters—had the scaled dragon not encountered it, his gaping would have been in vain.
He regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; one day, having finished the recitation, he passed away peacefully.
Chan Master Jing’an Zhuang of Mount Jingshan was a native of Taizhou. From childhood, he loathed the impurities of meat and wine and held the worldly dust of secular life in low esteem.

His parents allowed him to leave home at Guangci Hermitage. After some time, he traveled extensively to consult various masters of the Way until he thoroughly penetrated the source of the patriarchal lineage.

He served as abbot of two monasteries in the region of Yue; whenever things did not meet his expectations, he would immediately resign and depart. He subsequently went to rely upon Quanshi at Tianjie Monastery, where Quan placed him in charge.

He served as abbot twice. Not long after, he was appointed to Mount Jing. His spiritual influence flourished greatly. In the twelfth year of the Yongle era, he entered the capital by imperial decree to assist in the compilation of the Great Canon.

He resided at Tianjie Monastery for three years. Ministers such as Yao Gong, the Junior Tutor, submitted joint memorials recommending him to serve as the abbot, but he firmly declined and would not accept.
He returned to Mount Jing, where he passed away. His stupa was enshrined above the Small Pond on Water Ridge.
The senior monk Huainan You had long served in various monastic communities and was held in high esteem by his peers.

While staying at Tianwang Monastery in Dingzhou, he cultivated himself through the Way, remaining beyond the reach of intimacy or estrangement for others. After some time, he said to the assembly, "I am departing.
Some took this to be a jest; when pressed to provide a verse, he immediately sought out brush and paper and wrote in large characters: "Coming, I did not enter the gate; going—"
"Without leaving the door, he shattered the void; there was no longer any room for evasion. Clapping his hands and laughing 'he-he,' he said, 'Come back!
As the white clouds dispersed, the green mountains were revealed. Thereupon, he sat in *paryaṅka* and passed away. The attending monks hurriedly called out and shook him;

the Master opened his eyes again, raised his hand, and thanked them, saying, "Do not trouble yourselves further. Take good care of yourselves. At that time, the Prefectural Governor, Lord Su, was also present.
He went to pay his respects and, touching the master’s remains, remarked, "One may truly call him a monk who has brought his affairs to completion.
Chan Master Fumiao was a native of Kunming. He left the household life at Tianhua Temple and traveled to the capital in the sixteenth year of the Hongwu era.

He was granted a robe and alms bowl, and traveled with staff and mendicant’s bowl to Jingshan in Zhejiang. In the twelfth month of the fourth year of the Xuande era, he bathed, changed his robes, and wrote a verse, saying:
"Last year I was seventy-nine; this year I have reached eighty. Having traveled ten thousand *li* in search of the Way, my worldly ties are now at an end.
He cast aside his brush, sat upright, and passed away.

Chan Master Xueting of Xianlin in Hangzhou was the son of the Guì clan of Rénhé, Hangzhou. Having lost his father before the onset of puberty, he suffered from smallpox and a wind-disorder that left him with short-sightedness in both eyes;
consequently, he sought to leave the household life several times. He visited Xiūxiū at Xianlin, where they attained mutual accord upon their first meeting.
While reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he encountered a point of doubt regarding the passage: "Within a single hair-tip, a jeweled royal realm appears. Later, while at Qiánmíng in Jiāngyīn...
While at the temple, he suddenly beheld the Wanfo Ge (Ten Thousand Buddhas Pavilion), its golden and azure splendor towering before his very eyes; thereupon, he attained a profound realization.

Later, on New Year’s Eve, upon hearing the sound of the bell, he unconsciously shed the burdens of years of practice all at once. He spoke this verse: “The perfect resonance—the mind does not hear it.”
The great trichiliocosm is illuminated as one; he has brushed past the ultimate barrier and no longer harbors any notions of the profound or the mysterious.
The Master styled himself the "Hidden Man of Plum and Snow" and also called himself "Illusory Dweller. He once said: "Illusion is the trace of dwelling, and dwelling is the mark of illusion."
Illusion arises and rests upon non-existence; when resting is total, it is illusion. Illusion pursues and rests upon existence; when resting is total, it is non-existence.

When cataracts produce flowers before the eyes, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth appear; yet when the flowers do not arise from the cataracts, there is the true reality of emptiness. That illusion rests upon this—truly, it is but child’s play!
Chan Master Baiyun Mingxing of Mount Wugong in Jizhou was the son of the Zhang family from Changting in Min.

After shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. He suddenly sighed, saying, "If a great man has not yet accomplished the path of the Dharma, what can he do about birth and death?"
He then visited renowned masters everywhere until his spiritual affinity was established with one. He lived in seclusion at Mount Xiao for over twenty years.

When Governor Wang urged him to emerge from retreat and teach, the Master again moved deeper into the wilderness with his thatched hut. Disciples flocked to him, and it gradually became a formal monastery. One day, he took leave of the assembly, saying, "I am departing.
When the assembly asked where he was going, the Master presented this verse: "The bright moon falls into the heart of the waves; the white..."
"Clouds span across the ridges; if you wish to recognize the original mechanism, it is like an iron ox swallowing a great elephant. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at his home mountain.
Chan Master Jingshan Yuelin Jing of Hangzhou was a native of that province. From his youth, he was exceptionally gifted; he left home to become a monk at an early age.
He visited various renowned masters, who directed him to investigate the "original person. After a long time, he attained realization and composed this verse:
"The original person, the original person— Without a head and without a brain, how can one seek them? Suddenly, I grasp their nostrils; Look closely, and see what they originally are!"
The Commoner. Chan Master Yongning Guyuanqing of Jinling attained awakening upon hearing the crowing of a rooster. His verse says:
When the golden rooster crows to announce the dawn, Were it not for that sound, how could one know? The three thousandfold world is entirely like snow; It is mud at the bottom of the well.
Shewu Zhezhi (Snake Dance Zhazhi).
Funiu Wugai Mingli Chan Master was the son of He Shi of Fenzhou. He went to attend upon Master Songzhu Dafang and participated in the seven-day intensive retreat (*qijie*) with the assembly.
There, he uttered the line: "One sound shatters the void, revealing alone the King of Dharmas. Later, in the same month...
An Daoyuan entered Zhongnan Mountain. One day, while at the hermitage, An raised the koan concerning Gaofeng’s "silver mountains and iron walls.

The Master attained sudden enlightenment and composed a verse containing the lines: "When a single awakened mind arises, doubt vanishes; picking it up and letting it go, one is naturally carefree. He went to Fang to seek verification.
Fang said, "I do not ask about the seven-day retreat at Funiu; what is the meaning of this quiet chamber in Zhongnan? The Master—
Fang said, "At Fu-niu, we practiced the 'Seven Days' retreat; at Zhongnan, in a quiet hermitage, I emitted a great radiance.
Then I shouted, 'Where is this radiance right now? The Master stepped forward and gave me a slap. Fang laughed heartily and said, 'Just so! Just so!'"
Master Chanshi Zhu Hong, known as Yunqi Lianchi, was the son of the Shen family of Renhe County in Hangzhou. At the age of seventeen, he enrolled in the local prefectural school.
He would regularly write the four characters "The Matter of Birth and Death" (shēngsì shìdà) upon his desk. One day, by accident, he broke a tea bowl, which triggered a moment of awakening;
he recorded this realization in a poem titled "Seven Strokes of the Checkmark" (*qībǐgōu*). He then went to Mount Xishan to receive the tonsure under Master Xingtian and subsequently traveled north.
Sambyeon-yong later visited Sogwan at Ryugang to seek instruction. Sogwan said, "You have come from three thousand *li* away to receive instruction from me;
what instruction do I have to give? The Master was suddenly enlightened. He took his leave and returned home.

Passing through Dongchang, he heard the sound of the drum from the watchtower on the road and attained sudden awakening. He composed a verse: "The events of twenty years ago remain suspicious; Three thousand *li*..."
What is so strange about having an affair? Burning incense and throwing a halberd are but trivial matters; as for demons and Buddhas vying over right and wrong, they are all empty.
While dwelling at Yunqi, Minister Wang Zongmu asked, "Last night the mice were chirping incessantly; did they recite the entire Avataṃsaka Sūtra?
The Master said, "When the cat suddenly springs out, what then? Wang was speechless. The Master provided his own answer on his behalf: "They have run away."

The Dharma Master left behind his lecture notes and then composed this verse: "The mice squeak; the Avataṃsaka is clear and distinct. How strange! Vice Minister Wang was so deluded as to be led astray by animals. A cat suddenly darts out before the painted hall;
at the head of the couch, the preaching of the Dharma leaves no trace. No trace—this is the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the Great Vaipulya Scripture of the Buddha, Chapter One:

'The Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruling Lords.'"* *Note: This is a traditional Chinese commentary on the opening lines of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. "Mice" and "cat" are metaphors for worldly distractions and sensory attachments that obscure the profound teachings.*
Biyu Gong Chunxi asked about the circumstances of Huirui’s branding of five hundred sick monks.
The Master said, "Huirui was content to be a destitute son who abandoned himself to follow others; Xiuyuan, however, humiliated an ordinary citizen by leading him from life toward death.
It is a pity that those five hundred monks only knew how to be branded and depart, yet not one or two remained lying high and refusing to rise, thereby allowing Huirui to manifest his brilliance."

This will confuse the masses and bring calamity upon their descendants. Your Excellency, Lord of the Prefecture, deeply understands the ailments of the people; I, a mountain monk, am urgently pressed by the exigencies of the times.
In this haste, I have unfortunately lost my bamboo staff. I can do no more than brandish empty fists and strike a blow right upon the abscess of the layman.
I dare guarantee that the chronic ailment will burst open, the poisonous blood will flow forth, and the myriad channels shall circulate freely through the hundred limbs.
"Relaxing and at ease. Even so, how can one person cause the multitude to arise? Have you not seen it said: "When the yang returns, a single leaf appears;
when spring fills the world, it pervades a thousand forests"? Let this matter rest for a moment.

As for spending all day holding a bamboo staff, pointing east and waving west—it is better to remain constantly with the wooden block, upholding it in the morning and guarding it in the evening. Through guarding it again and again, suddenly it becomes withered.
"Wood layered with flowers is nothing other than the dead coming back to life. What need is there to mention bamboo and trees?

Take it for granted that all the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests of the entire world shall attain Buddhahood. Why is this? The void-nature beyond the green things is itself the Tathāgata’s solid and real heart.
[He] inscribed his own portrait, saying: "Ten strokes, nine do not resemble [me]; they have driven me to distraction, these brushstrokes and ink."
"Craftsman! I hope you are close to this. If you leave it here as a mere object of offering, if you say that this is it, it remains two separate things.
Not two separate things? Thirty blows! Question: "In the practice of Zen meditation and the recitation of the Buddha's name, can they be used in a harmonious integration?
The Master said: "If they were two distinct things, one could speak of their harmonious integration. Question: "When the World-Honored One remained silent for a long while, the non-Buddhist..."
This refers to [the story where] Mazu said, "He opened up my clouds of delusion. When Xingkong was sitting in meditation, he did not speak;

when Śakra spoke of the excellence of the Prajñāpāramitā, Mazu said, "If you wish to have your delusions cleared away while remaining for a long time in a state of silence, the gloom will persist for ten thousand miles. If you intend to hear the Prajñāpāramitā while sitting in meditation, it has already been explained for a long time.
Even so, as for those who "grasp the essential meaning at the tip of the whip" or see "flowers flying in the void," what exactly do they see?
"Ma! On the first day of the New Year, he addressed the assembly: 'Today we celebrate the New Year; the seasons have been renewed once more. What was it like yesterday? [O].
On the fourth day of the seventh month in the forty-third year of the Wanli era, as the Master was about to pass away, he took leave of the assembly in advance, saying:
'Half a month from now, I shall depart for another place. No one could fathom this. When the time arrived, he manifested a slight illness and turned his face toward the west."
He passed away.

Chan Master Daguang Zhenke of Mount Jing’s Zibai Temple was the son of the Shen family from Tanque in Wujiang. At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and began traveling to study under various masters.
Upon hearing the recitation of Zhang Zhuo’s verse, when it reached the lines, “To sever delusive thoughts is to increase one’s illness; turn toward the True,” he...

[He thought,] "This too is wrong; it is a great doubt. One day, while at his midday meal, he suddenly attained awakening and said, "If I had been under the guidance of Linji or Deshan, a single slap would have awakened me.
Why use such words as 'how' or 'what'? Thereupon, he traveled through Jiangnan, dwelling in no fixed location.
Later, while residing in Yan-shan, a lay practitioner mentioned the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "One should give rise to [the mind] without dwelling anywhere..."
Regarding the phrase on the mind, the Master said, "What is 'responding by giving rise to the mind while having nothing to dwell upon'? The scholar was bewildered.
The Master said, "Ask me, and I will explain it for you. The scholar then asked. The Master suddenly struck the desk and said, "Did you hear that?
He replied, "I heard it. The Master said, "Is this not giving rise to the mind? He asked again, "Do you hear with a mind, or do you hear without a mind? He replied, "Without."
Xinwen asked, "Is this not 'that which corresponds to non-abiding'? He then spoke a verse: "The wooden fish is struck so frequently;
Fearing the pain, it suddenly gives rise to anger. If you knew the place where it feels pain, The golden-scaled dragon would have passed through the Dragon Gate.

In the autumn of the Gui-mao year of the Wanli era, those who harbored malice toward the Master used other matters to entrap him, causing him to suffer hardship. Prior to this, Emperor Shenzong had personally inscribed [the name of] the Golden...
While reading the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, his sweat happened to soak the paper. Suspecting it should be replaced, he immediately dispatched an attendant to consult the Master.
The Master offered this verse in response: "A single drop of imperial sweat is a bridge for ten thousand generations; The inexhaustible treasury of Dharma shall from now on radiate light."
The Emperor was greatly pleased. On the day the Master was arrested, the Emperor saw his memorial petitions and felt deep compassion for him;

yet, as he could not escape the law, he was subsequently apprehended. An imperial decree was issued stating, "Let him be interrogated thoroughly, but that is all. During the interrogation, his countenance remained composed.

Though he endured every form of flogging and torture, he died with the thought that if the transmission of the Lamp were not continued, it would be a great failure for his life in this world as a teacher of wisdom. He had no other concern.

He said, "From beginning to end, I shall not yield. On the fifth day of the twelfth month, he entered prison. On the seventeenth day, the judicial authorities finalized the verdict and intended to execute the Master.
The Master spoke a verse, saying: "A single laugh has always had its own cause; Who would have known that the Great Mass of Earth could not tolerate even a speck of dust?
From this moment on, I gather up my mother-born feet; The iron peg shall bloom without waiting for spring. He further said, "The world..."
"If the Dharma is such as this, what is the use of it remaining for long? Having said this, he finished his bath and instructed his attendant, Xingtian, saying, "I am departing.
Please convey my thanks to all the Dharma protectors in Jiangnan. The attendant wept bitterly, but the Master rebuked him, saying, "You have served me for twenty years;

do you still act with such attachment to coming and going? At that time, there was a man surnamed Wu who attended him and inquired about the Great Dharma, to which the Master again gave an explanation.
The verse says: "Only when the matter arrives does one see the hero’s bones; did Master Da and Mr. Wu share a karmic affinity from of old? I shall return to the west while you go north;
our conversations over many lifetimes shall be even more serene. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
When the Censor Cao Xuecheng heard of this, he hurried there in haste. Seeing no one, he said, "The Master has departed well. The Master then opened his eyes, smiled, and bid him farewell.

Fragrant clouds did not dissipate within the prison for six days while he awaited his sentence, yet his countenance remained unchanged. Upon his release, he was given a floating funeral outside Ci’en Temple.
Later, his reliquary shrine was escorted to Mount Jing, where a stupa was erected. His works, known as the *Zibai ji*, were published and circulated throughout the world.
Chan Master Wunian Shendao of Huangbo in Ruizhou was the son of the Xiong family from Macheng in Huangzhou. At the age of sixteen, he was afflicted with smallpox and was on the verge of death.
His uncle and elder brother discussed allowing him to leave the household life, whereupon he recovered. He received the tonsure at Dangshan, where an old monk said to him:
"A single grain of rice from the ten directions is as heavy as Mount Sumeru; if you do not realize the Way, you shall wear fur and carry horns."
When Jue returned, the Master heard of this and was struck with awe; he immediately set out to seek instruction. Hearing a monk cite the question posed to Daixiu:
"What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? Daixiu replied, "Yellow gourd, eggplant. The Master was deeply perplexed by this and traveled throughout Jiangzhe to consult renowned masters.
He visited Chan Master Dajian of Mount Lu, who asked him, "What is your name? The Master replied, "Wunian (No-Thought). Dajian said, "Which one?"

"This is non-thought. The Master was at a loss. One night, he heard the sounds of laughter and weeping mingling together; suddenly, he attained awakening. By chance, he saw a basin of flour on the road;
he picked it up and thrust it into a cupboard. Seeing a fruit basket there, he pushed it away with his hand, but lost his grip without realizing it.
The lid of the cupboard struck him on the head, and sweat poured down his entire body. He laughed and said, "The whole earth is this very thing."
There is no-thought. What doubt could there be? Take these preceding doubts and obstructions and smash them all at once.
In the *wanshi* (wanli) year of *xinsi*, I went to Longhu together with the layman Li Zhuowu to Sima Mountain. A Dharma Master arrived, and the layman asked him:

"Originally pure and serene, how did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? After the monk had finished his lecture based on the text, the layman said, "Tell me this without conceptual thought.
As the Master was about to open his mouth, the layman pushed him on the knee and said, "What about this? The Master suddenly attained a profound realization;
he then understood that even a Bodhisattva of the Tenth Stage might dream of sentient beings whose bodies have fallen into a great river, and who desire to rescue and deliver them.
Therefore, one must give rise to a courageous mind and exert great diligence. Only when both person and phenomena are realized as empty does one first enter the gate;
[at that point, they] have no interference whatsoever. There is a verse that says: "For over forty years I did not rest in my practice; I sought and sought until the traces vanished.
Now, having sought to the point of no reliance, Only then do I regret my former misapplication of effort. A monk asked: "Is there truly a fruit? The Master said: "Fruit..."

[The student] asked, "What is it like when the four elements disperse? The Master raised his fist and said, "This does not belong to the four elements. [The student] asked about the ancients.

Chán Master Fāng Tàn of Yífēng at Bái Mǎ in Kuīzhōu was the son of the Luò family of Dázhōu. He investigated the question, "What is the pivot that ghosts and spirits cannot perceive?
After three years, he attained realization. He left the gorges to visit various spiritual teachers extensively and settled in a thatched hut at Shuāngxī.
One day at noon while cooking rice, he heard the sound of the steamer. Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment and composed a verse: The Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials have no origin;
Exhausting all clever thoughts, there is nowhere to seek them. Taking a step from before the window to the hearth door, White clouds and blue peaks nod their heads in unison.
Nodding their heads in unison— Nanyue and Tiantai share a single tally. He also said: "A girl of sixteen."
